title: GOTT: Object-centric Dexterous Manipulation with a Reusable Cross-Embodiment Primitive
summary: Foundation models and large-scale human data provide rich sources of manipulation intent, but translating this intent into multi-fingered robot behavior remains difficult. Dexterous hands still lack a reusable low-level primitive that reliably establishes contact across tasks and embodiments. We propose GOTT, a reach-acquire-move framework built around a single cross-embodiment contact-acquisition primitive. Given a robot-agnostic object trajectory and a reach specification, GOTT first brings the hand near a task-relevant contact region. The shared closed-loop primitive then establishes stable contact from this approximate initialization, and a pose-conditioned controller tracks the desired object motion. Reach specifications may come from future-aware planning, external models, or human demonstrations, while the primitive and tracking backend remain unchanged. Simulation and real-world experiments show that GOTT is able to establish robust contact across diverse objects, arm-hand platforms, and seen and unseen hand morphologies. It also consistently improves end-to-end task success over open-loop grasp execution.

Introduction Foundation models~ deepmind2026gemini31pro,openai2026gpt55 and large-scale human data~ yang2022oakink,banerjee2024introducing provide rich sources of manipulation intent. For parallel-jaw grippers, such intent can be translated into robot actions through mature low-level primitives such as grasping, placing, and trajectory following~ huang2023voxposer,huang2024rekep,liang2023code . However, the same approach does not directly extend to dexterous hands, which lack a comparable set of general-purpose low-level skills. These skills must establish complex contact configurations, coordinate high-dimensional actions, and adapt to different hand morphologies. Existing dexterous manipulation methods usually address these challenges through task-specific sim-to-real learning~ andrychowicz2020learning or hand-motion retargeting~ li2025maniptrans . However, these approaches are not well suited to converting high-level intent into robot behavior. Task-specific policies~ qi2022hand,qi2023rotateit,chen2023visual,nvidia2022dextreme require retraining for each new behavior, making them difficult to scale. Retargeting recovers kinematic targets from demonstrations~ mandi2025dexmachina , often without incorporating perceptual feedback~ pan2025spider . This lack of feedback makes contact-rich tasks difficult to execute in the real world. This raises a key question: what is the right interface for translating high-level manipulation intent into low-level dexterous execution? Object-centric motion representations provide a promising answer to this question. Prior work has shown that many rigid-object manipulation tasks can be described by the desired object motion~ kerr2024robot,patel2025robotic,heppert2024ditto , abstracting away embodiment-specific robot motion. However, an object trajectory specifies how the object should move, but not where and how the hand should establish contact. This distinction is critical for functional manipulation: a geometrically stable grasp may still be unsuitable for pouring, sweeping, or tool use. Prior methods address this gap by supplying a pre-grasp or hand reference~ chen2024object,liu2025dextrack , or by learning contact acquisition jointly with trajectory execution~ kedia2026simtoolreal,kuang2026dex4d . While effective, these designs do not expose contact acquisition as a reusable skill across high-level sources and robot embodiments. We propose General Object Trajectory Tracking ( ), a framework for executing diverse object motions across tasks and robot embodiments using a shared contact-acquisition primitive. We represent high-level manipulation intent using a desired object trajectory and a reach specification, which specifies how to bring the hand near a task-relevant contact region. These components may come from different sources. For example, the object trajectory may be extracted from a video, while the reach specification may be generated through affordance-aware planning or obtained by retargeting a human trajectory. implements this interface through a reach, acquire, and move decomposition. During reach, the robot follows the reach specification toward the selected contact region. During acquire, a learned closed-loop contact-acquisition primitive establishes stable contact from this approximate initialization. During move, an object-pose-conditioned controller tracks the desired object trajectory. The primitive uses only local hand-object geometry and proprioceptive history, while a canonical per-link representation allows the same policy to be shared across hands. Reach specifications can come from VLM-guided, future-aware planning, external models, or demonstrations, while the contact-acquisition primitive remains unchanged. We evaluate in simulation and the real world. First, we test whether the contact-acquisition primitive can robustly grasp diverse objects across different hands and transfer zero-shot to unseen hand morphologies. We then evaluate the full pipeline on object-trajectory tracking tasks, including trash cleanup, pouring, whiteboard erasing, and tool use. We compare against end-to-end trajectory learning, showing that our decomposition enables robustness to workspace shifts and reuse across robot arms. We also show that the same primitive supports high-level specifications from generated videos, keyframes, human demonstrations, and hand-object interaction datasets. Finally, we conduct ablations on the primitive's observation and reward design and the system's planning modules. Related Work Foundation models and human demonstrations can specify robot manipulation tasks through language, visual constraints~ huang2024rekep , code~ liang2023code , or generated videos~ patel2025robotic . ManipGen~ dalal2024local combines reusable local policies with foundation models and motion planning. Another line of work learns from human videos by extracting intermediate motion representations, such as point trajectories, object flow, or object-centric motion plans~ bharadhwaj2024track2act,wen2023any,xu2024flow,zhu2026vision,heppert2024ditto,li2024okami . SPOT~ hsu2024spot learns object-pose trajectory plans from human demonstrations and uses them to condition a robot policy. VLM-Scaffold~ de2026scaffolding adapts a similar pipeline to dexterous hands but relies on task-specific residual RL, making it challenging to scale across tasks and embodiments. LUCID~ gupta2026lucid learns embodiment-agnostic intent from unstructured human videos and connects it to embodiment-specific sensorimotor policies through object flow and a rough palm pose. In contrast, represents high-level intent using an object trajectory and a flexible reach specification, and connects these inputs to robot execution through a reusable dexterous contact-acquisition primitive. D-Grasp~ christen2022dgrasp combines reference-conditioned grasp control with global motion synthesis to move objects to target poses. Methods that start from a reference trajectory typically follow one of two strategies. The first performs trajectory-specific transfer, converting a human or object trajectory into robot motion through kinematic optimization, sampling~ pan2025spider , or reinforcement learning~ li2025maniptrans,mandi2025dexmachina . Human2Sim2Robot~ lum2025crossing uses a single object trajectory and a pre-grasp to learn a task-specific robot policy. ManipTrans~ li2025maniptrans and REGRIND~ feng2026regrind transfer hand-object interaction trajectories through residual learning, while SPIDER~ pan2025spider performs fast physics-informed retargeting. These transfer methods can reproduce a given demonstration but are often tied to a specific trajectory or embodiment. The second strategy trains policies conditioned on multiple reference trajectories. ObjDex~ chen2024object and DexTrack~ liu2025dextrack condition policies on object or hand trajectories. AdaDexTrack~ adalibieke2026adadextrack adds online modulation to improve tracking of noisy references. OmniGrasp~ luo2024omnigrasp learns to grasp diverse objects and follow object trajectories with a simulated humanoid. SimToolReal~ kedia2026simtoolreal and Dex4D~ kuang2026dex4d learn general object-centric policies conditioned on target object poses or point tracks, jointly handling contact acquisition and motion execution. Grasp to Act~ gupta2026grasp2act combines human-guided grasp optimization with residual RL for online finger adaptation. In contrast, factors execution into reach, acquire, and move: high-level inputs specify the desired object motion and a task-relevant reach, while a trajectory-agnostic primitive establishes contact before trajectory tracking begins. This decomposition enables the same contact-acquisition primitive to be reused across trajectories, objects, and robot embodiments. Existing learning-based methods develop generalizable tabletop grasping policies~ xu2023unidexgrasp,wan2023unidexgrasppp,lum2024dextrah,zhang2025robustdexgrasp . Grasp synthesis and evaluation methods instead generate or refine grasp targets~ chen2025bodex,wei2024dro,wang2022dexgraspnet,chen2024springgrasp,lum2024get,fang2025anydexgrasp . GraspXL~ zhang2024graspxl and ConGraspXL~ zhang2026congraspxl condition grasping motions on approach, contact-region, or pose constraints. Functional grasping methods use affordances, human grasp references, or language to select task-relevant grasps~ agarwal2023functional,huang2025fungrasp,wei2025afforddexgrasp . Cross-embodiment methods further share grasping policies or representations across hands: CrossDex~ yuan2025cross uses a unified observation space and retargeted eigengrasp actions, while OHRA~ wei2026one uses canonical hand representations and UniMorphGrasp~ wu2026unimorphgrasp conditions grasp generation on morphology. GET-Zero~ patel2025getzero studies zero-shot transfer to unseen hand structures for in-hand rotation. These works advance grasping and cross-hand transfer, while primarily focusing on grasp acquisition itself. In contrast, GOTT treats contact acquisition as a reusable intermediate primitive that refines an approximate, task-relevant reach into stable contact before downstream object-trajectory tracking. This enables the same primitive to be reused across objects, tasks, trajectories, and hand embodiments. Dexterous Manipulation via General Object Trajectory Tracking We propose , a reach-acquire-move framework (Section~ sec:decomposition ) for executing rigid-object motions with dexterous hands. Its high-level interface consists of a desired object trajectory and a reach specification that brings the hand near a task-relevant contact region. At its core, a reusable cross-embodiment contact-acquisition primitive grounds this interface by turning an approximate reach into stable contact (Section~ sec:rl ). In the object-centric setting, a future-aware planner constructs from the object mesh, desired trajectory, and task description (Section~ sec:planning ). Alternatively, external models or human demonstrations can provide (Section~ sec:inference ), while the primitive and tracking backend remain unchanged (Section~ sec:execution ). Reach-Acquire-Move Decomposition sec:decomposition Given a desired object trajectory where denotes the object pose at timestep , and a reach specification , decomposes dexterous execution into three stages. During reach, the robot follows the approach trajectory to an approximate initial configuration . During acquire, the contact-acquisition primitive uses closed-loop feedback to establish stable contact. During move, the pose-conditioned tracker moves the object along . This decomposition separates high-level reasoning about functional contact selection, collision-free approach, and long-horizon reachability from local contact-rich control. title: LatentQuant: Preserving the Policy-Facing Latent Contract under NVFP4 VAE Quantization
summary: Recent world action models (WAMs) reuse pretrained video VAEs whose encoder latents directly condition downstream action policies. Quantization must therefore preserve not only reconstruction fidelity but also the policy-facing latent contract expected by the frozen policy. Direct NVFP4 leaves W4A4 quantization error uncompensated, whereas joint quantization-aware training (QAT) can recover reconstruction by moving this representation. On Wan2.1, joint QAT nearly matches FP32 VBench-7 (0.7403 versus 0.7409), yet LIBERO success collapses from 95.5% to 10.5%. Controlled decoder-only experiments show that activation quantize-dequantize operations alter the reconstruction signal and decoder Jacobian, redirecting the gradient returned to the encoder and inducing persistent latent drift. Based on this mechanism, we introduce LatentQuant, a two-stage NVFP4 QAT framework that first aligns the quantized encoder with its high-precision counterpart, then freezes it while adapting the decoder. Across Wan2.1 and Wan2.2, LatentQuant preserves near-baseline control and high reconstruction quality, achieving 95.75% success on LIBERO and 68.8% on RoboTwin. On NVIDIA B300 GPUs, NVFP4 execution achieves 1.17x-1.26x end-to-end VAE speedups over BF16 cuDNN.

Across Wan2.1 and Wan2.2, LatentQuant preserves near-baseline control and high reconstruction quality, achieving success on LIBERO and on RoboTwin. On NVIDIA B300 GPUs, NVFP4 execution achieves 1.17×–1.26× end-to-end VAE speedups over BF16 cuDNN Introduction sec:introduction Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are conventionally evaluated by reconstruction fidelity~ yu2023magvitv2,chen2024dcae,nvidia2025cosmostokenizer . In recent world action models (WAMs), however, the encoder representation can also be consumed directly by a downstream action policy~ cheang2024gr2,li2025uva,li2026lingbotva,ye2026dreamzero . Closed-loop control further imposes a tight per-step latency budget, making the VAE worth optimizing even when its cost is secondary in offline video generation~ akbari2026actquant,xu2026daptq,zhang2026quantvla . The latent is therefore both an internal code and a policy-facing representation whose semantics must remain compatible with a pretrained policy, a requirement not captured by reconstruction-centric quantization. We call this requirement the policy-facing latent contract. Reconstruction constrains the composition of an encoder and decoder , but not their intermediate coordinates. For any invertible transformation , the transformed pair preserves reconstruction, whereas a fixed policy is generally not invariant to the same reparameterization: Hence, preserving does not guarantee preservation of the representation consumed by ; policy-facing VAE quantization must preserve both reconstruction fidelity and the latent contract. Standard joint quantization-aware training (QAT)~ jacob2018quantization,huang2025qvgen,zhang2026attnqat can strongly violate this contract. Under W4A4 NVFP4 QAT~ nvidia2025nvfp4 , the encoder and decoder co-adapt to quantization error by moving the latent while maintaining reconstruction. On Wan2.1~ wanteam2025wan , joint QAT nearly matches FP32 VBench-7~ huang2024vbench ( versus ), yet LIBERO~ liu2023libero success falls from to ; latent regularization recovers only . Reconstruction quality can thus conceal severe incompatibility with the frozen policy. Controlled interventions trace this mismatch to decoder activation quantization. By changing both the reconstruction signal and the decoder Jacobian, quantization redirects the gradient returned to the encoder; repeated optimizer updates consolidate this signal into a persistent latent shift. The failure is therefore a learned drift of the policy-facing representation, not merely an instantaneous perturbation at the encoder output. This analysis suggests a hard design constraint: reconstruction adaptation should not rewrite an established latent contract. We therefore propose LatentQuant, the two-stage NVFP4 QAT framework in Figure~ fig:overview . Stage~I aligns the quantized encoder with its high-precision reference under NVFP4 execution. Stage~II freezes the aligned encoder and adapts only the quantized decoder for reconstruction. This boundary permits low-precision adaptation while preventing decoder reconstruction gradients from modifying the policy-facing latent. Across Wan2.1 and Wan2.2~ wanteam2025wan , LatentQuant retains near-baseline control and high reconstruction quality: versus success on LIBERO, and versus on RoboTwin~ chen2025robotwin . A native packed-NVFP4 convolution backend on NVIDIA B300 GPUs further demonstrates that contract preservation is compatible with end-to-end VAE acceleration. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We formulate the policy-facing latent contract for quantizing VAEs consumed by fixed downstream policies, and show that reconstruction fidelity can conceal severe policy incompatibility. We identify an optimization-induced latent-contract violation mechanism under joint low-bit QAT, showing that decoder-side quantization redirects reconstruction gradients returned to the encoder and consolidates them into persistent learned latent drift. We propose LatentQuant, a two-stage QAT method which separates quantized encoder alignment from decoder adaptation to preserve the established latent contract. On NVIDIA B300 GPUs, NVFP4 execution achieves 1.17 --1.26 end-to-end VAE speedups over BF16 cuDNN. Related Work sec:related-work WAMs and policy-consuming latents. Recent video-action models couple latent visual representations with action prediction through diverse architectures. A growing class of WAMs builds directly on latent video generators and inherits their pretrained VAEs. GR-2 jointly predicts future videos and actions, while UVA learns a joint video--action latent representation with separate decoding heads~ cheang2024gr2,li2025uva . More recent WAMs, including WALL-WM, LingBot-VA, and DreamZero, further couple video generation and action prediction through different unified or causal architectures~ li2026wallwm,li2026lingbotva,ye2026dreamzero . Despite the various WAM architectures, the latents produced from the encoder of VAEs are consumed by the downstream action policy. As a result, it is critical to preserve the latent while quantizing VAEs. This compatibility concern also appears in video-VAE design, where latent-space alignment is used to retain compatibility with a pretrained generator~ zhao2024cvvae,cai2026davae . Our setting is stricter: the downstream action policy is frozen, so the established latent coordinates cannot be adapted after quantization. Low-bit quantization for generative models. Existing quantization studies for generative models have primarily focused on the Transformer backbone. Q-Diffusion, SVDQuant, and ViDiT-Q develop low-bit quantization methods for diffusion models, while QVGen introduces QAT for video diffusion models at 4-bit and below~ li2023qdiffusion,zhao2025viditq,li2025svdquant,huang2025qvgen . In contrast, VAE quantization has received substantially less attention than the Transformer backbone in low-bit diffusion pipelines. PassionSR~ zhu2025passionsr is among the few works that explicitly quantize the VAE, but it focuses on W8A8/W6A6 PTQ for image super-resolution. Complementary video-VAE work targets compression and decoder efficiency rather than low-bit weight-and-activation execution~ wu2025h3ae,zhu2026flashvaed . Although PTQ is time efficient, QAT can achieve higher accuracy, which is critical for downstream action policy. With native NVFP4 support in NVIDIA's low-precision training stack~ nvidia2025nvfp4 , an effective VAE-specific NVFP4 QAT method is needed for practical low-bit acceleration. Interface-aware quantization. Recent work has shown that low-bit quantization can affect intermediate representations and downstream behavior, not only final outputs. Quantized feature distillation and quantization-aware distillation use teacher-guided objectives to mitigate such degradation~ zhu2023qfd,xin2026qad , while QuantWM, QuantVLA, ActQuant, and DA-PTQ study quantization-induced degradation in world models and vision-language-action policies~ fu2026worldquant,zhang2026quantvla,akbari2026actquant,xu2026daptq . Analyses of nonuniform floating-point training also identify systematic shrinkage bias in low-bit optimization~ zhao2026ufp4 . Studies of latent geometry and frequency structure further show that a reconstruction-preserving latent can still be unfavorable to a downstream generator~ yao2025vavae,chen2025dcae15,skorokhodov2025diffusability,kouzelis2025eqvae . In contrast, we focus on a different failure mode arising during joint QAT of a pretrained video VAE, where reconstruction optimization persistently shifts the policy-facing encoder representation. We therefore formulate latent preservation as a representation contract during low-bit VAE adaptation. Problem Setting sec:problem_setting Policy-Facing VAE Quantization sec:policy_facing_vae We consider WAMs in which the representation produced by a pretrained video VAE conditions a fixed downstream action policy. Given an observation clip , the high-precision encoder produces and the corresponding action prediction is abstracted as where denotes the task condition and remains frozen throughout VAE quantization. Let and denote the quantized encoder and decoder, with trainable parameters and , and let denote the quantized encoder representation. Conventional VAE quantization primarily seeks to preserve reconstruction through . In the policy-facing setting, this objective is insufficient: the quantized representation must also remain compatible with the representation expected by the fixed downstream policy. We therefore view VAE quantization as reconstruction adaptation subject to preservation of the policy-facing latent contract, where the notion of latent deviation used for evaluation is specified in Section~ sec:experiments . NVFP4 Quantization sec:nvfp4_setting We study W4A4 quantization under the Blackwell NVFP4 format nvidia2025nvfp4 . NVFP4 represents data values in E2M1 and uses two-level scaling consisting of an FP32 per-tensor scale and an E4M3 scale for each contiguous 16-element block. We apply NVFP4 QDQ to the weight and activation operands of convolutional and linear layers. Normalization, nonlinearities, residual additions, and the VAE input and latent boundaries remain in higher precision. During QAT, master parameters and optimizer states remain in FP32, while the selected operands follow the NVFP4 QDQ contract in the forward pass with a straight-through estimator for backpropagation. Direct quantization uses the same arithmetic and layer coverage without parameter adaptation. All low-bit baselines therefore share the same numerical contract, isolating the effect of the optimization strategy. Detailed scaling rules, operand layouts, and mixed-precision scopes are provided in Appendix~ app:nvfp4-details . Mechanism of Latent-Contract Violation under Joint QAT sec:mechanism Joint QAT optimizes the encoder and decoder jointly under reconstruction objectives. Although this flexibility compensates for quantization errors, it also allows reconstruction adaptation to modify the policy-facing latent representation. We analyze this optimization pathway through three stages: latent drift under low precision, decoder-induced gradient perturbation, and persistent encoder representation change. title: WAMJET: A Harness for World Action Model Acceleration
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) leverage pretrained video foundation models for robot manipulation, but their large backbones and video-action co-prediction are expensive. Although existing acceleration techniques offer many ways to reduce this cost, selecting and composing them requires substantial engineering for each model and hardware platform. To tackle this bottleneck, we present WAMJET, an agentic harness that accelerates WAM inference by equipping coding agents with reusable optimization guidance and measurement and validation tools. WAMJET follows a bottleneck-driven workflow where the agent profiles inference, modifies targeted code, validates effects, and iteratively refines the acceleration stack as bottlenecks shift, while preserving action quality. Experiments span six WAMs, three coding agents, and two GPU architectures. WAMJET achieves up to 9.95x lossless speedup over upstream implementations. Approximation and hardware-aware optimization yield additional latency reductions, with comparable success rates. The results show that WAMJET can produce effective acceleration stacks for WAM deployment.
full_text: World Action Models (WAMs) leverage pretrained video foundation models for robot manipulation, but their large backbones and video-action co-prediction are expensive. Although existing acceleration techniques offer many ways to reduce this cost, selecting and composing them requires substantial engineering for each model and hardware platform. To tackle this bottleneck, we present WAMJET, an agentic harness that accelerates WAM inference by equipping coding agents with reusable optimization guidance and measurement and validation tools. WAMJET follows a bottleneck-driven workflow where the agent profiles inference, modifies targeted code, validates effects, and iteratively refines the acceleration stack as bottlenecks shift, while preserving action quality. Experiments span six WAMs, three coding agents, and two GPU architectures. WAMJET achieves up to 9.95× lossless speedup over upstream implementations. Approximation and hardware-aware optimization yield additional latency reductions, with comparable success rates. The results show that WAMJET can produce effective acceleration stacks for WAM deployment. Introduction sec:introduction Building generalist policies requires not only mapping visual observations to actions but also understanding and predicting the consequences of actions in diverse environments. Video generation models learn representations of such dynamics from large-scale video datasets. Many of these videos contain intentional behavior like object manipulation and scene changes because someone or something acted. That makes video models attractive backbones for generalist manipulation. Before seeing any robot actions, the backbone already encodes useful links between language, visual change, and plausible object interactions. World Action Models (WAMs) build on these models and extend them with action-generation capabilities. They inherit priors from video pretraining and couple action generation with video-based world modeling for more robust robot manipulation across diverse environments. Compared with Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs), WAMs are appealing because predicting the future states of the environment may help capture better physical dynamics and temporal information. Modern video generation models are often billion-scale parameter models and continue to scale toward higher generation quality and higher fidelity. This scaling provides stronger priors about how visual scenes evolve but also increases inference cost. The same backbones that make WAMs attractive also make them expensive to run. Inference may involve sampling a large video model, several denoising steps, and repeated vision-language processing. Beyond those computations, data movement, synchronization, and cache updates can also add substantial latency. This computational burden poses a significant challenge for real-time control in robotics, where timely decision-making is crucial. Many techniques can accelerate inference, including compilation, kernel fusion, caching, and quantization. The difficulty is deciding which techniques to apply and how to combine them. A model dominated by repeated conditioning needs different optimizations from one governed by attention or memory transfers. Hardware also affects which kernels or data types are efficient. Moreover, optimizations can interact, which means removing one bottleneck can expose another, and a change that initially gives little benefit may become useful later. Developing an effective acceleration strategy, therefore, requires repeated profiling, implementation, and measurement for each deployment. Preserving the policy's behavior adds another challenge. Reusing a prompt embedding while the instruction is unchanged can avoid redundant computation. Reusing visual features after the observation changes, however, approximates the policy's input. Quantization can introduce further error, whose effect on manipulation may be difficult to predict from tensor differences alone. An optimization process must account for both inference speed and the effect of its changes on robot actions. Accelerating WAM inference is not a one-time optimization but requires a recipe that composes techniques for a specific model, hardware stack, and task. The best recipe for a certain WAM may not directly transfer to other models. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:fig1_harness_overview , hand-crafting an acceleration strategy that works well on a specific model and hardware setup requires substantial engineering effort and may not generalize to other scenarios. LLM coding agents offer a way to automate this process, but reliable optimization over many iterations requires clear constraints, appropriate tools, and feedback on both latency and correctness. Harness engineering provides this structure through agent-readable workflows, measurement tools, and explicit validation criteria~ lee2026meta . This shifts human effort toward designing reusable guidance, while the agent conducts experiments, assesses their outcomes, and uses the evidence to guide subsequent optimizations. In this work, we present WAMJET, an agentic harness for accelerating WAM inference. WAMJET equips coding agents with optimization guidance and tools for profiling, latency measurement, numerical comparison, and paired task analysis. Starting from a runnable policy, the agent identifies bottlenecks, implements lossless or approximate accelerations, and benchmarks and validates each candidate. It retains useful changes and repeats the process within a specified budget. Throughout the search, the agent adapts its optimization choices to the target hardware, records experiment outcomes, and stores reusable findings in external memory. This iterative process produces acceleration stacks tailored to the target policy and hardware. Our contributions can be summarized in several aspects: We introduce WAMJET, a harness that combines reusable optimization guidance with measurement and validation tools for accelerating WAM inference. We develop a bottleneck-driven workflow that iteratively composes acceleration techniques and checks their effects on outputs, recurrent state, and task performance. We evaluate WAMJET across different WAMs and GPU architectures, examining the optimizations found by different agent campaigns, the benefit of further search, and the gains and limitations of approximate inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our training-free framework can achieve significant acceleration. Related Work sec:related_work Foundation Models for Robot Manipulation Foundation models support robot manipulation through both direct action prediction and higher-level decision making. RT-2 transfers vision-language pretraining into control by representing robot actions as tokens, while OpenVLA provides an open-source vision-language-action (VLA) model trained on diverse robot demonstrations~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla . combines a pretrained vision-language backbone with flow-matching action generation, and Octo learns a generalist diffusion policy from heterogeneous robot data~ black2024pi0,octo2024 . Other approaches leverage language models: SayCan selects skills based on learned affordances~ ahn2022saycan , while Code as Policies generates executable programs for robot control~ liang2022codeaspolicies . A related line connects policy learning with future visual prediction. UniPi formulates planning as text-conditioned video generation and extracts executable actions from the resulting visual plans~ du2023unipi . Unified models couple video and action learning: UVA learns a shared latent representation with decoupled diffusion heads, while UWM integrates video and action diffusion in a single transformer with independently controlled diffusion timesteps~ li2025uva,zhu2025uwm . DreamZero builds on a pretrained video diffusion backbone to jointly predict future observations and robot actions~ ye2026dreamzero . WAMJET accelerates the inference code of a trained policy, with numerical and task evaluations used to assess the effect of each optimization. Accelerating Video Generation and World Action Models Diffusion acceleration operates at several levels of the inference computation. DPM-Solver reduces the number of model evaluations through higher-order numerical integration, whereas progressive distillation trains a student to reproduce a longer sampling process with fewer steps~ lu2022dpmsolver,salimans2022distillation . Training-free caching methods instead exploit redundancy along the denoising trajectory: TeaCache uses timestep-conditioned input changes to guide reuse, and TaylorSeer forecasts intermediate features rather than simply reusing them~ liu2025teacache,liu2025taylorseer . Sparse VideoGen reduces attention computation through spatial-temporal sparsity, token merging reduces redundant token processing, and SVDQuant enables low-bit diffusion inference with a high-precision low-rank branch~ xi2025sparsevideogen,bolya2023tomesd,li2024svdquant . These approximations differ from implementations such as FlashAttention, which accelerates exact dense attention through IO-aware tiling and reduced memory traffic~ dao2022flashattention . WAM-specific works explore both architectural efficiency and deployment-time optimization. DreamZero combines caching, quantization, compilation, kernel optimization, and asynchronous execution in a model-specific control stack~ ye2026dreamzero . Fast-WAM retains video co-training but removes test-time future-video generation~ yuan2026fastwam . Light-WAM further adopts a compact video backbone and state-fusion action decoding, predicting action chunks without a generative action expert~ li2026lightwam . These methods require retraining and thus are not drop-in optimizations for arbitrary checkpoints. In contrast, C ache is a training-free WAM accelerator that reuses action-expert residuals across consecutive inference chunks, exploiting cross-chunk redundancy~ zhao2026c3ache . While these methods offer complementary acceleration mechanisms, they differ in the evaluation criteria: numerical equivalence, perceptual similarity, and task success are not interchangeable, e.g., video fidelity alone does not ensure manipulation performance. WAMJET builds on these techniques, selecting and combining them according to the bottlenecks of each model and hardware platform. Agentic Workflows and Harness Engineering Agentic systems make iterative tool use and external feedback central to problem-solving. ReAct introduced the reasoning–action loop~ yao2022react , SWE-agent built an agent–computer interface for solving software engineering tasks~ yang2024sweagent , and agent harnesses go further by designing the whole runtime system around the agent~ zhong2026harness . In performance engineering, CUDA-LLM and CudaForge use executable correctness checks and hardware-level performance measurements to iteratively improve GPU kernels~ chen2025cudallm,zhang2025cudaforge . Robotics harnesses apply these ideas to different stages of the robot-learning lifecycle. HARBOR automates robot RL training by coordinating specialized agents from environment setup to reward tuning and to policy training~ li2026harbor . Nautilus standardizes policy-benchmark-robot integration through typed contracts and validated workflows~ jin2026nautilus . Show-Harness instead operates within the embodied control loop: it exposes compact semantic actions to a VLM and deterministically maps them into robot motion, with execution feedback from observations~ chen2026showharness . WAMJET instead applies agentic optimization to the inference code of a trained WAM. title: SUAVE: Unified Video-Action Models via Masked Diffusion
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) inherit strong semantic grounding from pretrained vision-language backbones but are typically optimized for predicting actions rather than future observations. They can see and act, but they do not imagine the future before acting. World action models (WAMs) built on video diffusion backbones can imagine but treat language as frozen conditioning on a continuous latent space. Unified models bring these modalities into one architecture, but they either decode autoregressively, one token at a time, or keep video continuous with an auxiliary action head. In this work, we present SUAVE, a Single vocabulary Unified Action-Video modEl in which a masked diffusion transformer generates video and actions conditioned on language, with all three modalities represented as discrete tokens in a shared sequence. Choosing which tokens to mask at inference turns the same network into a world model, a robot policy, or a video-action model. For action-free co-training, the action positions of unlabeled video are filled with mask tokens and excluded from the loss. Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate two findings. First, a single SUAVE model predicts long-horizon video and acts as a policy, competitive with dedicated world models and specialized action policies on static and dynamic manipulation tasks. On a real robot, our model generates subgoal images and an action chunk spanning one second of motion in 1,030 ms on an RTX 5090 GPU, sustaining closed-loop control at 2.5 actions per second. Second, pretraining on robot video and co-training on human video substantially improves policy performance and zero-shot robustness to distribution shift. Together, these results show that masked diffusion is a practical and versatile foundation for unified video-action modeling.

Bottom: SUAVE can imagine a goal and then reach it, for various static and dynamic object scenes. Together, these results show that masked diffusion is a practical and versatile foundation for unified video-action modeling. Imitation Learning, Deep Learning in Grasping and Manipulation, Model Learning for Control Introduction Robot learning has recently experienced a paradigm shift towards end-to-end policies trained on large datasets. This shift has been driven by two complementary model families. Vision-language-action models (VLAs)~ kim2024openvla, black2024pi_0, intelligence2025pi_ adapt pretrained vision-language backbones to output actions and inherit strong semantic grounding. World action models (WAMs)~ ye2026world adapt pretrained video diffusion backbones to output actions alongside predicted frames and inherit an understanding of physical dynamics. Both families have shown that a pretrained backbone plus robot actions is a viable recipe for general-purpose control. However, each family imposes architectural assumptions that limit its suitability for robotics. A VLA sees and acts, but it is not trained to anticipate. It maps the current observation to an action chunk without explicitly predicting the visual consequences. Because the standard VLA objective is defined only over actions, it cannot learn from video that lack action labels, which represent a large portion of all video that exists. A WAM is trained to anticipate as a product of its future video prediction, but it does so in a continuous latent space. Although video prediction and control are often jointly trained, many architectures retain separate representations or prediction heads for the two outputs, making them inherently decoupled. Recent work on visual chain of thought~ zhao2025cot shows that predicting a subgoal image before acting improves VLA performance, which suggests that the two families are converging on the same idea: a policy should be able to imagine the future before acting. This motivates a single generative model over language, video, and actions, rather than separate modules for each. We model the three modalities in a shared sequence using masked diffusion, a method that is analogous to continuous diffusion but in the discrete space. If every video frame, action, and language token is drawn from one vocabulary, then a transformer trained to unmask tokens can learn to fill in video and actions across a few denoising steps. Which conditional the model samples at inference time is decided entirely by which positions are masked: mask the future frame and it becomes a world model, mask the actions and it becomes a robot policy, mask both and it becomes a video-action model that generates a visual subgoal and the actions needed to reach the subgoal. Excluding masked action positions from the loss allows video without action labels to enter the same batch as labeled demonstrations, enabling robot video with actions and human video without actions to share one training stage and one unified objective. Because all masked positions are predicted in parallel, decoding at inference only takes a handful of steps rather than one step per token. This is in contrast to fully autoregressive methods, which make generating a subgoal image alongside actions prohibitively slow for closed-loop control, as each image and action token needs to be predicted sequentially. The discrete formulation enables strong versatility, allowing the same model weights to control the robot, roll out long-horizon video, and learn from human video all in one objective. We propose SUAVE, a Single-vocabulary Unified Action-Video modEl built on a masked diffusion transformer. SUAVE arranges a video context, a language instruction, a predicted goal frame, and an action chunk as one token sequence. Because every token is predicted by the same objective, the mask at inference selects whether the model acts as a world model, a robot policy, or a video-action model. Experiments in simulation and on a real robot support two findings: One model is a competitive world model and robot policy. A single SUAVE checkpoint predicts long-horizon video at a quality comparable to dedicated world models. As a policy, it is competitive with specialized action policies on static manipulation tasks and exceeds every baseline on dynamic manipulation tasks. We show our results for real world tasks, LIBERO, LIBERO-PLUS, and the DOMINO benchmark. Pretraining and co-training on video substantially improve performance and zero-shot robustness. Pretraining on robot video and co-training on action-free human video more than double the real robot task scores of models trained from scratch and roughly triple them under distribution shift, with the gap statistically significant in nearly every task and condition. Related Work Vision-language-action models VLAs adapt a pretrained vision-language backbone to robot control by treating actions as an additional output modality. RT-2~ brohan2023rt and OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla discretize actions into tokens and decode them autoregressively. OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025fine replaces sequential decoding with parallel regression over an action chunk. ~ black2024pi_0 , -FAST~ pertsch2025fast , and ~ intelligence2025pi_ attach flow-matching heads or compressed action tokenizers to pretrained VLM backbones. All of these map the current observation and language instruction to action. CoT-VLA~ zhao2025cot extends this by predicting a single subgoal image before acting and shows that this visual chain of thought approach improves success through better grounding. However, because the subgoal is generated token by token, the authors report a 7 slowdown in control. These models generate actions and at most one frame, however none model multi-step video. As their objectives are defined over actions, none can train on video that lacks action labels. World models and world action models A parallel line of work starts from video generation. iVideoGPT~ wu2024ivideogpt , Interactive World Simulator~ wang2026interactive , and Cosmos~ agarwal2025cosmos learn action- or latent action-conditioned video predictors. Recent world action models, such as DreamZero~ ye2026world , adapt pretrained video diffusion backbones to output actions alongside predicted frames. These models can imagine the future well, but they typically operate in a continuous latent space: when language is present, it enters only as conditioning from a frozen text encoder, and actions are produced by a separate head. Video, actions, and language are therefore handled by different components with different objectives. SUAVE takes the opposite approach: all three are represented as discrete tokens and processed by one network under a shared objective. Unified video-action and unified multimodal models Several recent works generate video and actions jointly. UWM~ zhu2025unified and UVA~ li2025unified are continuous diffusion models over frames and actions. UWM samples independent noise levels for the two modalities so that one network can act as a policy, a forward model, or an inverse dynamics model. It is the closest continuous analog to our approach, and our independent per-modality mask rates are the discrete counterpart of its independent time steps. UniVLA~ wang2026unified unifies vision, language, and action as discrete tokens but decodes them autoregressively, one token at a time. On the language-model side, LLaDA~ nie2026large showed that masked diffusion scales to LLM-sized text models, and MMaDA~ yang2026mmada extends it to a shared text and image vocabulary with parallel decoding. SUAVE brings this backbone to robotics by adding video and actions. Existing designs fall into three families: models that decode autoregressively over discrete tokens, models with continuous diffusion over frames and actions, and hybrid models that combine a language model with diffusion heads. SUAVE presents a fourth design: one generative mechanism over one discrete vocabulary for every modality, so that all cross-modal interaction happens under a single objective, with subgoal frames and the action chunk decoded in parallel. Pretraining and co-training on video for robot policies Large scale video is a promising source of transferable supervision for robotics. Prior works have found several ways to use it in training. UniVLA~ wang2026unified post-trains on video before learning a policy. UWM~ zhu2025unified sets the action diffusion timestep of action-free clips to maximum noise, allowing them to train alongside labeled demonstrations. SUAVE achieves this in the discrete setting by filling action positions with mask tokens and excluding them from the loss, so a human video clip and a robot demonstration share a batch. Our evaluation methodology follows LBM~ barreiros2025careful , which shows controlled comparisons of data recipes on a fixed architecture with quantified uncertainty. We evaluate on LIBERO~ liu2023libero , LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025libero for robustness to perturbations, and DOMINO~ fang2026towards for dynamic manipulation. Our contribution on this axis is a controlled evaluation of the effects of robot-video pretraining and action-free human video co-training, conducted under one protocol in simulation and on a real robot. title: Return-to-Home Feasible Micro-Aerial Vehicle Exploration for 3D Gaussian Splatting Reconstruction
comment: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on INTELLIGENT ROBOTS & SYSTEMS 2026
summary: Micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) enable rapid indoor 3D reconstruction for inspection and time-critical situational awareness, but must operate under strict flight-time budgets and safety constraints that require explicit return-to-home (RTH) feasibility with a conservative margin. We present a topology-first active reconstruction framework that decouples high-fidelity rendering from navigation. A dense 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) map is optimized as the reconstruction target, while a lightweight Truncated Signed Distance Field (TSDF)/occupancy scaffold supports conservative collision checking and online construction of a sparse 3D Voronoi skeleton roadmap. Since directly extracting roadmaps from TSDF geometry can be unstable under noisy and incomplete online fusion, we validate nodes and edges using carved free-space consistency and dense visibility checks, which suppress behind-wall phantom structure and stabilize planning. Viewpoints are selected on the roadmap using a flight-time-budget-aware objective and a lightweight receding-horizon lookahead to improve non-myopic exploration behavior. We evaluate on photorealistic indoor simulation benchmarks (ReplicaCAD, Gibson, and HM3D), reporting reconstruction coverage/error, RTH success, and computational cost. Results demonstrate improved or competitive performance relative to recent GS-based baselines under identical flight-time budgets.
full_text: Micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) enable rapid indoor 3D reconstruction for inspection and time-critical situational awareness, but must operate under strict flight-time budgets and safety constraints that require explicit return-to-home (RTH) feasibility with a conservative margin. We present a topology-first active reconstruction framework that decouples high-fidelity rendering from navigation. A dense 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) map is optimized as the reconstruction target, while a lightweight Truncated Signed Distance Field (TSDF)/occupancy scaffold supports conservative collision checking and online construction of a sparse 3D Voronoi skeleton roadmap. Since directly extracting roadmaps from TSDF geometry can be unstable under noisy and incomplete online fusion, we validate nodes and edges using carved free-space consistency and dense visibility checks, which suppress behind-wall phantom structure and stabilize planning. Viewpoints are selected on the roadmap using a flight-time-budget-aware objective and a lightweight receding-horizon lookahead to improve non-myopic exploration behavior. We evaluate on photorealistic indoor simulation benchmarks (ReplicaCAD, Gibson, and HM3D), reporting reconstruction coverage/error, RTH success, and computational cost. Results demonstrate improved or competitive performance relative to recent GS-based baselines under identical flight-time budgets. Introduction Micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) are increasingly attractive for indoor search-and-rescue (SAR) and first-responder missions because they can quickly enter confined or hazardous spaces and provide situational awareness before humans are deployed kumar2012opportunities . In these environments, autonomy must handle cluttered, GPS-denied navigation through narrow doorways and corridors under strict flight-time limits. If the MAV exhausts its battery deep inside a structure, safe recovery is not guaranteed and the mission may fail prematurely. Consequently, a central operational requirement is return-to-home (RTH) feasibility. In multi-room indoor layouts, return cost is highly non-Euclidean, and straight-line distance can severely underestimate the true time required to navigate around walls and through doorways. Therefore, viewpoint selection must trade off expected reconstruction gain against travel time while maintaining a conservative safety margin for possible interruptions during the return flight (Fig.~ fig:demo ). Beyond geometric coverage, responders often require high-fidelity reconstructions that preserve appearance and fine structure for inspection and decision making. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233dgs enables photorealistic reconstruction by representing scenes with explicit Gaussian primitives and fast differentiable rasterization, making online refinement feasible at interactive rates. This has motivated active reconstruction systems that couple viewpoint planning with online map updates. However, bringing 3DGS-based active reconstruction to MAVs is challenging because informative viewpoint selection must remain execution-aware under the above non-Euclidean travel and RTH constraints, and because a 3DGS map is rendering-centric and does not directly provide watertight surfaces or conservative free-space semantics for collision checking. Practical autonomy therefore typically requires an auxiliary geometric scaffold for safe navigation and feasibility reasoning. While recent work has begun coupling Gaussian splatting with active viewpoint planning, reliably integrating high-fidelity mapping with an execution-ready navigation abstraction under budget constraints in multi-room indoor scenes remains challenging. ActiveGS~ jin2025activegs uses a voxel scaffold to represent unexplored space and guide exploration, which can become costly to maintain and query as the explored 3D volume grows. ActiveSplat~ li2025activesplat enables efficient planning using a planar topological abstraction, but this 2D workspace does not explicitly capture the 3D connectivity and occlusions that arise in indoor flight. To bridge these gaps, we take a topology-first approach that decouples photorealistic reconstruction from conservative navigation reasoning. The MAV incrementally optimizes a dense 3DGS map as the reconstruction output, while simultaneously fusing the same posed RGB-D observations into a lightweight TSDF and occupancy grid that provide explicit surfaces and conservative free-space evidence for planning. From this evolving geometric scaffold, we construct a sparse 3D Voronoi skeleton roadmap whose vertices lie near the medial axis of free space and naturally provide high-clearance waypoint candidates, similar in spirit to classical Voronoi-graph roadmaps used for sensor-based exploration~ choset2000sensor . Since online TSDF geometry is incomplete early in exploration and can contain holes and transient artifacts, directly extracting a roadmap can introduce behind-wall phantom nodes that waste flight time and jeopardize safe return. We therefore apply conservative validation using carved free-space consistency and dense visibility checks to keep the roadmap stable for MAV execution. On the resulting roadmap, we formulate viewpoint actions as (node, yaw) pairs and select goals using a budget-aware objective that trades off information gain against shortest-path travel time while enforcing an explicit RTH safety margin. Finally, to reduce myopic oscillations, we use a lightweight two-step receding-horizon selection, motivated by receding-horizon next-best-view planning for aerial exploration~ bircher2016receding . In summary, our main contributions are as follows: We introduce a drone-centric hybrid planning architecture that decouples photorealistic reconstruction from conservative navigation: a dense 3DGS map is optimized as the reconstruction target, while a lightweight TSDF occupancy scaffold enables collision checking and stable online extraction of a sparse 3D Voronoi skeleton roadmap via carved-free-space validation, behind-wall suppression, and free-space node injection. We propose a budget-aware flight-time mechanism that couples structural awareness (information gain and frontier cues) with a travel-cost model. The resulting objective explicitly enforces a return-to-home safety margin and adaptively trades off information gain against travel time as remaining flight-time budget decreases. We provide evaluation under continuous-time MAV execution in photorealistic simulation, including comparisons to recent GS-based active reconstruction baselines and ablations isolating the effect of roadmap construction and non-myopic selection. Related Work Autonomous Exploration and Informative Path Planning Informative Path Planning (IPP) selects sensing actions to maximize information gain or coverage under constraints such as time, range, or energy~ zhu2021online . In unknown environments, IPP is commonly solved online using an evolving map so that viewpoint selection adapts to newly observed structure. For UAV exploration in large 3D spaces, scalable representations and clearance-aware planning are important; examples include low-memory mapping for exploration~ huang2024efficient and Voronoi-guided planning with adaptive layering~ dong2025voronoi . Complementary work targets robust state estimation and globally consistent geometric mapping, such as GO-SLAM~ zhang2023go , Voxgraph~ reijgwart2019voxgraph , and Kimera~ rosinol2020kimera . High-Fidelity Scene Reconstruction NeRF-based methods produce high-quality view synthesis but rely on expensive volume rendering, which limits real-time closed-loop use. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233dgs provides an efficient alternative via explicit Gaussian primitives and fast rasterization, enabling interactive rendering and online refinement and motivating NBV-style active reconstruction~ bircher2016receding,charrow2015information . Recent systems estimate view utility from renderability or uncertainty cues~ chen2025activegamer,xie2025gaussmi,li2025active3d . Since 3DGS is rendering-centric and does not provide conservative free-space semantics, many approaches pair it with auxiliary geometric scaffolds or sparse navigation abstractions for safe planning, such as ActiveGS~ jin2025activegs , ActiveSplat~ li2025activesplat , and neural-map exploration methods~ kuang2024active . UAV-Based Indoor Reconstruction and Unresolved Gaps Indoor UAV reconstruction systems study exploration and mapping under practical sensing and execution constraints~ zhang2025autonomous,wu2024optimally . Recent 3DGS-focused planners also target quadrotor autonomy, including GS-Planner~ jin2024gs and HGS-Planner~ xu2024hgs . Despite progress, robust autonomous reconstruction in cluttered multi-room indoor scenes remains challenging. Dense voxel scaffolds for unknown-space reasoning can become expensive as explored volume grows, while planar abstractions can miss 3D connectivity and occlusions important for indoor flight. Moreover, return-to-home feasibility is inherently non-Euclidean indoors because return cost must respect doors and walls, and sparse roadmaps extracted from online fusion can become unstable early in exploration without conservative validation. These limitations motivate hybrid architectures that optimize 3DGS as the reconstruction target while planning and safety reasoning are performed on a lightweight geometric scaffold under explicit budget and RTH feasibility constraints. Methodology sec:methodology Method Overview We address edge-assisted budgeted autonomous exploration for high-fidelity indoor reconstruction using an RGB-D equipped micro aerial vehicle. A fundamental challenge in active radiance-field mapping is that representations optimized for photorealistic rendering (e.g., 3DGS) lack the explicit, conservative free-space semantics required for safe navigation. To resolve this, our framework (Fig.~ fig:framework ) adopts a hybrid perception--action loop. Specifically, the system: (i) incrementally optimizes a dense 3DGS map as the primary reconstruction target, while concurrently (ii) fusing depth into a lightweight TSDF to serve as a geometric scaffold for extracting a sparse 3D topological roadmap. Using this roadmap, (iii) a budget-aware planner selects and executes next-best viewpoints to maximize coverage while enforcing return-to-home (RTH) feasibility. Gaussian Splatting We represent the scene as a set of explicit 3D Gaussian primitives kerbl20233dgs . Each Gaussian is parameterized by a mean , an anisotropic covariance , a color , and an opacity . Given a camera pose, the per-pixel contribution of Gaussian at pixel can be written as where denotes the 3D point associated with pixel in the camera coordinate frame. Rendered color is obtained by standard front-to-back -compositing: with Gaussians ordered by increasing depth. Depth and accumulated opacity are computed analogously using the same compositing rule (inherited from li2025activesplat ). 3D Voronoi Roadmap Construction subsec:voronoi_roadmap We construct a sparse, topologically meaningful abstraction of the environment: a 3D Voronoi roadmap whose nodes approximate the medial axis of free space and whose edges maximize obstacle clearance. To ensure the roadmap remains stable under continuous map updates, we employ a pipeline that fuses depth into a TSDF, extracts temporally smoothed obstacle sites, computes a 3D Voronoi tessellation, and rigorously filters the resulting graph using explicit volumetric carving. title: VolS-GS: Relightable Gaussian Splatting with Volumetric Subsurface Scattering
summary: We present VolS-GS, a relightable Gaussian splatting framework that reconstructs objects from one-light-at-a-time (OLAT) captures and renders them under novel lighting and viewpoints. Relightable Gaussian Splatting methods typically model appearance independently at each primitive, which makes non-local effects difficult to represent. This limitation is particularly apparent for subsurface scattering, where light entering the object at one location can emerge at another. Rather than modeling this effect solely with a neural network or a local kernel at each primitive, we use the spatial support of the Gaussian scene as the domain of a differentiable finite-volume transport solver, so that light can propagate through the object's interior. A small network predicts scattering and absorption coefficients for each Gaussian, and the solve redistributes incident light through the resulting field. The coefficients are fit to images rather than measured, so the solve supplies a transport-shaped path for aggregating per-primitive appearance, not a measurement of the material. To keep the learned shadow and specular terms from taking over the other components, our shadow term is predicted from visibility together with the transmittances and the scattering the solve produces, and a regularizer suppresses specular highlights in regions the shadow term predicts to be unlit. Experiments on three OLAT benchmarks show that VolS-GS consistently improves relighting quality on held-out lights and views.
full_text: Experiments sec:exp Setup sec:setup Datasets. We evaluate on three OLAT datasets covering subsurface-dominant, opaque, and anisotropic material regimes. The SSS-GS benchmark~ dihlmann2024sssgs , built for subsurface scattering, provides five synthetic translucent objects and three real light-stage captures. The NRHints set~ zeng2023nrhints contributes seven real captured objects, most of which are not strongly translucent. The GS synthetic set~ bi2024gs3 adds six scenes spanning metal, fur, and mixed materials. Baselines. The methods that appear in qualitative comparisons are retrained from public implementations under matched resolution, splits, and training budgets. More details are listed in Appendix~ app:impl . These are GS ~ bi2024gs3 , a general relighting system, SSD-GS~ zheng2026ssdgs , a recent relightable Gaussian baseline with an explicit subsurface component that is the local-kernel counterpoint to our solve, RNG~ fan2025rng , and SSS-GS~ dihlmann2024sssgs , which introduces a dedicated subsurface scattering component. The per-scene tables in Appendix~ app:perscene also list 3DGS~ kerbl20233dgs and GI-GS~ chen2025gigs with the numbers reported by zheng2026ssdgs as additional reference points; both fall well below the retrained baselines. We use a fixed hyperparameter configuration across all scenes, following each baseline's official codebase. Implementation. All timings are measured on one A6000, with the per-scene transfer basis precomputed once and excluded. VolS-GS renders the five SSS-GS synthetic scenes at FPS. On the SSS-GS synthetic scenes, training takes under 3.5 hours and under 8\,GiB of GPU memory per scene. Per-scene frame times, primitive counts and the rest of the implementation are in Appendix~ app:impl . Main results sec:sssbench Quantitative Results. Table~ tab:sss shows that VolS-GS achieves the best average performance across all three datasets. All per-scene metrics are provided in Appendix~ app:perscene . The improvement is most consistent on the SSS-GS benchmark, where subsurface scattering is the dominant effect. The gains also carry over to NRHints and GS , which contain less translucent and more diverse materials. Qualitative Results. Figure~ fig:qual shows relighting results across translucent and opaque objects. GS and SSS-GS reproduce the overall appearance but their predictions become less accurate around shadows and fine appearance details. SSS-GS in particular does not optimize stably on four of the seven NRHints scenes, and we report and show those rows as measured. RNG also captures the overall illumination but tends to lose high-frequency details, particularly on and . SSD-GS produces competitive results but still struggles with intricate shadow patterns and complex subsurface effects. Material Decomposition. sec:decomp Figure~ fig:decomp shows the learned decomposition into diffuse, specular, shadow, SSS, and normal components. The SSS channel captures the broad glow visible in backlit regions while the specular and shadow branches remain more localized. More detailed investigations across SSD-GS and SSS-GS are in Appendix~ app:compare . Ablations sec:ablation We ablate the main components of VolS-GS to understand their individual roles. We consider four variants: (1) Volumetric SSS, which removes the volumetric scattering component; (2) transport cues on shadow, which prevents the shadow branch from using transport-derived cues; (3) shadow term multiplied onto SSS, which applies the learned shadow to the SSS component as well; and (4) shadow term, which removes the learned shadow component. Figure~ fig:abl and Table~ tab:ablation give the visual and the metric comparison of these variants. Removing the volumetric SSS channel (1) changes the rendered appearance of and wherever transported light contributes. Removing the transport cues (2) changes the shadow decomposition, most visibly on , where the predicted shadow no longer follows the same attenuation pattern. Multiplying the shadow onto the SSS channel (3) changes the render only slightly but rewrites the shadow channel, degrading its interpretability, and the cost on held-out lights is visible in Table~ tab:ablation . Removing the shadow term (4) flattens the shading. The specular leakage regularizer contributes to cleaner decomposition, whose investigation is reported in Appendix~ app:specreg .

title: Grounded in Time: A Multi-Source Dataset and Benchmark for Temporal Grounding in Robotic Manipulation
summary: Robotic manipulation often requires inferring task-relevant states from past interactions when the current observation alone is insufficient to determine the appropriate action. Despite progress in benchmarking memory-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) models, application-oriented tasks requiring history-dependent semantic inference remain underrepresented. We introduce GiT (Grounded in Time), a dataset and benchmark for grounding manipulation decisions in past events across biolaboratory, household, and industrial scenarios. It includes real-robot and Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) style demonstrations covering 18 bimanual tasks, together with simulation data and a ManiSkill-based evaluation suite covering nine tasks. Fine-grained subtask annotations and annotated counterfactual task pairs, in which similar current observations require different actions depending on prior events, support policy learning and targeted evaluation of history use. Evaluations of representative end-to-end VLA models in simulation and on selected real-world tasks reveal substantial room for improvement in history-dependent manipulation. The dataset and benchmark are available at the project page.

It includes real-robot and Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) style demonstrations covering 18 bimanual tasks, together with simulation data and a ManiSkill-based evaluation suite covering nine tasks. Evaluations of representative end-to-end VLA models in simulation and on selected real-world tasks reveal substantial room for improvement in history-dependent manipulation. The dataset and benchmark are available at the project page . > X INTRODUCTION Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have strengthened visual understanding and instruction following liu2024improved . Building on these advances, vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated generalizable manipulation across tasks and environments shao2025large , including long-horizon household activities kim2025openvla,black2025pi05 . In such long-horizon settings, current observations may be insufficient for action planning, motivating memory-augmented policies that support spatial recall, action sequencing, and task-progress tracking fang2025sam2act,shi2026memoryvla . Within this broader effort to leverage interaction history, we focus on a specific capability crucial for following history-dependent instructions: associating past interaction events with objects and task-relevant states in the current scene to determine appropriate actions. For example, when several bowls look alike, executing ``Put the bowl I just used back in the cupboard'' requires identifying the target from interaction history rather than appearance alone. This capability is particularly relevant to household assistance and collaborative assembly, where actions by humans or other robots can determine the referents and requirements of subsequent instructions. Existing robotic memory-centric benchmarks, such as dai2026robomme, chen2026rmbench focus on in-episode state tracking, primarily assessing memory through abstract, purpose-built manipulation tasks. While useful for isolating specific memory skills, these settings offer limited coverage of everyday workflows in which prior interactions determine the meaning of subsequent instructions. In such workflows, a new request may refer to interactions completed before it was issued, including those performed by humans or other robots. When the current observation provides insufficient evidence to identify the intended objects or task-relevant states, the robot must interpret these earlier events and link them to the current scene. We term this capability pre-episode semantic grounding: grounding a current instruction in scene objects and task-relevant states using interactions completed before the current task episode begins. To support pre-episode semantic grounding, we introduce Grounded in Time (GiT), a multi-source dataset and benchmark for history-dependent bimanual manipulation in biolaboratory, household, and industrial settings. The GiT dataset combines simulated trajectories from ManiSkill3 DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2410-00425 , real-robot demonstrations collected through virtual reality (VR) teleoperation, and human demonstrations collected with a sensorized handheld gripper inspired by the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) chi2024universal . It comprises over 4,680 episodes across 18 tasks, totaling more than 3.3 million steps and more than 30 hours of interaction. Each sample pairs a pre-episode interaction video with a manipulation instruction and execution trajectory. Both the training and test splits include annotated counterfactual A--B pairs with matched scenes at the start of the current task but different pre-episode histories and required actions. The GiT benchmark uses the test-set pairs to assess whether policies ground current instructions in the relevant prior interactions. Our main contributions are as follows: A multi-source dataset. We introduce the GiT dataset, linking pre-episode interaction histories to subsequent bimanual manipulation across three application domains. A semi-automated annotation pipeline. We develop a pipeline for hierarchical trajectory and segment level annotation, covering 180 subtask categories. A benchmark and empirical evaluations. We establish the GiT benchmark and evaluate selected end-to-end VLA policies, revealing limitations in history-dependent manipulation. We complement these evaluations with small-scale real-robot experiments. Related Work Datasets for Robotic Learning Robotic manipulation datasets have expanded the coverage of tasks, environments, and embodiments available for policy learning. Simulation-based resources such as RLBench james2020rlbench and LIBERO liu2023libero provide diverse tasks with generated or human-collected demonstrations. In the real world, BridgeData V2 walke2023bridgedata and DROID khazatsky2024droid broaden skill and scene coverage, while Open X-Embodiment embodiment2024openx and RoboMIND wu2025robomind support learning across robotic embodiments. Human demonstrations provide another source of supervision: RH20T fang2024rh20t pairs human videos with robot executions, and UMI chi2024universal enables manipulation data collection using handheld grippers. Domain-specific efforts such as AutoBio lan2025autobio and LabUtopia li2025labutopia target biology-laboratory automation with high-fidelity simulation of fluid handling, instrument interfaces, and chemically meaningful interactions, emphasizing precise protocol execution rather than memory-dependent instruction grounding. These resources primarily support learning how to execute specified tasks across diverse conditions. However, greater trajectory diversity and access to demonstration videos do not by themselves ensure supervision for interpreting requests whose referents depend on earlier interactions. The GiT dataset targets the challenges by linking pre-episode interaction videos to subsequent instructions and execution trajectories, with counterfactual A--B pair annotations in both training and test splits. Memory‑centric benchmarks for robotic manipulation Robotic manipulation benchmarks evaluate different aspects of task execution. Table tab:benchmark summarizes a comparison of representative robotic manipulation benchmarks along key dimensions. BEHAVIOR-1K li2023behavior emphasizes realistic, long-horizon everyday activities, while RoboEval wang2025roboeval assesses bimanual execution quality through fine-grained behavioral metrics. However, task realism and execution quality alone do not isolate the need for historical information. To evaluate history dependence more directly, RMBench chen2026rmbench organizes manipulation tasks by memory complexity, whereas RoboMME dai2026robomme evaluates counting, object permanence, reference resolution, and motion imitation, including tasks that identify manipulation targets from prior videos. These controlled tasks help isolate specific memory skills, but success on such tests alone does not establish reliable grounding of history-dependent instructions in practical workflows. Compared with prior benchmarks, our benchmark uniquely targets the pre‑episode memory capability. It requires policies to reason over completed historical episodes for decision‑making, rather than maintaining and updating continuous task states within ongoing interactions. Moreover, our benchmark complements previous efforts by focusing on pre-episode semantic grounding in application-oriented biolaboratory, household, and industrial tasks. Methodology Problem Formulation We investigate temporal grounding under perceptual ambiguity in VLA models, examining whether they can use historical demonstrations to guide subsequent manipulation decisions when the current observation and language instruction alone are insufficient to identify the instruction-relevant manipulation target. An instruction may refer to object properties, relations, or event order established through interactions completed before the current task episode. When the current scene provides insufficient evidence of these distinctions, the intended target or task requirements cannot be reliably determined from the current observation and instruction alone. For example, visually similar objects may undergo different interactions without lasting changes to their appearance and subsequently return to similar spatial configurations, such that only their distinct interaction histories reveal which object satisfies the instruction. Formally, we formulate temporal grounding at decision step of each benchmark instance as a mapping from the historical visual sequence , the current observation , and the language instruction to the instruction-relevant manipulation specification : Here, specifies one or more target objects together with, where applicable, a required execution order, relational configuration, or target state. The function abstractly represents how this specification is determined from historical evidence, the current observation, and the language instruction, without imposing any particular model architecture. Hardware Setup and Data Acquisition The GiT dataset is collected through three pipelines: VR-based real-robot teleoperation, UMI style human demonstration collection, and simulation. The real-robot and simulation pipelines share a dual-arm embodiment comprising two PiperX manipulators, while the UMI style pipeline uses handheld grippers matched to the robot gripper geometry. The left and right controller poses and button states are acquired through oculus reader orbik2021oculusreader and mapped to the corresponding robot arms. A ROS-based teleoperation system processes these inputs into Cartesian end-effector targets and gripper commands, with the end-effector targets subsequently converted into joint commands for coordinated bimanual execution. title: TacOT: Learning Contact-Rich Dexterous Manipulation from Human Demonstrations via Tactile-Guided Optimal Transport
summary: Learning contact-rich dexterous manipulation from human demonstrations provides a scalable source of interaction data, yet transferring such skills to robots remains challenging due to unreliable human--robot correspondence. Existing human-to-robot transfer methods typically rely on visual appearance or motion similarity, which may associate similar motions with different contact states and force patterns. Tactile dynamics provide interaction-aware cues to distinguish manipulation processes with similar motions but different contact states. We introduce tactile-guided optimal transport (TacOT), a framework for human-to-robot contact-rich manipulation. TacOT leverages action--tactile dynamic time warping to identify human--robot demonstration correspondences with consistent interaction dynamics and uses these correspondences to guide soft optimal transport alignment in a shared policy representation space. This enables human demonstrations to provide contact-rich supervision for robot policy learning without requiring predefined frame-level human--robot pairing. Across four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks, TacOT improves closed-loop success rates over action-guided OT by up to 17 points on in-distribution tasks and 20 points under targeted human-to-robot out-of-distribution transfer. Further analyses show that tactile-guided correspondence selects demonstration pairs with more consistent contact dynamics and produces latent representations that better reflect interaction-state evolution. These results demonstrate that tactile dynamics provide an effective semantic signal for establishing reliable human-to-robot correspondence in contact-rich dexterous manipulation.
