This enables human demonstrations to provide contact-rich supervision for robot policy learning without requiring predefined frame-level human--robot pairing. Across four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks, TacOT improves closed-loop success rates over action-guided OT by up to 17 points on in-distribution tasks and 20 points under targeted human-to-robot out-of-distribution transfer. Further analyses show that tactile-guided correspondence selects demonstration pairs with more consistent contact dynamics and produces latent representations that better reflect interaction-state evolution. These results demonstrate that tactile dynamics provide an effective semantic signal for establishing reliable human-to-robot correspondence in contact-rich dexterous manipulation. INTRODUCTION Learning contact-rich skills with dexterous robot hands remains constrained by the scarcity of robot demonstrations. Collecting multi-finger interactions on physical robots is slow, labor-intensive, and difficult to scale across objects, scenes, and contact conditions. Automated demonstration generation and visuo-tactile pretraining improve data efficiency~ dexmimicgen2025,vital2025 , while large multi-embodiment datasets broaden the coverage of robot learning~ open_x_embodiment . Yet dexterous manipulation remains underrepresented because its critical variations lie not only in appearance and motion, but also in how contact is established, maintained, and released. Human demonstrations offer a scalable source of this missing interaction diversity. Wearable and in-the-wild systems can capture natural hand motion, visual observations, and contact signals across diverse manipulation behaviors~ umi,mimicplay,dexwild2025,mimictouch . However, leveraging human data raises a fundamental correspondence question: which human interactions provide meaningful supervision for robot behavior despite differences in embodiment? Existing approaches commonly rely on visual similarity or end-effector motion~ egomimic,egobridge . These cues are insufficient for contact-rich dexterous manipulation: similar wrist motions can correspond to free-space motion, contact establishment, or forceful interaction, while morphologically different human and robot motions may realize the same physical behavior. Consequently, demonstrations can appear aligned in vision or kinematics while differing substantially in finger contacts and force distributions. We therefore cast human-to-robot imitation as identifying interaction-consistent behavior rather than merely closing appearance- or motion-domain gaps. The relevant unit of correspondence is a temporally extended action--contact pattern, not an individual visually similar frame. Tactile trajectories disambiguate interaction phases that vision and kinematics leave uncertain. Here, tactile information serves not only as a policy observation but also as a supervision signal for matching human and robot demonstrations with consistent interaction dynamics. Although prior work has demonstrated the value of touch for policy conditioning, tactile representation learning, and cross-sensor transfer~ mimictouch,sparsh,xu2026vt, transferable_tactile_transformers,tactalign,unitachand , using joint action--tactile dynamics to establish human–robot behavioral correspondence remains underexplored. The same interaction may exhibit temporal variations between human and robot demonstrations, and multiple human segments may correspond to similar robot behaviors. Therefore, effective correspondence requires flexible alignment beyond frame-wise matching. Dynamic time warping (DTW) addresses the temporal requirement through order-preserving sequence alignment~ sakoe1978dtw . To support soft correspondence, we adopt entropy-regularized optimal transport (OT), which couples human and robot policy representations without predefined one-to-one pairing~ cuturi2013sinkhorn,peyre2019cot . The key challenge is to define a transport cost that reflects interaction compatibility between human and robot behaviors. We use joint action--tactile dynamics to guide this cost, favoring correspondences consistent in both motion and contact. We present tactile-guided optimal transport (TacOT), a framework for contact-rich human-to-robot manipulation. TacOT combines DTW distances computed separately over action and tactile trajectories to identify interaction-consistent human--robot demonstration pairs. These pairs guide OT by reducing their latent transport costs, favoring compatible interactions while retaining soft coupling across all pairs. Optimized jointly with a multimodal flow-matching objective, this alignment allows contact-rich human demonstrations to supervise a shared policy space anchored by robot data. Our contributions are as follows: We formulate human-to-robot imitation for contact-rich dexterous manipulation as an interaction-consistent correspondence learning problem, using joint action--tactile dynamics to guide soft optimal transport alignment. We develop a matched-sensing human--robot platform and a multimodal flow-matching policy for joint learning from visual, motion, and tactile demonstration data from human and robot systems. We evaluate TacOT on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks. Compared with action-guided OT, TacOT improves success rates by up to 17 percentage points in-distribution and 20 percentage points under targeted human-to-robot transfer. RELATED WORK Dexterous Imitation Learning. Dexterous imitation learning models high-dimensional, contact-rich hand--object interactions across tasks and embodiments. Video-based methods derive robot-executable supervision through physics-aware policy learning or hand--object reconstruction and retargeting~ chen2025vividex,paliwal2026dexterous . Being-H0, VITRA, and Being-H0.5 scale dexterous VLA pretraining through hand-motion modeling and action representations shared across human and robot embodiments~ luo2025being,li2025scalable,luo2026being , while DexHiL incorporates coordinated arm--hand interventions for policy adaptation~ han2026dexhil . These methods broaden supervision beyond robot teleoperation, but transferring human manipulation skills still requires alignment between human and robot representations and often robot-specific adaptation data. Tactile Representation and Transfer. Recent work learns tactile representations transferable across sensors, objects, and tasks. Self-supervised methods extract reusable tactile features~ sparsh , while multi-sensor approaches learn representations across heterogeneous visuo-tactile platforms~ anytouch,transferable_tactile_transformers . MimicTouch incorporates human tactile demonstrations into contact-rich robot learning~ mimictouch , and UniTacHand learns shared representations for human-to-robot tactile transfer~ unitachand . These studies emphasize tactile representation learning and transfer; TacOT additionally uses tactile trajectories to guide human--robot demonstration matching during policy learning. Learning from Human Demonstrations. MimicPlay learns long-horizon robot behaviors from human play data~ mimicplay , while EgoMimic co-trains human and robot demonstrations through visual and action-space alignment~ egomimic . EgoBridge constructs pseudo-pairs from end-effector trajectories to guide optimal-transport alignment between human and robot representations for robots with two-finger grippers~ egobridge . However, similar motions can involve different contact states in dexterous manipulation. TacOT therefore combines end-effector motion, hand actions, and tactile evolution to identify correspondences consistent in both motion and contact dynamics. SYSTEM AND METHOD TacOT learns human-to-robot dexterous manipulation by jointly leveraging human and robot demonstrations with synchronized visual, motion, and tactile observations. We first construct matched human and robot demonstration systems for multimodal data collection (Fig.~ fig:hardware_system ). The collected observations are then converted into unified representations for multimodal policy learning and action--tactile-guided latent alignment, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:pipeline . The following sections describe the hardware design and data collection (Sec.~III-A), human–robot representation alignment (Sec.~III-B), multimodal flow policy learning (Sec.~III-C), and action--tactile-guided latent alignment (Sec.~III-D). Hardware Design and Data Collection To support human-to-robot transfer, we construct two matched-sensing demonstration systems for multimodal data collection. The human demonstration system records natural hand--object interactions, whereas the robot demonstration system maps human motion to executable arm--hand commands through teleoperation. Both systems collect visual, motion, and tactile observations for human–robot representation learning. The human and robot datasets are collected independently and are not linked by shared timestamps, episode identifiers, or recorded cross-embodiment pairings. Fig.~ fig:hardware_system summarizes their hardware configurations and sensing modalities. Human demonstration system. The human system records hand motion and fingertip contact forces using a Manus data glove, a Vive Tracker with base stations, and five three-axis Paxini force sensors. Each sensor is fixed to a Manus fingertip using a 3D-printed mount, providing repeatable placement across demonstrations. Two Intel RealSense D435 cameras record synchronized RGB observations at a resolution of \(640 480\), providing wrist-view and third-person views of the interaction. Robot demonstration system. The robot system consists of a UR5 manipulator equipped with an XHand dexterous hand. During teleoperation, the human wrist trajectory is mapped to the UR5 end effector (EEF), while glove signals are converted online into XHand joint commands. The glove and tracker signals used for teleoperation are not stored and are not used for training. The robot system records only robot-side EEF and hand trajectories, fingertip contact forces measured by tactile sensors integrated into the XHand hand, and dual-view RGB observations using two D435 cameras. title: Frame-Level Temporal Alignment for Human-to-Robot Visual Adaptation
summary: Transferring visual representations pretrained on human videos to robot manipulation requires learning reliable correspondences between human and robot demonstrations. However, paired demonstrations can differ in execution rate and in the proportion of non-key frames that do not directly reflect task progress. Frames at the same relative timestamp may therefore represent different task stages, which can cause correspondence learning to fail. To address these issues, we propose Frame-Level Temporal Alignment (FLTA), a framework that uses two temporal priors to adapt visual encoders pretrained on human videos for robot manipulation. It learns shared task-progress representations without frame-level correspondence annotations, allowing frames at different relative temporal positions to match. A global progress prior combines normalized temporal positions with visual similarity to construct a soft correspondence target. A local temporal order prior penalizes backward transitions while allowing stays and varying forward rates to accommodate execution-rate differences. With ResNet-50 and ViT encoders, our method achieves relative improvements of 46.93% and 65.96%, respectively, over the best baselines in average simulation success rates and achieves higher task success rates on real-world manipulation tasks. These results also suggest that effective human-robot adaptation depends less on the number of parameters updated than on which parameters are selected. Our project page is available at https://rtx5090ultra.github.io/FLTA-Project-Page/.

These results also suggest that effective human--robot adaptation depends less on the number of parameters updated than on which parameters are selected. Our project page is available at . Introduction sec:intro Vision-based robotic manipulation relies on visual representations that capture task-relevant state information for action prediction. Learning such representations solely from robot demonstrations is challenging because robot data are costly to collect and often cover a limited range of tasks. Human videos provide a scalable, complementary source of interaction data, as they are relatively inexpensive to obtain, widely available, and rich in object manipulation experience~ Grauman_2022_CVPR,bahl2023affordances,pmlr-v235-li24cr,Srirama-RSS-24,zhang2026provable . Pretraining on human videos can encode these experiences into transferable, task-relevant visual representations that support downstream policy learning and generalization beyond task-specific robot demonstrations~ pmlr-v205-nair23a,radosavovic2023real,pmlr-v202-ma23b,pmlr-v235-li24cr . However, differences in movement capabilities and appearance between humans and robots create a substantial domain gap between human videos and robot observations~ Zhou_2025_CVPR,ben2006analysis,ganin2016domain . As such, visual representations need to distinguish task progress because the downstream policy selects its next action based on the current observation~ pmlr-v205-nair23a,Srirama-RSS-24 . HRAlign~ Zhou_2025_CVPR , the state-of-the-art solution, uses paired human-robot videos for video-level contrastive alignment, learning shared task semantics to reduce this domain gap. However, frames sampled from paired human and robot videos may show different task stages despite sharing the same task instruction. Aligning their aggregated video representations does not explicitly establish which human and robot frames correspond to similar task progress. This distinction is apparent for paired datasets such as RH20T~ fang2024rh20t , which provides human and robot demonstrations of the same task. As shown in Figure~ fig:motivation figure , these videos exhibit two temporal differences. First, the videos contain different proportions of non-key frames, which do not directly reflect task progress. As a result, the action starts at different relative positions in the two videos. Second, execution-rate mismatch changes the duration of each task stage. Frames sampled at the same relative time may show different task progress. Statistics across tasks and video pairs are provided in Appendix~ app:temporal_differences . For example, sampled human non-key frames and robot key frames may contribute to a video-level positive pair. The aggregated video representations are pulled together even though the sampled frames show different task progress. Such stage mismatch may reduce the strength of the alignment signal used to learn task-progress representations, making it harder for downstream policies to select appropriate actions. To address these issues, we propose a frame-level temporal alignment framework that adapts pretrained visual encoders using paired human and robot videos, without frame-level correspondence annotations. As shown in Figure~ fig:motivation figure , we guide correspondence learning with the inductive bias that human and robot demonstrations generally progress toward task completion over time~ Hadji_2021_CVPR,pmlr-v164-zakka22a . First, we introduce a global progress prior that combines normalized temporal positions with visual similarity to construct a soft correspondence target between human and robot frames. It allows each frame to match multiple candidate frames while penalizing large differences in normalized temporal position, rather than requiring same-position matches. Second, we introduce a local temporal order prior to guide the order of matches for consecutive sampled frames. As time progresses from the current human frame to the next sampled human frame, encourages the corresponding robot match to stay or move forward by penalizing backward transitions. This encourages temporal order while allowing for execution-rate differences. During adaptation, we update only the affine parameters of normalization layers, a restricted parameterization previously used for domain adaptation~ wang2020tent . This restricts the parameter search space during adaptation, with the aim of improving the visual representations for downstream robotic manipulation. On AGNOSTOS~ zhou2026exploring , our method achieves a relative improvement in average success rate over HRAlign with R3M-RN50~ pmlr-v205-nair23a initialization. With D4R-ViT~ pmlr-v229-dasari23a initialization, it achieves a relative improvement over HRP~ Srirama-RSS-24 . With D4R-ViT initialization, it also improves success rates on all four real-world manipulation tasks compared with the Frozen and HRP baselines. Our experiments further show that effective human--robot adaptation does not require a large number of trainable parameters. Updating only 53.1K normalization-affine parameters achieves higher success rates than the late-adapter variant, despite using approximately fewer trainable parameters. Adaptation only takes approximately 13 hours on a single NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU, without multi-GPU training. These results suggest that effective human--robot adaptation depends less on the number of parameters updated than on which parameters are selected. Human-to-Robot Domain Adaptation sec:Preliminaries and Methodology We formulate the human-to-robot domain gap as a representation adaptation problem. For paired human and robot videos of the same task with different temporal structures, video-level alignment does not explicitly establish frame-level correspondences, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:motivation figure . We therefore adapt a pretrained visual encoder through frame-level temporal alignment without frame-level correspondence annotations. The adapted encoder is then frozen for downstream robot policy learning. In the human-video pretraining paradigm, a visual encoder is first pretrained on human videos. The policy then takes the encoded representation , rather than the raw robot observation , as its visual state input. To handle the human-robot domain gap, we adapt using . The adapted encoder provides visual representations better suited to robot observations , helping the downstream policy predict the next action more reliably. Framework Overview subsec:Framework Overview As shown in Figure~ fig:ours_framework , our framework learns frame-level temporal correspondences using visual similarity, a global progress prior, and a local temporal order prior. An auxiliary frame discrimination loss supports cross-domain matching. title: AgenticTactileVLA: Contact-Guided Execution-Time Supervision for Generalizable Dexterous Manipulation without VLA Retraining
summary: Vision-language-action policies may predict a transferable manipulation strategy yet fail to realize it reliably on the encountered object: objects compatible with the same grasp differ in geometry and compliance, and visual feedback degrades under closure occlusion. AgenticTactileVLA is presented as an execution-time supervisor that shifts part of object-specific adaptation from prediction to physical interaction. A fixed VLA provides the approach and hand targets; the supervisor decides whether to remain transparent, refine finger flexion, retain or release the corrected configuration, return control to the VLA for retry, or select a compliant hand-control regime. It uses finger-position and motor-effort feedback as proprioceptive contact evidence and requires neither tactile sensors nor VLA retraining. On a Unitree G1 with a BrainCo Revo2 hand, a randomized matched-block evaluation on five objects held out from VLA training yields 61.3% completion for the base VLA, 72.0% for unconditional close-to-stall control, and 84.0% for the supervisor under a shared budget; the gain is positive on every object and persists under moderate pose perturbations. Ablations show the gain is not explained by extended closure alone, and that selective triggering reduces correction episodes by 65.7% with no detected change in completion. A retention audit shows acceptance predicts retention in 88.9% of held-out cases, while compliant objects expose conservative false rejection. A thin-walled-cup study demonstrates contextual routing to compliant control, matching an always-compliant reference. These results suggest that contact-guided execution-time adaptation can improve the object-level generalization of a fixed VLA to held-out objects by adapting physical realization without object-specific retraining.
full_text: Vision-language-action policies may predict a transferable manipulation strategy yet fail to realize it reliably on the encountered object: objects compatible with the same grasp differ in geometry and compliance, and visual feedback degrades under closure occlusion. AgenticTactileVLA is presented as an execution-time supervisor that shifts part of object-specific adaptation from prediction to physical interaction. A fixed VLA provides the approach and hand targets; the supervisor decides whether to remain transparent, refine finger flexion, retain or release the corrected configuration, return control to the VLA for retry, or select a compliant hand-control regime. It uses finger-position and motor-effort feedback as proprioceptive contact evidence and requires neither tactile sensors nor VLA retraining. On a Unitree G1 with a BrainCo Revo2 hand, a randomized matched-block evaluation on five objects held out from VLA training yields 61.3 completion for the base VLA, 72.0 for unconditional close-to-stall control, and 84.0 for the supervisor under a shared budget; the gain is positive on every object and persists under moderate pose perturbations. Ablations show the gain is not explained by extended closure alone, and that selective triggering reduces correction episodes by 65.7 with no detected change in completion. A retention audit shows acceptance predicts retention in 88.9 of held-out cases, while compliant objects expose conservative false rejection. A thin-walled-cup study demonstrates contextual routing to compliant control, matching an always-compliant reference. These results suggest that contact-guided execution-time adaptation can improve the object-level generalization of a fixed VLA to held-out objects by adapting physical realization without object-specific retraining. Introduction A central challenge in robot learning is to generalize manipulation policies to new objects while maintaining reliable physical execution. For vision-language-action (VLA) models, this is particularly important in contact-rich manipulation. Objects compatible with the same broad grasp strategy may differ in geometry and compliance, changing the finger contacts and interaction conditions required for successful execution. A VLA may therefore generate a suitable approach yet still leave fingers without sufficient support, produce an unsuitable terminal hand configuration, or over-compress a fragile object. Such failures are difficult to resolve visually during closure, when the hand increasingly occludes the contact region. Many objects can be handled using a limited repertoire of broad grasp strategies cutkosky1989grasp,feixgrasp , while their physical realization may still require object-specific finger contacts and interaction effort. This motivates reusing a fixed policy while adapting these physical details during execution rather than through object-specific retraining. We investigate a division of responsibility in which the VLA provides the transferable manipulation strategy, while an execution-time supervisor adapts its physical realization to the encountered object (Fig.~ fig:platform ). The supervisor can modify finger flexion and gate progression of the VLA-generated body reference, but does not replace the VLA approach policy or learn a residual action model. Prior work has explored tactile-conditioned VLA adaptation vlatouch,unitacvla and execution monitoring and recovery planar,volo . Our work lies at their intersection and asks: Can execution-time physical adaptation improve the realization of a fixed VLA policy on objects outside its training set without object-specific retraining? AgenticTactileVLA augments a fixed VLA with a stateful execution supervisor. At the terminal phase of nominal closure, it evaluates proprioceptive support evidence. If support is sufficient, execution remains transparent to the policy. Otherwise, body-reference progression is paused while whole-body stabilization remains active, and unsupported fingers are corrected independently. An accepted correction is retained; a rejected correction releases the hand override and returns control to the VLA for subsequent policy-generated retry. A key principle is selective intervention: the supervisor acts only when the policy-proposed closure is not sufficiently realized physically. To separate this effect from simply closing farther or longer, we compare against unconditional close-to-stall control under the same execution budget and use component ablations to examine selectivity, effort-assisted stopping, and verdict-dependent release. Geometric correction alone is insufficient when the interaction regime must also change. Fragile objects may deform before proprioceptive resistance is large enough for reactive correction. AgenticTactileVLA therefore also selects between nominal position control and a predefined compliant mode before closure. Explicit handling cues can request compliant interaction, while a vision-language model (VLM) can select between the two modes from image and task context. The VLM selects only the interaction mode and does not generate controller parameters or material estimates. We use the term agentic to denote this bounded, stateful supervision: deciding whether to remain transparent or intervene, adapting individual finger references, accepting or releasing the corrected grasp, returning control to the VLA for retry, and selecting the interaction regime. This distinguishes the layer from low-level reflexes by enabling high-level decision-making based on multimodal context. The framework uses finger position and motor-effort signals as device-specific proprioceptive evidence and requires neither additional tactile sensors nor object-specific VLA retraining. The main contributions of this work are: A contact-guided execution-time supervisor for a fixed VLA, combining selective intervention, bounded per-finger correction, grasp acceptance or release, and policy-mediated retry. A proprioceptive execution mechanism using finger position and motor-effort feedback without additional tactile hardware, together with language- or vision-conditioned selection between nominal and compliant interaction modes. Real-hardware evaluation on a Unitree G1 with a BrainCo Revo2 hand under matched execution budgets, including unconditional close-to-stall control, component ablations, pose perturbations, retention diagnostics, and fragile-object interaction tests. The intended scope is adaptation of feasible policy-generated manipulation strategies, not recovery from arbitrary incompatible approach errors. Within this scope, we view execution-time physical adaptation as a step toward more scalable object-level generalization of fixed VLA policies, reducing the need for object-specific retraining while preserving the policy's reusable manipulation strategy. Related Work Contact Sensing from Motor Feedback Motor feedback can reveal physical robot--object interaction without dedicated tactile sensors. Current as Touch currentastouch , Transferring Contact, Not Just Motion contacttransfer , and Pseudo-Tactile pseudotactile use actuator or gripper signals for contact-aware manipulation. AgenticTactileVLA uses finger positions and motor-effort signals as device-specific evidence of interaction resistance rather than calibrated contact force. This evidence determines whether the nominal closure provides sufficient support and, when necessary, guides local finger correction and grasp acceptance or release. Tactile Feedback for VLA Adaptation Tactile feedback complements vision when physical interaction is difficult to infer from images alone. VLA-Touch vlatouch combines a frozen VLA with semantic tactile feedback and learned action refinement. TLA tla and VTLA vtla incorporate tactile observations into action generation, while UniTacVLA unitacvla predicts contact changes to refine action chunks. RoboTacDex robotacdex provides multimodal data for visual--tactile dexterous humanoid manipulation. In contrast, AgenticTactileVLA does not train a tactile-conditioned VLA or a learned residual policy. Adaptation is placed in an external, nonlearned execution layer while the VLA remains fixed. The supervisor stays transparent when the policy-generated closure already provides sufficient support and intervenes only when physical correction is required. Execution Supervision and Interaction Control Execution supervision connects predicted actions with observed consequences. PLanAR planar verifies expected effects and replans after deviations, VoLo volo combines monitoring with recovery, and VLAs Fail Differently failsdifferently analyzes failure structure in motor-command sequences. This work brings supervision to the closure-to-motion transition in dexterous manipulation. The supervisor determines whether the physical realization of the VLA action is sufficient, whether individual fingers should be corrected, whether the resulting grasp should be retained or released, and whether control should return to the VLA for another approach. A separate interaction-mode layer selects between nominal position control and current-limited compliant control before closure. AgenticTactileVLA thus combines selective intervention, contact-guided finger adaptation, grasp acceptance or release, policy-mediated retry, and contextual interaction-mode selection within a single execution-time layer over a fixed VLA policy. Method sec:method The architecture separates policy prediction from physical execution. The fixed VLA generates body-motion tokens and hand targets, while the execution supervisor monitors how these commands are physically realized. When the policy-generated grasp is sufficiently realized, execution remains unchanged. Otherwise, the supervisor can pause body-reference progression, adapt individual fingers, or return control to the VLA for another approach. A separate interaction-mode layer selects nominal or compliant hand control before closure, while whole-body stabilization remains active throughout execution (Fig.~ fig:architecture ). System Overview and Execution Supervisor sec:supervisor Nominal VLA execution GR00T-N1.6-3B groot , fine-tuned on teleoperated manipulation demonstrations, is deployed on a Unitree G1 with a BrainCo Revo2 hand and remains fixed during agent-assisted execution. Let denote the policy observation, including the ego-view image, robot state, and measured hand positions, and let denote the natural-language instruction. The VLA produces an action chunk where is the body-motion token and contains the nominal position targets for the six hand channels. GEAR-SONIC sonic realizes the body-motion tokens, while a dedicated driver executes thumb flexion (0), thumb opposition (1), index (2), middle (3), ring (4), and little finger (5). Thumb opposition preserves the policy-selected grasp arrangement; execution-time correction modifies only the flexion channels. The hand publishes measured finger positions and a motor-effort proxy . These signals provide the proprioceptive feedback used by the supervisor. Motor effort is treated as a device-specific indicator of interaction resistance, not as a calibrated measurement of contact force. Agentic execution supervisor The execution agent wraps the fixed VLA as a stateful supervisory layer: where stores issued hand references, measured positions, and motor-effort feedback; is the visual observation and the internal execution state. The outputs define execution authority. The mode selects the hand-control regime, selects nominal execution or intervention, contains override finger references, and gates progression of the body reference. The agent does not replace the VLA arm policy: body motion continues to originate from policy-generated tokens. The supervisor operates at the boundary between policy completion and physical grasp completion. A closure is visible in the action chunk as progressive flexion-target motion. title: WasserMan: Benchmark for Underwater Manipulation Policy Learning
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
summary: Underwater manipulation couples visual decisions, contact forces and a thruster-controlled floating base. We introduce WasserMan, to our knowledge the first multi-task simulation benchmark for visuomotor learning of floating-base underwater contact manipulation. It provides ten expert-solvable tasks, two vehicle-arm platforms, a bimanual configuration and underwater dynamics. Nine tasks have learned-policy evaluations. We compare ACT, diffusion policies (DP) and behavioral cloning on six tasks, with three training runs and equal sampled-window budgets. Pretrained SmolVLA adds evaluations on three tasks. In the tested settings, removing integral action can prevent completion, while changing action interfaces can reduce learned-policy success despite successful expert replay. Currents produce task-dependent changes in completion and actuation effort. Versioned tasks, demonstrations and per-episode evidence support a protocol separating expert feasibility, learned completion and execution effort.
full_text: Underwater manipulation couples visual decisions, contact forces and a thruster-controlled floating base. We introduce WasserMan, to our knowledge the first multi-task simulation benchmark for visuomotor learning of floating-base underwater contact manipulation. It provides ten expert-solvable tasks, two vehicle--arm platforms, a bimanual configuration and underwater dynamics. Nine tasks have learned-policy evaluations. We compare ACT, diffusion policies (DP) and behavioral cloning on six tasks, with three training runs and equal sampled-window budgets. Pretrained SmolVLA adds evaluations on three tasks. Introduction Underwater manipulation couples arm motion, contact and a thruster-controlled floating base~ fossen . Intervention platforms~ girona , valve turning under currents~ carrera and dual-arm control~ simetti2015 study this coupling. A learning benchmark must distinguish an infeasible command interface from a learned policy that fails to produce useful commands. WasserMan formalizes this distinction. To our knowledge, it is the first multi-task simulation benchmark for visuomotor learning of floating-base underwater contact manipulation. Its ten-task catalogue spans panel interaction, object collection, connector insertion and shipwreck intervention. The main learning protocol covers PressButton, RotateValve, OpenHatch, CollectShell, PushSlider and PullLever. Separately versioned ACT/DP evaluations cover HotStab, CabinRecovery and CargoRelease, giving nine tasks with learned-policy results. Wall Toss adds an expert delivery scenario. Two native vehicle--arm systems and a custom twin-arm configuration support platform and bimanual comparisons. We make three contributions. First, we provide extensible task contracts, physical experts, floating-base platforms, distributable procedural assets, demonstrations and fixed evaluation cohorts. Second, we report ACT, DP and chunked-BC results on six tasks, with three independent training runs per configuration. Third, a diagnostic protocol links expert replay to policy evaluation and interventions on controllers, action interfaces and currents. Contact, mechanism progress and vehicle response reveal differences hidden by success alone. Related Work Marine simulation and manipulation. UUV Simulator, DAVE and Stonefish support marine simulation and intervention~ uuv,dave,stonefish,stonefishml . DAVE supports stabilized bimanual manipulation. Stonefish provides articulated dynamics and learning interfaces. MarineGym reports PPO studies of station keeping and trajectory tracking~ marinegym . Earlier intervention benchmarks studied tracking under visibility and current changes, and reconstruction~ sanz2015benchmark . WasserMan standardizes learning for visual-contact tasks through common demonstrations, checkpoints and physical scoring. Bi-AQUA studies bilateral imitation with lighting-aware action chunking~ biaqua . UMI-Underwater evaluates affordance-conditioned diffusion policies in pool experiments~ umiunderwater . ULOHA combines underwater bimanual hardware with ACT, DP and SmolVLA~ uloha . WasserMan enables controlled simulation comparisons. Published BlueROV2 damping identification~ vonbenzon2022 supplies a separate coefficient condition. Benchmarks and policies. AM-Bench evaluates policies, control interfaces and embodiments in aerial manipulation~ ambench . WasserMan evaluates underwater contact tasks under its own task, data and execution contracts. RLBench, robosuite, ManiSkill, Meta-World and CALVIN provide manipulation suites~ rlbench,robosuite,maniskill,maniskill2,metaworld,calvin . LIBERO, BEHAVIOR and RoboCasa broaden evaluation settings~ libero,behavior,robocasa . Robomimic motivates implementation-aware comparisons~ robomimic . ACT and DP combine transformer and diffusion methods with visual encoders~ act,dp,transformer,ddpm,ddim,resnet,clip . R3M/VC-1 and DAgger offer representation and data-aggregation alternatives~ r3m,vc1,dagger . Simulation and appearance. Isaac Gym, Orbit and Isaac Lab provide GPU simulation and learning infrastructure~ isaacgym,orbit,isaaclab . MuJoCo and SAPIEN are complementary engines~ mujoco,sapien . Underwater image formation, restoration, lighting, refraction and calibration motivate optical controls~ akkaynak,seathru,illumination,refractive,calibration . Visual and dynamics randomization motivates transfer tests~ tobin,peng,rubik . WasserMan exposes optical controls and frozen-policy current interventions. Benchmark Tasks and Contracts Task and asset version The open-procedural-v1 profile supplies primitive arm visuals and two-segment box fingers. Evaluation Design Data and implementations A predefined stream of 400 candidate resets per task supplies the first 80 successful expert demonstrations. Each run (seeds 17/43/101) uses 320,000 non-padded sampled windows. ACT and BC use batch 32 for 10,000 updates, and DP uses effective batch 64 for 5,000. title: VCURF: Virtual Camera-based Uncertainty of Radiance Fields
summary: Radiance fields, implemented with either implicit (NeRF) or explicit (Gaussian Splatting) representations, are advancing the state of the art in novel view synthesis at a rapid pace. Even though the rendered views they generate are often compelling, they are not free of errors. In this paper, we propose a new approach for pixel-wise uncertainty quantification based on measuring the inconsistencies among renderings by the radiance field model in virtual cameras sampled near the target viewpoint. We named our approach VCURF for Virtual Camera-based Uncertainty of Radiance Fields. VCURF treats the radiance field model as a black box, only assuming that it is capable of rendering color and depth on demand. This property makes our approach applicable to both NeRF and GS models without any modification. Our experiments on a combination of datasets, radiance field models and baselines demonstrate VCURF's effectiveness in pixel-wise uncertainty estimation. We conclude the paper with findings that question the way view selection is tackled by the majority of the current literature.
full_text: Radiance fields, implemented with either implicit (NeRF) or explicit (Gaussian Splatting) representations, are advancing the state of the art in novel view synthesis at a rapid pace. Even though the rendered views they generate are often compelling, they are not free of errors. In this paper, we propose a new approach for pixel-wise uncertainty quantification based on measuring the inconsistencies among renderings by the radiance field model in virtual cameras sampled near the target viewpoint. We named our approach VCURF for Virtual Camera-based Uncertainty of Radiance Fields. VCURF treats the radiance field model as a black box, only assuming that it is capable of rendering color and depth on demand. This property makes our approach applicable to both NeRF and GS models without any modification. Our experiments on a combination of datasets, radiance field models and baselines demonstrate VCURF's effectiveness in pixel-wise uncertainty estimation. We conclude the paper with findings that question the way view selection is tackled by the majority of the current literature. Introduction sec:intro Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) mildenhall2020nerf have had tremendous impact on Novel View Synthesis (NVS). This is due to their ability to synthesize plausible images without striking artifacts under adverse imaging conditions and errors in camera geometry estimation. More recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) kerbl20233dgs emerged as an alternative to NeRF. Unlike NeRF, which relies on implicit representations, Gaussian Splatting employs an explicit representation in the form of a set of 3D Gaussian splats. Following recent literature, we will use the term Radiance Fields (RF) to describe both. (We will also use GS to denote Gaussian Splatting in general, and 3DGS for the method of Kerbl et al. kerbl20233dgs .) Despite their success, RF-based maps are not perfect in practice: limited views, appearance challenges, dynamics, and pose errors can cause local failures in geometry and appearance. This motivates pixel-wise uncertainty estimation that predicts the expected rendering error without ground truth. Such estimates provide useful signals for identifying unreliable regions, filtering artifacts, and assessing local reconstruction quality. They have also been widely used as proxies for information gain in next-best-view (NBV) selection and active reconstruction. However, these two uses should be distinguished. Pixel-wise uncertainty characterizes where the current model is likely to be wrong, whereas the utility of a candidate view additionally depends on whether it contributes novel and non-redundant observations relative to the existing training set. A highly uncertain view is therefore not necessarily the view that will most improve the RF after retraining. We revisit this distinction experimentally after establishing the accuracy of our uncertainty estimator. In practice, we seek an uncertainty module that is easy to deploy as a plug-in, is training-free, memory-friendly, and avoids modifying or accessing internal RF parameters, which simplifies integration across diverse backbones. In this paper, we use black-box to denote estimators that require only outputs and no knowledge of model parameters, and white-box to denote methods that require modifying the RF model and/or introducing additional training objectives. Motivated by these constraints, we propose Virtual-Camera-based Uncertainty of Radiance Fields ( ), a black-box pixel-wise uncertainty estimator applicable to both implicit and explicit RFs. is based on the principle that inconsistency indicates uncertainty: it perturbs the viewpoint via a set of virtual cameras around the target view, warps renderings across views, and derives uncertainty from discrepancies in warped color and depth (Fig.~ fig:overview ). Compared to uncertainty estimators that require stochastic inference, posterior approximations, or additional model instances/components (e.g., ensembles, dropout, entropy, Bayesian/variational methods)~ sunderhauf2023density,sun2024ph,zhan2022activermap,xue2024neural,lyu2024manifold , is a lightweight plug-in estimator that queries only renderings to virtual cameras, avoiding retraining and the storage overhead of maintaining multiple model instances while still producing accurate pixel-wise uncertainty. Two recent methods rely on Fisher Information to estimate uncertainty: Bayes' Rays goli2024bayes for NeRF and FisherRF jiang2024fisherrf for GS. Both approaches derive uncertainty from a Hessian matrix and impose the Laplace approximation to make computation tractable. These formulations are elegant, but the range within which the approximations are valid may be limited. , on the other hand, does not impose any restrictions on the posterior of the model. As a result, uncertainty cannot be computed in closed form, given model parameters, but we are able to measure the effects of relatively large perturbations in camera pose. Our experimental results show higher accuracy in uncertainty prediction compared to FisherRF. The main contributions of our paper are: a new approach for estimating pixel uncertainty of implicit and explicit RF models based on virtual-camera cross-view consistency; the algorithm, a training-free, memory-friendly plug-in uncertainty estimator that treats the RF model as a black box (no model modification and no access to parameters) and does not require storing multiple models; extensive experiments on multiple datasets comparing with various uncertainty estimators on an implicit and an explicit RF model. Related Work sec:related_works As the literature on Radiance Fields (RFs) expands rapidly, providing a comprehensive survey is beyond the scope of this paper. We refer readers to recent overviews bao2025_3dgs_survey,dalal_2024_gaussian,fei2024survey and focus on uncertainty estimation for NeRF and Gaussian Splatting (GS). Klasson et al. klasson2024sources evaluate uncertainty predictors for both representations and categorize common sources of uncertainty as noise, occlusions, outliers, and imprecise camera poses. Their study evaluates uncertainty quantification due to each source separately without considering identifying the sources. Uncertainty estimation for NeRF. A common approach augments the reconstruction objective with a negative log-likelihood (NLL) term kendall2017uncertainties . NeRF-W martin2021nerfwild uses this formulation to account for transient occluders and other outliers, while Neu-NBV jin2023neu , ActiveNeRF pan2022activenerf , the Colorized Surface Voxel approach kim2024active , and NARUTO feng2024naruto use related predictive uncertainty formulations in active reconstruction. Neural Visibility Fields xue2024neural jointly model visibility and uncertainty in a Bayesian formulation that also incorporates an NLL objective. Entropy along a ray has likewise been used as an uncertainty signal zhan2022activermap,lee2022uncertainty,yan2023activeimplicit , while NeurAR ran2023neurar uses transmittance-weighted rendering variance but requires ground-truth depth during training. Ensembles provide another widely used estimate of epistemic uncertainty. S\"underhauf et al. sunderhauf2023density measure variation among RGB renderings and incorporate predicted density, outperforming naive ensembles. He et al. he_chaudhari2024active form distributions over color, depth, voxel occupancy, and semantic labels. Dropsembles susmelj2025uncertainty construct an ensemble by fine-tuning several dropout-thinned instances on noisy inputs, while Yan et al. yan2023activeneuralmapping perturb network weights during exploration and use the resulting rendering variation to identify uncertain regions. Monte Carlo Dropout gal2016dropout can also be viewed as an efficient mechanism for constructing an implicit ensemble and is widely used as an uncertainty baseline shen2021stochastic,shen2022conditional,sunderhauf2023density,yan2023activeneuralmapping . Rather than maintaining a finite set of models, Conditional-Flow NeRF (CF-NeRF) shen2022conditional learns a distribution over possible RFs using conditional normalizing flows and estimates uncertainty from multiple samples. Shen et al. shen2024estimating instead combine an NLL-based prediction with a 3D uncertainty field that distinguishes observed from unobserved regions. Zeng et al. zeng2023efficient learn an approximation to a volumetric information-gain field. Bayes' Rays goli2024bayes defines a spatial perturbation field and estimates uncertainty through the Hessian of the posterior over network parameters: regions are considered uncertain when large perturbations produce little change in the objective. Evidential Neural Radiance Fields duan2026evidential is a probabilistic approach for distinguishing between epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty. Uncertainty estimation for Gaussian Splatting. WildGaussians kulhanek2024wildgaussians uses an NLL loss to predict uncertainty caused by occlusions, dynamic objects, and illumination changes. ActiveGS jin2025activegs derives the uncertainty of each splat from the density and angular diversity of its observing cameras, while Gauss-MI xie2025GauSS-MI associates reliability variables with the splats and uses them to estimate information gain. Variational formulations have been introduced by Savant et al. savant2025modeling , who incorporate an AUSE-based term into the training objective, and by Li et al. li2024variational , who use multi-scale analysis. Manifold sampling lyu2024manifold provides a differentiable uncertainty formulation based on variational inference. RT-GuIDE tao2024rt uses the magnitude of Gaussian-parameter updates as its uncertainty signal, whereas Gottwald et al. gottwald2025uncertainty attach visibility and training-error features to the primitives and train a regressor to predict pixel-wise uncertainty. Xue et al. xue2026uncertainty estimate an anisotropic volumetric visibility field for explicit RFs, from which uncertainty can be derived. FisherRF jiang2024fisherrf uses Fisher information to estimate the information carried by a view or pixel about the underlying RF. It obtains a tractable estimate from a diagonal Laplace approximation to the Hessian of the rendering objective. This approximation is particularly suitable for representations with structured local parameters, such as 3DGS kerbl20233dgs and Plenoxels fridovich2022plenoxels . PUP 3D-GS hanson2024pup also computes Fisher information for Gaussian primitives, but uses a block-wise rather than diagonal approximation and evaluates uncertainty indirectly through pruning. Representation-agnostic estimators. Only a few uncertainty estimators can directly work with both implicit and explicit RFs. FisherRF is applicable to both, although its approximation can be poorer for fully connected implicit models. Ewen et al. ewen2025these use low- and high-order moments of rendered color, depth, and semantic labels. PH-Dropout sun2024ph inserts dropout into either a trained NeRF or a GS model, increases the dropout ratio while preserving training-view accuracy, and measures uncertainty from the variance of repeated renderings. Like our method, WarpRF safadoust2026warprf estimates uncertainty through cross-view consistency without modifying the RF architecture. title: Agentic AI with Structured CoT for Enhancing AI's Spatial Intelligence: Visualization and Reasoning of Rotation
summary: Recent studies show that artificial intelligence (AI) with language and vision capabilities still experiences limitations in spatial reasoning. In this paper, we have studied the spatial capabilities of advanced generative AI to understand the rotations of objects in 3D space, utilizing AI's image processing and language processing features. We trained and examined the spatial intelligence of a generative Agentic AI model (GPT-5.6) to understand the spatial rotation process with rotation diagrams based on the revised Purdue Spatial Visualization Test: Visualization of Rotations (Revised PSVT:R). We improvised the Revised PSVT:R by superimposing additional graphical and contextual features to evaluate how different Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning strategies influence model performance. The results indicate that structured CoT reasoning improves the spatial reasoning performance of the base GPT-5.6 model in both datasets (PSVT:R and PSVT:R with coordinate system). We used three CoT approaches - (1) Structured CoT, (2) few-shot Structured CoT, and Structured CoT with Self-optimized Prompt. The three CoT approaches evaluated in this study showed no significant performance difference. Results showed that combining structured CoT reasoning with relevant contextual information leads to considerable improvements in VLM performance on 3D rotation tasks, demonstrating the potential of agentic AI for more effective spatial reasoning. However, when contextual information is removed, structured CoT reasoning alone provides limited improvement, and the models continue to exhibit notable difficulties in understanding spatial transformations. These findings suggest that effective spatial reasoning in VLMs relies on the integration of visual, textual, and reasoning-based information in future agentic AI systems for spatial intelligence.

Generative AI, Spatial Intelligence, Agentic AI, Chain-of-Thought, CoT, PSVT:R Introduction Spatial visualization is a significant part of spatial skills. Spatial skill and spatial guidance can greatly benefit understanding spatial transformations and additionally support processes like assembly, construction, and manufacturing, as well as learning in AEC (Architecture/Engineering/Construction), STEM, and medicine that require precise 3D spatial understanding. The impact of spatial visualization skill is both educational and practical. AI with spatial reasoning skills can greatly benefit educational and practical tasks. In education, despite having access to various computer-assisted learning resources for geometry, spatial transformations, and mathematical concepts, many STEM students struggle with visualization tasks garmendia2007first , andrews2017hypothetical . When conversational AI is added to an immersive visual learning approach, learners can receive personalized, real-time assistance, allowing them to ask questions, correct misunderstandings, and practice spatial reasoning interactively wei2025multiple . In practice, in construction, manufacturing, disaster response, and emergency field operations, AI's understanding of spatial relationships can facilitate assembly, avoid misplacement of components, help navigation, and facilitate prompt response. Generative AI, encompassing technologies that can create new content such as text, images, 3D models, audio, and video, has rapidly evolved in recent years, driven by advancements in deep learning and neural network architecture. Large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-4 and its successors have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in generating coherent and contextually relevant text. GPT-4o and GPT-5 with vision have capabilities to analyze user-input images and show unprecedented ability in understanding visual inputs, spatial relationships of humans and objects achiam2023gpt , han2026decoupling . However, current vision-language models still have limitations in spatial reasoning, especially when interpreting three-dimensional transformations such as rotation, translation, scale, orientation, and perspective changes han2020spare3d . This creates a critical knowledge gap: AI systems can describe images and objects, but they are not yet consistently reliable as spatial guides in complex real-world environments where decisions may affect safety, infrastructure, and human life anthi2025role , lee2025agentic . Therefore, improving AI’s spatial intelligence is essential for building trustworthy human-AI interaction systems that can support users in dangerous, high-pressure, and visually complex settings speiser2026agentic . Spatial reasoning, a key area in psychometrics, has several datasets for evaluating these skills. Some widely used tests for rotation visualization are the Purdue Spatial Visualization Test (PSVT)/The Purdue Visualization of Rotations Test bodner1997purdue , the Revised Purdue Spatial Visualization Test: Visualization of Rotations (Revised PSVT:R) yoon2011psychometric , and the Mental Rotation Tests vandenberg1978mental . We can use both a verbal and visual description to explain spatial rotations and convey how objects change orientations in 3D space lacey2013multisensory . Previous studies have shown that Vision Language Models (VLMs) struggle with spatial reasoning tasks despite using methods like fine-tuning and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) xu-etal-2025-defining . The aim of this study is to enhance AI’s capability of understanding 3D spatial rotations by training currently available VLMs through an Agentic AI approach and performing a series of tests based on Revised PSVT:R. The research questions that guide this study are as follows: What is an efficient process for improving generative AI models' performance in Revised PSVT:R using an Agentic AI system? title: Fine-Tuning VLM for Enhancing AI's Spatial Intelligence: Understanding 3D and 2D Rotations
summary: Spatial intelligence is a fundamental skill in multiple domains, such as Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM), Medicine, Architecture, and Construction. Recent studies indicate that Vision-Language Models (VLMs) still face limitations in spatial reasoning, which inhibits artificial intelligence (AI) from performing practical spatial tasks. Using multiple object-rotation datasets developed for training and evaluation, our experiments demonstrated promising improvements in both 2D and 3D rotation detection. Fine-tuned Google DeepMind-built Gemma-4 mixture-of-experts (MoE) models significantly outperformed fine-tuned Gemma-4 generalist models in predicting rotations defined by both their axes and angles. Fine-tuning also substantially improved angle estimation for 2D representation without requiring an explicit coordinate system. Furthermore, identifiable objects did not improve angle-detection accuracy; instead, objects with prominent linear features showed improved performance.

title: ForeAct3D: Policy-Grounded Future World Modeling for VLA Policies
summary: Robots need to anticipate how their actions will change the world, since manipulation success hinges on the resulting contacts and object motions. However, existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies that predict future observations from shared features leave the forecast decoupled from the actions the policy will actually execute, and impose no physical constraints on how the scene may evolve. We introduce ForeAct3D, a framework for policy-grounded future world modeling within VLA policies. Learnable geometric queries decode depth, semantic segmentation, and camera pose from the policy representation into current and future semantic 3D scene states, and the future queries are conditioned on the policy-generated action chunk to ground the forecast in the planned interaction. A physical-consistency closure relates the two states through background staticity and instance-level rigidity, and anchors the wrist-camera pose to end-effector kinematics. These objectives shape the shared representation used for action generation during training, and no future prediction is required at inference. Without robot pretraining, ForeAct3D achieves 98.3\% average success on LIBERO and an average task length of 3.73 on CALVIN, outperforming its base policy on every suite. Ablations show that semantic 3D supervision, physical consistency, and action conditioning each improve manipulation performance, and that action conditioning substantially improves future object localization. Real-world experiments on spatial placement, object insertion, and sequential manipulation further raise average success from 6.7\% to 37.8\% over the base policy. The project page and code are available at https://github.com/anthonytao80-crypto/ForeAct3D.
full_text: Method sec:method Problem Formulation sec:problem . To anticipate the consequences of a planned manipulation, we perform future world modeling through semantic 3D scene prediction within a VLA policy. The model estimates the current scene and predicts its future state over the policy's action horizon. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:pipeline , structured geometry defines the state, physical-consistency constraints relate the two states across time, and explicit action conditioning grounds the predicted future in the policy's planned action. At time , the robot receives a language instruction and an observation set containing images from an external agent camera and a robot-mounted wrist camera, where denotes these two views. The policy maps to an action chunk of horizon , which also defines the future prediction time . This shared horizon aligns future-state supervision with the scene changes induced by the planned action chunk. We predict the scene state at the action horizon's endpoint without generating a sequence of observations for the intermediate action steps. 3D scene state. To capture the geometry relevant to manipulation, we represent each scene state using depth, three-class semantic masks, and camera pose. Depth encodes spatial structure, semantic masks separate background, robot, and object regions, and camera pose places each view in a common world frame. All objects share a single object class; the prediction neither assigns instance identities nor establishes object correspondence across the current and future states. For each view , depth , known intrinsics , and camera pose define a point cloud by back-projection . The semantic mask labels these points, so the scene state combines metric geometry with the semantic role of each region: ForeAct3D estimates the current state from the instruction and observations, and additionally conditions the future estimate on the planned action chunk. Both estimates live in the same semantic 3D representation, which allows physical constraints to relate the observed scene to its configuration after the action chunk: The current estimate recovers the scene the policy observes, whereas the future estimate predicts the consequences of the action it generates. This formulation supervises both endpoints of the interaction in a single representation and makes their geometric relationship part of policy learning. Semantic Geometry from Policy Features sec:object3d queries. To extract a structured scene state from the policy representation, we introduce six learnable queries , indexed by geometric quantity and prediction time . Each query cross-attends to the final backbone features to produce a query feature ; future queries are further conditioned on the action chunk as described in Section~ sec:actionconditioned . View embeddings are added before decoding: depth and segmentation queries serve both cameras, while pose queries use the wrist-view embedding to predict only the wrist-camera pose. Depth and segmentation share a decoder that attends to intermediate-layer backbone features of the corresponding view, followed by separate output heads. Because all queries read from the policy backbone, geometric supervision directly shapes the representation used for control. Ground-truth instance IDs provide supervision distinct from the three predicted semantic classes. The rigidity constraint in Section~ sec:closure uses these IDs to partition the predicted geometry into individual objects and applies Kabsch alignment to each instance using pairs at shared valid pixels. This supplies instance-level physical supervision without requiring the segmentation head to predict object identities or establish object correspondence between the current and future scene states. Physical-Consistency Closure sec:closure We impose three complementary constraints on predicted geometry and camera pose: background staticity, instance-level rigidity, and end-effector kinematics. The two geometric constraints operate on agent-view point clouds back-projected from predicted depth with ground-truth intrinsics and extrinsics. Since the agent camera is fixed, its extrinsics are identical at both endpoints, and the resulting points are directly comparable in world coordinates. Labeled calibration isolates depth consistency from pose prediction errors, while kinematics supervises the wrist-camera pose. staticity. To keep the static environment fixed over time, we compare current and future background points back-projected from predicted depth at the same image pixels. A shared mask retains pixels labeled as valid background at both endpoints, thereby excluding regions occluded by the robot or objects at either time. The background loss averages a Smooth-L1 distance over these paired points; the same distance is used in the rigidity term below. -level rigidity. To preserve object shape under motion, we require each instance's current and future geometry to be related by a rigid transform. Ground-truth instance IDs select pixels that belong to the same object and are valid at both endpoints. For each instance with at least 32 such pixels, we form paired world point sets and . Kabsch alignment estimates the rigid transform between them, and the residual after alignment defines the rigidity loss over the retained instance set : Same-pixel pairing approximates temporal correspondence without tracking surface points; it is a short-horizon approximation, since shared instance membership does not guarantee that paired pixels observe the same material point under large motion. The weight down-weights instances likely being grasped: when the gripper is closed and the current instance centroid lies within 0.10,m of the end effector, and otherwise. At the batch level, is averaged with equal weight over samples that have valid future targets and at least one retained instance. -effector kinematics. To anchor the predicted wrist-camera pose to the robot configuration, we supervise both endpoints using a reference pose from forward kinematics and the fixed hand--eye transform. The pose loss sums equally weighted translation MSE and geodesic rotation distance in radians over both prediction times. We convert the predicted 6D rotation into a rotation matrix before computing the loss. Pose supervision is separate from the background and rigidity constraints, which reconstruct world points using predicted depth and labeled camera poses. . The three constraints are combined into a single regularization objective, with coefficients , , and controlling their relative contributions: Together, these constraints encourage a static background, approximately rigid object motion, and wrist-camera poses grounded in robot kinematics. Since geometric predictions are decoded from the policy backbone, these constraints directly regularize its representation for action generation. Action-Conditioned State Prediction sec:actionconditioned The current scene alone does not determine an interaction's outcome: different actions can produce different future states from the same observation. The future branch therefore receives the policy-generated action chunk, explicitly tying its prediction to the planned interaction. -conditioned prediction. To inject the planned action into future prediction, we project the action chunk into the query feature space with a small network . After all six queries have read scene information from the backbone (Section~ sec:object3d ), only the three future queries are additionally conditioned on the action. Each future query cross-attends to the concatenation of the projected backbone features and the action features : This step fuses scene context with the planned action into the future query features . Current queries skip this step and keep their scene-only features . View embeddings are then added to both sets of queries before decoding depth, segmentation, and wrist-camera pose, as in Section~ sec:object3d .

title: PerturBot: Breaking Shortcut Priors in Vision-Language-Action Models with Perturbative Training
summary: A vision--language--action (VLA) policy can complete complex tasks while ignoring the evidence that should determine its actions. An object held near the wrist camera can displace the instructed target. Language and action show the same pattern: a familiar noun can trigger the operation it was paired with in training even after the verb changes, and a gripper that closed on nothing may lift anyway. We call these dependencies modality shortcuts: regularities in successful demonstrations make visual, lexical, or motor cues sufficient to predict expert actions without the task evidence needed for the underlying decision. More demonstrations of the same kind can raise task success while leaving these shortcuts intact. We propose Perturbot which makes task-relevant evidence easier to use and shortcuts insufficient on their own: it applies task-preserving wrist-view perturbations, enriches instructions with decision-relevant captions, and adds random and failed trajectory segments relabeled with the behavior they contain. It complements scaling by changing what is scaled, and leaves inference unchanged. Moreover, we propose GroundingFscore, an offline score that diagnoses how severely a policy relies on modality shortcuts. Task success rate shows whether a policy improves, while GroundingFscore reveals whether the policy scales healthily, relying on task evidence rather than shortcuts. Together, Perturbot and GroundingFscore provide a training-and-evaluation framework for disentangling VLA decisions from shortcut priors while preserving responsiveness to task-relevant evidence.

We call these dependencies : regularities in successful demonstrations make visual, lexical, or motor cues sufficient to predict expert actions without the task evidence needed for the underlying decision. More demonstrations of the same kind can raise task success while leaving these shortcuts intact. We propose , which makes task-relevant evidence easier to use and shortcuts insufficient on their own: it applies task-preserving wrist-view perturbations, enriches instructions with decision-relevant captions, and adds random and failed trajectory segments relabeled with the behavior they contain. It complements scaling by changing what is scaled, and leaves inference unchanged. Moreover, we propose , an offline score that diagnoses how severely a policy relies on modality shortcuts. Task success rate shows whether a policy improves, while reveals whether the policy scales healthily, relying on task evidence rather than shortcuts. Together, and provide a training-and-evaluation framework for disentangling VLA decisions from shortcut priors while preserving responsiveness to task-relevant evidence. Introduction sec:intro ``Success is a lousy teacher.''\\ --- Bill Gates, The Road Ahead (1995) Vision--language--action (VLA) policies can now perform complex manipulation tasks zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,ghosh2024octo,black2025pi0 , yet a simple change in view can still divert them ( ). An object held near the wrist camera can displace the instructed target; changing ``pick up the bowl'' to ``push the bowl'' may still elicit a grasp; and a gripper that closes on nothing may lift anyway. Task success cannot tell whether the policy uses the scene, instruction, and observed outcome to decide what to do, or merely replays an action when a familiar cue appears. We call such dependencies , a multimodal instance of shortcut learning geirhos2020shortcut closely related to causal confusion in imitation learning dehaan2019causal,wen2020fighting . A modality shortcut is not an unimportant input but an easily decoded cue that stands in for the evidence a decision requires. Such cues arise from the regularity of successful demonstrations: the target dominates the wrist view as the expert reaches for it, each object name may be paired with a single operation, and gripper closure is reliably followed by a lift. Behavior cloning rewards agreement with the demonstrated action, not the evidence used to predict it, so nothing in the objective stops the policy from relying on the cue. This matters for scaling. Larger and more diverse demonstration corpora are central to generalist robot learning oneill2024open,khazatsky2024droid,lin2025scaling , but if new trajectories preserve the same correlations, the shortcut rule and the intended rule keep prescribing the same actions, and more data cannot distinguish them. Higher success on familiar tasks then need not mean more reliable target selection, instruction following, or outcome assessment: the policy grows more proficient where shortcut and evidence agree yet stays brittle where they disagree, which makes modality shortcuts a bottleneck for scaling. Addressing this requires changing what the training data demand, not weakening an input modality: the evidence a correct decision needs should be easier to use, and shortcuts should be insufficient on their own ( ). does so with three training-time data interventions and no extra model or forward pass at deployment: task-preserving wrist-view perturbations add plausible distractors without changing the target or invalidating the recorded action; decision-relevant captions make object attributes, spatial relations, and requested operations explicit, each supported by the recorded behavior; and caption-grounded trajectory expansion adds random-motion and failed-execution segments relabeled with the behavior they contain, which add behavioral support rather than recovery skills, since relabeling cannot create an unrecorded correction. thus changes what is scaled: as data grow, it expands not only repetitions of familiar behavior but also the range of decisions that depend on the scene, instruction, and observed outcome. Whether scaling achieves this cannot be read from task success: when shortcut and evidence agree, policies relying on either can succeed, and robustness to distractors can come from simply ignoring vision. We therefore propose , an offline score that diagnoses how severely a policy relies on modality shortcuts. It pairs each input with edits that should leave the action unchanged, such as an off-path distractor, and edits that should change it in a known way, such as naming a different object; a high score requires both, so ignoring an input does not help. Because it needs no robot rollouts, can be computed for every checkpoint as data grow: task success shows whether a policy improves, and whether it improves for the right reason. With a backbone, we evaluate all eight component combinations on 50 real-robot General PnP cases and cover broader skills in RoboTwin~2.0 chen2025robotwin2 ; ablations test whether success and evidence use rise together as data grow and whether predicts online failures. Our contributions are threefold: We identify in VLA learning , unifying , , and , and explain why scaling demonstrations that preserve these correlations need not remove them. We propose , three independently ablatable data interventions that keep action supervision valid, change what is scaled, and leave inference unchanged. We introduce , an offline score that, unlike task success, indicates whether a policy scales healthily and cannot be raised by ignoring useful evidence. Related work sec:related Scaling VLA policies. Vision--language--action (VLA) policies map observations and instructions to actions; they are trained on large robot datasets and often initialized from pretrained vision--language models brohan2023rt1,zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,ghosh2024octo,black2025pi0,black2025pi05,wang2025vq,liu2025gae,liu2026stamo . Their progress has followed the growth of demonstration data across tasks and embodiments oneill2024open,khazatsky2024droid,walke2023bridgedata and studies of how data diversity and composition shape transfer lin2025scaling,hejna2024remix,zha2025factored , while evaluation has expanded from nominal simulation benchmarks liu2023libero,mees2022calvin,li2024evaluating to perturbed scenes and instructions fei2025liberoplus,zhou2025liberopro,zhao2026instructmove . Success alone cannot show whether a policy improves by using task evidence or by using a shortcut more consistently. measures shortcut reliance offline; unlike action sensitivity to task-preserving perturbations, which has been used to select demonstrations durso2026cfn , it also requires the action to change when task-relevant evidence changes. Shortcut learning. Neural networks often rely on features that are predictive in training but fail under distribution shift, as studied under shortcut learning, simplicity bias, and dataset bias geirhos2020shortcut,shah2020pitfalls,torralba2011unbiased . Visual question answering models can answer from language priors without grounding the evidence in the image goyal2017making,agrawal2018dont,cadene2019rubi , and in imitation learning, causal confusion and the copycat problem show that matching expert actions need not identify the evidence that should control behavior dehaan2019causal,wen2020fighting,park2021object . Recent VLA studies find that policies can underuse language or let vision override instructions xu2025bayesvla,lian2026langforce,fang2026visionoverrides , and diagnose or regularize how modalities are used shi2026vlatrace,xu2026unmasking,jia2026guidedvla,lin2026lit . These accounts usually examine one modality at a time; we tie each shortcut to the decision it affects and trace all three to the regularity of successful demonstrations. Data interventions for robust policies. Data-centric methods improve robustness by varying appearance through augmentation and domain randomization tobin2017domain,laskin2020reinforcement,bharadhwaj2023roboagent , synthesizing or counterfactually editing demonstrations mandlekar2023mimicgen,ameperosa2025rocoda , enriching or relabeling instructions kim2026demian,glossop2025cast , and widening behavioral coverage with corrective, perturbed, or unstructured data ross2011reduction,laskey2017dart,lynch2019play,hu2025rac,liu2026perfect . Perturbative training has likewise reduced language-prior hallucinations in vision--language models chen2025perturbollava . Each of these interventions is typically designed for one axis of variation, such as appearance, geometry, language, or coverage; instead targets the cue that substitutes for evidence in a given decision, while keeping every action label valid and leaving inference unchanged. Method sec:method We first model modality shortcuts ( ), then describe the three data components of ( ) and how measures the resulting evidence use ( ). In (what to manipulate), an object near the wrist camera can divert a reach from the instructed target; in (which semantics apply), a policy that has pushed other objects but only picked up the bowl may grasp it when asked to push it; in (how to move), a gripper that closed on nothing may lift anyway. In each, a cue that is reliable in successful demonstrations stands in for the required evidence: wrist-view salience for the instruction, the noun for the verb, and the close--lift sequence for visual grasp feedback.
