title: RoboIRS: Inference-Time Internal Representation Steering for Generalist Robot Policies
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) often degrade under out-of-distribution task variations despite retaining partial task capability. To recover such capability, we propose RoboIRS, an inference-time internal representation steering method that uses successful and failed rollouts to train linear classifiers, select outcome-relevant intervention locations, and derive task-specific steering directions without updating policy parameters. On 15 simulation tasks with a frozen $π0.5$ policy, RoboIRS improves the average success rate from 44.4% to 66.2%, outperforming alternative inference-time intervention baselines while adding little inference time. We further validate RoboIRS on real-robot manipulation using the same $π0.5$ policy and demonstrate its applicability to a world-action model Cosmos Policy, where the average success rate improves from 35.4% to 55.4%. These results show that directly steering internal robot-policy representations can improve the performance of robot policies at inference time. Project website is available at https://rollingoat.github.io/roboirs/.
full_text: Jiuzhou Lei , Chang Liu , Dayou Li , Zhiyuan Zhang , Xiao Liang , Yu She , Zhiwen Fan , Minghui Zheng Jiuzhou Lei, Chang Liu, Dayou Li, and Minghui Zheng are with the J. Mike Walker '66 Department of Mechanical Engineering, Texas A M University, College Station, TX 77843, USA. Emails: \ jiuzl, changliu.chris, dayou519, mhzheng\ @tamu.edu Yu She and Zhiyuan Zhang are with the Edwardson School of Industrial Engineering, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA. Emails: \ yushe, zhan5570\ @purdue.edu Xiao Liang is with the Zachry Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Texas A M University, College Station, TX 77843, USA. Email: xliang@tamu.edu Zhiwen Fan is with the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Texas A M University, College Station, TX 77843, USA. Email: zhiwenfan@tamu.edu Vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) often degrade under out-of-distribution task variations despite retaining partial task capability. To recover such capability, we propose RoboIRS, an inference-time internal representation steering method that uses successful and failed rollouts to train linear classifiers, select outcome-relevant intervention locations, and derive task-specific steering directions without updating policy parameters. On 15 simulation tasks with a frozen policy, RoboIRS improves the average success rate from 44.4 to 66.2 , outperforming alternative inference-time intervention baselines while adding little inference time. We further validate RoboIRS on real-robot manipulation using the same policy and demonstrate its applicability to a world-action model Cosmos Policy, where the average success rate improves from 35.4 to 55.4 . These results show that directly steering internal robot-policy representations can improve the performance of robot policies at inference time. Project website is available at https://rollingoat.github.io/roboirs/ . Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAMs) have recently emerged as promising architectures for robotic manipulation by integrating visual perception, language-conditioned task understanding, and action generation with future prediction in a unified policy. However, their performance often degrades on out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs, such as unseen scenes, novel object layouts, and new object appearances zhou2025libero, fei2026libero . Importantly, this degradation does not necessarily imply complete incapability: a policy may still succeed on a subset of these OOD tasks, albeit at a lower success rate. This suggests that the policy may retain some of the internal computations required for successful execution even when its behavior becomes unreliable. A similar phenomenon has already been observed in LLMs, which may produce both truthful and untruthful responses despite being queried under similar conditions. This inconsistency suggests that the model may already contain internal representations associated with the desired behavior, even when they are not reliably expressed in its outputs li2023inference . Recent progress in mechanistic interpretability and activation steering for large language models provides evidence that internal representations can be causally manipulated to alter model behavior. Here, internal representations refer to intermediate output that encode information during model computation; in transformer-based models, these may include residual-stream activations passed between layers, as well as activations associated with individual neurons, attention heads, or other localized model components zhang2026locate . Prior work has shown that high-level behaviors such as truthfulness, refusal, sentiment, and task execution can be localized in hidden representations and modified through activation-space interventions. Li et al.~ li2023inference steer LLMs toward truthful answers by intervening on truth-related activations, while Turner et al.~ turner2023steering and Rimsky et al.~ rimsky2024steering show that contrastive activation directions can control generation behavior without retraining the model. Zou et al.~ zou2023representation frame such methods as representation engineering, where internal activations are treated as controllable objects for modifying model behavior. Motivated by the findings in LLM, can we similarly steer the internal representations of a robot policy at inference time to improve its performance on OOD tasks? Recent work has already extended mechanistic interpretability to vision-language-action (VLA) models. Grant et al.~ grant2026not and Swann et al.~ swann2026sparse use sparse autoencoders to identify interpretable residual-stream features associated with robot behaviors, but do not demonstrate how these features can improve downstream policy performance. Häon et al.~ haon2025mechanistic and Buurmeijer et al.~ buurmeijer2026observing go further by intervening on internal representations to steer behaviors such as motion speed and end-effector height; however, their evaluations are limited to a small set of predefined behavioral attributes rather than general task performance. Hong et al.~ hong2026steering instead use an LQR controller to steer the diffusion transformer’s hidden activations such that the resulting activations lead to robust robot behaviors and require constructed contrastive residual-stream pairs from matched nominal and perturbed observations to provide target activation levels. In this work, we aim to improve the performance of a frozen robot policy under distribution shift through inference-time steering of its internal representations. Rather than retraining the policy, we use these outcome-labeled activations to identify representations associated with successful and failed rollouts and intervene on the policy at inference time using a steering vector. The goal is to bias an already capable but unreliable policy toward internal states that are more predictive of successful action selection. Inspired by li2023inference , we first train a linear classifier to classify the internal representations and then use the classifier weight as steering vectors to change the internal representations such that the predicted actions are more favorable of successful rollouts. We evaluate the proposed approach on two representative robot policies: the vision-language-action model \( _ 0.5 \)~ intelligence2025pi and the world-action model Cosmos Policy~ kim2026cosmos . We conduct experiments in both simulation and real-world robotic settings to assess whether inference-time internal representation steering improves task success rates under distribution shift. The main contributions of this work are as follows. We propose RoboIRS, which adapts the internal representation-steering paradigm from LLMs to robot policies and enables inference-time intervention on frozen policies using steering vectors derived from the internal representations of successful and failed rollouts. We conduct simulation and real-robot experiments showing that RoboIRS improves the average SR of a fully trained policy under distribution shift from to , outperforms alternative inference-time intervention baselines, improves real-robot manipulation performance, and is also effective on Cosmos Policy despite its different training recipe and model architecture, increasing the average SR from to . Related Work sec: related work Mechanistic Interpretability and Steering in LLMs Mechanistic interpretability increasingly studies how high-level concepts are represented in neural activations and whether these representations can be causally manipulated~ zhang2026locate,geiger2025causal . Many intervention methods build on the observation that properties such as truthfulness and sentiment can be represented by linear directions or low-dimensional subspaces~ lieanrRepresentationHypothesis,marks2023geometry,tigges2023linear . Activation-steering methods exploit this structure by constructing directions from contrastive examples or demonstrations and injecting them into hidden states to control behavior without retraining~ turner2023steering, rimsky2024steering, hendel2023context, todd2023function . Such interventions have been applied to truthfulness, hallucination, and refusal behavior~ li2023inference,zhang2024truthx,wang2025adaptive,arditi2024refusal . Mechanistic Interpretability and Internal Representation Steering of Robot Policy Models Recent robotics work has begun to apply mechanistic interpretability techniques to characterize the internal representations of VLA policies, with several studies further showing that the discovered features can serve as causal handles for behavior steering. Khan et al.~ khan2025controlling use sparse autoencoders to identify action-related latent directions from contrastive action pairs and show that these directions can be manipulated to steer VLA action outputs without retraining. Grant et al.~ grant2026not conduct a cross-architecture mechanistic study using activation injection, sparse autoencoders, and linear probes to analyze how visual, language, and action-generation pathways contribute to VLA behavior. Swann et al.~ swann2026sparse use sparse autoencoders to identify interpretable features in VLA hidden states, distinguishing transferable motion primitives from episode-specific memorization, and causally validate selected features through steering experiments. Several VLA papers move from feature discovery to explicit control of robot behaviors. Buurmeijer et al.~ buurmeijer2026observing formalize feature observability and controllability in VLA models and use lightweight linear interventions to steer encoded features during closed-loop execution. Häon et al.~ haon2025mechanistic identify sparse semantic directions in transformer activations and use those directions to control policy behavior without retraining. Mitra et al.~ mitra2025mechanistic identify task-relevant attention heads and selectively update them, framing policy adaptation as targeted modification of relevant internal mechanisms. COAST~ miao2026contrastive constructs success- and failure-associated conceptor from rollout hidden states to steer VLA activations toward success-critical representations at inference time. COAST is evaluated on imperfect policies, such as early fine-tuning checkpoints, using tasks drawn from the original benchmark distribution, whereas RoboIRS focuses on recovering the performance of fully trained frozen policies under unseen task perturbations. Hong et al.~ hong2026steering take a control-based approach to representation steering, constructing contrastive directions from paired nominal and perturbed inputs and using them to define robustness-relevant latent feature subspaces and target feature setpoints. RoboIRS instead derives its intervention directly from successful and failed rollouts without requiring matched nominal and perturbed observation pairs. Inference-Time Intervention of Robot Policies Another line of work improves robot policies at inference time through action selection or generative guidance. V-GPS~ nakamoto2025steering samples actions from a frozen policy and re-ranks them with an offline-RL value function, while RoboMonkey~ kwok2025robomonkey , MG-Select~ jang2026verifierfree , and RoVer~ dai2025rover select or refine VLA action candidates using learned verifiers, intrinsic confidence, or process rewards. Related methods intervene directly during action generation: value-guided diffusion~ zhang2024valueguided biases diffusion trajectories with value gradients. Guided Action Flow~ yang2026guided keeps the VLA frozen and uses gradients from a critic trained on successful and failed rollouts to steer flow-matching action generation toward higher-return actions. PPGuide~ wang2026ppguide trains a performance predictor and uses its guidance signal to steer pretrained diffusion policies away from predicted failure modes during inference. Proposed Approach sec:proposed-approach

title: CellSplat4D: PSF-Aware 4D Gaussian Splatting for Sparse Robotic Live-Cell Imaging
summary: A robotic microscope watching living cells cannot afford to look as often as it would like. Every volume it acquires costs photons the specimen does not get back, and time owed to other wells. What such a platform exists to produce is a record of individual cells through time: which cell is which from one volume to the next, and which cell divided into which two. Sampling sparsely breaks that record exactly where it matters, and the fault lies in the acquisition schedule rather than in the analysis software. We fill the gaps by reconstructing them, fitting a 4D Gaussian model to whatever volumes the hardware could afford. The model is a cloud of light-emitting blobs, each carrying a position, a shape and a lifetime. Being continuous in time, it renders any missing volume on demand, decoupling how often the robot analyses from how often it can afford to look. The microscope's point-spread function is measured from the data rather than inherited from acquisition metadata or left to the optimizer, because metadata inflates it and the optimizer cannot recover it at all: a wider blur around a smaller blob fits the images equally well. Each blob's lifetime is stored in frames rather than as a fraction of the recording, so that it denotes a fixed duration on any sequence. Unmeasured timesteps are supervised at coarse scale by a 3D U-Net that predicts the intermediate volume directly and estimates no motion field, since a dividing cell becomes two and no motion describes that. On two Cell Tracking Challenge sequences, a C. elegans embryo and a Chinese Hamster Ovarian (CHO), with fidelity scored per cell nucleus, our reconstruction holds the highest nucleus fidelity at every distance from an acquired frame, has the flattest decay across the gap, and best recovers focal planes it was never shown with graceful degradation across the gap.

Introduction Robotic platforms now run live-cell experiments end to end, and the most advanced decide what to image next from what they have just seen conrad2011micropilot,mahecic2022event,pinkard2021pycromanager ; micro-robotic systems close a tighter loop still, acting on individual cells under visual servoing sun2002biological,nelson2010microrobots . All are limited by the same resource. A volumetric acquisition costs stage travel and photons the specimen does not get back, excess exposure changes the biology rather than merely adding noise icha2017phototoxicity,laissue2017assessing , and a platform serving many wells must divide that budget huisken2004spim,chen2014lattice,royer2016adaptive . So it samples sparsely in time and accepts the gaps. The gaps are where the robot's autonomy fails. Linkers lose identities across the jump, lineage graphs fragment at the divisions they exist to record, and a controller choosing its next target reasons over a state it does not have. These are documented failure modes as the sampling interval grows ulman2017objective,maska2023ctc , and the deficiency is in the acquisition, not the tracker. Our response is to give the robot a continuous-time 4D state of the specimen, fitted to whatever the hardware could afford and queried by rendering (Fig.~ fig:workflow ). Three things follow. It decouples the analysis rate from the acquisition rate: every downstream module was designed for a densely sampled sequence, and a rendered volume enters the pipeline where an acquired one would. It produces a physical state rather than pixels, primitives with positions, extents and lifetimes that can be asked where an emitter is and how long it persists, which interpolated images cannot supply. And it changes the acquisition design space: the sampling interval becomes a parameter the robot trades rather than a constraint it lives under, which reframes what we ask of a dynamic representation. Not whether it fits the acquired frames, since all do, but how gracefully its per-nucleus fidelity decays with distance from the nearest acquired frame. Flatness, not peak accuracy, is what buys a longer acquisition interval, and it is the axis on which we evaluate. Gaussian splatting kerbl20233dgs and its dynamic extensions yang2024deformable,duan20244drotor,li2024spacetime, yang2024realtime4dgs,luiten2024dynamic are the natural substrate: explicit, fast to render, and exposing per-primitive temporal parameters that can be inspected rather than probed. Designed for multi-view video of opaque surfaces at full frame rate, three of their assumptions break under sparse volumetric fluorescence. Their temporal gate is a fraction of the training window, so a fixed initialization denotes a different duration on every sequence (Sec.~ sec:gate ). Their forward model treats axial blur as free or defaulted, when it is a physical constant the default overstates and the optimizer cannot recover (Sec.~ sec:whypsf , Sec.~ sec:psf ). And their densification statistics ignore the gate, diluting the growth signal in proportion to window length (Sec.~ sec:densify ). Each failure is silent: training loss and full-image PSNR register none of them, and Sec.~ sec:psnrfails shows PSNR ranks the fixes backwards. We contribute (1) a completion framework that turns a sparse acquisition into a continuous-time 4D state, scored on the decay profile of nucleus fidelity across the gap rather than on aggregate image quality (Sec.~ sec:exp ); (2) three changes that make 4D splatting work at this sampling rate: frame-unit temporal gates (Sec.~ sec:gate ), an axial PSF pinned to a measured physical constant, against which both the metadata default and a learned width fail (Sec.~ sec:psf ), and gate-aware residual-driven densification under an exact budget (Sec.~ sec:densify ); and (3) an evaluation protocol of masked, nucleus-level metrics (Sec.~ sec:eval ). Related Work Preliminaries: 3D and 4D Gaussian splatting sec:prelim 3D Gaussian splatting kerbl20233dgs represents a scene as anisotropic primitives, primitive a Gaussian of mean and covariance , projected under an EWA approximation of the pinhole map zwicker2001ewa and accumulated front-to-back over depth-sorted primitives, with for opacity and the projected 2D Gaussian. Its appeal here is that every term is an explicit, physically interpretable parameter, not a network activation. Dynamic extensions add time in one of two ways. Deformation-field methods pumarola2021dnerf,yang2024deformable,wu20244dgaussians warp a canonical primitive set with an MLP, often over a low-rank spacetime factorization cao2023hexplane,fridovichkeil2023kplanes . Native-4D methods yang2024realtime4dgs,duan20244drotor instead lift each primitive into spacetime with a temporal centre and extent , so that marginalizing at time scales it by a temporal gate We build on the native-4D family because states how long the model believes each emitter persists, which is what a sparse-acquisition analysis needs to inspect and where Sec.~ sec:gate finds a failure. Why the forward model must carry the PSF sec:whypsf Equation~ encodes two assumptions that fail for a fluorescence microscope. First, fluorophores are self-luminous and, in thin specimens, neither occlude one another nor vary with viewing direction, so the occlusion-aware composite collapses to a linear accumulation of emission, with a scalar emission weight. This removes depth sorting and view dependence, making the rendered quantity a measurement of integrated intensity rather than a colour, the same reduction X-ray splatting makes cai2024xgaussian . Second, the instrument is not a pinhole: the detector records the emission field convolved with the point-spread function , where the axial width far exceeds the lateral one and is a property of the objective, not of the specimen. Since convolving two Gaussians sums their covariances, an emitter of true extent is observed with extent This has two consequences. A model omitting absorbs into , recovering the specimen convolved with the optics and inflated anisotropically in . One that includes but leaves free inherits a non-identifiability instead: shrinking every while growing leaves unchanged on every supervised plane, and only planes the model never saw break the tie. Pinning removes that degenerate direction and lets be read as a statement about the specimen. GaussianPile gaussianpile already encodes a finite-thickness PSF in its projection operator, using the theoretical value. Our renderer inherits that operator and lifts its primitives to 4D under Eq.~ ; what we add concerns the value of inside it, where Sec.~ sec:psf finds failure modes on both sides of the theoretical choice. Dynamic scene representations Neural radiance fields mildenhall2020nerf,muller2022instantngp established volumetric inverse rendering before splatting displaced them on speed. We compare against a deformation-field representative yang2024deformable and a radiative 4D variant built for sparse-view angiography liu20244drgs , which shares the emission-only regime of~ . Feature-based li2024spacetime and persistent luiten2024dynamic spacetime splatting both assume dense capture, as does every method here. Sparsity has been attacked in the angular domain by few-shot splatting zhu2024fsgs ; ours is temporal, the missing quantity being the specimen's state between measurements rather than an unobserved viewing angle. Our contribution is accordingly not a new dynamic representation but an account of which of their components are load-bearing when most frames are absent. Temporal completion Video frame interpolation is dominated by flow-based architectures that estimate a motion field and warp along it jiang2018superslomo,huang2022rife,reda2022film . That design rests on brightness constancy, which a dividing nucleus violates: it brightens and becomes two objects where there was one, so no displacement field explains the pair. Our completion network is therefore a 3D U-Net ronneberger2015unet,cicek20163dunet regressing the intermediate volume directly, baselined against the alternative it declines to be farneback2003twoframe,teed2020raft . Microscopy reconstruction and evaluation Content-aware restoration weigert2018care established that learned priors transfer across fluorescence modalities but can hallucinate structure that image-level metrics reward. Putting the PSF inside the reconstruction inverts the classical deconvolution arrangement, where it instead drives an iterative restoration of the acquired volume sage2017deconvolutionlab2 ; the constant supplied is the same, and so is the requirement that it be right. Ours is the standard Gaussian approximation to the widefield axial response zhang2007gaussianpsf,bornwolf1999principles . Sequences and foreground masks follow the Cell Tracking Challenge protocol ulman2017objective,maska2023ctc . title: Sparse-GS2Mesh: 3D Gaussian Splatting Guided by Novel Stereo Views and 2DGS for Sparse View Surface Reconstruction}
comment: 13, pages, 7 figures, accepted to NIPS 2026 PhysWorldAI workshops
summary: Surface reconstruction under sparse-view settings remains challenging due to limited geometric cues. Volume rendering methods based on signed distance functions often produce over-smoothed surfaces, while 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), though time-efficient, suffers from incomplete geometry due to the lack of reliable depth supervision and the limitation of being optimized only from given input views. In this paper, we present Sparse-GS2Mesh, a stereo-aware framework for surface reconstruction from sparse views. While 3DGS and stereo matching have been leveraged for surface reconstruction under dense view settings, we extend them to operate effectively under sparse view conditions by first initializing 3DGS using epipolar depth priors to mitigate the 3DGS overfitting problem, followed by our three key components: (I) adaptive baseline selection, (II) fine-tuning with a stereo matching network, and (III) 2D/3D co-regularized fine-tuning. Given a warmed-up 3DGS initialized with epipolar depth, the adaptive baseline selection automatically determines a baseline to synthesize for each sparse view. We then fine-tune 3DGS by backpropagating depth-refining gradients from the stereo matching network, effectively specializing the 3DGS for stereo matching. The 2D/3D co-regularization further helps obtain stable reconstruction, addressing weak geometric cues in close stereo views. Sparse-GS2Mesh achieves a 15\% improvement over state-of-the-art methods in little-overlap settings and comparable results in large-overlap settings. Codes will be publicly available.

Volume rendering methods based on signed distance functions often produce over-smoothed surfaces, while 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), though time-efficient, suffers from incomplete geometry due to the lack of reliable depth supervision and the limitation of being optimized only from given input views. We then fine-tune 3DGS by backpropagating depth-refining gradients from the stereo matching network, effectively specializing the 3DGS for stereo matching. The 2D/3D co-regularization further helps obtain stable reconstruction, addressing weak geometric cues in close stereo views. Given sparse views as input, our method reconstructs high fidelity 3D geometry with novel stereo-view rendering and 2D/3D GS co-regularization. Teaser Introduction sec:intro 3D surface reconstruction is a long-standing problem and plays a crucial role in various domains such as autonomous driving li2023bevdepth, zhuopeng2023read , robotics qiyu2023graspnerf, zihan2022niceslam, moreau2021lens , and virtual reality (VR) weicai2021superplane, matt2023objaverse . Despite recent progress, reconstructing accurate geometry from sparse inputs remains challenging yet practically important, since real-world applications often allow only a limited number of images. Previous surface reconstruction methods oechsle2021unisurf, tong2022voxurf, wang2023neus2 are built upon neural radiance fields (NeRF) mildenhall2020nerf , representing a scene as continuous radiance/density fields and optimizing them via differentiable volume rendering. Although several studies long2022sparseneus, ren2023volrecon, youngju2024uforecon, huang2024neusurf have explored sparse-view reconstruction (i.e., only a few different view images as input) and achieved promising results, their major bottleneck lies in long training time, which ranges from several hours to days per scene. Recent studies~ yu2024gof, yu2024gsdf, zhang2024nsdgs have extended 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) kerbl20233dgs to surface reconstruction. 2DGS huang20242dgs directly reconstructs surfaces from 3DGS by flattening Gaussian elements and applying additional geometric regularization. On the other hand, GS2Mesh yaniv2024gs2mesh generates stereo-aligned image pairs through 3DGS rendering and extracts accurate depth using a pre-trained stereo model. In sparse-view settings, pre-trained multi-view stereo (MVS) networks xiong2023cl have also been utilized jiang2025sparse2dgs to initialize Gaussian elements and to enforce depth consistency during optimization. Despite these developments, reconstructed surfaces in sparse-view settings still suffer from geometric inaccuracies due to extremely limited information. To address the aforementioned challenges, we propose Sparse-GS2Mesh, a novel framework designed for surface reconstruction under sparse-view settings. While the original GS2Mesh yaniv2024gs2mesh was developed for dense-view settings, our key idea is that leveraging stereo-aligned renderings as additional geometric cues becomes more effective under sparse-view conditions, where geometric information is extremely limited. However, in such sparse-view settings, 3DGS tends to overfit to training views, leading to a rapid degradation in novel-view rendering quality as the viewpoints move away from the training views. Moreover, initializing 3DGS from sparse SfM points further intensifies overfitting, resulting in unstable Gaussians. Therefore, our method initializes the 3DGS using epipolar depth priors following the strategy of NexusGS~ yulong2025nexusgs , to obtain more reliable stereo renderings in the early stage. Instead of using a fixed baseline as in prior works, we adaptively determine the baseline for each view using a multi-view feature score, avoiding the manual setup of baseline parameters. Afterwards, we fine-tune the 3DGS using a pre-trained stereo matching network together with a 2D/3D co-regularization scheme. The stereo matching network is leveraged to propagate gradients that directly improve its depth estimation quality, guiding the 3DGS toward stereo-consistent geometry. Meanwhile, 2D/3D co-regularization provides geometrically stable optimization by complementing the strengths of 2D and 3D Gaussian representations. It is particularly important in large-overlap settings where the synthesized stereo images become similar to the existing input images, making them redundant and thereby weakening the effect. The fine-tuned 3DGS is specialized for stereo-view rendering, from which accurate depth maps are extracted using a pre-trained stereo network. High-quality images rendered from the fine-tuned 3DGS offer additional geometric cues under sparse-view settings, improving our method to preserve more accurate geometry compared to prior works jiang2025sparse2dgs, han2025fatesgs , which rely solely on information derived from the given sparse views. Experiments were conducted on the DTU dataset aanaes2016dtu , and surface reconstruction qualities are evaluated using the Chamfer Distance metric. We also perform qualitative experiments on the BlendedMVS yao2020blendedmvs dataset to demonstrate the generalization of our method. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose Sparse-GS2Mesh, the pipeline specializing 3DGS for stereo matching under sparse inputs, with three novel components: (I) adaptive baseline selection, (II) fine-tuning with a stereo matching network, and (III) 2D/3D co-regularized fine-tuning. We use synthesized stereo images from 3DGS as geometric cues and leverage epipolar depth priors in initialization to enhance reconstruction quality. Sparse-GS2Mesh achieves Chamfer Distance (mm) of 1.07 on the DTU dataset with three little-overlap images, outperforming the SOTA (1.27), and 0.95 under the large-overlap setting, which is comparable to the SOTA (0.92). Related Work Dense View Surface Reconstruction Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)~ mildenhall2020nerf represent 3D scenes implicitly for novel view synthesis via differentiable volume rendering. Subsequent studies extend this formulation to surface reconstruction; NeuS~ peng2021neus improves geometric fidelity via weighted volume rendering, while RegSDF~ zhang2023regsdf regularizes geometry using SfM point clouds. However, these radiance-field methods require heavy computation and degrade significantly under sparse-view conditions due to insufficient geometric cues. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233dgs models scenes using explicit Gaussian primitives optimized by photometric consistency. Recent works extend 3DGS to dense surface reconstruction: 2DGS~ huang20242dgs flattens Gaussians for surface alignment, GS2Mesh~ yaniv2024gs2mesh predicts depth from rendered stereo pairs using a pre-trained stereo model, and PGSR~ chen2024pgsr integrates unbiased depth rendering with cross-view regularization. Despite high quality under dense views, their dependence on dense observations limits performance in sparse scenarios, motivating our approach. Sparse-View 3D Reconstruction Novel View Synthesis. Although both NeRF mildenhall2020nerf and 3DGS kerbl20233dgs achieve impressive performance in novel view synthesis under dense-view settings, they tend to overfit to training views when the number of input images is constrained, leading to a significant degradation in novel view rendering quality. To alleviate this issue, DS-NeRF~ deng2022dsnerf leverages depth priors from SfM points to constrain scene reconstruction, and InfoNeRF~ kim2022infonerf reduces reconstruction uncertainty via entropy-based regularization on ray densities. Cor-GS~ zhang2024corgs extends 3DGS with a dual-field co-regularization scheme to enhance multi-view geometric consistency. Unlike Cor-GS, our framework enforces co-regularization between 3DGS and 2DGS, leading to a more robust 3DGS representation, particularly well-suited for surface reconstruction. NexusGS~ yulong2025nexusgs exploits geometric initialization by computing epipolar depth from optical flow estimation. Our method follows the same initialization strategy as NexusGS, and further refines the geometry through fine-tuning using the stereo matching model and 2D/3D Co-Regularization. Surface Reconstruction. Beyond novel view synthesis, surface reconstruction also faces challenges under sparse-view settings due to limited geometric observations. To address this issue, NeuSurf~ huang2024neusurf integrates on-surface priors into neural implicit representations, while SparseNeuS~ long2022sparseneus learns generalizable geometric priors from large-scale datasets using signed distance functions (SDF) and image features, though it still requires per-scene fine-tuning. FatesGS~ han2025fatesgs , a 2DGS~ huang20242dgs based method, improves geometric alignment by enforcing both multi-view feature consistency and intra-view depth consistency. Sparse2DGS~ jiang2025sparse2dgs further strengthens 2DGS by introducing a geometry-prioritized enhancement strategy that combines the advantages of MVS and 2DGS. Despite these advances, their performance remains limited under extremely sparse observations (i.e., a little overlap setting), often yielding noisy or incomplete geometry. These methods rely solely on the information available from the given views without leveraging additional geometric cues. This motivates our stereo-guided Sparse-GS2Mesh framework, which effectively leverages high-quality stereo cues to achieve robust geometry reconstruction under sparse-view conditions. Deep Learning Based Stereo Matching Stereo matching aims to estimate disparity from a pair of stereo images captured from closely spaced viewpoints. Recent deep-learning methods~ chang2018pyramidstereo, shen2021cfnet, zhang2019ganet, wen2025foundationstereo , particularly recurrent architectures~ lipson2021raft, xu2023igev, zhao2023dlnr , iteratively refine disparity predictions for high accuracy. Among them, DEFOM-Stereo~ jiang2025defomstereo integrates monocular depth estimation on the reference view with recurrent stereo refinement. To fully exploit the information from the ground-truth image alongside our synthesized 3DGS stereo rendering, we adopt DEFOM-Stereo to iteratively refine the monocular depth within its recurrent framework. Method We introduce Sparse-GS2Mesh, a method to reconstruct high-fidelity 3D geometry from sparse-view inputs. Our framework first goes through a 2D/3D GS~ huang20242dgs, kerbl20233dgs warm-up stage, and then adaptively selects stereo baselines without manual tuning to synthesize reliable stereo-aligned images. During the fine-tuning stage, the stereo matching network~ jiang2025defomstereo adapts 3DGS specifically for stereo matching, while the 2D/3D co-regularization improves their robustness by allowing two modules to compensate for each other's strengths. Finally, we render high-quality stereo views from 3DGS and extract accurate depth maps using the pre-trained stereo matching network to obtain high-quality meshes. title: Synthetic-to-Real ViT-Based Pose Estimation of a Noncooperative UAV
summary: Remote pose estimation of noncooperative Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) from imagery is critical, as they cannot be influenced or instrumented in advance. Deep-learning-based approaches offer a promising solution; however, their development is constrained by the cost and difficulty of acquiring large-scale real-world datasets with accurate pose labels. Synthetic imagery provides an alternative, but models trained on synthetic data must overcome the synthetic-to-real domain gap to generalize to real-world imagery. This work investigates the inherent synthetic-to-real generalization capability of a Vision Transformer (ViT)-based model for monocular UAV pose estimation. The proposed approach employs a self-supervised DINOv2 backbone and is trained exclusively on labeled synthetic imagery while being evaluated on labeled real-world imagery. Pose ambiguity-aware strategies are incorporated during training and inference to address ambiguities arising from the projection of a three-dimensional target onto a two-dimensional image plane and from target symmetries. An $α$-$β$ filter is further integrated during inference to improve pose estimations. To assess the model under operational requirements, it is evaluated in terms of Mean Angular Error (MAE) and inference time, both before and after filtering, using a real-world dataset containing 77,077 labeled UAV images. Before filtering, the model achieves an MAE of $19.18^{\circ}$ and an inference time of $13.25$ ms, whereas after filtering, these values are $8.74^{\circ}$ and $13.42$ ms, respectively.

Introduction Remote pose estimation of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) from imagery is essential for applications such as autonomous navigation pessanha2024fixed , aerial refueling gong2023research , and directed-energy systems herrera2025deep . The latter application motivates this work, where accurate pose estimation of noncooperative UAVs is critical to automate operational scenarios that are difficult or impractical for human operators. Since noncooperative targets cannot be instrumented or influenced in advance, camera-based remote sensing provides an attractive approach for estimating UAV pose from imagery. To estimate pose from this imagery, deep learning-based methods have emerged as a powerful solution due to their ability to learn visual representations directly from image data. Deep-learning-based pose estimation models have shown significant promise in recent years guan2024survey, ordoumpozanis2025reviewing, liu2026deep . However, their performance is often limited by the availability of labeled training data. Collecting and annotating large-scale real-world data, especially in the noncooperative UAV context is costly and time-consuming, particularly when accurate pose labels are required. Synthetic data generation provides an attractive alternative by producing large quantities of labeled imagery under controlled variations such as pose, lighting, and viewing conditions. Nevertheless, models trained on synthetic data must overcome the synthetic-to-real domain gap to generalize effectively to real-world imagery. Similar domain gap challenges have been observed in satellite pose estimation. The second international Satellite Pose Estimation Competition (SPEC2021), co-hosted by the European Space Agency (ESA) and Stanford University's Space Rendezvous Laboratory (SLAB), highlighted the challenge of generalizing models trained on synthetic imagery to realistic imagery park2023satellite , motivating research into methods for bridging the synthetic-to-real domain gap. Although focused primarily on satellite pose estimation, the underlying problem is also relevant to noncooperative UAV pose estimation, where acquiring large quantities of accurately labeled real-world pose data is costly and often impractical. This work investigates whether a Vision Transformer (ViT)-based model can generalize from synthetic to real UAV imagery for pose estimation. The proposed model is based on the self-supervised DINOv2 oquab2023dinov2 and is trained exclusively on synthetic imagery and evaluated on real-world imagery for direct pose estimation. This experimental setting is intentionally adopted to assess the inherent synthetic-to-real generalization capability of the ViT-based model. Techniques such as adversarial training ganin2016domain and domain randomization tobin2017domain could be employed to reduce the synthetic-to-real domain gap. However, the primary interest of this study is the inherent synthetic-to-real performance of the ViT-based model without incorporating explicit domain-gap reduction techniques. ViT leverages self-attention mechanisms to capture global contextual information dosovitskiy2020image . ViT has demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of computer vision tasks. However, its effectiveness for synthetic-to-real UAV pose estimation remains insufficiently explored. In this work, the proposed ViT-based model is designed to account for pose ambiguity, a significant challenge in monocular pose estimation arising from the projection of a three-dimensional target onto a two-dimensional image plane and from target symmetries. As illustrated in Figure fig:ambiguous_poses , distinct target poses may produce nearly identical image appearances, potentially leading to large pose prediction errors. To mitigate this issue, ambiguity-aware strategies are incorporated during both training and inference. The proposed model is evaluated using two criteria that are critical for practical deployment: prediction accuracy, quantified by mean angular error, and inference time. In addition, an filter is integrated during inference to smooth the estimations. Accuracy and inference time are evaluated before and after filtering to quantify its effect. The UAV imagery used in this research consists of labeled synthetic and real-world datasets. The synthetic dataset was generated in simulation using a 3D UAV virtual model, whereas the labeled real-world dataset was acquired using a laboratory testbed with 3D printed UAV model, as detailed in herrera2023deep . A total of 77,077 labeled real-world images were used in this study. Preliminaries sec:prelim This section fixes notation and introduces the four ingredients the method builds on: the rotation representation and error metric ( ), the continuous six-dimensional parametrization the network regresses ( ), the four-branch symmetry group that formalizes the pose ambiguity ( ), and the radar-cue signal used to resolve it. Rotation representation and error metric sec:rot A three-dimensional orientation is an element of the special orthogonal group , the group of proper rotations. is a three-dimensional curved manifold rather than a Euclidean space, and this curvature is the source of both the parametrization difficulties ( ) and the need for a manifold-aware error metric. Orientations are represented by an axis-angle (Rodrigues) vector , where is the unit rotation axis and is the rotation angle; this is the parametrization in which ground-truth labels are supplied. The corresponding rotation matrix is recovered by the matrix exponential, which for takes the closed form known as the Rodrigues formula, where is the skew-symmetric matrix such that for all . Labels are converted to matrices via before any loss is computed. The discrepancy between a predicted and a ground-truth orientation is measured by the geodesic distance on , the length of the shortest rotation carrying one onto the other, equivalently the angle of the residual rotation : Unlike a Euclidean distance between rotation matrices or quaternions, it reflects true angular displacement and does not saturate or double-count near large rotations. All errors are reported in degrees. Continuous six-dimensional rotation representation sec:sixd The continuous six-dimensional representation of Zhou~ ~ zhou2019continuity is used. The network emits two raw vectors , mapped to a valid rotation matrix by Gram--Schmidt orthonormalization, The resulting is orthonormal with determinant by construction, so no post-hoc projection onto is required, and the map is continuous and surjective. This removes the discontinuities that afflict Euler-angle and quaternion outputs and degrade accuracy near their seams. Pose ambiguity and the four-branch symmetry group sec:ambiguity The defining challenge of this task is that the silhouette of a fixed-wing UAV is approximately invariant under two independent reflections: one exchanging nose and tail, one exchanging top and bottom. As a consequence, a single image is geometrically consistent with four distinct orientations, illustrated in . Given a true rotation , these are where is the nose--tail flip, the top--bottom flip, and their composition. Every is itself a proper rotation and hence a legitimate regression target: is a rotation by about the body -axis, and the two-sided action in composes two reflections of determinant , one on each side, so each product has determinant . The four transforms form a Klein four-group under composition: the identity together with the two reflections and their product, in which each nontrivial element is its own inverse and composing any two distinct flips yields the third. The set is thus the orbit of under this group, the complete collection of poses the image cannot distinguish, and a pose in general position has exactly four such preimages. Two properties of this structure are what make the ambiguity tractable rather than merely troublesome. First, the orbit is small and of fixed size: there are precisely four candidates, not an open-ended confusable set, so disambiguation is a two-bit decision. Second, the group acts faithfully on a pair of physically measurable sign bits: no nontrivial group element leaves both bits unchanged, so the four orbit members carry four distinct bit patterns and two bits suffice to identify the correct pose, as formalized next. Radar cues. To resolve the ambiguity at inference without access to the ground-truth pose, the two radar-cue sign bits of~ herrera2025 are adopted, computed from a rotation matrix as with , , and the convention . The nose--tail sign is the sign of the -component of the rotated body -axis and encodes which end of the fuselage points toward the sensor. Physically this is the sign of the radar range rate, positive when the nose approaches and negative when the tail does. The top--bottom sign is the sign of the -component of the rotated body -axis and encodes whether the target is upright or inverted. Each of the three reflections in flips a different combination of the two bits, so the four orbit members carry four distinct bit patterns ( ) and two physically measurable bits identify the correct pose among the four. Method sec:method Model Architecture sec:arch presents the model pipeline from left to right. An image crop containing the UAV is first passed through a Vision Transformer backbone, which divides the image into a grid of small patches and produces one feature vector for each patch. These patch features are then used by the rest of the network. The first decoder stage predicts three keypoints that are relatively easy to identify: the nose, the tail, and the small fin beneath the tail. These three points are used to compute a geometric cue that captures the direction of the fuselage in the image and indicates which side of the aircraft the fin lies on. The second decoder stage takes this cue, together with the same patch features, and predicts the four remaining keypoints: the two wingtips and the two horizontal tail surfaces. title: A differentiable Lagrangian-coupled 3D Gaussian Splatting-SPH model for forward simulation and inverse analysis in solid mechanics
summary: Recent advances in generative world models have increased interest in digital models that reproduce both the appearance of real objects and their response to physical interaction. Three-dimensional reconstruction techniques, including 3D Gaussian Splatting, capture detailed surface geometry and appearance from images and videos. However, extending these representations beyond plausible animation to mechanically interpretable models for constitutive behavior, boundary conditions, and inverse parameter identification remains less explored. In this work, a differentiable Lagrangian-coupled 3DGS-smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) model is proposed for forward simulation and inverse analysis of deformable solids. The observed object is first reconstructed from multi-view calibrated visual dataset as a 3DGS rendering model. An envelope-based procedure then generates an independent SPH support for the solid-mechanics model, avoiding the direct use of rendering primitives as mechanical particles. A reference-configuration Lagrangian transfer maps SPH deformation to Gaussian positions and covariances, thereby coupling the physical model and the image observation model while preserving a differentiable computational path. The SPH formulation supports linear elastic, hyperelastic, and Kelvin--Voigt viscoelastic responses, together with fixed, free, and Robin-type boundary conditions. Numerical studies validate the SPH response against finite-element results, assess accuracy and efficiency against a conventional model using Gaussian centers as surface SPH particles, and demonstrate forward simulations on beam, bridge, and liver-shaped examples. Inverse analyses further estimate constitutive and boundary parameters from rendered deformation observations, including noisy cases, demonstrating the feasibility of the proposed model for mechanics-based parameter identification from image data.
full_text: A differentiable Lagrangian-coupled 3D Gaussian Splatting--SPH model for forward simulation and inverse analysis in solid mechanics Tian Xu, Soroush Atashi, Tianju Xue Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Recent advances in generative world models for physical artificial intelligence have increased interest in digital models that reproduce both the appearance of real objects and their response to physical interaction. Three-dimensional reconstruction techniques, including 3D Gaussian Splatting, capture detailed surface geometry and appearance from images and videos, while physics-integrated representations extend these capabilities to simulating the mechanical response of deformable solids. However, extending these representations beyond plausible animation to mechanically interpretable models for constitutive behavior, boundary conditions, and inverse parameter identification remains less explored. In this work, a differentiable Lagrangian-coupled 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)--smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) model is proposed for forward simulation and inverse analysis of deformable solids. The observed object is first reconstructed from multi-view calibrated visual dataset as a 3DGS rendering model. An envelope-based procedure then generates an independent SPH support for the solid-mechanics model, avoiding the direct use of rendering primitives as mechanical particles. A reference-configuration Lagrangian transfer maps SPH deformation to Gaussian positions and covariances, thereby coupling the physical model and the image observation model while preserving a differentiable computational path. The SPH formulation supports linear elastic, hyperelastic, and Kelvin--Voigt viscoelastic responses, together with fixed, free, and Robin-type boundary conditions. Numerical studies validate the SPH response against finite-element results, assess accuracy and efficiency against a conventional model using Gaussian centers as surface SPH particles, and demonstrate forward simulations on beam, bridge, and liver-shaped examples. Inverse analyses further estimate constitutive and boundary parameters from rendered deformation observations, including noisy cases, demonstrating the feasibility of the proposed model for mechanics-based parameter identification from image data. Keywords:\\ 3D Gaussian splatting, smoothed particle hydrodynamics, inverse analysis Introduction Recent advances in generative world models for physical artificial intelligence are extending visual scene generation toward interactive simulation for robot learning and action evaluation nvidia2025worldsimulation . Alongside these developments, reconstructing deformable objects from videos for subsequent physical simulation is bringing vision and mechanics into closer connection jiang2025phystwin . Translating these capabilities into mechanical analysis requires more than visually plausible motion: the deformation must be governed by constitutive relations and balance laws under specified boundary conditions, with physical parameters that can be inferred from observations willcox2021imperative . This requires a physical model of the solid coupled with a rendering model that relates its deformation to the observed appearance. In forward simulation, these models describe the mechanical response and its rendered appearance; in inverse analysis, they enable physical parameters to be estimated by comparing simulated and observed images. A consistent and differentiable connection between vision and solid mechanics is therefore needed to support both deformation simulation and parameter identification from images or videos. Modern visual reconstruction methods provide the geometric and appearance description required to start from images. In particular, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) represents a scene by anisotropic Gaussian primitives and has become an effective representation for view synthesis kerbl2023gaussian . A 3DGS model, however, is primarily an observation-space representation. Its Gaussian centers, covariances, colors, and opacities are optimized for rendering, and do not by themselves define a constitutive model, material volume, or boundary condition for solid-mechanics analysis. Physics-integrated Gaussian models have made important progress in forward deformation simulation of 3DGS representations. PhysGaussian couples co-located Gaussians to the material point method (MPM), while Spring-Gaus uses a spring--mass representation; subsequent methods broadened the constitutive range to learned or mixed material responses xie2024physgaussian,zhong2024springgaus,cao2024neuma, lin2025omniphysgs,huang2026gaussianfluent . These formulations provide a direct kinematic link between simulation and rendering and can produce plausible deformation under prescribed material and loading settings. For solid mechanics, however, co-locating mechanical supports with visual primitives would result in a high-dimensional physical discretization, with the mechanical supports tending to be distributed non-uniformly and densely over the object surface. Several recent methods therefore use reduced or proxy physical representations to improve the efficiency of forward deformation. Sparse controls can drive dense Gaussians without a constitutive model huang2024scgs ; PhysSplat employs adaptively sampled MPM driving particles, with material property distributions supplied by multimodal language model priors; PHYSPLAT derives appearance agnostic simulation proxies from reconstructed Gaussian scenes; and GASP groups or selects Gaussians for an external physics engine zhao2025physsplat,alfonso2026physplat,borycki2026gasp . Most closely, PhysTalk fixes rest pose particle neighborhoods and blends particle displacements and deformation gradients back to the original Gaussians collorone2025phystalk . These studies show that reduced physical representations are promising for efficient forward animation. Nevertheless, the physical representation in the aforementioned methods often serves as a proxy or control model for rendered motion. Without adequate constitutive and boundary modeling, visual agreement alone cannot establish mechanical accuracy under different loading conditions. Beyond computational efficiency and physical fidelity in forward simulation, a further objective is to identify the constitutive parameters and boundary conditions responsible for the observed deformation. Full-field methods such as finite-element model updating and the virtual fields method have established the value of spatially resolved observations for constitutive identification avril2008fullfield . Related elasticity inverse problem studies have shown that material parameters and boundary conditions can be jointly identified from partial or local observations when the forward mechanics model and observation operator are properly formulated xu2022fembased,xu2023multiple . These methods commonly use displacement or strain fields extracted before the inverse solve. In rendered inverse physics, PAC-NeRF couples neural rendering with differentiable MPM for system identification from multiview videos; PhysDreamer and NeuMA use image-space supervision to infer material behavior; and TopoGaussian, PhysTwin, and MonoPhysics estimate topology, physical digital-twin parameters, or joint geometry--appearance--physics states from visual observations li2023pacnerf,zhang2024physdreamer,cao2024neuma, xiong2025topogaussian,jiang2025phystwin,rho2026monophysics . These works confirm the relevance of rendered identification. However, examples such as TopoGaussian mainly emphasize internal topology or material related recovery, whereas boundary condition identification and its coupling with constitutive parameters remain less developed in mechanics-oriented Gaussian deformation models. For a differentiable model supporting both forward simulation and inverse analysis, the solid discretization and the evaluation of parameter sensitivities must be considered together. Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) provides a suitable physical discretization for this purpose because it is mesh-free and naturally Lagrangian compared to the MPM lucy1977sph,gingold1977sph,monaghan1992sph . Corrected and corotated SPH formulations further improve the consistency and stability of elastic solid simulation randles1996sph,bonet1999variational,becker2009corotated,peer2018implicit . Extending these solid discretization formulations to gradient-based inverse analysis further requires sensitivities of the simulated response to the unknown physical parameters. Differentiable numerical frameworks provide this capability: JAX-FEM supports sensitivity analysis and inverse design in solid mechanics xue2023jaxfem , while JAX-SPH enables differentiation through SPH fluid simulations for inverse analysis toshev2024jaxsph . However, differentiable SPH formulations for solid mechanics remain less explored, particularly for the joint identification of constitutive parameters and boundary conditions. Despite these advances, constructing mechanical models from visual observations remains challenging when efficient forward simulation must preserve physical and rendering fidelity with fewer mechanical degrees of freedom. Extending the same model to inverse analysis poses the additional challenge of identifying constitutive parameters and boundary conditions from images within a unified differentiable formulation. To address these challenges, this work develops a Lagrangian-coupled 3D Gaussian Splatting--SPH model for forward simulation and inverse analysis in solid mechanics. In the proposed model, the observed object is first represented by a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model reconstructed from multi-view images or video frames. An envelope-based procedure is then used to generate an SPH particle support from the reconstructed Gaussian geometry, while the solid-mechanics response is computed on the SPH model rather than directly on the Gaussian primitives. The deformation of the SPH model is transferred back to the Gaussian representation through a reference-configuration Lagrangian mapping, which reconstructs Gaussian centers and covariance deformation from neighboring SPH particle displacement and local deformation. The coupled simulation, transfer, and rendering process is implemented in JAX, allowing the same model to be used for both forward deformation rendering and gradient-based inverse analysis. The main contributions of this work are reflected in three aspects. First, a differentiable Lagrangian SPH-GS transfer is proposed to bridge the 3DGS rendering model and the SPH physical model. This enables a lower-dimensional mechanical discretization to drive a dense Gaussian representation, improving simulation efficiency while retaining physical and rendering fidelity. Second, the corrected corotated SPH model is extended to incorporate hyperelastic and Kelvin--Voigt viscoelastic responses together with Robin-like boundary conditions, expanding the physical modeling capabilities of the coupled model beyond elastic deformation under fixed or free constraints. Third, forward simulation and inverse analysis are connected within the same differentiable 3DGS-SPH model, enabling joint identification of constitutive parameters and boundary conditions from image or video observations. The JAX implementation provides parameter gradients through simulation, Lagrangian transfer, and rendering to support gradient-based optimization. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~2 presents the mathematical formulation of the forward simulation and inverse analysis problems. Section~3 introduces the proposed 3DGS-SPH model, including the 3D Gaussian representation, envelope-based SPH support generation, corrected solid SPH formulation, Lagrangian SPH-GS transfer, and inverse analysis formulation. title: ExStereo: Lifting 2D Vision-Language-Action Models to 3D with Explicit Stereo Representations
summary: Three-dimensional perception is critical for robotic manipulation, particularly for high-precision tasks, as recovering metric depth and precise 3D object positions from monocular RGB observations is inherently ill-posed. However, many Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models rely solely on RGB observations for perception. Leveraging recent advances in foundation models for stereo matching, we introduce ExStereo, a stereo module that augments pre-trained 2D VLAs with 3D perception. ExStereo reconstructs scene geometry from stereo image pairs and renders multi-view observations as an explicit stereo representation for stereo feature extraction. The action tokens from the action expert selectively attend to the resulting stereo tokens through our proposed action-stereo cross-attention mechanism, enabling the policy to generate robot actions conditioned on 3D scene information. To learn robust 3D representations, we introduce a mid-training stage before task-specific post-training, using a self-supervised learning objective on large-scale stereo data. We validate our approach by fine-tuning two publicly available VLAs, $π_{0.5}$ and SmolVLA, and evaluate them in simulation and on a real-world bimanual PiPER platform. Across both settings, VLAs fine-tuned with ExStereo consistently outperform baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of stereo perception for robotic manipulation. Our project website is at: https://exstereo-vla.github.io/ExStereo/.

Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation~ kim24openvla,intelligence2025pi05,liu2024rdt , demonstrating impressive visuomotor capabilities. By building on large-scale pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs)~ radford2021clip,dosovitskiy2020vit , these policies learn from semantic priors, acquire diverse skills from demonstrations, and generalize across objects and instructions. However, most VLA models operate on monocular RGB observations processed through pre-trained 2D vision encoders to extract features for downstream action generation. Operating on 2D visual tokens, these policies lack precise depth and geometric information. While effective in controlled settings, real-world interactions often require accurate spatial relationships and object locations, as well as robustness to occlusions and visual variations. Recent work has explored injecting 3D structure into VLAs~ li2025bridgevla,li2025pointvlainjecting3dworld,sun2025geovlaempowering3drepresentations,zhen20243dvla , achieving strong performance on 3D manipulation tasks. However, these methods depend on RGB-D sensors, which require precise calibration and are sensitive to sensor noise. Meanwhile, StereoVLA~ deng2026stereovlaenhancingvisionlanguageactionmodels and StereoPolicy~ han2026stereopolicyimprovingroboticmanipulation leverage stereo image pairs to obtain implicit stereo features for policy learning. StereoVLA requires training its VLA from scratch, while StereoPolicy provides only modest improvements to pre-trained VLAs. In this work, we show how effectively leveraging explicit stereo representations can equip 2D VLAs with metric 3D perception and substantially improve their performance. We propose lifting 2D Vision-Language-Action models to 3D with plicit Representations (ExStereo), a stereo module that equips pre-trained, off-the-shelf VLAs with 3D spatial perception. It takes a stereo image pair as input and employs a pre-trained stereo foundation model~ wen2026fastfoundationstereo to obtain a disparity map. Using the camera intrinsics and stereo baseline, the disparity map is transformed into a metric depth map and 3D point cloud. The point cloud is rendered from four orthogonal viewpoints (Top, Front, Left, and Right) using z-buffering. The four views are then tiled horizontally to form a multi-view observation, which is fed into a Vision Transformer (ViT)~ dosovitskiy2020vit to obtain stereo tokens. The stereo tokens are utilized for action generation through the proposed action-stereo cross-attention mechanism, where the action tokens serve as queries and the stereo tokens serve as keys and values. This allows the action tokens to selectively attend to relevant 3D visual features without modifying the large prefix token sequence or the weights of VLMs, enabling pre-trained robot policies to efficiently integrate the stereo module during post-training. See~ for an overview. To learn robust 3D representations, we introduce a mid-training stage with a masked autoencoding objective prior to post-training. During mid-training, patches of the multi-view observation are randomly masked, and the VLA is trained on a large-scale stereo dataset to reconstruct the missing patches while learning to extract relevant visual features for action generation from incomplete observations. During post-training, the stereo module is frozen to prevent overfitting to task-specific demonstrations. We evaluate ExStereo on ten simulated RoboTwin~ chen2025robotwin tasks and three real-world tasks using a bimanual AgileX PiPER platform. ExStereo improves the average simulation success rate of from 51.2 to 76.4 and its real-world success rate from 16/60 to 50/60 trials, while also outperforming point-cloud and implicit-stereo baselines. The contributions of this paper are: We propose , a novel stereo module that lifts any 2D VLA to 3D for fast adaptation without requiring additional pre-training of the base policy. We demonstrate that explicit stereo representations, when used appropriately, yield stronger downstream manipulation performance than implicit representations. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments show that VLAs equipped with ExStereo greatly improve upon the performance of their base VLAs while outperforming other strong baselines. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models sec:related_VLA Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, also commonly referred to as robotic foundation models, fine-tune pretrained VLMs to output robot actions, such as end-effector pose deltas or joint targets, by training on large-scale teleoperation data~ open_x_embodiment_rt_x_2023 . Representative systems include RT-2, OpenVLA~ kim24openvla , SmolVLA~ shukor2025smolvlavisionlanguageactionmodelaffordable , and the family~ black2024pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel, intelligence2025pi05,intelligence2025pi06vlalearnsexperience,intelligence2026pi07 . We refer the reader to~ FMs_robotics_2023_survey_1,FMs_robotics_2023_survey_2 for surveys. Early VLAs discretized actions into tokens and predicted them autoregressively~ rt22023arxiv, kim24openvla , whereas recent policies attach a dedicated action expert trained with diffusion or flow matching to produce smooth, high-frequency action chunks~ black2024pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel, intelligence2025pi05,shukor2025smolvlavisionlanguageactionmodelaffordable . Camera configurations have broadened in parallel, from a single third-person view to wrist-mounted cameras and to multi-camera rigs that observe the workspace from several sides~ intelligence2025pi05 . Across these variants, each view is still processed by a monocular 2D encoder so metric scale and inter-object spatial relations must be inferred from appearance. Prior work has addressed these limitations by incorporating depth sensors~ liu2026clamp,jia2024lift3dfoundationpolicylifting,wei2024droma , such as RGB-D cameras. However, these sensors often degrade on transparent~ wei2024droma and reflective surfaces and are sensitive to sensor noise, calibration errors, and point cloud artifacts, making high-quality 3D reconstruction challenging. Beyond these hardware limitations, visual representations remain a key bottleneck. Existing 2D vision backbones~ radford2021clip,Tschannen2025SigLIP2M,simeoni2025dinov3 generalize well across diverse visual domains but lack explicit 3D structure. In contrast, 3D vision backbones directly capture geometry from point clouds~ wu2025sonata,wu2023masked,wu2024ptv3,PointContrast2020 , but tend to underperform their 2D counterparts due to the scarcity of large-scale 3D training data. These limitations motivate a 3D perception approach that preserves the scalability and representational strengths of 2D vision while providing explicit geometric information. Stereo setups are common on robot platforms and can recover such geometry from binocular disparity, yet the second image is rarely exploited by the policy. ExStereo builds on this observation and equips pre-trained VLAs with an explicit 3D representation computed from a stereo pair. Stereo Vision in Computer Vision sec:related_stereo Stereo matching recovers metric depth by estimating disparity between a rectified left--right image pair without active depth sensors. Previous classical methods build a cost volume and refine disparity with 3D convolutions or recurrent updates~ chang2018pyramidstereomatchingnetwork,lipson2021raft,xu2025igev . More recently, the field has moved toward stereo foundation models that generalize zero-shot across domains by transferring priors from monocular depth models. FoundationStereo~ wen2025stereo establishes this direction through large-scale pretraining, and later work improves robustness on transparent, reflective, and textureless surfaces where depth sensors fail~ Bartolomei_2025_CVPR,guo2024stereo . Fast-FoundationStereo~ wen2026fastfoundationstereo distills these models for near real-time inference. We leverage it in to obtain an explicit 3D representation. Stereo Vision in Robotics Stereo cameras recover depth from binocular disparity, making them more reliable for transparent, specular, and textureless objects, where conventional depth sensors often struggle. Prior work has applied stereo vision to challenging materials such as glass~ wei2024droma,bai2024cleardepth , as well as to stereo-based grasping and tracking~ yu2025pogs . More recently, StereoPolicy~ han2026stereopolicyimprovingroboticmanipulation and StereoVLA~ deng2026stereovlaenhancingvisionlanguageactionmodels extract features from stereo modules, which we characterize as implicit representations (see Section sec:multiviewobservationrendering for details), and combine them with language or RGB image features as inputs to a VLM for policy learning. In contrast, we use a stereo module to construct an explicit 3D representation of the scene and feed the corresponding tokens directly into the action expert for policy learning. title: LoCoSplat: Real-Time Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting with Minimal 3D Reasoning
summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) increasingly aggregates multi-view evidence with heavy learned 3D networks. We propose LoCoSplat (Local-Context Splatting), motivated by the observation that a Gaussian is a local primitive: once depth is predicted, what the 3D stage must add (scale, rotation, opacity) depends on the point cloud around each anchor, and a fixed local average of that neighbourhood is enough to supply it, no heavy network required. LoCoSplat realises exactly this average: it splats a 16-d linear projection of the point features into a fine and a coarse grid and reads both back at each anchor with a 0.14M-parameter pointwise MLP; with no learned 3D network and no dynamic sparse computation, its whole encoder runs as one fp16 CUDA graph. On RealEstate10K, LoCoSplat outperforms every prior feed-forward method on PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS at 6, 12, and 24 views, with a margin that widens as views densify (+3.3 PSNR over VolSplat, the prior voxel-aligned state of the art, at 24 views) and grows further under zero-shot transfer to ACID and fine-tuning on ScanNet. It reconstructs a 6-view scene in 33 ms on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU, the fastest of seven feed-forward methods and $4.2\times$ faster than the previous state of the art, trains $2.7\times$ faster ($5.9\times$ at 24 views), and uses $6.7\times$ less inference memory.

Introduction sec:introduction Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting~ charatan2024pixelsplat,chen2024mvsplat,xu2025depthsplat predicts the Gaussian primitives of 3DGS~ kerbl20233d from a handful of posed images in a single forward pass, replacing the per-scene optimization of NeRF and 3DGS~ mildenhall2021nerf,kerbl20233d with a learned prior. Pixel-aligned prediction, the dominant approach, suffers from multi-view misalignment and resolution-bound Gaussian budgets, and the field's answer has been to reason with ever-heavier learned modules, mostly by moving prediction into 3D: sparse 3D U-Nets and CNNs~ wang2025volsplat,zhang2022nerfusion , 3D cost-volume networks, or long-sequence Mamba/transformer models over image tokens~ ziwen2024long . ~ wang2025volsplat , the state of the art of the depth-guided voxel-aligned family, predicts depth, voxelizes the unprojected pixels into anchors, and then refines the sparse volume with a 17M-parameter sparse 3D U-Net before decoding Gaussians. That U-Net is its largest inference cost ( 7 scenes per second): a dynamic-shape sparse computation~ choy20194d that cannot be captured in a CUDA graph and barely benefits from mixed precision, and the dominant training memory as views grow (24-view training takes 159 hours). Behind this trajectory lies an implicit assumption: that aggregating multi-view evidence in 3D requires substantial learned 3D capacity. Our motivation is a local view of the 3D stage: what a Gaussian needs from its neighbours is the kind of low-order local information that a grid computes for free, not a learned 3D network. With no learned 3D network and no dynamic sparse computation, the whole encoder runs as one fp16 CUDA graph. The motivation is structural: a 3D Gaussian is a local primitive. Once depth is predicted, each anchor's colour and position are determined by its own pixel. The 3D stage must add scale, rotation, and opacity, the layout of the surface around the anchor; no single pixel observes this layout, but it is determined by the neighbouring points, which a fixed average over a coarser neighbourhood, computed for free by a grid, can summarize. The anchors are also so sparse at the working voxel size (99.6 have no occupied neighbour at 6 views) that a sparse convolution over them is already pointwise ( ), so any context must come from a coarser scale, which the coarse grid supplies. title: SelectOccFlow: Selective Spatiotemporal Aggregation for 3D Occupancy and Scene Flow Prediction
summary: Comprehensive 3D scene understanding for autonomous driving requires modeling geometry, semantics, and motion. However, camera-based occupancy and scene flow prediction are sensitive to unreliable spatial and temporal aggregation, caused by semantically incompatible image features, misaligned historical observations, and incomplete voxel structures. To address this issue, we propose SelectOccFlow, a selective spatiotemporal aggregation framework that progressively refines contextual evidence across image, temporal, and voxel domains. To obtain semantically compatible image evidence, we design Semantic-Guided Sampling (SGS) to regulate feature sampling with semantic priors. Since reliable image evidence alone cannot resolve temporal inconsistency, we then present State-Conditioned Temporal Aggregation (SCTA) to selectively retrieve historical evidence according to voxel states. To further enhance the structural completeness of voxel representations, we introduce Extent-Aware Spatial Aggregation (ESA), which exploits directional structural support to refine foreground geometry. Experiments on OpenOcc demonstrate that SelectOccFlow achieves a state-of-the-art OccScore of 44.9, improving the previous best by +4.2%. It also maintains competitive occupancy performance on Occ3D-nus and improves the mean OccScore under nuScenes-C corruptions by +11.1%, demonstrating improved robustness to visual corruptions. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/muchen1021/SelectOccFlow.
