Introduction Reliable autonomous driving requires a comprehensive understanding of the geometry, semantics, and motion of surrounding environments. Camera-based 3D semantic occupancy prediction provides a dense voxel-level representation of scene geometry and semantic categories~ tong2023scene,behley2019semantickitti,tian2023occ3d . However, occupancy primarily describes the instantaneous scene state and does not explicitly characterize motion at occupied voxels. This limitation is particularly important in dynamic traffic, where geometrically similar scenes can evolve differently. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:fig1 (a), similar occupancy states may correspond to different scene flows, implying distinct interactions with the ego path and potential risks. Scene flow complements occupancy by estimating the voxel-wise direction and magnitude of motion~ liao2025stcocc,chen2025alocc,liu2024let,timoneda2026selfoccflow . Together, 3D occupancy and scene flow provide a more complete representation for dynamic scene understanding. Recovering this representation from multi-view images requires effective aggregation of complementary spatial and temporal evidence. Existing camera-based approaches extract image features and lift them into BEV or 3D voxel space~ wei2023surroundocc,ma2024cotr,huang2023tri,zhang2023occformer,li2023voxformer , while temporal extensions incorporate historical observations~ liao2025stcocc,li2024viewformer,ye2024cvt . However, contextual evidence is not uniformly reliable. Spatial evidence can be incompatible across object boundaries, whereas temporal evidence can become unreliable due to independent object motion, changing occlusions, or degraded observations. Indiscriminate aggregation may therefore propagate errors throughout the prediction pipeline. The key challenge is thus not only where and how to aggregate spatial and temporal evidence, but also which evidence to select at each stage. Spatial incompatibility can arise both before and after image-to-3D transformation. Before lifting, image features near object boundaries or crowded regions may mix foreground, background, and neighboring objects. Adverse visual conditions can further degrade visual evidence~ kong2023robodepth,xie2025benchmarking , thereby aggravating feature mixing near object boundaries. After lifting, incomplete or noisy voxel features require spatial support, while indiscriminate aggregation may propagate errors across semantic boundaries. Reliable spatial aggregation should therefore preserve semantically compatible image evidence before lifting and exploit structurally consistent voxel support afterward to recover foreground geometry. Historical observations provide complementary cues for estimating scene dynamics, but their reliability depends on temporal alignment and observation quality. Although ego-motion compensation aligns static structures, independently moving objects may remain misaligned across frames. Changing occlusions and degraded visual observations can further produce incomplete or noisy histories~ dong2023benchmarking . Moreover, temporal evidence varies across voxel states: stable voxels benefit from longer histories, motion-sensitive voxels require recent observations and adaptive spatial sampling, while free-dominant voxels need only limited temporal support. A shared temporal range and sampling strategy may retrieve stale, misaligned, or noisy evidence. Temporal aggregation should therefore adapt historical retrieval to voxel states through state-specific temporal ranges and spatial sampling. Based on these observations, we propose SelectOccFlow, a selective spatiotemporal aggregation framework for 3D occupancy and scene flow prediction. It adaptively selects context according to spatial compatibility and temporal reliability. Specifically, Semantic-Guided Sampling (SGS) uses semantic priors to regulate image-space sampling before lifting. State-Conditioned Temporal Aggregation (SCTA) retrieves historical evidence with state-specific temporal ranges and spatial sampling. Extent-Aware Spatial Aggregation (ESA) exploits structural voxel support to refine geometry. Extensive experiments on OpenOcc~ tong2023scene and Occ3D-nus~ tian2023occ3d validate the effectiveness of SelectOccFlow for 3D occupancy and scene flow prediction. As shown in Fig.~ fig:fig1 (b), SelectOccFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance on OpenOcc across occupancy (RayIoU), scene flow (mAVE), and overall evaluation, with an OccScore of . It also maintains competitive occupancy performance on Occ3D-nus. Under nuScenes-C corruptions~ xie2025benchmarking , SelectOccFlow further improves the mean OccScore across six corruption types on OpenOcc by , demonstrating improved robustness under degraded visual conditions. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We propose SelectOccFlow, a selective spatiotemporal aggregation framework that selects evidence based on spatial compatibility and temporal reliability. We develop SGS, SCTA, and ESA for progressive image, temporal, and voxel aggregation, regulating sampling, historical retrieval, and voxel refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on OpenOcc, competitive performance on Occ3D-nus, and improved robustness on nuScenes-C. Related Work 3D Occupancy and Scene Flow Prediction Camera-based 3D occupancy prediction methods lift features from monocular images~ li2023voxformer,cao2022monoscene,li2025voxdet or surround-view observations~ wei2023surroundocc,huang2023tri,zhang2023occformer into 3D space to estimate voxel-wise occupancy states and semantic categories, providing dense representations of surrounding environments. Recent approaches further extend occupancy prediction through unified panoptic, compact, and sparse formulations~ ma2024cotr,wang2024panoocc,liu2024fully,wang2024opus . However, occupancy representations primarily describe scene geometry and semantics at a given time without explicitly encoding the motion of occupied voxels. Scene flow complements occupancy prediction by estimating the motion of occupied voxels over time. Recent methods incorporate scene flow into occupancy frameworks to model semantic geometry and scene dynamics within a unified representation~ zhu2025voxelsplat,chen2025alocc,liu2024let,timoneda2026selfoccflow,li2024viewformer . Despite this progress, occupancy and scene flow remain closely coupled because inaccurate spatial structures can impair motion estimation, while unreliable temporal cues may hinder the recovery of both 3D occupancy and scene flow. Consequently, reliable dynamic scene understanding requires effective modeling of spatial observations and temporal evidence. Spatiotemporal Modeling Spatiotemporal modeling has been widely explored in camera-based 3D perception to enhance scene representation and dynamic understanding~ liao2025stcocc,li2024viewformer,li2024bevformer,qin2023unifusion . Existing methods model spatial context through dense BEV or voxel representations~ wei2023surroundocc,zhang2023occformer,li2024bevformer and sparse query-based aggregation~ wang2024opus,wang2022detr3d,tang2024sparseocc . Dense representations aggregate context over structured grids, whereas sparse queries retrieve features around task-specific reference locations. However, spatial compatibility during feature aggregation before and after lifting remains less explored, and evidence from a single frame may be incomplete or ambiguous. Temporal modeling mitigates this limitation by incorporating historical observations to complement current evidence and capture scene evolution. Existing methods encode temporal context through recurrent BEV features~ li2024bevformer,chang2024recurrentbev , aligned multi-frame perspective features~ qin2023unifusion,liu2023petrv2 , or propagated object queries~ wang2023streampetr,papais2025foresight . For occupancy prediction, recent approaches further employ multi-frame streaming temporal attention~ li2024viewformer , perform sparse voxel updates~ liao2025stcocc , or introduce historical predictions as memory priors~ leng2025occupancy,yuan2025lmpocc . Although effective, these methods determine how history is represented and fused, while variations in the relevance of historical evidence across voxel states remain insufficiently addressed. Degraded visual observations caused by adverse weather, illumination changes, and sensor failures~ kong2023robodepth,xie2025benchmarking,dong2023benchmarking,wu2025see,jiang2025acdepth can weaken spatial evidence and reduce the reliability of historical cues, while scene dynamics increase discrepancies between current and historical evidence. title: $R^2$-WAM: Repair-and-Reject Post-Training for World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) emerge as a promising foundation for policy refinement by predicting the consequences of sampled actions. However, visually plausible predictions can mislead policy refinement if they fail to reflect the input actions. To address this mismatch, we introduce $R^2$-WAM, a two-stage repair-and-reject post-training framework that first improves the consistency of predicted futures with input actions, then uses these futures to select inferior action samples for negative fine-tuning. The repair stage grounds imagination in observed robot behavior through a kinematic alignment score that measures agreement between predicted and demonstrated motion, enabling the predicted video to faithfully reflect its input actions. Using the repaired video model, the rejection stage compares imagined outcomes of sampled and demonstrated actions, selectively applying negative fine-tuning to samples whose predicted task progress falls below the demonstrated reference by a prescribed margin. Together, the two stages extend video prediction from representation learning to consequence-based policy refinement without additional environment interaction or changes to the inference procedure. $R^2$-WAM achieves 93.8% average success on RoboTwin 2.0 across clean and randomized settings. On the long-horizon real-world Fold Shirt task, it achieves 87.5% average success, compared with 0% for Fast-WAM.

Introduction sec:introduction World Action Models (WAMs) have recently emerged as a promising approach to robotic control by guiding action generation with predicted visual outcomes. Existing WAMs typically learn to predict video and actions jointly in pixel or latent space ye2026world,zhu2025unified,Bi_2026_CVPR,li2026causal,yuan2026fast , thereby grounding action generation in predicted scene dynamics. Beyond direct robot control, recent studies have explored using action-conditioned world models as simulators to predict the consequences of candidate actions and provide feedback for policy improvement guo2026ctrl,yang2026rise . This is particularly useful when demonstrations provide limited coverage of execution errors and collecting physical trials is costly chandra2025diwa,jiang2025world4rl,xiao2025worldenv,jiang2026wovr . A key prerequisite for effective policy post-training with a world model is that it faithfully predicts how the environment changes in response to actions. Although modern video generation models can produce visually plausible predictions~ wan2025 , they do not necessarily preserve physical properties such as kinematics and dynamics. Consequently, generated videos may appear realistic while failing to reflect the supplied actions yang2026mirabench . Evaluating actions with such predictions can mistake video model errors for policy failures, causing the policy to learn from outcomes its actions would not produce jiang2026wovr,chen2026worldsync . To reduce mismatch between imagined and actual consequences, prior methods ground generated videos in robot motion using inverse dynamics wang2026eva or extracted 3D flow dharmarajan2025dream2flow . These methods rely on auxiliary components to obtain motion feedback, but do not ensure that the video faithfully follows a supplied action. Recent methods improve imagined feedback by fine-tuning world models on real policy rollouts guo2026vlaw , updating the model as the policy evolves from task-critical keyframes jiang2026wovr , or training on diverse actions with supervision~ chen2026worldsync . These methods improve action grounding, but leave open how observed demonstration outcomes can identify unreliable predictions before they are used to evaluate sampled policy actions. To fill this gap, we propose repairing the video expert using observed consequences of demonstrated actions, then using the repaired expert to reject sampled actions with inferior predicted task progress (Figure~ fig:teaser ). To this end, we introduce , a two-stage repair-and-reject post-training framework comprising predictive repair and action rejection (Figure~ fig:pipeline ), comprising the following modules: 1) Predictive repair turns each demonstration into a test of action fidelity: given the same observation and action, the video expert generates a future that can be compared with what the robot actually did. A kinematic alignment score measures whether the generated robot motion follows the observed motion and selects predictions with substantial discrepancies for negative fine-tuning. This stage improves the video expert before its imagined consequences are used to judge sampled policy actions, reducing the risk that prediction errors become misleading training signals. 2) Action rejection uses the repaired video expert to judge what sampled actions are likely to achieve. With the expert frozen, we predict futures for sampled and demonstrated actions from the same initial observation, then compare their task progress using STEAM~ liu2026steam . Sampled actions whose predicted progress falls below the demonstrated reference by a prescribed margin are selected for negative fine-tuning, while demonstrations remain the positive targets. This directs policy updates toward actions with evidence of inferior consequences. Together, the two stages turn video prediction into feedback for policy post-training without additional environment interaction or changes to the inference procedure. We conduct an extensive empirical study across 50 RoboTwin~2.0 tasks and two real-world manipulation tasks, evaluating action fidelity, negative-selection accuracy, and downstream policy success. improves average success over action-conditioned Fast-WAM by 3.3 percentage points in simulation and raises average success on the long-horizon real-world Fold Shirt task from 0 with Fast-WAM to 87.5 . Predictions can also guide control through visual representations~ hu2024video or explicit motion plans: RoboFlow4D~ lin2026roboflow4d predicts multi-frame 3D motion to condition action generation. We build on Fast-WAM to use predicted consequences for policy post-training. Policy post-training. RECAP~ intelligence2025pi refines policies through advantage-conditioned learning from experience. title: PreAct-Nav: Agentic Reasoning Before Action for Urban Navigation
summary: Urban navigation requires embodied agents to pursue long-horizon goals through local decisions based on egocentric observations. However, existing agentic navigation methods often struggle to translate distant goals into coherent local decisions in large-scale physical environments. Their reliance on linguistic reasoning over transient observations or limited history constrains anticipation of the consequences of actions and future conditions, despite the importance of such foresight for navigating long and complex urban routes. To bridge this gap, we propose PreAct-Nav, an agentic navigation framework that equips frozen policies with anticipatory reasoning for robust urban navigation. Our central idea is to anchor local decisions in persistent medium-horizon subgoals, assess the consequences of predicted actions before execution, and continually update the reasoning context using actual outcomes. At its core, a navigation memory module maintains the active subgoal and relevant experience across decisions, translating distant goals into actionable intermediate objectives. We further introduce a predictive world sandbox that uses an action-conditioned world model (AC-WM) to forecast world dynamics conditioned on candidate movements. A vision-language model (VLM) reasoner interprets these predictions under the current subgoal to retain or revise actions. After execution, real observations are used to assess outcomes, correct inconsistent assumptions, and update memory to continue or reformulate the subgoal. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed PreAct-Nav improves action selection through memory updates and visual prediction, with more pronounced gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.

Introduction Urban navigation requires embodied agents to reach a destination described in language through a sequence of local movements~ Mei_2026 . The agent sees only part of its surroundings, while the route may extend beyond several intersections and turns. A locally feasible movement is therefore not necessarily useful for reaching the destination. As an example, the route in Figure~ fig:concept first requires approaching a crossing before continuing toward the goal. Thus, reliable navigation in such environment requires connecting such intermediate steps to the long-horizon goal while anticipating how local actions may affect subsequent progress. Recent language and vision-language models (VLMs) have enabled navigation agents to reason explicitly about instructions, observations, and possible actions~ zhou2024navgpt,long2024discussnav,ruan2026brain . Rather than directly executing a policy prediction, these agents use reasoning to assess where to move next. EvoNav~ dai2026evonav further incorporates historical experience and future thoughts by retrieving past experience and predicting subsequent actions and landmarks. These advances establish reasoning over experience as a practical way to improve navigation decisions. Despite this progress, connecting local reasoning to long-horizon navigation remains challenging in two respects. First, historical context records past observations and actions, but provides limited guidance for subsequent movements toward the long-horizon goal. Local decisions may therefore be reasonable in isolation yet inconsistent across steps. Second, reasoning about future actions and landmarks in language does not provide visual evidence of what a proposed movement might reveal. A passage that appears plausible from the current view may remain occluded or fail to lead toward the intended route. These limitations make it difficult to determine whether a locally plausible action will support progress toward the destination. In this paper, we propose , a training-free agentic reasoning harness that equips frozen navigation policies with anticipatory reasoning. Our central idea is to maintain medium-horizon subgoals to guide local decisions, evaluate proposed actions using predicted visual outcomes before execution, and update navigation memory using execution feedback. A shared VLM reasoner uses the current subgoal, relevant experience, and visual predictions to decide whether to retain or revise the proposed action. This reasoning loop connects action evaluation and revision before execution with memory updates afterward, without updating model weights. Specifically, the harness organizes a VLM reasoner and two callable tools into a four-stage reasoning loop (Figure~ fig:architecture ). During Action Preview, the reasoner reads Navigation Memory, which maintains the current subgoal and relevant experience across decisions. If the available evidence is insufficient, it queries the Predictive Sandbox, which uses an action-conditioned world model (AC-WM) to generate future views for the proposed movement~ Bar_2025_CVPR . During Action Review, the reasoner uses predicted visual cues to assess whether the proposed action makes progress toward the current subgoal. It retains a supported action or revises a contradicted one; a revised action returns to preview and review within a fixed reasoning budget. In Action Execute, the agent follows the accepted movement. Finally, Memory Update compares the expected cues with the next real observation, records the outcome, and updates subgoal progress for the next decision. By coordinating context, tool use, and execution feedback, the harness maintains medium-horizon guidance across local actions: prediction guides revision, and real feedback updates memory. We evaluate on UrbanNav with three navigation policies and two VLM reasoners. Our method achieves relative improvements of 6.71 in success rate (SR) and 4.19 in success weighted by path length (SPL) over the benchmark's original policy. Experiments with other policies and reasoners further assess its applicability beyond a single backbone. Component ablations and analyses of individual decisions examine the roles of memory and prediction, with larger prediction gains on longer routes and routes with more turns. In summary, our contributions are: We introduce , a training-free navigation harness that reviews and revises policy actions using memory and visual prediction before execution. We develop Navigation Memory to maintain medium-horizon subgoals alongside observed experience and update their progress through execution feedback. We expose an action-conditioned world model as a Predictive Sandbox, providing future visual cues for action reasoning under the current subgoal. We evaluate the harness across navigation policies and VLM reasoners, with component ablations and analyses of memory, prediction, and navigation difficulty. Related Work Navigation reasoning. Vision-and-language navigation grounds instructions in observed scenes, from navigation graphs to continuous environments~ anderson2018vln,krantz2020vlnce . Learned policies translate observations and goals into local movements~ Mei_2026,sridhar2024nomad,hirose2026omnivla , while CityWalker learns urban navigation from web videos~ liu2025citywalker . LM-Nav composes pretrained models without fine-tuning~ shah2023lmnav , while CompassNav supervises feasible-action decisions~ li2026compassnav . Explicit reasoning supports instruction interpretation~ zhou2024navgpt,qiao2025opennav , multi-expert assessment~ long2024discussnav , and retrieved experience with future thoughts~ dai2026evonav . ReAct and Inner Monologue interleave reasoning with feedback~ yao2023react,pmlr-v205-huang23c , while Toolformer learns when and how to call tools~ schick2023toolformer . Our frozen reasoner coordinates memory and prediction through a harness to review and revise movements before execution. Agent memory. Memory enables agents to reuse experience without encoding every interaction in model weights. Reflexion stores verbal reflections~ NEURIPS2023_1b44b878 , REMem retrieves temporally grounded events~ ICLR2026_5b93eda3 , and M3-Agent builds multimodal episodic and semantic memories~ long2026m3agent . Agentic Context Engineering incrementally updates contextual playbooks using execution feedback~ zhang2026ace . In navigation, DUET combines a growing topological map with local observations~ chen2022duet , and PanoNav retains exploration history to avoid repeated local deadlocks~ Jin_2026 . Our Navigation Memory couples observed experience with an active medium-horizon subgoal that provides shared context for action review and revision. Execution feedback updates its objective and progress cues, so memory tracks both past outcomes and the current purpose of navigation. Action-conditioned world models. Video generation provides a visual representation of future plans: UniPi generates goal-conditioned videos and extracts control actions from them~ du2023unipi . Action-conditioned world models instead predict observations for a specified movement. Navigation World Models use such predictions to plan paths or rank proposed trajectories~ Bar_2025_CVPR , while Cosmos Policy fine-tunes video models for visuomotor control and planning~ kim2026cosmospolicy . In computer-use agents, R-WoM grounds language-model simulations in retrieved tutorials~ mei2026rwom . Access to a world model, however, does not ensure effective use of its predictions~ qian-etal-2026-current . Our focus is how visual prediction informs navigation reasoning. The Predictive Sandbox exposes the world model as a callable tool; the VLM interprets predicted visual cues against the current subgoal to retain or revise a movement. Real observations subsequently establish progress and update memory, linking predictive reasoning to execution feedback. title: DiVeR: Decision-Critical Verifier Learning for VLA Test-Time Scaling
summary: Scaling robot data and model capacity has improved Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, but further progress is constrained by the high cost of robotic data. Verifier-guided test-time scaling offers an efficient alternative by sampling multiple action candidates and selecting the one most likely to lead to task success at inference time. Existing classification-based verifiers learn from trajectory-level outcomes but treat all visited states equally, even though their value for candidate discrimination can vary across a trajectory. At many states, plausible actions are similar and provide limited discrimination signal, while only a sparse set of decision-critical states admits meaningfully different actions that can substantially affect downstream outcomes. To address this, we propose DiVeR, which estimates decision criticality from the dispersion of sampled action representations. DiVeR then uses this signal to reweight verifier learning toward states where action selection is most consequential, without requiring step-level annotations or additional environment interaction. Across LIBERO, RoboCasa, and real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 robot, DiVeR consistently improves task success through more effective verifier-guided action selection, while adding negligible verifier inference overhead.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi_,intelligence2025pi,bjorck2025gr00t learn generalist robot policies from large-scale multimodal demonstrations, but further scaling remains limited by the high cost of robotic data collection~ ma2026survey . Test-Time Scaling (TTS) ~ snell2024scaling,jang2025verifier,kwok2025robomonkey offers a complementary route to improving VLA performance without collecting new demonstrations or retraining the base policy. Rather than executing a single sampled action, a pretrained VLA can be viewed as a stochastic generator that proposes multiple candidate action chunks at each decision step. Since this distribution may contain both successful and unsuccessful continuations, a verifier can rank the candidates and select the one most likely to make task progress. This naturally leads to verifier-guided Best-of-N (BoN) sampling, a generator--verifier framework that converts additional inference-time computation into better action selection. A practical approach to verifier learning is to train lightweight classification-based verifiers~ yang2025steering,tsao2026learning,attarian2026update from trajectory-level success and failure outcomes, avoiding costly step-level supervision~ zhang2026progress and the inference overhead of external VLM-based judges~ liang2026robometer,kwok2025robomonkey,kwok2026llm . However, existing approaches propagate each trajectory outcome uniformly across all visited states or state–action pairs, implicitly treating them as equally informative for candidate discrimination. This assumption can be problematic in long horizon robotic execution, where the informativeness of trajectory-level supervision for candidate discrimination can vary substantially across states. Our key observation is that not all states are equally consequential for action selection. As illustrated in~ (a), at states such as free-space motion or post-grasp transport, sampled action candidates remain highly similar. We refer to these as routine states , where candidate selection is relatively inconsequential and provides limited signal for learning to discriminate among actions. In contrast, at decision-critical states , such as pre-grasp or pre-placement alignment, plausible candidates diverge more strongly, and small differences in action choice can substantially affect downstream outcomes. (b) further shows that such high-criticality states are sparse and temporally localized rather than uniformly distributed throughout a trajectory. This pattern echoes findings in language generation, where only a sparse subset of high-entropy minority tokens can lead to divergent continuations and steer generation toward distinct downstream trajectories~ wang2026beyond . Together, these observations suggest that uniformly weighting all visited states can dilute the supervision signal from the relatively few states where accurate candidate discrimination matters most. In this paper, we introduce , a Decision-criticality-weighted VeRifier for VLA test-time scaling that focuses learning on states where action selection matters most. Our key idea is to estimate decision criticality from disagreement among plausible actions under the frozen VLA policy. At each visited state, we sample multiple action candidates and measure the dispersion of their action-expert representations. Low dispersion characterizes routine states where the policy proposes similar behaviors, whereas high dispersion identifies states where plausible actions diverge and candidate selection can substantially affect downstream outcomes. This provides a practical proxy for decision criticality without requiring step-level supervision or additional environment interaction. uses this signal to reweight the verifier objective, concentrating trajectory-level supervision on states where accurate candidate discrimination is most consequential. We evaluate on two simulated manipulation benchmarks and a real-world robotic platform using and . Across policies and environments, improves task success by up to +13.6 over single sample inference and +3.4 over the strongest baseline. Notably, also surpasses the VLM-based verifier by +4.6 success rate while reducing verifier inference latency by over . These results demonstrate the effectiveness of focusing verifier learning on the sparse states where candidate differences matter most. Our key contributions are summarized as follows: We identify a limitation of uniform verifier training, showing that routine states dominate trajectories while providing limited signal for candidate discrimination, whereas sparse decision-critical states are more consequential for action selection. We propose , a novel decision-criticality-weighted verifier that uses action-expert representation variance as a practical proxy for decision criticality and places greater emphasis on states with stronger candidate disagreement. We validate across simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, demonstrating consistent improvements in task success through more effective verifier-guided Best-of-\(N\) action selection, with negligible verifier overhead at inference. Recent approaches further improve these policies along several complementary directions, including geometry-aware representations that enhance 3D spatial understanding~ qu2025spatialvla, li2026pointvla , memory mechanisms for long-horizon tasks~ shi2025memoryvla, torne2026mem, sridhar2025memer , and world models that capture environment dynamics~ ye2026world, cen2025rynnvla, gao2026dreamdojo . While effective, these directions strengthen the policy itself and thus require additional data collection, architectural modification, or retraining. In contrast, we treat the pretrained VLA as a frozen stochastic action generator and improve its execution purely at inference time, making our approach complementary to these advances. Focusing supervision on these forking tokens can therefore yield disproportionate gains, suggesting that the value of supervision may vary across a trajectory. Accordingly, we focus verifier learning on these sparse states rather than treating all states uniformly. Test-time Scaling in VLAs. title: A Unified Dynamics Framework for Reinforcement Learning and Classical Control of a Six-DOF Pipeline-Tracking ROV in NVIDIA Isaac Sim
summary: Reinforcement learning controllers for underwater vehicles are usually trained against one physics representation and deployed against another, so reported performance does not always describe behavior outside training. This paper presents a pipeline-tracking architecture for a six-degree-of-freedom remotely operated vehicle (ROV) in which one Universal Scene Description (USD) scene supplies the real BlueROV2-Heavy mass, added-mass, damping, buoyancy, and thruster parameters to both halves of the system: a vectorized NumPy implementation of Fossen's marine-craft equations, and an interactive NVIDIA Isaac Sim deployment applying the identical equations as PhysX forces at every step. The Coriolis-centripetal term is the primary dynamics model in both branches; a controlled ablation on PPO and TRPO shows that including it does not destabilize either algorithm and modestly improves tracking, about 19 percent lower standoff RMS error for TRPO. Five reinforcement learning algorithms, PPO, soft actor-critic, TD3, DDPG, and TRPO, are trained against one environment, reward, and randomized evaluation harness through a checkpoint-compatibility layer scoring any policy with the same code. The pipeline is extended with six classical baselines, PID, sliding-mode, fuzzy logic, feedback linearization, model predictive control, and an adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system, driven by the same guidance geometry and thruster allocation as the learned policies. Under Coriolis-enabled dynamics, PPO, TRPO, and feedback linearization reach the strongest combination of 100 percent success and competitive accuracy; PID, fuzzy control, and the neuro-fuzzy baseline also reach 100 percent success with looser tracking; DDPG and TD3 each show a specific, explainable failure mode rather than a general weakness of off-policy learning; and classical control remains a strong baseline against the best learned policies.
full_text: A Unified Dynamics Framework for Reinforcement Learning and Classical Control of a Six-DOF Pipeline-Tracking ROV in NVIDIA Isaac Sim Cheng~Siong~Chin, M.~Venkateshkumar, and Jianhua~Zhang Chin et al.: Unified Fossen-Dynamics Framework for RL and Classical Control of a Pipeline-Tracking ROV Reinforcement learning controllers for underwater vehicles are usually trained against one physics representation and, when a live simulator or hardware is available, deployed against another, so reported tracking performance does not always describe what the controller will do once it leaves the training environment. This paper reports a pipeline-tracking control architecture for a six-degree-of-freedom remotely operated vehicle (ROV) in which a single Universal Scene Description (USD) scene supplies the real BlueROV2-Heavy mass, added-mass, damping, buoyancy, and eight-thruster allocation parameters to both halves of the system: a vectorized NumPy implementation of Fossen's marine-craft equations, and an interactive NVIDIA Isaac Sim deployment in which the identical equations are applied as forces to a PhysX rigid body at every physics step. The Coriolis-centripetal coupling term C( ) is included as the primary dynamics model in both branches, and a controlled ablation restricted to proximal policy optimization (PPO) and trust region policy optimization (TRPO) shows that including the term does not destabilize either algorithm and modestly improves tracking accuracy, an approximately 19 percent reduction in standoff root-mean-square error for TRPO. Five reinforcement learning algorithms, PPO, soft actor-critic (SAC), twin-delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3), deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG), and TRPO, are trained against an identical environment, reward, and 30-episode randomized evaluation harness through a checkpoint-compatibility layer that lets any trained policy be scored by the same evaluation code. The same shared-dynamics pipeline is extended with six classical and model-based control baselines, proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control, sliding-mode control, fuzzy logic control, feedback linearization, model predictive control, and an adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS), each driven by the identical guidance geometry and thruster-allocation map as the learned policies, so that any performance difference reflects the control law itself. Under Coriolis-enabled dynamics, PPO, TRPO, and feedback linearization achieve the strongest combination of a 100 percent success rate and competitive-to-best tracking accuracy; PID, fuzzy logic control, and the ANFIS surrogate also reach 100 percent success with somewhat looser tracking; DDPG and TD3 each show a specific, explainable failure mode rather than a general weakness of off-policy learning; and classical, model-based control remains a strong, competitive, low-cost baseline against the best learned policies on this task. reinforcement learning, remotely operated vehicle, proximal policy optimization, soft actor-critic, twin-delayed deep deterministic policy gradient, deep deterministic policy gradient, trust region policy optimization, sliding-mode control, fuzzy logic control, feedback linearization, model predictive control, adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS), NVIDIA Isaac Sim, NVIDIA Omniverse. Introduction Subsea pipelines carry oil, gas, and slurry across seabeds that divers and tethered inspection vehicles cannot reach cheaply or safely, and the standard inspection task for a remotely operated vehicle (ROV) is to fly a fixed standoff distance above the pipeline while avoiding rock outcrops and the seafloor itself b1 . The six coupled degrees of freedom of an underwater vehicle, surge, sway, heave, roll, pitch, and yaw, make the task difficult to hand-code, since damping, added mass, Coriolis-centripetal coupling, and buoyancy interact nonlinearly with vehicle attitude b2 . Reinforcement learning (RL) offers an alternative to hand-tuned controllers: a policy trained against a physics model learns the coupling directly from reward signal rather than from a linearized approximation of it, and recent work reports reinforcement-learning controllers b3,b4,b5 that track paths, hold depth, and dock autonomous underwater vehicles under disturbances that defeat a fixed-gain proportional-integral-derivative loop. Most of this work is validated inside the same simulator used for training, with a single algorithm, and rarely against a classical or model-based controller built from the same dynamics model. A policy is trained and evaluated against one instance of a dynamics model, sometimes with domain randomization applied to the model's own parameters, and the paper reports how that policy performed inside the training loop b6,b7 . Whether the same policy behaves identically once handed to a different physics engine, whether a reported result generalizes across the family of algorithms used for continuous control, and whether a learned policy actually outperforms a well-tuned classical controller given the same dynamics model and guidance geometry, are typically left open b8 . NVIDIA Isaac Sim narrows the first question for many robot classes by pairing a GPU-accelerated PhysX engine with a Universal Scene Description (USD) scene graph that serves as a single source of truth for a robot's geometry and physical parameters b9,b10 , and a recent underwater-specific extension, MarineGym, adapts Isaac Sim's physics backbone to marine hydrodynamics at high simulation throughput b11 . A worked architecture in which the same, Coriolis-coupled equations of motion, read from one parameter set, drive a vectorized trainer, an interactive deployment scene, and a shared bank of classical baselines alike, has not been reported for a pipeline-tracking task. This paper builds a USD scene encoding a 6-DOF ROV's mass, added mass, linear and quadratic damping, buoyancy, and eight-thruster allocation matrix as scene attributes, parsed by two independent code paths: a NumPy-vectorized implementation of Fossen's marine-craft dynamics b2 , with the Coriolis-centripetal coupling term C( ) included as part of the default governing equation, integrated with a fixed-step fourth-order Runge-Kutta scheme across 64 parallel environments; and an interactive Isaac Sim deployment in which a controller reads the live PhysX pose and velocity of the rigid body at every physics step, computes the identical Coriolis, damping, thruster, and buoyancy terms, and applies them as a body-frame force and torque, letting PhysX integrate the vehicle in place of a second Runge-Kutta solver. A controlled ablation, restricted to two of the five compared reinforcement-learning algorithms, shows that including this term is safe and modestly beneficial, motivating its use as the primary model throughout rather than as a simplification to be engineered around. Against this Coriolis-inclusive architecture, five reinforcement learning algorithms are derived, trained, and evaluated: PPO b12 with generalized advantage estimation b13 , SAC b14 , TD3 b15 , DDPG b16 , and TRPO b17 , scored through a single checkpoint-compatibility layer built around PPO's own evaluation code; and six classical and model-based controllers, PID, sliding-mode control, fuzzy logic control, feedback linearization, model predictive control, and an adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system, are added as baselines under the identical guidance geometry and thruster-allocation map, so that any performance difference reflects the control law rather than the task setup. Sections III through V present the shared architecture, dynamics, and RL environment; Sections VI and VII derive the five reinforcement-learning algorithms; Section VIII presents the six classical and model-based baselines; Section IX describes the Isaac Sim deployment; Sections X and XI give the evaluation protocol and the resulting comparison; Section XII discusses the comparison and its limitations. Related Work Guidance and control for underwater vehicles Line-of-sight guidance coupled with proportional-integral-derivative or sliding-mode control remains the reference approach for autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) path following; a recent survey documents three decades of refinements to the guidance law, from constant look-ahead distance to adaptive and time-varying variants that cope with current disturbances b1 . These methods are computationally cheap and well understood, but each new disturbance model or actuator constraint typically requires a new stability proof, and the resulting controllers do not adapt online to dynamics they were not designed against. Reinforcement learning for underwater tracking and following Deep deterministic policy gradient and its twin-delayed variant have been used for AUV path following and depth tracking under current disturbance, with reported reductions in cross-track error of up to two-thirds relative to a PID baseline once a recurrent state encoder and a learnable guidance parameter are added b4 . Proximal policy optimization has been used for three-degree-of-freedom motion planning without a prior disturbance model b8 , and soft actor-critic variants, sometimes combined with a long short-term memory encoder, produce adaptive trajectory-tracking controllers for underwater vehicles b18,b19 . Obstacle-aware extensions add a real-time avoidance term to the reward or the action space, closer to the pipeline-tracking task addressed here, since a policy that only tracks a centerline still routes around fixed and moving obstacles b20 . Across this literature, a learned policy generalizes across current strength and payload changes that would require re-derivation of a classical controller; the recurring gap is that a policy is validated inside the dynamics model it was trained against, with sim-to-real or sim-to-sim transfer left as future work b3,b5 , that a single algorithm is typically reported per task, and that a classical baseline built from the same dynamics model is rarely reported alongside the learned policy. Off-policy and trust-region continuous control DDPG combines a deterministic policy with an actor-critic architecture and a replay buffer, extending value-based deep reinforcement learning to continuous action spaces, and is sensitive to function-approximation error in its single critic and to exploration-noise scale b16 . TD3 addresses this with twin critics under clipped double-Q learning, delayed policy updates, and target-policy smoothing noise, reporting more stable learning than DDPG on standard continuous-control benchmarks b15 . SAC frames the objective as maximum-entropy reinforcement learning, adding an entropy bonus to the reward and automatically tuning the temperature coefficient against a target entropy b14 . TRPO constrains each policy update to a trust region bounded by the Kullback-Leibler divergence between successive policies, computed via a conjugate-gradient approximation to the natural gradient and enforced with a backtracking line search, and is the on-policy predecessor PPO's clipped surrogate objective was designed to approximate more cheaply b17 . Comparisons spanning all of these families against one environment, reward, and evaluation code are less common than single-algorithm reports, which motivates the comparison undertaken here. Simulation platforms and the sim-to-real gap Purpose-built underwater simulators such as HoloOcean and UNav-Sim provide photorealistic rendering and sensor models for AUV research but were not designed for the throughput population-based reinforcement learning needs b21,b22 . General-purpose GPU-accelerated simulators built for terrestrial and aerial robots, most visibly Isaac Gym and its successor Isaac Sim, solved the throughput problem by vectorizing physics and observation computation on the GPU b9,b23 . title: PB-STDG: A Prediction-Based Short-Term Decentralized Greedy Guidance Algorithm for a Drone Road System
summary: In recent years, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) or drones have been increasingly adopted in urban environments for applications such as parcel delivery, infrastructure inspection, emergency response, and drone light shows. A non-negligible issue is how to manage the increasing number of drones operated by different entities, to enable them to cooperatively avoid potential collisions and determine conflict-free short-term flight paths in urban airspace. This paper presents a Prediction-Based Short-Term Decentralized Greedy (PB-STDG) guidance algorithm for a structured Drone Road System (DRS). PB-STDG extends the original STDG algorithm by introducing a prediction mechanism that enables drones to anticipate the decisions of neighboring drones using additional information shared in beacon packets, aiming to address the over-conservative behavior observed in the STDG algorithm. Several simulation scenarios are conducted to evaluate and compare the proposed algorithm with STDG. The results show that PB-STDG improves traffic efficiency while maintaining a safety level comparable to that of STDG.

Drone, Congestion Control, Guidance and Navigation, Road System, Wireless Communication numbers,open= [ ,close= ] Introduction Continuous advances in drones, or unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), technology have significantly expanded the range of drone applications, attracting growing interest from both academia and industry. Although drones were initially developed for military operations ko2021drone, bousquet2018eye , their applications have gradually expanded into a wide range of civilian and commercial fields, such as aerial photography jung2022improved,ri2024drone,xiao2022aerial , emergency response soni2024medical , and infrastructure inspection lekidis2022electricity, raja2022adversarial . More recently, drone applications have expanded into delivery and entertainment. Commercial drone delivery services are now being used for last-mile parcel distribution by companies such as Amazon Prime Air amazon_prime_air and Google Wing wing_delivery . Food delivery by drones has also entered commercial operation in cities including Shenzhen, China, where Meituan operates urban drone delivery routes meituan_drone . Beyond delivery, large-scale drone light shows have become a popular feature of public celebrations, such as the drone show program at Darling Harbour in Sydney darling_harbour_drone , where coordinated drone swarms are deployed for regular night-time performances. With the growth of these drone applications, the number of deployed drones is continuously increasing dii2025 . These drones generally share the same low-altitude airspace, particularly in urban environments. Unlike traditional ground traffic systems, most current drone operations are conducted in an unstructured and free-flight manner. Each drone independently plans its trajectory based on its own algorithms and available information. Although such an approach provides flexibility, it becomes increasingly difficult to maintain safety and manage large-scale drone operations involving different operators and service providers. Conflicts between competing flight paths may lead to traffic congestion or even collisions as the number of drones increases, which can degrade overall system efficiency and pose risks to public safety. To address this challenge, several studies on structured airspace management have been proposed, aiming to organize low-altitude airspace into predefined aerial structures and constrain drone movements within them. A representative example is the NASA drone traffic management concept jang2017concepts . In this framework, the low-altitude airspace is organized into multiple layers based on altitude. High-speed fixed-wing UAVs are typically assigned to higher layers, while low-speed rotary-wing UAVs operate in lower layers. Within each layer, the airspace is further structured into different types of aerial structures, including sky-corridors, sky-tubes, and sky-lanes. Drones are allowed to fly freely within sky-corridors, whereas sky-tubes impose directional constraints on movement. Sky-lanes provide an additional level of restriction by regulating lateral motion, preventing drones from cruising in parallel within the same lane. Several studies have explored layer-based approaches for drone traffic management, using different altitude layers to regulate drone movement and heading directions aerospace8020038,svaigen2022biomixd,9256627 . Other studies have proposed more structured drone road systems inspired by ground transportation networks, including corridor-based and lane-level structures ijgi10050338,9476745 . Building on these concepts, qu2025drone proposes a Drone Road System framework consisting of structured roads and ramps. All road segments are designed to be unidirectional, with a defined number of lanes and an allowed speed range, to support safe and predictable drone movement. The system can also be encoded in XML format, enabling flexible updates and efficient distribution across different platforms. While drone traffic management systems such as drone road systems provide a structured framework for organizing low-altitude airspace, conflicts between drones can still occur within the constrained network, particularly under high-density traffic conditions. In such environments, drones may compete for optimal routes, and different types of conflicts may arise due to speed differences or directional changes during navigation. Therefore, effective drone guidance and collision avoidance mechanisms remain essential. A large body of research has been devoted to UAV navigation and collision avoidance in free-flight environments. These include approaches such as farid2022modified and wang2022trajectory , which determine short-term collision-free paths for UAVs in environments containing obstacles and other dynamic constraints. The Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) approach abhishek2020hybrid iteratively updates drone positions based on individual and global best solutions. Another widely studied approach is Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) han2025deep, almahamid2025agile, liu2025flexible , which learns drone control policies through interaction with the environment. These methods typically use sensory inputs such as images, video streams, or onboard sensor data to generate control actions via deep neural networks. By optimizing a reward function, drones can learn collision-free navigation in dynamic and complex environments. Specifically, several studies have investigated safe guidance and collision avoidance algorithms for drone delivery scenarios. In droneincity3 , three collision avoidance strategies are proposed to manage large numbers of drones delivering goods to random destinations in urban environments. Similarly, droneincity1 presents a centralized navigation approach for a fleet of drones to achieve safe point-to-point parcel delivery missions. In addition, droneincity2 introduces two centralized algorithms to ensure safe delivery operations within a simplified two-layer airspace structure. However, these approaches suffer from several limitations: (i) they often rely on global information of other agents, (ii) they require multiple types of onboard sensors, and (iii) they are primarily designed for free-flight environments and cannot be directly adapted to structured airspace systems. In the large-scale drone traffic system we focus on, where drones are owned by different operators and perform diverse tasks, these limitations become more critical. Specifically, global coordination is difficult to achieve in practice, as it is unrealistic for each drone to obtain or maintain global knowledge of all other drones in the city-scale airspace. Moreover, different navigation algorithms across different drones further increase system uncertainty, since individual drones are unable to accurately predict the behavior of others under inconsistent or unknown algorithms. They will also make different assumptions about the available sensors, and in this paper, we make very minimal assumptions, requiring only GPS and wireless communication. Based on these challenges and assumptions, a research gap can be identified in the guidance of large-scale drone traffic under limited coordination. Existing approaches often rely on assumptions about the available sensing, communication, or coordination capabilities of drones. However, in a large-scale drone road system, drones may be operated by different manufacturers or service providers and may therefore have limited ability to coordinate with one another. There is therefore a need for a guidance approach that can manage interactions among a large number of independently operating drones without relying on extensive coordination or additional sensing capabilities. To address this research gap, a baseline guidance algorithm for structured drone road systems is required that can be applied to different types of drones while relying on minimal information and limited sensing capabilities. In our previous studies drones6120411, qu2026stdg , STDG was proposed to address drone route navigation and collision avoidance challenges on the standardized Drone Road System introduced in qu2025drone . The STDG algorithm relies only on position and velocity information exchanged between drones through beacon packets, and provides short-term, coordination-free, and decentralized guidance. Drones periodically execute STDG to make short-term lane and speed decisions based on the current traffic conditions and potential collision risks. Previous simulation results for STDG revealed a key limitation: significant speed loss when avoiding potential collisions. Since the algorithm is coordination-free (i.e., drones only exchange beacon packets, with no other form of coordination) and only position and velocity information is shared, it is difficult for drones to accurately estimate or predict the decisions of others. As a result, lane switching may be suppressed when multiple neighboring drones simultaneously select the same lane to switch. In such cases, drones tend to remain in their current lanes and may further reduce their speed or even come to a complete stop until the surrounding traffic conditions change. This behavior significantly degrades traffic throughput and system efficiency. In our previous study, the algorithm settings that allow some potential risks to be disregarded result in an increase in average speed from around 7 m/s to 10 m/s, approaching the preferred speed of 12.5 m/s, with only a slight increase in the collision rate (i.e., from 1 to 5 collisions among 150,000 drones). The results show that STDG has room to improve its average speed, as a substantial speed increase can be achieved by slightly relaxing its treatment of potential collision risks with only a small increase in actual collisions. This motivates the prediction of neighboring drones' future actions to better distinguish potential risks from likely collisions, thus allowing drones to make more effective lane-switching and speed-selection decisions without unnecessary stops or slowdowns and avoiding additional collisions that may occur in such situations. In this paper, we focus on designing a prediction-based extension to the previous STDG guidance algorithm. title: Vela: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models with Adaptive Action Curve Parametrization
summary: Most vision-language-action models represent future motion as fixed-rate action chunks, tying temporal resolution and prediction horizon to a fixed output budget. This pointwise representation wastes capacity on highly correlated neighboring actions, leaves temporal continuity and smoothness to be learned implicitly, and forces a tradeoff between long-horizon coverage and the local precision required for contact-rich manipulation. To address these limitations, we introduce Vela, a vision-language-action foundation model that represents future robot behavior as continuous trajectories. Vela combines a compact spline-based action representation with motion-dependent temporal support and a shared action interface for heterogeneous embodiments, allowing a fixed output budget to adapt its temporal resolution across motions. We pretrain Vela on large-scale multi-embodiment robot data and evaluate it on LIBERO-X, EBench, and two real-world long-horizon tasks, egg-cake cooking and potato shredding, obtaining promising results across simulation and physical manipulation. These results highlight the potential of continuous action representations as a foundation for future embodied foundation models. Project page and more results: https://clementine24.github.io/Vela/ .

Introduction Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models are rapidly scaling to larger datasets, broader task distributions, and more diverse robot embodiments~ intelligence2026pi,yuan2026qwen,ma2026internvla . Yet most VLAs still represent future motion as a fixed-length sequence of actions sampled on a predetermined temporal grid. This pointwise interface assigns separate prediction capacity to highly correlated neighboring actions and couples the output budget to both prediction horizon and temporal resolution: representing a longer future requires more action points, while a fixed budget forces coarser sampling. Conversely, spreading the same budget over a long horizon can remove the local precision needed for contact-rich manipulation. Because temporal continuity is learned implicitly, execution also relies on a predefined sampling grid. These limitations reflect a mismatch between current VLA representations and the objects they control: robot actions are not isolated points but samples from continuous motions. A trajectory-level representation provides a more natural action space. Instead of predicting every temporal sample, a policy can predict a compact set of parameters that defines a continuous trajectory and query that trajectory at the desired temporal locations. This representation compresses correlated actions, exposes temporal continuity, and decouples trajectory geometry from the time span over which it is executed. The same fixed parameter budget can therefore describe a long, smooth motion or a short, finely resolved one, while supporting different control frequencies. Splines provide a practical realization of this idea: a small set of control points specifies a continuous curve that can be evaluated on arbitrary temporal grids. Trajectory-level representations have a long history in robotics, including dynamical and probabilistic movement primitives~ ijspeert2013dynamical,paraschos2013probabilistic . Recent learning-based policies have explored dynamical-system parameterizations~ bahl2020ndp , differentiable trajectory optimization~ wan2024difftori , and geometric curve representations~ li2026gpi . Spline-based policies have further studied compact action tokenization, asynchronous execution, and temporal rescaling~ zhou2026beast,yang2026abpolicy,han2026b . These studies show the value of structured motion representations, but they mainly focus on task-specific policies, individual robot platforms, or downstream action tokenization and execution. Whether trajectory-level action modeling can serve as the output space for foundation-scale VLA pretraining across large, heterogeneous robot datasets remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we build a VLA that learns future motion in trajectory space and make this representation trainable at foundation scale. A shared cross-embodiment action interface and scalable supervision procedure allow the same model to absorb heterogeneous robot corpora. We further make the temporal span of each prediction motion-dependent: with a fixed number of spline control points, each demonstrated motion is assigned a sample-specific horizon by selecting the longest span that adequately represents it under a noise-aware criterion. Smooth motions can therefore use longer spans, whereas motions with rapid local variation can use shorter spans without changing the output budget. We train this framework on large multi-embodiment robot data and evaluate its transfer to downstream manipulation tasks. Our main contributions are: We show how trajectory-space action modeling can be scaled to VLA pretraining through a shared cross-embodiment action interface and a training procedure designed for large heterogeneous robot corpora. We introduce motion-dependent horizon adaptation, selecting for each demonstrated motion the longest temporal span that a fixed spline budget can represent under a noise-aware criterion. We evaluate the framework with controlled comparisons, downstream manipulation benchmarks, and ablations, showing improvements from trajectory-space modeling, large-scale pretraining, and horizon adaptation, particularly under contact-rich, long-horizon, and distribution-shifted tasks. Related Work -Language-Action Foundation Models. Extensive research on vision-language models has advanced cross-modal alignment and downstream visual reasoning~ li2024unified, li2025revseg . Building on this progress, vision-language-action (VLA) foundation models scale robot learning across heterogeneous tasks, data, and embodiments by coupling pretrained vision-language representations~ beyer2024paligemma,bai2025qwen3 with generalist action policies~ team2024octo,black2024pi_0,bjorck2025gr00t . Recent systems further improve cross-task and cross-embodiment generalization through heterogeneous co-training, embodiment alignment, and predictive supervision~ intelligence2025pi_, intelligence2026pi, yuan2026qwen, zheng2026x, cai2026internvla, ma2026internvla, zhou2026tau0wm, wang2026mvista4d ; related robot-control work also studies structured visual representations~ jiang2026learning,wang2024gsrl . Yet the low-level motion interface of modern chunk-based VLAs remains largely organized around fixed-resolution sequences of sampled future actions. Recent work begins to relax this temporal rigidity: MoH~ jing2025mixture models multiple prediction horizons, while AutoHorizon~ wang2026vla and AAC~ liang2026adaptive use attention patterns and action entropy to determine execution lengths. These methods still operate on sampled action sequences. In contrast, makes temporal support part of the action representation itself, using a fixed set of control points to parameterize continuous trajectories with motion-adaptive future spans. -Based Robot Policies. Structured representations of robot motion have long been studied through dynamical and probabilistic movement primitives~ ijspeert2013dynamical,paraschos2013probabilistic . Recent work incorporates splines into learned policies for efficient action tokenization ~ zhou2026beast , asynchronous execution~ yang2026abpolicy , and structured action generation across policy backbones~ tian2026spline . B-spline Policy~ han2026b accelerates visuomotor policies through adaptive spline fitting and temporal rescaling. These works primarily study splines as policy-level representations, tokenizers, or execution interfaces. To our knowledge, is the first VLA foundation model established in trajectory space through large-scale pretraining on multi-embodiment robot data. Our framework is designed to support this scaling: a unified action interface accommodates heterogeneous embodiments, while a noise-calibrated horizon procedure constructs spline targets on the fly. Together, constructs consistent trajectory targets from heterogeneous datasets, investigates spline trajectories as the output space of a foundation model. Methodology sec:methodology We develop by treating demonstrated actions as samples of a continuous trajectory and learning to predict a compact representation of that trajectory. Building on this formulation, we describe the policy, construct motion-dependent horizons, and scale training to heterogeneous robot data. title: Sparse-View 4D Gaussian Splatting via Spatiotemporal Priors and Generative Assistance
comment: 4 pages, 5 figures, Accepted to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Workshops (SA Workshops '26)
summary: We present a 4D Gaussian Splatting framework for the Sparse-View Track of the SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Volumetric Video Challenge, which requires dynamic scene reconstruction from only six cameras with wide baselines. To achieve robust dynamic reconstruction under such sparse views, our framework integrates three components. (1) Region-adaptive spatial priors: We use foreground masks to guide Gaussian initialization and mask voting to control densification separately for the dynamic foreground and static background. Background geometry is regularized using monocular depth aligned to metric scale. (2) Motion-consistent temporal priors: We provide supervision at intermediate times through frame interpolation and constrain projected Gaussian motion with estimated optical flow. (3) Generative assistance: We place virtual cameras in the widest angular gaps and restore their rendered images using a diffusion-based model conditioned on camera poses. The restored images are iteratively incorporated into training as pseudo-supervision. On the validation set, our framework improves full-frame PSNR from 25.60 dB for the baseline to 29.75 dB. On the official test benchmark, it achieves 30.04 dB full-frame PSNR and 27.88 dB foreground PSNR, ranking first overall in the Sparse-View Track.

The Sparse-View Track of the SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Volumetric Video Challenge challenges this reliance by requiring dynamic reconstruction from only six wide-baseline cameras. Under such sparse-view settings, 4DGS reconstruction faces three interrelated challenges. ~ : Uniform densification can overpopulate the background, which occupies most image pixels, while leaving the dynamic foreground underrepresented. This imbalance can lead to background overfitting and degrade foreground rendering at novel viewpoints. ~ : Rapid motion can produce blur and large inter-frame displacements, while residual timing differences across cameras cause nominally simultaneous images to capture different motion states. These factors limit the reliability of photometric supervision for continuous motion reconstruction. ~ : Wide angular gaps and occlusions leave some regions weakly observed or unseen. Holes and incomplete structures may therefore persist despite improved capacity allocation and motion regularization. To address these interrelated challenges, we combine three complementary components (Fig.~ fig:pipeline ): ~ (Sec.~ sec:spatial ) use foreground masks to guide initialization, mask voting to adapt densification, and monocular depth aligned to metric scale to regularize background geometry. ~ (Sec.~ sec:temporal ) provide supervision between captured frames through interpolation and constrain projected Gaussian velocities with estimated optical flow. ~ (Sec.~ sec:gen ) places virtual cameras in the widest angular gaps, restores their rendered images using ArtiFixer~ delutio2026artifixer , and iteratively incorporates the restored views into training as pseudo-supervision. Extensive validation confirms that our framework effectively stabilizes sparse dynamic reconstruction, ultimately earning 1 place in the official Sparse-View Track. Region-Adaptive Spatial Priors sec:spatial We build on spatiotemporal Gaussians~ yang2026imvid , where each primitive has a temporal center , a temporal extent , and a 3D velocity . We precompute two scene priors: per-frame foreground masks obtained using YOLO11~ jocher2023ultralytics and tracked with SAM~2~ ravi2024sam2 , and monocular depth predictions from DA2~ yang2024depthanythingv2 . The masks guide Gaussian initialization and densification separately for the foreground and background, while the depth predictions regularize background geometry. Per-Frame Dynamic Initialization sec:init Following~ wang2025freetimegs , we initialize Gaussian primitives by triangulating multi-view correspondences obtained with RoMa~ edstedt2024roma . Foreground primitives are initialized at every frame, with temporal centers and short temporal extents to capture localized motion. In contrast, background primitives are initialized every frames with larger temporal extents . Parameter values are provided in Sec.~ sec:impl . Mask-Voting Densification sec:densify During training, we update each primitive's foreground or background label through multi-view mask voting, using the tolerance introduced in Sec.~ sec:init . Following the adaptive density control of 3DGS~ kerbl3Dgaussians , we densify primitives whose accumulated absolute view-space gradients~ ye2024absgs exceed the threshold assigned to their region. We use a lower threshold to encourage foreground refinement and a higher threshold to limit excessive background densification. Background Depth Regularization sec:depth We align monocular depth predictions to metric scale using depth samples derived from triangulated RoMa points. RANSAC is used to estimate the scale and shift , yielding . To provide additional supervision at these viewpoints, we render images from virtual cameras and restore them using a diffusion model conditioned on camera poses and reference views. The restored images are iteratively incorporated into 4DGS training as pseudo-supervision.
