title: EvoMem-VLA: State-Evolution Memory for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
summary: Most vision-language-action (VLA) models rely on current observations and lose task-relevant evidence once it leaves view, limiting performance on long-horizon, memory-dependent tasks. Existing efforts incorporate compressed historical features or sparse visual keyframes. However, isolated snapshots can leave the policy uncertain about what changed during past interactions and which action should follow. To overcome this limitation, we propose EvoMem-VLA, which constructs state-evolution memory by explicitly encoding and retaining observed changes between historical states. These change representations preserve evidence of interaction outcomes, allowing the policy to track task progress beyond isolated snapshots. Specifically, we introduce conditional delta tokenization to encode ordered frame pairs into directional, source-conditioned delta tokens, each associated with its corresponding state evidence. A shared VLM backbone supports task-adaptive routing: normal long-horizon tasks follow a direct action route, whereas multi-stage tasks use a subtask route that generates an executable subtask as an additional input for action generation. With a single jointly trained policy for each simulation benchmark, EvoMem-VLA achieves success rates of 80.7\% on RMBench, 82.0\% on RoboMME and 83.8\% across four real-world tasks spanning two robot embodiments. These results represent substantial improvements over the previous state of the art in all three evaluation settings.
full_text: Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer pretrained visual and semantic knowledge to robot control, enabling increasingly general instruction following and manipulation across tasks~ rt2,openvla,pi0,xvla . However, their performance remains limited on long-horizon, memory-dependent tasks. This is because a policy conditioned only on the current observation and instruction lacks access to past events that determine future actions~ hamlet,memoryvla,eventvla . As a result, the policy may lose track of task progress and generate an incorrect action. Recently, there have been efforts to augment VLAs with historical memory. Existing approaches represent history using discrete state features~ hamlet,memoryvla,roboflamingo or sparse visual keyframes~ eventvla,kcvla,memer . However, task-relevant changes often remain implicit in the stored history (Figure~ fig:evomem_overview (a)). Long-horizon control requires the policy to relate remembered states to changes during task execution. Without an explicit representation of these changes, the policy must extract them from sparse state evidence when determining task progress and selecting the next action. This motivates a memory representation that retains both what was observed and how it changed relative to an earlier observation. To address this limitation, we propose EvoMem-VLA, a state-evolution memory paradigm that explicitly encodes and retains observed interaction changes between sparse historical observations (Figure~ fig:evomem_overview (b)). By linking change representations to corresponding visual states, this memory preserves evidence of interaction changes. Therefore, compared with VLAs that rely on discrete state memory, our policy can distinguish interaction processes that discrete history alone leaves ambiguous and use explicit change evidence to generate the appropriate next action. We instantiate this paradigm as a unified VLA with multi-scale state-evolution memory and task-adaptive routing. Specifically, to explicitly represent the visual change from the source frame to the target frame, we introduce conditional delta tokenization~ deltatok to encode ordered frame pairs sampled from recent observations and selected keyframes into delta tokens. We then construct state-evolution memory by arranging these delta tokens alongside the initial frame, recent historical frames, and selected keyframes~ eventvla in temporal order. Next, the state-evolution memory is fed into a shared VLM backbone together with the task instruction and current observation. Additionally, the VLM backbone supports task-adaptive routing: for normal long-horizon tasks without multi-stage planning, it predicts actions directly; for multi-stage tasks, it first generates an executable subtask and then appends it to the original input context to guide action generation~ wla0 . Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose EvoMem-VLA, a state-evolution memory paradigm that explicitly retains observed interaction changes alongside historical states. This enables policies to use remembered change evidence for action generation rather than infer what happened from sparse historical states alone. We develop a unified VLA that organizes conditional delta tokens with initial, recent, and keyframe observations into multi-scale state-evolution memory. Its shared VLM backbone supports task-adaptive routing for direct action prediction or action generation conditioned on an executable subtask. EvoMem-VLA achieves state-of-the-art success rates of 80.7 on RMBench~ rmbench , 82.0 on RoboMME~ robomme , and 83.8 across four real-world tasks on two robot embodiments. We use one jointly trained policy per simulation benchmark, with RMBench ablations further validating the contribution of conditional delta tokenization. Related Work sec:related_work Vision-Language-Action Models. Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt pretrained vision-language representations to language-conditioned robot control~ spatialvla,smolvla . RT-2 and OpenVLA formulate action generation as autoregressive prediction over discretized action tokens~ rt2,openvla . More recent approaches introduce continuous or hybrid action generation~ openvlaoft : uses a flow-matching action expert~ pi0 , CogACT and DexVLA condition diffusion-based action experts on VLM features~ cogact,dexvla , and HybridVLA combines autoregressive prediction with diffusion action generation~ hybridvla . X-VLA studies policy scaling across heterogeneous robot embodiments~ xvla . Despite advances in action representation and policy scaling, these models do not inherently maintain a persistent record of task execution. When earlier evidence leaves the observation window, a policy may lose track of what it has observed or completed, even when this history is needed to disambiguate visually similar states requiring different actions. Memory Augmented Vision-Language-Action Models. History-aware policies address this limitation by retaining or transforming past observations~ fourdvla,swiftvla,sam2act,mem . RoboFlamingo compresses temporal vision-language features into an LSTM policy state~ roboflamingo , while TraceVLA overlays tracked point trajectories on current images as visual motion prompts~ tracevla . HAMLET encodes observations as temporally discriminative moment tokens and aggregates them through a lightweight causal memory module~ hamlet . MemoryVLA maintains perceptual and cognitive representations in long-term memory and retrieves relevant entries for action prediction~ memoryvla . EventVLA retains the initial observation and a recent history window alongside event-triggered keyframes in bounded memory~ eventvla . MemER uses a high-level policy to select and consolidate keyframes, predict the current language subtask, and delegate execution to a separate low-level controller~ memer . Complementary approaches use language and reasoning to guide action generation~ ecot,rth,thinkact : on multi-subtask data, predicts a semantic subtask before generating the corresponding action chunk~ pi05 , while WLA-0 jointly learns textual-subtask prediction, future-state prediction, and action synthesis~ wla0 . These methods provide remembered states, motion cues, and subtask context through distinct interfaces. However, the cited state-oriented memories lack dedicated inter-state change representations, while TraceVLA's short-window motion traces are not integrated with sparse long-term state evidence. MemER provides history to its high-level policy, but its controller receives only the predicted subtask, current images, and robot state. In contrast, EvoMem-VLA organizes multi-scale visual states and learned inter-state changes in state-evolution memory shared by subtask and action prediction. Tasks without textual-subtask supervision retain a direct action route through the same VLA policy. Method sec:method EvoMem-VLA constructs state-evolution memory by organizing initial, recent, and selected keyframe observations alongside delta tokens that explicitly encode observed changes between frames. At each replanning step, a shared VLM backbone takes this memory, the current observation, and the task instruction as input and supports task-adaptive routing. For tasks without multi-stage planning, it predicts actions directly; for multi-stage tasks, it first generates an executable subtask and appends it to the input context to guide action generation. A lightweight Keyframe Head selects task-relevant observations to update the keyframe memory online. Figure~ fig:evomem_architecture summarizes the architecture. title: FLEX-WAM: Flexible Block-Causal World-Action Models for Long-Horizon Imagination and Planning
summary: World--action models (WAMs) promise a unified model that predicts action-conditioned futures, generates feasible actions, and supports planning in imagination. However, existing joint video--action models often use computationally heavy, fixed-horizon backbones ill-suited to streaming inference and stable long-horizon open-loop rollouts. We introduce FLEX-WAM, a Flexible and Efficient Block-Causal World--Action Model for unified simulation and policy inference. FLEX-WAM supports variable-length contexts and non-causal prediction horizons, as well as infinite autoregressive generation frame by frame or block by block. Its block-causal, KV-cacheable architecture combines axial attention and blockwise diffusion forcing to enable efficient real-time rollout and deployment-time latency--throughput tradeoffs without retraining. Joint training can nevertheless produce plausible futures that weakly respond to commanded actions. We address this failure mode by balancing state and action flow-matching gradient contributions across the state--action diffusion-noise grid and regulating world-model sampling using Forward-Dynamics (FD) elasticity, an efficient training-time proxy for action responsiveness. Across simulated and real-world datasets, FLEX-WAM achieves superior multi-step prediction quality and latency while producing stable joint state--action rollouts for thousands of steps. As a joint action proposer and simulator within MCTS, it solves long-horizon PushT and all five OGBench Puzzle-4x4 tasks entirely in imagination. On a bimanual OpenArm-based robot, a single checkpoint jointly serves as a play policy and expected-outcome predictor, enabling real-time identification and collection of model--reality mismatches for future self-improvement.
full_text: World--action models (WAMs) promise a unified model that predicts action-conditioned futures, generates feasible actions, and supports planning in imagination. However, existing joint video--action models often use computationally heavy, fixed-horizon backbones ill-suited to streaming inference and stable long-horizon open-loop rollouts. We introduce FLEX-WAM, a Flexible and Efficient Block-Causal World--Action Model for unified simulation and policy inference. FLEX-WAM supports variable-length contexts and non-causal prediction horizons, as well as infinite autoregressive generation frame by frame or block by block. Its block-causal, KV-cacheable architecture combines axial attention and blockwise diffusion forcing to enable efficient real-time rollout and deployment-time latency--throughput tradeoffs without retraining. Joint training can nevertheless produce plausible futures that weakly respond to commanded actions. We address this failure mode by balancing state and action flow-matching gradient contributions across the state--action diffusion-noise grid and regulating world-model sampling using Forward-Dynamics (FD) elasticity, an efficient training-time proxy for action responsiveness. Across simulated and real-world datasets, FLEX-WAM achieves superior multi-step prediction quality and latency while producing stable joint state--action rollouts for thousands of steps. As a joint action proposer and simulator within MCTS, it solves long-horizon PushT and all five OGBench Puzzle-4x4 tasks entirely in imagination. On a bimanual OpenArm-based robot, a single checkpoint jointly serves as a play policy and expected-outcome predictor, enabling real-time identification and collection of model--reality mismatches for future self-improvement. An embodied agent must answer two complementary questions: what will happen after executing an action, and what action will achieve a given task? World models address the former by predicting action-conditioned futures for imagined rollouts, planning, and control finn2016unsupervised,finn2017deep,hafner2019learning,hafner2025mastering,khorrambakht2025worldplanner ; policies and inverse-dynamics models address the latter by generating feasible actions. Since these capabilities are complementary views of the same state--action trajectory distribution, jointly modeling them promises a unified model that can act, predict, and evaluate action consequences. Recent work has pursued this objective through joint video--action generative models. GR-1 jointly denoises future images and actions wu2024unleashing,guo2024prediction , while UVA learns a shared representation with decoupled diffusion heads for policy learning, forward and inverse dynamics, and video prediction li2025unified . Most closely related to our setting, UWM couples video and action diffusion in a shared transformer with independently controlled diffusion timesteps zhu2025unified . Varying the state--action noise configuration allows a single UWM model to operate as a policy, world model, inverse-dynamics model, or video generator. More recently, pretrained video generators have also shown promise as scalable world--action models bi2026motus,ye2026world . However, joint modeling and flexible inference do not by themselves guarantee balanced learning, stable long-horizon generation, or real-time open-loop simulation. Most existing approaches either rely on fixed-horizon, computationally heavy video backbones that are poorly suited to streaming and infinite-horizon generation, or expose such capabilities only as a simulator hafner2025trainingagentsinsidescalable or a policy ye2026world . We introduce FLEX-WAM, a Flexible and EfficientNet Block-Causal World--Action Model, together with a training procedure for unified simulation and policy inference. FLEX-WAM supports variable-length context histories, variable-length non-causal prediction horizons, and infinite autoregressive rollouts generated block by block or frame by frame. Its block-causal, KV-cacheable architecture enables stable rollouts over thousands of real-time steps while supporting efficient real-time generation. A central challenge in training a unified world--action model is preserving simulation capability (action responsiveness) while learning history-driven state--action prediction vector fields in policy and video-generation modes. We address this challenge with two training-time components. First, we numerically estimate and balance the gradient contributions of independent state and action flow-matching losses across the state--action noise grid. Second, we introduce Forward-Dynamics (FD) elasticity, an efficient proxy for world-model action responsiveness. We monitor its degradation throughout training and use it to adaptively bias sampling toward world-model mode. Because a world--action model must first learn action-conditioned dynamics to serve as both a simulator and generator, our training procedure begins in pure world-model mode and gradually transitions to joint WAM training. During this transition, FD elasticity regulates the sampling schedule to preserve world-modeling capability. We evaluate FLEX-WAM's efficiency, long-horizon stability, and unified multi-mode capabilities by deploying it jointly as a simulator and action proposer within Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). Planning entirely in FLEX-WAM's imagination, the resulting system solves long-horizon, multi-step puzzle tasks from OGBench park2025ogbench as well as real-world PushT motion-planning tasks. We further present preliminary bimanual-robot results in which a single FLEX-WAM checkpoint jointly serves as a policy and expected-outcome predictor. This unified deployment enables real-time detection and automatic collection of counterfactual examples, providing a path toward improving learned world models through real-world interaction. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce FLEX-WAM, an open-source Code and checkpoints are omitted for anonymous review and will be released upon acceptance block-causal world--action model that supports frame-by-frame and block-by-block autoregressive prediction, variable context horizons, and KV-cacheable rollouts stable over thousands of real-time steps. We introduce a gradient-calibrated, feedback-regulated two-stage training procedure that measures and preserves the action responsiveness required for temporally dense simulation. We evaluate the proposed architecture on simulated and real-world datasets, demonstrating competitive prediction quality and rollout efficiency relative to representative state-of-the-art world--action models. We show that FLEX-WAM can solve long-horizon planning tasks entirely in imagination when deployed jointly as an action proposer and simulator within MCTS. We demonstrate the potential of unified world--action models to identify and collect counterfactual examples for self-improvement during real-world deployment. Method WAM as a Joint Flow Matching Model sec:joint We define a WAM as a joint generative model of state ( ) and action ( ) sequences: We merge ideas from~ hafner2025trainingagentsinsidescalable, chen2024diffusion and model this distribution as a flow matching model with per-modality and per-timestep independent state and action signal levels and . The per-modality independence allows diverse training and inference modes including world model ( ), inverse dynamics ( ), video model ( ) and joint state-action generative model ( ). On the other hand the per-frame noise control allows any subset of the model input tokens to serve as clean context or prediction horizon and improves the model long-horizon rollout stability by exposing it to various context perturbations that effectively reduce the distribution mismatch between a context filled with the model's own predictions during inference and ground-truth during training time chen2024diffusion . FLEX-WAM: Architecture Our core axial attention efficient transformer architecture and multi-modal tokenizer are based on the DreamerV4 world model hafner2025trainingagentsinsidescalable (Fig.~ fig:overview ). However, we extend this framework both architecturally and training-wise both necessitated by the joint state-action modeling. Block-Causal Axial Transformer sec:backbone We build our tokenizer and dynamics model on top of block-causal axial transfomer blocks described in this section. Stacking per-timestep token sets along time and fusing them spatiotemporally is subject to compute complexity due to attention operations. Instead, we adopt axial attention where each layer only fuses information spatially or temporally and is subject to lower computational complexity of ho2019axialattentionmultidimensionaltransformers . We adopt RoPE su2024roformer as positional embedding in each layer and interleave the architecture with AdaLN layers in case text/task conditioning is required (in this paper we do not use text/class conditioning because text and action are competing information regarding the future of a rollout and impair the model's capability as a simulator). Instead of training the model fully causally as in~ hafner2025trainingagentsinsidescalable (reduced quality in predicting long horizons), fully bi-directionally~ zhu2025unified (not KV-cacheable), or with partitioned causal context and bi-directional horizon~ agarwal2026cosmos (committing to a fixed horizon length set in training time), we propose variable block size block causal attention as a randomized knob during training and configurable setting during inference. Specifically, frames are partitioned into contiguous blocks of frames where frame may attend to frame iff , where is the block index: attention is bidirectional within a block and strictly causal across blocks (Fig~ fig:overview .d). During training, we draw once per forward pass, from , shared by every sequence in the batch. As a result, block size is a deployment-time choice that allows our model to operate either completely causally ( ) or block-by-block ( ) when a predictive horizon larger than one is needed. Multi-View Tokenizer sec:tokenizer As formulated in hafner2025trainingagentsinsidescalable , our tokenizer is a masked auto-encoder~ he2021maskedautoencodersscalablevision , trained to reconstruct spatially and temporally randomly masked modalities. The encoder attention mask is set such that, each modality can only attend to itself while the latent tokens can attend to the modalities and themselves. On the other hand in the decoder each modality can attend to itself and the latent while the latent can only attend to itself. This ensures that during encoding, cross modality information has passed the latents and in the decoding they are decoded purely from latents and not affected by each other. In this paper, encoder and decoder are both fully causal in time ( ) and block sizes larger than one is unnecessary. title: PermVLA: Factorization Order as a Regularizer for VLA Learning
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies commonly learn action chunks through a fixed left-to-right (LTR) factorization, although the same expert trajectory distribution admits many valid chain-rule factorizations. We identify factorization order as an overlooked regularization choice and introduce causally anchored permutation (CAP), which samples action reveal orders with a tunable chronological prefix. Its auxiliary objective trains one shared policy to predict actions from different known subsets of the same expert chunk, while deployment retains deterministic LTR control. We call this conditional-set augmentation: it creates multiple conditional prediction problems from one expert chunk without adding demonstrations. This discourages reliance on the single chronological prefix used by ordinary teacher forcing. Controlled experiments show that CAP consistently outperforms standard LTR training on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, with the same advantage appearing in cross-dataset CALVIN evaluation. A diagnostic that measures the expected squared difference between a chunk's joint log likelihood under two reveal orders verifies that CAP training internalizes agreement across reveal orders. These findings position sampled subset-conditioned auxiliary objectives as a general recipe for constructing VLA regularizers, illustrated by an extension to diffusion action generators.

Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) systems learn a conditional joint distribution over a chunk of future actions. Recent work has explored robot pretraining, action tokenization, diffusion and flow objectives, post-training, and asynchronous execution kim2024openvla,kim2025oft,black2024pi0,pi2025pi05,shukor2025smolvla . The chain rule introduces another modeling choice: the order in which action variables are revealed and predicted. Autoregressive VLA training usually fixes this order to chronological action time, conventionally modeled left-to-right (LTR), leaving factorization order hidden inside the action objective. We study it as an independent modeling choice and ask whether alternative valid factorizations can regularize VLA training. Under LTR training, each action slot is always predicted from the same family of preceding physical actions. Complete expert chunks make many other valid conditioning subsets available. We hypothesize that exclusive training on one teacher-forced chain encourages the policy to rely on that single reveal order. Predicting the same physical action from different known subsets should instead favor conditional dependencies among action steps that remain predictive across conditioning patterns. This may improve closed-loop control when visual, linguistic, or embodiment context shifts. We instantiate this idea as , a deliberately minimal VLA that conditions a diagonal-Gaussian autoregressive action head on pretrained vision-language model (VLM) embeddings. This design prioritizes controlled analysis and attribution of causally anchored permutation (CAP) regularization; closed-loop success measures its contribution within the fixed architecture. CAP adds an auxiliary permutation likelihood to the standard LTR objective. The tunable prefix length \(K\) fixes the first \(K\) actions in physical-time order; \(K=0\) allows every reveal order. The shared policy minimizes \((1- ) L_ + L_ \), then deploys through deterministic LTR receding-horizon control. Each expert chunk supplies prediction problems conditioned on different known action subsets, with physical action identities and the deployment procedure unchanged. We call this conditional-set augmentation. Figure~ fig:teaser illustrates these conditioning patterns and summarizes their effect in matched LIBERO comparisons. Permutation modeling has established foundations in orderless density estimation, XLNet, and autoregressive diffusion uria2014deep,yang2019xlnet,hoogeboom2022ardm . Random autoregressive factorization has also been applied to same-time multi-agent trajectories rudolph2022conditional , while Uni[MASK], MaskDP, and Masked Trajectory Models learn completion under variable masks carroll2022unimask,liu2022maskdp,wu2023mtm . We assign alternative factorizations a distinct VLA role: a training-only regularizer over future physical actions, with a tunable chronological prefix and paired with the exact LTR deployment objective. This formulation makes factorization order directly measurable under a fixed controller. Sample-matched LTR-1pass and decoder-compute-matched LTR-2pass controls isolate the training objective. LIBERO~ liu2023libero tests in-distribution control, LIBERO-Plus~ fei2026liberoplus tests zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness, and CALVIN~ mees2022calvin tests whether the gains extend to another benchmark. In the matched reference experiments, CAP improves closed-loop success over both LTR controls across these benchmarks. Likelihood diagnostics show greater agreement across reveal orders while retaining the fit under LTR, connecting the training objective to a measurable change in the learned policy. This approach suggests a broader design principle: varying known action subsets can construct auxiliary objectives for other action generators while retaining their deployment procedures. We illustrate it with , which conditions on clean action subsets and denoises the remaining slots. Our contributions are: We identify action-chunk factorization order as a previously overlooked VLA inductive-bias axis and formulate its regularization effect as conditional-set augmentation. We introduce CAP, an auxiliary factorization objective with tunable prefix length that diversifies action conditioning during training and preserves standard LTR deployment. Matched controls, parameter studies, OOD evaluation, and CALVIN demonstrate the empirical benefits. Likelihood diagnostics provide evidence of agreement across reveal orders, and a diffusion extension illustrates the broader design space. Related Work sec:related VLA action modeling. RT-1 and RT-2 established scalable vision-language robot policies with tokenized control brohan2022rt1,brohan2023rt2 ; Octo and OpenVLA extended open robot pretraining across datasets and embodiments octo2024,kim2024openvla . Recent action generators include the Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policy zhao2023act , conditional denoising in Diffusion Policy chi2023diffusion , flow matching in \( _0\) black2024pi0 , and compressed action tokens in FAST pertsch2025fast . OpenVLA-OFT, WorldVLA, \( _ 0.5 \), and SmolVLA further study chunk decoding, auxiliary prediction, heterogeneous pretraining, and asynchronous execution kim2025oft,cen2025worldvla,pi2025pi05,shukor2025smolvla . CAP fixes the backbone and continuous action generator to isolate factorization order as a training intervention. Order-agnostic and masked sequence modeling. Orderless Neural Autoregressive Distribution Estimation (NADE) trains one density estimator across autoregressive orders uria2014deep ; XLNet combines permutation language modeling with two-stream attention yang2019xlnet ; and autoregressive diffusion models (ARDMs) connect order-agnostic autoregression to absorbing diffusion hoogeboom2022ardm . rudolph2022conditional carry the same mechanism into trajectory modeling, pairing random autoregressive factorizations with conditional two-stream attention for the same-time movements of multiple agents. Uni[MASK], MaskDP, and Masked Trajectory Models learn behavior from variable trajectory masks carroll2022unimask,liu2022maskdp,wu2023mtm . In each case, permutation or masking constitutes the primary training objective itself, defined over unordered variable sets or completion-style tasks. Permutation training as a VLA regularizer. Our contribution is to import the permutation idea of XLNet into VLA learning in the form of a regularizer: the permuted likelihood enters as an auxiliary term on top of the chronological density objective. Two properties of physical-world action imitation make this transfer practical. The first is computational feasibility: expert action chunks are short (\(H=8\)--\(16\) slots), so evaluating normalized likelihoods under \(M\) sampled reveal orders adds modest decoder computation, while the parameter count and deployment cost remain fixed. The second is temporal adherence: the chronological LTR objective remains the dominant training path and the only deployment path, so the policy keeps physical-time ordering as its primary interface to control. The auxiliary CAP term then predicts each target action from varied known subsets, discouraging over-reliance on one generation path and on the visual correspondences specific to that path. CAP assigns an ordered, normalized likelihood to each sampled order within one future action chunk, whereas masked-completion objectives score unordered variable sets with completion-style losses. The tunable prefix length \(K\) controls the order family, including fully unrestricted orders at \(K=0\). Our reference configuration draws only \(M=1\) sampled order per example, with a \(M=4\) ablation, so the computational-efficiency argument above is validated only in the low-\(M\) regime; scaling \(M\) further and mapping the resulting computation--regularization trade-off remains an open direction. title: Bayesian Data Augmentation for DNN Retraining with Binomial Outcomes in Vision-Based UAV Landing
summary:
In GPS-denied or cluttered urban environments, vision-based landing is essential for reliable UAV missions. Real-world landing sites are often unstructured and highly variable, requiring strong generalization by the perception system. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) trained with synthetic data augmentation offer a scalable solution for learning landing-site features across diverse vehicle and environmental states. However, computationally expensive DNN retraining, along with challenging performance validation via test flights, limits exhaustive model fine-tuning and necessitates an optimized retraining pipeline. In this work, we deploy a Bayesian data augmentation framework integrated with a photorealistic simulator featuring high-fidelity vehicle dynamics to iteratively retrain the helipad detector DNN, maximizing landing performance as the objective function.
  We validate our framework with experiments in a photorealistic simulator under different environmental conditions and vehicle states, demonstrating improved landing performance and tighter confidence intervals on predicted landing outcomes.
full_text: Bayesian Data Augmentation for DNN Retraining with Binomial Outcomes in Vision-Based UAV Landing In GPS-denied or cluttered urban environments, vision-based landing is essential for reliable UAV missions. Real-world landing sites are often unstructured and highly variable, requiring strong generalization by the perception system. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) trained with synthetic data augmentation offer a scalable solution for learning landing-site features across diverse vehicle and environmental states. However, computationally expensive DNN retraining, along with challenging performance validation via test flights, limits exhaustive model fine-tuning and necessitates an optimized retraining pipeline. In this work, we deploy a Bayesian data augmentation framework integrated with a photorealistic simulator featuring high-fidelity vehicle dynamics to iteratively retrain the helipad detector DNN, maximizing landing performance as the objective function. We validate our framework with experiments in a photo- realistic simulator under different environmental conditions and vehicle state, demonstrating improved landing performance and tighter confidence intervals on predicted landing outcomes. Bayesian Optimization, UAV Landing, DNN Introduction Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have gained significant popularity in recent times for a wide range of military and civilian applications. Traditional navigation methods for UAVs rely on GPS waypoint following, which can be unreliable in cluttered urban environments or provide insufficient accuracy when a high-precision landing is required. Vision-based landing can be a suitable alternative for such scenarios if the landing pad can be reliably detected and tracked throughout the landing maneuver. However, real-world landing sites are often unstructured with variable features, making consistent detection challenging. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) demonstrate superior performance in learning such complex features compared to traditional computer vision methods, and have been applied in a wide range of perception tasks~ grigorescu2020survey,voulodimos2018deep . However, training DNNs with random helipad images is not sufficient, as the same helipad may appear in different sizes, shapes, and appearances depending on the vehicle pose, environmental conditions, and camera parameter settings. For real-time object detection and control, general-purpose frameworks such as YOLO (You Only Look Once)~ redmon2016you are therefore trained with domain-specific datasets~ diwan2023object with data augmentation to improve the generalization of the model for different sizes, lighting, and aspect ratios of the object. This augmentation process can be validated and refined further based on the vision-based landing performance of the UAV. However, collecting such landing performance data would involve using expensive aircraft for extended periods to cover varying scenarios, altitude ranges, times of day, and weather conditions. Photorealistic simulators can substantially reduce this burden by providing controlled, repeatable environments for generating task-specific performance data at scale~ HowTrainDefect2023, dallel2023digital, unity_autonomous_vehicle_training Despite these advances, retraining and deployment of DNNs remains a challenging task. For example, each iteration of refinement is computationally expensive, requiring substantial resources and time~ thompson2020computational . This high computational demand often becomes a bottleneck in the optimization process, necessitating improvements in the efficiency of the retraining process itself. The blackbox nature of the DNNs makes the task additionally challenging. Bayesian optimization can be a prominent method for such scenarios, as it systematically searches the decision variable space, balancing exploration and exploitation to identify optimal decision variables without knowing the objective function explicitly~ shahriari2015taking . By leveraging feedback from simulation outcomes, such as the number of successful landings over a finite number of landing attempts, Bayesian optimization can iteratively refine the model, ensuring effective adaptation to varying vehicle and environmental states. In this work, we address this challenge by introducing a retraining and deployment framework for perception DNNs, specifically for the autonomous landing operation of UAVs, as illustrated in Figure~ framework . First, we introduce an iterative DNN retraining process leveraging Bayesian optimization, which optimizes the binomial outcome of the landing attempts (success/failure) by efficiently applying data augmentation to the DNN retraining pipeline. This process consists of two phases. The first phase evaluates the binomial outcome (landing success/failure) as a performance measure of the vision-guided landing system, given the operation scenarios in a photorealistic simulation. In the second phase, the corresponding performance measure is used in a Bayesian optimization loop that applies the Gaussian Process (GP) prior and Laplace approximation of the posterior to generate the next set of hyperparameters for retraining the model. Finally, the updated model is evaluated in the first phase. These phases close the loop in the DNN refinement process. To evaluate our approach, we use a simulation environment~ bansal2025airtaxisim built in Unreal Engine that models realistic aerial scenarios, including cluttered urban landscapes, varying altitudes, and dynamic lighting. This environment enables thorough testing of the proposed framework, allowing us to study the effect of uncertainty, limited observability, and control feedback in closed-loop settings. Our key contributions are: We present an iterative retraining pipeline for landing pad detection DNN, integrated to a photorealistic simulator, that optimizes the binomial landing outcomes within the simulator as an objective function leveraging Bayesian optimization with GP prior and Laplace approximation of the posterior distribution. Literature Review UAVs are being used for a wide range of applications, including terrain mapping~ templetonAutonomousVisionbasedLanding2007 , road following~ frewVisionbasedRoadfollowingUsing2004 , shoreline investigation~ templinApplicationLowCostFixedWing2018 , wildlife monitoring~ olivares2015towards , and autonomous package delivery~ saundersAutonomousAerialRobotics2024 . Among different UAV configurations, multirotor planes with lift-and-cruise capability have gained popularity in the context of Advanced Air Mobility (AAM)~ johnson2022nasa, silva2018vtol . These aircraft combine the cruise characteristics of fixed-wing aircraft with the vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) capability of multirotors. Unlike fixed-wing runway operations, vertical landing requires precise localization of the landing site directly beneath the aircraft. Vision-based perception has emerged as the dominant sensing modality for high-precision autonomous landing in GPS-denied or cluttered environments~ gautam2014survey, xin2022visionlanding . Despite significant progress, generalized DNN training for diverse landing environments, robustness under lighting and texture variations, and a generalized exploration policy for the landing pad from different UAV poses remain open research directions. Early vision-based autonomous landing systems relied on cooperative visual markers of specific features, placed on the landing surface. One of the first implementations of such systems demonstrated helicopter landing using image processing-based tracking saripalli2003vision . Later, vision-based quadrotor landing was achieved on a moving platform using an onboard camera and nonlinear control biImplementationAutonomousVisual2013,falanga2017landing . Vision-based autonomous landing was also demonstrated in GPS-denied environments using customized landing pad design, state estimation, and stabilization~ langeVisionBasedOnboard2009 . These works established the feasibility of marker-based autonomous landing even under motion and disturbances. However, these solutions face challenges in real-world adoption in unknown environments, as the landing markers may not follow a specific feature, shape, or orientation. A Faster Region-based Convolutional Neural Network (Faster R-CNN)-based landing sign identification was proposed to identify the position and direction of the landing sign~ chenIdentificationAutonomousLanding2017 . Later, YOLO~ redmonYOLOv3IncrementalImprovement2018 has been widely integrated for safe landing area detection, pose correction, and navigation of UAVs~ leeLandingSiteInspection2020, symeonidis2021vision . However, training such perception models for autonomous landing requires large amounts of data collected covering diverse environments and vehicle states. For UAV perception, collecting data at scale can be expensive and unsafe, especially in the early stages of development. Moreover, comprehensive scenarios of varying environmental conditions and vehicle states can be challenging to recreate with real test flights. Photorealistic simulators equipped with high-fidelity vehicle dynamics can substantially reduce this gap by providing task-specific training data~ HowTrainDefect2023, dallel2023digital, unity_autonomous_vehicle_training . CARLA~ dosovitskiy2017carla and AirSim airsim2017 have been widely used for such synthetic data generation and control validation. However, the simulation-to-real gap still remains a major challenge for UAV perception model deployment, which can be further reduced by synthetically augmenting the training data itself through careful tuning of training parameters such as scale and brightness. Though such fine-tuning enables the DNNs to generalize well across varying altitude and lighting conditions, each iteration of retraining and validation is computationally expensive, which motivates the use of Bayesian optimization to efficiently search the hyperparameter space for optimal performance~ shahriari2015taking . Bayesian optimization based on stochastic binary outcomes is successfully demonstrated for different robotics applications~ tesch2013expensive, rofer2024bayesian . However, to the best of our knowledge, none of the prior works optimized perception DNNs for the autonomous landing task with a binomial simulation outcome. In this work, we place a Gaussian prior over the true unknown function and adopt a binomial observation model. We deploy the Laplace approximation method to approximate the non-Gaussian posterior. Finally, we leverage upper confidence bound (UCB) as an acquisition function to explore the hyperparameter space~ nickisch2008approximations . Problem Formulation The Bayesian optimization in this work aims to maximize the landing success rate within a defined altitude range in varying lighting conditions by iteratively retraining the object detection DNN (YOLO). We consider scale augmentation factor (S) and brightness augmentation (B) as relevant hyperparameters and define them as decision variables: . title: When to Switch: Reliable Action-Chunk Extension for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models serve as unified policies for robotic manipulation, yet their expensive inference forces robots to pause between policy calls, resulting in stop-and-go execution that interrupts smooth motion and prolongs task completion. Extending the action chunk reduces policy calls and hence these pauses, but predicting farther into the future makes long-chunk execution unreliable. To understand where this unreliability arises, we analyze action errors within long chunks and find that they concentrate around transitions between manipulation subskills, growing sharply with chunk length. This suggests the importance of transition timing, i.e., when to switch subskills within a chunk. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RACE (Reliable Action-Chunk Extension), a framework that predicts the transition timing from an auxiliary one-step denoising pass and conditions action generation on it. By learning and conditioning on transition timing, RACE reduces errors at subskill transitions and enables reliable execution of longer action chunks. Across simulation benchmarks, RACE outperforms fine-tuning at the same chunk length; with 2x longer chunks, it surpasses recent state-of-the-art and efficient VLAs in success rate, and with 4x longer chunks, it remains competitive. On a real robot, RACE uses 4x longer chunks, which reduces the idle time caused by stop-and-go execution by about 5x, while achieving a higher success rate than fine-tuning with the same chunk length. Code and a real-robot demo are available at https://github.com/Seonghoon-Yu/RACE-VLA
full_text: Experiments Experimental Setup sec:setup Dataset and Metric. For simulation experiments, we evaluate our framework on three manipulation benchmarks: VLABench~ vlabench , RoboCasa-H50~ robocasa , and LIBERO~ libero , with the LIBERO results reported in Appendix~ app:comparison_on_libero . We follow the standard evaluation protocols of each benchmark, with the dataset and protocol details provided in Appendix~ app:dataset . Throughout, denotes the number of actions executed per policy call. For each , we post-train RACE on top of the fine-tuned for that benchmark, together with a fine-tuned variant trained with the same recipe; both predict and execute a full chunk of actions. The original instead predicts actions and executes only the first , following its official protocol. As evaluation metrics, we measure the task success rate and the speedup relative to the baseline , measured as the reduction in cumulative policy-inference time per episode, excluding simulator execution time (Appendix~ app:speedup_measure ). The real-world setup and metrics are in Appendix~ app:real-world . Implementation Details. We build our framework on the official ~ pi05 checkpoints fine-tuned for each benchmark, with denoising steps. For the transition-conditioned generation (Sec.~ sec:cond ), we initialize every gate to and optimize it during training. In the training objective, we set and . We train for 40K steps on VLABench and 20K steps on the other benchmarks using AdamW with a learning rate that decays from to following a cosine schedule, and a batch size of 64 on four NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs. Ablation Study We conduct ablation studies with an execution chunk length of on VLABench. Effect of Each Component and Training Objective. In Tab.~ tab:ablation , we add each component and training objective one at a time, starting from the fine-tuned with only . Adding alone, without the prediction head, yields only a small improvement, so the extra denoising objective contributes little by itself. Adding the prediction head with raises the success rate, even though the prediction is not injected into generation. Since the head reads the action-expert features from the auxiliary pass, back-propagates into the action expert and makes its features transition-aware. Conditioning on the predicted prior improves it further under the same training objectives, showing that timing supervision and timing conditioning provide complementary gains. Finally, keeps the auxiliary pass a valid denoiser, which may provide better features for the head. Ablation within Transition-timing Prediction Head. (a) Transition labels (Tab.~ tab:design_choices_labels ). Replacing the PELT labels with the random transitions shrinks the learned modulation offsets by more than an order of magnitude; the model learns to ignore the uninformative prior and falls back to na\"ive fine-tuning. Further results with other PELT settings are reported in Appendix~ app:sensitivity_pelt . (b) Information sources (Tab.~ tab:design_choices_information ). The action-expert features alone come second, and combining both performs best (further ablations are in Appendix~ appendix:additional_ablation ). Understanding the Effectiveness of RACE subsec:understanding Where Errors Arise in Longer Chunks. To examine where errors arise as chunks grow longer, we compare actions predicted from demonstration states with the demonstrated actions on VLABench at (Fig.~ fig:drift_error ; Appendix~ app:action_error_measure ). We compare errors at transitions with those of non-transition actions at the same chunk position. Both errors grow toward the end of the chunk, as expected from open-loop prediction farther ahead. However, errors at transitions remain generally higher, and this gap widens at . This indicates that transitions pose additional difficulty beyond the growth with prediction horizon. RACE reduces errors at transitions over the fine-tuned , particularly near the end of the chunk, while also lowering errors at non-transition actions. For the gripper, whose binary command mainly reflects when it switches, RACE switches within one step of the correct step more often and misses fewer switches than the fine-tuned , with a similar false-switch rate (Tab.~ tab:gripper_timing of Appendix~ app:action_errors_dimension , with transition errors by action component in Tab.~ tab:transition_error_by_component ). This trend is consistent with our motivation to improve action generation around subskill transitions. The detailed statistics of each task are provided in Appendix~ app:statistics_transitions . Gains on Longer Chunks. Fig.~ fig:gain_vs_chunk shows the gain of RACE over the fine-tuned across chunk lengths on VLABench. The gain is positive at every and grows as the chunk becomes longer. Since a longer chunk is more likely to span one or more subskill transitions, this pattern indicates that transition timing is an obstacle to chunk extension and that RACE relieves it. To verify that RACE reliably executes longer action chunks that reduce idle time on a real robot, we fine-tune each policy on 30 demonstrations of a pick-and-place task and evaluate it over 50 trials (details in Appendix~ app:real-world ; demo videos on GitHub ). All methods use asynchronous execution with real-time chunking~ rtc , generating the next chunk while the current one is executed; each policy thus predicts a chunk twice as long as it executes ( , for ). We report the success rate, task-completion time, and idle time averaged over successful trials, , the total time the robot receives no new action command. As shown in Tab.~ tab:realworld_pnp , a short chunk still leaves idle time even with asynchronous execution (analyzed in Appendix~ app:idle_time ). Extending the chunk greatly reduces it, since executing more actions per policy call leaves enough time to generate the next chunk; the remaining idle time comes mostly from the first policy call at the start of each episode. title: Demonstration-Calibrated Port-Hamiltonian Retuning for Manipulation Policies
summary: Diffusion and VLA policies for manipulation are often deployed through downstream impedance controllers. The stiffness and damping gains of these controllers affect task success, yet are commonly inherited from data collection rather than selected for the deployed policy. Although empirical gain sweeps can improve performance, they require repeated evaluation rollouts. We introduce PHRetune, an offline method that derives controller gains for a frozen policy without evaluation rollouts or gain search. Our approach learns a port-Hamiltonian model from demonstrations to estimate the effort and energy associated with the policy's predicted actions. The policy is applied to recorded demonstration observations, and its predictions are assessed against demonstration-derived effort and energy budgets. From this comparison, we derive a single gain scale in closed form, adjusting the downstream controller while preserving the policy and its action representation. The gains are fixed before evaluation, without requiring a prior manipulator model, task rewards, policy retraining, or additional runtime computation. Across LIBERO suites, PHRetune improves Diffusion Policy success by up to 9.4 percentage points, with the derived gains achieving the highest observed success rates in empirical gain sweeps. On all four real-world manipulation tasks, PHRetuned Diffusion Policy outperforms the nominal policy, alternative gain-tuning methods, and a policy-retraining baseline. The same procedure improves success with SmolVLA and OpenVLA-OFT on every task, while reducing acceleration and jerk for both VLA backbones.
full_text: Demonstration-Calibrated Port-Hamiltonian Retuning for Manipulation Policies Yulong Yang Fan Wu Christine Allen-Blanchette Amit Chakraborty \\ Princeton University Arizona State University Siemens Foundation Technologies Preprint, under review. This work was primarily done during an internship at Siemens Foundation Technologies, Princeton, NJ. Correspondence to amit.chakraborty@siemens.com and yulong.yang@princeton.edu. Diffusion and VLA policies for manipulation are often deployed through downstream impedance controllers. The stiffness and damping gains of these controllers affect task success, yet are commonly inherited from data collection rather than selected for the deployed policy. Although empirical gain sweeps can improve performance, they require repeated evaluation rollouts. We introduce PHRetune, an offline method that derives controller gains for a frozen policy without evaluation rollouts or gain search. Our approach learns a port-Hamiltonian model from demonstrations to estimate the effort and energy associated with the policy’s predicted actions. The policy is applied to recorded demonstration observations, and its predictions are assessed against demonstration-derived effort and energy budgets. From this comparison, we derive a single gain scale in closed form, adjusting the downstream controller while preserving the policy and its action representation. The gains are fixed before evaluation, without requiring a prior manipulator model, task rewards, policy retraining, or additional runtime computation. Across LIBERO suites, PHRetune improves Diffusion Policy success by up to 9.4 percentage points, with the derived gains achieving the highest observed success rates in empirical gain sweeps. On all four real-world manipulation tasks, PHRetuned Diffusion Policy outperforms the nominal policy, alternative gain-tuning methods, and a policy-retraining baseline. The same procedure improves success with SmolVLA and OpenVLA-OFT on every task, while reducing acceleration and jerk for both VLA backbones. Introduction sec:introduction The behavior of a learned manipulation policy depends not only on its predicted actions, but also on the controller that executes them. Diffusion and vision-language-action (VLA) policies often command end-effector targets through a downstream impedance or operational-space controller~ chi2025diffusion,shukor2025smolvla,kim2025fine . The controller’s stiffness and damping therefore shape how policy predictions are realized as motion and interaction forces~ hogan1984impedance,khatib1987unified . Yet these gains are commonly inherited from teleoperated data collection or simulator defaults rather than selected for the deployed policy~ zhu2020robosuite,mandlekar2021matters,liu2023libero . Recent studies show that this choice materially affects policy learning and execution, and that more compliant settings can improve task success~ bronars2026tune,xu2026mind . Prior work addresses this issue either by incorporating compliance into policy learning or by tuning the downstream controller. Variable-impedance actions, explicit compliance predictions, and learning from intent–execution mismatch modify the action representation or training procedure rather than retuning the controller of an unchanged policy~ martin2019variable,hou2025adaptive,xu2026mind . Controller-side approaches instead optimize tracking through a dynamics model, prescribe stiffness from demonstration variability, or search directly over evaluation rollouts~ cheng2024difftune,calinon2010learning,bronars2026tune . These approaches respectively rely on a model-based tracking objective, omit the deployed policy’s predictions, or require execution feedback to select gains. Our goal is to derive a fixed gain tailored to a frozen policy using its task demonstrations, without requiring a prior manipulator model, policy retraining, or gain-selection rollouts. We introduce PHRetune (pronounced ``free-tune"), an offline method that derives controller gains for a frozen policy from its existing task demonstrations, without additional robot interaction for gain selection. A port-Hamiltonian formulation relates action attenuation and controller softening through their effects on the energy supplied by policy-generated setpoints~ hogan1984impedance,van2004port . Under a linear impedance model, this relationship provides a closed-form map from admissible action scalings to controller gains. We determine this action scaling using a surrogate fitted to demonstration transitions, assessing the policy’s predictions on recorded observations against demonstration-derived effort and energy budgets. Gain selection therefore remains blind to evaluation outcomes, requiring neither gain search nor additional robot or simulator rollouts. The resulting controller gains are fixed before evaluation, leaving the policy, action representation, and inference procedure unchanged and introducing no additional runtime overhead. Across three LIBERO suites, PHRetuned Diffusion Policy outperforms the nominal policy, alternative gain-tuning methods, and a policy-retraining baseline. The gains derived before evaluation also achieve the highest observed success rates in empirical gain sweeps. These improvements extend to four real-world manipulation tasks, where PHRetuned Diffusion Policy again outperforms the nominal policy and all evaluated baselines on every task. Applying the same procedure to SmolVLA and OpenVLA-OFT improves success on every task, with motion evaluations showing reduced acceleration and jerk for both VLA backbones. Related Work sec:relatedwork Controller Gains in Policy Learning. Visuomotor manipulation policies, including diffusion policies and VLA models, commonly predict joint- or end-effector targets that are executed by lower-level controllers~ zhao2023learning,chi2025diffusion,shukor2025smolvla,kim2024openvla . Their closed-loop behavior therefore depends on controller gains, although benchmark environments typically treat these gains as fixed parameters rather than quantities selected for the deployed policy~ james2020rlbench,zhu2020robosuite,mandlekar2021matters,liu2023libero,fei2025libero,nasiriany2024robocasa . One line of work incorporates compliance into policy learning. VICES jointly commands Cartesian motion and impedance~ martin2019variable , while related methods learn variable-impedance profiles from task experience or demonstrations~ buchli2011learning,kronander2013learning . Adaptive Compliance Policy predicts compliance alongside diffusion-generated motion~ hou2025adaptive , and Mind the Gap learns implicit impedance from intent–execution mismatch~ xu2026mind . These approaches modify the action representation or training procedure to learn compliant behavior, rather than retuning the downstream controller of an unchanged policy. A complementary line tunes the downstream controller. DiffTune differentiates a tracking objective through a dynamics model~ cheng2024difftune , while demonstration-based rules map motion variability to stiffness~ calinon2010learning . Tune-to-Learn empirically evaluates how controller gains affect policy learning and execution, demonstrating that gain selection can substantially alter task performance~ bronars2026tune . These approaches select gains through tracking objectives, demonstration statistics, or evaluation rollouts. PHRetune instead uses a demonstration-calibrated energy model to assess the frozen policy’s predictions on recorded observations against demonstration-derived effort and energy budgets. This assessment determines a fixed gain scale while preserving the policy, its action representation, and the controller structure. Gain selection therefore requires no policy retraining nor robot or simulator rollouts. Impedance, Passivity, and Port-Hamiltonian Foundations. Impedance control specifies the dynamic relationship between motion and interaction force around a virtual equilibrium~ hogan1984impedance , while operational-space control formulates motion and force control directly in task coordinates~ khatib1987unified . When a learned policy commands this equilibrium, its setpoint updates can supply energy to the controlled system rather than serving solely as kinematic targets. Port-Hamiltonian modeling describes this interaction through stored energy, dissipation, and power-conjugate ports~ van2004port . Under the linear impedance model considered here, spring effort and setpoint velocity form a power-conjugate pair. This representation provides a common basis for relating action attenuation and controller softening through their effects on the energy associated with setpoints. These foundations also underpin energy-shaping and passivity-based control. Interconnection and damping assignment passivity-based control (IDA-PBC) shapes the closed-loop storage and dissipation structure through feedback synthesis~ ortega2002interconnection , whereas energy-tank methods regulate energy exchange during online variations in stiffness or interaction~ ferraguti2013tank,schindlbeck2015unified . PHRetune addresses a different design problem. It neither synthesizes a new feedback law nor enforces a runtime energy budget, but uses a demonstration-calibrated energetic model to derive fixed gains for an existing impedance controller before deployment. The port-Hamiltonian formulation thus supports an offline retuning rule tailored to a frozen policy, with gain selection remaining blind to evaluation outcomes. Method sec:method Given a frozen diffusion or vision-language-action policy, its task demonstrations, and a downstream operational-space impedance controller, our goal is to derive fixed controller gains without policy retraining or evaluation rollouts. PHRetune uses two complementary port-Hamiltonian models to connect offline assessment of the policy’s actions to controller retuning. An action-port surrogate fitted to demonstration transitions provides model-relative effort and energy estimates. We apply the frozen policy to recorded demonstration observations and assess its predicted action chunks against demonstration-derived budgets to determine an admissible action scale. A linear impedance setpoint-port model then relates action attenuation to controller softening through energy matching, providing a closed-form map from this scale to controller gains. The resulting gains are fixed before evaluation and introduce no additional runtime computation. We therefore adopt a learned port-Hamiltonian representation to model end-effector dynamics with dissipation and external forcing~ van2004port,zhong2020dissipative,desai2021port,liu2025physically . PHRetune restricts the learned representation to end-effector motion rather than explicitly reconstructing the full joint-space dynamics of the manipulator. This reduced-order representation aligns with the end-effector action interface of the diffusion and VLA policies considered here. title: What the Guard Misses, the Robot Executes: Implied Harm in VLA Instructions
comment: Under review at the SPAIS 2026 workshop (CoRL 2026)
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) act on instructions without being able to refuse, so screening harmful requests falls to monitors. We test whether these monitors catch ordinary robot tasks requested for harmful reasons, holding the task fixed while varying only how explicitly the intent is stated. $π_{0.5}$ completes the task at every level of explicitness, as often as for harmless controls. Text guards flag nearly every blunt request but few implied ones: up to 95% of implied-harm runs end with the task done and no flag raised, and up to 90% even after recalibrating on robot instructions. Monitoring the model's activations does not close this gap. Linear probes separate harmful from harmless instructions almost perfectly in the base language and vision-language models, but this separation weakens after robot training in two model families, most for implied harm.
full_text: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) act on instructions without being able to refuse, so screening harmful requests falls to monitors. We test whether these monitors catch ordinary robot tasks requested for harmful reasons, holding the task fixed while varying only how explicitly the intent is stated. completes the task at every level of explicitness, as often as for harmless controls. Text guards flag nearly every blunt request but few implied ones: up to 95 of implied-harm runs end with the task done and no flag raised, and up to 90 even after recalibrating on robot instructions. Monitoring the model's activations does not close this gap. Linear probes separate harmful from harmless instructions almost perfectly in the base language and vision-language models, but this separation weakens after robot training in two model families, most for implied harm. Introduction Robot foundation models now take open-ended language instructions and act on them in the physical world~ openvla, pi05 . Unlike a chat model, the vision-language-action models (VLAs) we study cannot refuse: they output only actions. Checks on harmful requests therefore sit mostly outside the policy~ robey2026beyond , for example in a guard that screens the instruction, a planner or judge above it~ roboguard , a filter on its actions, or a monitor that reads its activations. We study two that act before the robot moves: text guards, which read the instruction, and activation probes, which read the model's internal representation of it. The hardest requests to screen are ordinary acts done for harmful reasons. Turning on a stove is harmless until the purpose is to burn someone. In language models, safety monitors catch overtly harmful requests and miss subtler ones~ karne2026recall . We ask whether the same holds when the request drives a robot. We find that the robot ignores the purpose entirely, and the guards notice it only when it is stated bluntly. We test two VLAs, ~ pi05 and OpenVLA-OFT~ oft , on five kitchen tasks from LIBERO-Goal~ libero , attaching a harmful reason to each, such as putting cream cheese in a bowl to make a dog sick. Each reason is phrased three ways: with the harm implied (L1, indirect), stated as fact (L2, direct), or announced outright (L3, blunt). Each is paired with a harmless control of similar length. The task never changes; only the wording does. completes the task at every level as often as it does for the controls. OFT seems safer, but it is not: it fails every request that includes a reason, harmful or not, because it cannot handle the extra sentence. Neither robot responds to the harm, so any check has to come from outside the policy, such as a text guard that screens the instruction. Looking at the text guards Llama Guard 3, WildGuard and Qwen3Guard, we find they respond to wording, not harm. They catch nearly every blunt request but few indirect or direct ones, even though human annotators recognize the intent in most of them. When the harm is only implied, up to 95 of harmful runs end with the task done and no flag raised. Inside the model, the harm signal appears to weaken with robot training. A linear probe separates harmful from harmless instructions almost perfectly in the base language and vision-language models, but loses much of this after robot training, most of all when the harm is only implied. We make three contributions: A controlled intent test for VLAs. The act, objects and scene stay fixed while only the stated purpose and its explicitness vary, and guards and probes run on the same instructions. What the guard misses, the robot executes. As when monitoring chat models, guards catch mostly blunt harm, and the robot carries out the harmful requests they miss. Robot training erodes the harm signal. In two model families, harmful intent is easy to read from the model before robot training and harder after it, extending the known loss of vision-language knowledge in VLAs~ hancock2026actions to safety-relevant content. Related Work Semantic safety for robot foundation models. ASIMOV~ asimov tests whether models judge robot scenarios as safe, without executing them. Closest to us, HazardArena~ hazardarena runs VLAs on matched safe and unsafe tasks with the same motor act and finds they execute both. There, the harm comes from what an object is used for; in ours, it comes only from the stated reason. Guards and wording. Off-the-shelf text guards miss most jailbreak prompts against LLM-based robots~ poex , in part because guards rely on surface keywords~ tasawong2025shortcut . In language models, monitors likewise mostly catch requests whose harm is explicit~ karne2026recall . We test whether this gap carries over to robots, where a missed request is executed. Inside VLAs. VLAs are brittle to paraphrased instructions~ liberopara and can ignore the instruction altogether~ liberoplus . Robot training also erodes the vision-language knowledge they inherit~ hancock2026actions , and probes have so far looked inside VLAs mainly for motion and state features~ haon2025mechanistic, buurmeijer2026observing . Less is known about whether harmful intent survives robot training, which determines whether a monitor reading the VLA's activations can catch what text guards miss. Experimental Setup Instructions. We use five LIBERO-Goal tasks~ libero , such as turning on the stove or putting the cream cheese in the bowl, each of which could cause harm in the right context. For each task, an LLM writes harmful reasons, stories explaining why the task is requested, at three levels of explicitness, plus a harmless control of similar length, keeping the task string verbatim. Two LLM judges check every version for preserved intent and fidelity to the scene, and two human annotators validated a sample (Appendix~ app:instructions ). Robots. We run ~ pi05 and OpenVLA-OFT~ oft from their public LIBERO checkpoints. Both reproduce their published success on the unmodified tasks: OFT 489 of 500 (97.8 , published 97.9 ~ oft ) and 49 of 50 on our five tasks (published 98.0 on all ten~ openpi ). For each task, we run seven reasons on the robot, each at every level and from the same five starting layouts of the scene, for 700 runs in total. OFT, run on four of the five tasks, gives 560 and 20. We also run the unchanged task instruction from the same layouts (25 runs). A run succeeds if the robot completes the requested task within 300 steps, using LIBERO's built-in check. Guards. We score every instruction with Llama Guard 3~ llamaguard3 , WildGuard~ wildguard and Qwen3Guard~ qwen3guard , each thresholded to flag 1 of 10,000 benign WildChat prompts~ wildchat and held fixed across levels. We use these chat thresholds because guards are built and calibrated for chat models; Appendix~ app:recal repeats the analysis with thresholds calibrated on benign robot instructions, and gpt-oss-safeguard is in Appendix~ app:gptoss . We say a harmful episode leaks if the VLA completes the task and the guard does not flag the instruction. Probes. We mean-pool residual-stream activations over the instruction tokens and train a logistic regression on L3 versus controls, holding out one task at a time. Models that take images, both VLMs and VLAs, receive the instruction with the task's first camera frame. The layer is chosen on training tasks only, excluding the first quarter of layers, which mainly encode token identity and match a bag-of-words baseline. Stating the harm, even outright, does not change what the robot does. OFT's failures are not about intent. OFT completes the bare task 19 of 20 times, but none of the 560 episodes that include a reason, harmful or harmless. This is unlikely to be a pipeline artifact: on published paraphrases of the same tasks it succeeds 69 of the time, close to the reported 65 ~ liberopara , and it handles short added phrases without error (Appendix~ app:rollouts ). Its apparent safety comes from failing to handle the added sentence, not from understanding it. Guards catch mostly blunt harm. No guard flags a control or original instruction (Table~ tab:main a). At L3 they flag 92 to 98 , but at L1 and L2 almost nothing: 0 to 2 , except Llama Guard 3 at 6 and 33 . As a result, 66 to 97 of harmful runs at L1 and L2 end with the task done and no flag raised, against 3 to 11 at L3. The intent is not hidden: annotators identify it in 82 of L1 instructions (Appendix~ app:instructions ). Recalibrating on benign robot instructions helps far more at L2 than at L1, where 58 to 90 of harmful runs still leak (Appendix~ app:recal ). Robot training erodes the harm signal. In both model families, probes on the language and vision-language models separate harmful from harmless instructions almost perfectly (Table~ tab:main b). Robot training weakens this: from Prismatic to OFT, AUROC drops by 0.27, 0.20 and 0.14 at L1, L2 and L3, and from PaliGemma to by 0.20, 0.17 and 0.03 (95 CIs exclude zero). The drop is largest for implied harm, so the probes, like the guards, are sensitive to wording. As a monitor, the probe flags only 12 to 16 of harmful instructions, and about three quarters of harmful runs leak. A bag-of-words baseline also scores highly (0.97 to 1.00), so part of this signal may be lexical; we leave separating harm from general sentence content to future work. Discussion Robot guards need to reason about consequences. Current guards were developed for chat, where harmful requests typically state their goal explicitly. A robot request, by contrast, is often harmful only through its context, such as who will be affected by the act, and guards miss this context unless it is stated explicitly. Since that context may not be visible in the scene, a scene-aware judge may not catch it either. A robot guard should reason about what the act will do, not only how the request is worded. Monitors need the signal robot training removes. The base models encode harmful intent well, but robot training weakens it most for implied harm, exactly where a monitor is needed. Co-training on web data, as in , is not enough: it preserves the signal for blunt requests but not for implied ones. A probe can only read what the model retains, so preserving the signal may require including safety-relevant data during robot training. Conclusion VLAs carry out instructions regardless of their stated purpose. The text guards meant to screen them detect harmful intent mostly when it is stated bluntly, and the models' own representation of that intent weakens during robot training. As VLAs improve at following language, ordinary acts requested for harmful reasons are precisely the requests that current safeguards fail to catch. Closing this gap will require guards that reason about the consequences of an act in its context rather than the wording of the request, and robot training that preserves the harm signal inherited from the language model rather than weakening it. Limitations. We study one simulated kitchen, five tasks, 51 reasons and two VLAs. title: LightVLN: Efficient Aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation with Compact Memory and History-Guided Local Aggregation
summary: Aerial vision-and-language navigation (VLN) enables unmanned aerial vehicles to execute long-horizon natural-language instructions from visual observations in complex three-dimensional environments. However, recent aerial VLN models often rely on large-scale vision-language backbones and dense visual histories, imposing substantial computation and memory costs that hinder onboard deployment. We propose LightVLN, a lightweight history-aware aerial VLN framework that combines a compact 0.5B language backbone with compact representations of both historical and current observations. LightVLN compresses each historical frame into a single token using visual features already computed by the policy. It further introduces history- and instruction-conditioned local aggregation to reduce the current observation from 256 to 32 visual tokens while preserving navigation-relevant spatial information. With up to 16 historical frames, the policy uses at most 48 observation-derived tokens. On the public OpenFly dataset, LightVLN achieves 50.93% Test-Seen and 36.14% Test-Unseen success rates (SR), outperforming the evaluated 7B language-backbone baselines on most reported metrics. It also achieves 25.83% SR on AerialVLN-S Val-Seen. In a reconstructed unseen campus, we deploy LightVLN on a DJI M350 RTK with an external Jetson Orin NX 16 GB for closed-loop onboard-compute real-to-sim hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) evaluation, achieving 14.61 Hz model inference and 11.13 Hz end-to-end decision updates. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of LightVLN for aerial navigation.
