Introduction Aerial vision-and-language navigation (VLN) enables unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to follow long-horizon natural-language instructions from visual observations in complex three-dimensional environments~ liu2023aerialvln . It requires the UAV to connect instructions with visual observations and predict a sequence of actions toward the navigation goal. The AerialVLN benchmark established a foundation for this task through simulated aerial environments, annotated navigation trajectories, and a cross-modal alignment baseline~ liu2023aerialvln . Subsequent platforms expanded the realism and scale of aerial navigation data, supporting the development of more advanced navigation models~ wang2025openuav,gao2025openfly . Recent methods further improve spatial reasoning and long-horizon decision making through explicit spatial representations, semantic subgoals, grounded targets, and learned multimodal policies~ gao2024stmr,citynavagent2025,lookasidevln2026,xu2026fly0,aeroact2025 . Aerial navigation models have increasingly adopted larger language backbones and richer visual histories. Video-based navigation models~ zhang2024navid,navila2025 and aerial foundation-model policies~ gao2025openfly,aeroact2025,deng2026dreamfly use large pretrained multimodal backbones for visual grounding and action prediction. Meanwhile, long-horizon aerial navigation has motivated retaining information across observation sequences through selected-frame histories~ gao2025openfly,aeroact2025 , structured spatiotemporal memory~ ding2026hett,jiang2025longfly , and relevance-aware or causal history integration~ ma2026s2d,deng2026dreamfly . These mechanisms provide access to historical visual information for subsequent navigation decisions. However, the use of larger language backbones and richer visual histories also brings substantial computation and memory demands at inference~ zhang2024navid,wu2025vlaan . Deploying aerial navigation models on resource-constrained UAV platforms remains challenging~ wu2025vlaan . In particular, large backbones and extensive visual context increase computation and memory demands at inference. Recent deployment-oriented systems improve efficiency through optimized inference pipelines, lightweight action generation, shared perception, and fast--slow or asynchronous execution~ wu2025vlaan,zhu2026fsdvln,zheng2026onfly . Complementary to these deployment-oriented techniques, we target a compact language backbone and compact representations of both historical and current observations. Lightweight aerial VLN therefore also requires reducing the intrinsic resource demands of the navigation policy while preserving its navigation capability. Designing such a policy poses two challenges: constructing low-cost historical memory that remains useful for action prediction, and compressing the current observation while preserving navigation-relevant spatial information. First, for historical memory, existing aerial VLN methods typically control temporal redundancy and computation through keyframe selection or compact history representations~ gao2025openfly,aeroact2025,jiang2025longfly . These strategies reduce memory cost by limiting the number of retained observations or compressing their representations. NativeMEM~ wang2026nativemem addresses this trade-off by compressing each historical frame into a single action-supervised token, enabling substantially longer and denser visual histories. It constructs memory through a separately optimized visual-encoding path initialized from the policy's vision encoder. Second, for current-view compression, existing methods reduce visual redundancy through learned-query bottlenecks, regional aggregation, or language-conditioned token selection~ li2023blip2,li2024tokenpacker,zhang2024navid,song2026evocomp . These methods effectively compress the current observation but do not exploit navigation history. DreamFly~ deng2026dreamfly incorporates historical context to enhance current-view representations through causal memory, but does not target lightweight visual token compression or low-cost memory construction. These observations motivate an integrated lightweight design that combines low-cost historical memory with compact current-view representations. To address these challenges, we propose , a lightweight history-aware aerial VLN framework that combines a compact 0.5B language backbone with compact representations of both historical and current observations (Fig.~ fig:overview ). Each historical frame is compressed into a single token using visual features already extracted by the policy. For the current observation, history- and instruction-conditioned local aggregation reduces 256 visual tokens to 32 while preserving navigation-relevant spatial information. With up to 16 historical frames, the resulting visual context contains at most 48 observation-derived tokens. We evaluate on the public OpenFly splits~ gao2025openfly and AerialVLN-S~ liu2023aerialvln and conduct extensive same-backbone ablations on OpenFly. We further reconstruct a campus environment and construct a 500-episode unseen evaluation set, where is deployed on a DJI M350 RTK with an external Jetson Orin NX 16\,GB for closed-loop onboard-compute real-to-sim HIL evaluation. The main contributions are: We propose , a lightweight history-aware aerial VLN framework that combines a compact 0.5B language backbone with low-cost historical memory and compact current-view representations. With at most 48 observation-derived tokens, provides a compact visual interface for aerial VLN with a substantially smaller language backbone. We develop two complementary lightweight designs: single-token historical compression that reuses visual features already extracted by the policy, and history- and instruction-conditioned local aggregation that reduces the current observation from 256 to 32 visual tokens while preserving spatial information relevant to navigation. We evaluate on OpenFly and AerialVLN-S and conduct extensive same-backbone ablations on OpenFly. achieves 50.93 Test-Seen and 36.14 Test-Unseen SR on public OpenFly, outperforming the evaluated 7B baselines on most reported OpenFly metrics, and achieves 25.83 SR on AerialVLN-S Val-Seen. We further conduct closed-loop onboard-compute real-to-sim HIL evaluation in a reconstructed unseen campus, where reaches 14.61\,Hz model inference and 11.13\,Hz end-to-end decision updates on Jetson Orin NX 16\,GB. Related Work Aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation Existing aerial VLN methods broadly include structured reasoning and learned multimodal navigation approaches. Structured methods introduce explicit spatial or semantic representations to support navigation reasoning. STMR~ gao2024stmr constructs spatial representations for language-guided reasoning, while CityNavAgent~ citynavagent2025 performs hierarchical semantic planning with global memory. LookasideVLN~ lookasidevln2026 incorporates direction-aware reasoning, and Fly0~ xu2026fly0 uses persistent metric anchors for zero-shot navigation. Learned multimodal approaches directly predict navigation decisions from visual observations and language instructions. AerialVLN~ liu2023aerialvln establishes an early cross-modal navigation baseline, while OpenFly-Agent~ gao2025openfly scales aerial VLN with pretrained multimodal models and historical observations. AeroAct~ aeroact2025 further integrates spatial, temporal, and embodied reasoning within a unified navigation model. Efficient Aerial VLN and Onboard Deployment Existing work improves the efficiency of aerial VLN through lightweight inference, decoupled decision making, and computation reuse. VLA-AN~ wu2025vlaan combines lightweight action generation with an optimized inference pipeline for onboard deployment. FSD-VLN~ zhu2026fsdvln adopts a fast--slow dual-system architecture, separating high-level semantic reasoning from frequent navigation updates. OnFly~ zheng2026onfly shares perception features and reuses memory across decision steps to reduce redundant computation and support real-time onboard execution. Compact Historical and Current Visual Representations Existing work reduces visual redundancy from two complementary aspects: historical representation and current-view compression. For historical representation, OpenFly-Agent~ gao2025openfly and AeroAct~ aeroact2025 retain selected historical observations to provide temporal context while controlling the number of stored views. HETT~ ding2026hett organizes historical information through history-enhanced spatial representations, while LongFly~ jiang2025longfly integrates compact spatiotemporal context for long-horizon navigation. S2D~ ma2026s2d further emphasizes relevance-aware historical information for decision making. Beyond aerial VLN, NativeMEM~ wang2026nativemem compresses each historical frame into a single action-supervised token, enabling much denser temporal memory. It constructs memory through a separately optimized visual-encoding path initialized from the policy's vision encoder. Our memory directly reuses the policy's existing patch features. For current-view compression, BLIP-2~ li2023blip2 uses a learned query bottleneck to extract a compact set of visual features, while TokenPacker~ li2024tokenpacker aggregates local visual tokens to preserve spatial structure with fewer tokens. NaVid~ zhang2024navid introduces language-conditioned visual compression for navigation, and EvoComp~ song2026evocomp selects task-relevant visual tokens through semantic guidance. AeroAct~ aeroact2025 also employs regional visual aggregation in aerial navigation. These methods mainly focus on compressing the current observation itself, whereas navigation history is usually handled as a separate source of context. DreamFly~ deng2026dreamfly instead uses causal memory to enhance current-view representations with historical information. title: Triggering Generalist Reasoning via Predictive Uncertainty for Dual-System VLA
summary: Dual-system Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models improve real-time robotic control by pairing a slow, reasoning-capable generalist with a fast specialist action expert. However, existing methods invoke the generalist at a fixed frequency, ignoring the fact that decision-making complexity varies throughout a rollout. This static strategy wastes computation in easy phases and can delay renewed reasoning when the scene changes unexpectedly. We propose TUD (Triggering generalist reasoning via predictive Uncertainty for Dual-system VLA), an adaptive inference framework that selectively skips unnecessary generalist calls. TUD measures the cross-step dispersion of action re-predictions at the upcoming chunk slot under the cached generalist context, as a predictive uncertainty signal. This signal captures how much the future action plan shifts as new observations arrive and is computed from forwards the architecture already runs, requiring neither manual phase labels nor an auxiliary uncertainty model. On VLA-Arena, it achieves a higher success rate at matched call budgets than alternative uncertainty baselines while maintaining low wall-clock overhead, and more consistently separates successful from failed rollouts. Also, TUD finds a more favorable cost-success trade-off than non-adaptive baselines, tracing an entire operating curve as a single threshold is varied, and substantially reduces VLM calls at matched success rate. The same trade-off appears in our real-robot experiments, where TUD cuts generalist calls by 75% relative to the strongest fixed-interval baseline while achieving an even higher success rate. Our results suggest that predictive uncertainty provides a practical criterion for adaptive reasoning in efficient VLA control.

Introduction sec:introduction Enabling robots to perform diverse tasks across varying environments has been a long-standing challenge. Conventional robot learning has largely focused on policies tailored to specific tasks and robot platforms, which achieve high accuracy within their target scenario but generalize poorly to novel instructions or scenes~ mees2022calvin, VLA_Benchmark_zhang2024vlabench . Recent work addresses this limitation by leveraging pretrained large language or vision-language models~ PaliGemma_beyer2024paligemma, Prismatic_karamcheti2024prismatic to reformulate manipulation as a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) problem~ VLA_Archi_kim2024openvla, VLA_not_black2024pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel, kim2025fine, bu2025univla, shukor1844smolvla , enabling broader generalization across instructions and scenes. The deployment of single-system VLAs is, however, bottlenecked by limited inference throughput, as billion-scale VLMs are too slow for real-time contact-rich manipulation. To reconcile reasoning with fast control, a body of work adopts dual-system architectures~ VLA_Dual_bu2024towards, VLA_Dual_zhang2024hirt, VLA_Dual_shentu2024llms, VLA_Dual_cui2025openhelix, VLA_Dual_chen2025fast, VLA_Dual_zhouchatvla , inspired by the separation between slow deliberative reasoning and fast reactive behavior~ kahneman2011thinking . The generalist (System 2) is a large VLM that consumes the full multimodal context and emits high-level reasoning or a long-horizon action plan. The specialist (System 1) is a lightweight action expert that generates low-latency action chunks conditioned on the generalist's plan. This decoupling amortizes the heavy VLM forward across many specialist steps while allowing the specialist to absorb fresh observations between generalist calls. This gain comes with a new design question that does not exist in single-system policies: when should the generalist be re-invoked? Existing dual-system VLAs leave this question unanswered and use a fixed call interval that interleaves generalist call and specialist at a static frequency~ VLA_Dual_bu2024towards, VLA_Dual_chen2025fast, VLA_Dual_cui2025openhelix . OneTwoVLA~ VLA_Dual_lin2025onetwovla instead learns a decision token to toggle between reasoning and acting modes, but requires manually annotated phase boundaries, which limits scalability and transfer to unseen tasks. In reality, scene difficulty changes step by step within a single rollout, so any fixed call interval wastes generalist calls on easy phases (e.g., a static scene) and reacts too slowly when an unexpected event (e.g., a moved obstacle) arises. An effective re-invocation signal should capture how the long-horizon action plan shifts in response to changes in the surrounding environment. When the scene evolves away from what the cached plan assumed, the predicted actions for upcoming time steps diverge from the existing plan, and a useful trigger must reflect this divergence. To preserve the throughput advantage that motivated the dual-system split in the first place, the signal should also be computable from the specialist forwards the architecture already runs at inference time, without auxiliary uncertainty models or manually labeled phase boundaries. We propose TUD (Triggering generalist reasoning via predictive Uncertainty for Dual-system VLA), which adapts generalist invocation using predictive action-plan dispersion. At each step, the specialist re-predicts the upcoming action chunk against the most recent generalist context. The dispersion is the standard deviation of these re-predictions, remaining low when the cached plan still fits the current scene and increasing when it becomes stale. The invocation rule then defers the generalist call at each decision point when the running mean of the dispersion stays below a threshold, ensuring that the cached plan does not drift too far from a fresh specialist re-prediction. We adapt the single-system ~ VLA_not_black2024pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel backbone into a dual-system. On VLA-Arena~ zhang2025vla , the dispersion provides a more effective invocation signal for adaptive generalist calling than alternative uncertainty signals~ Uncertainty_Dagger_lee2025diff-dagger,kou2024bayesdiff, de2025diffusion, jazbec2025generative, Uncertainty_VLA_ACC_Liang_2026_CVPR , achieving the highest success rate with low wall-clock under the matched budgets. It also consistently separates successful from failed rollouts and tracks within-rollout difficulty. Empirically, TUD finds a more favorable cost--success trade-off than non-adaptive baselines as the threshold is varied. Against the baseline, TUD substantially reduces VLM calls at a matched success rate. Furthermore, we validate TUD on a real SO-101 robotic arm and show that, averaged across three tasks, TUD achieves a higher success rate with fewer generalist calls than all baselines. Our contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=*, topsep=2pt, itemsep=1pt, parsep=0pt, partopsep=0pt] We surface adaptive generalist calling as a central design axis of dual-system VLAs and identify two preconditions missing from existing fixed-interval designs, an interval-flexible architecture and a cheap online invocation signal. We propose TUD, a framework that triggers the generalist via the predictive action-plan dispersion, an inference-time signal computed from existing specialist forwards. A simple thresholding rule turns this signal into a call-or-skip decision, and varying the threshold traces an entire operating curve in the (task success rate, VLM-call budget) plane. TUD finds a more favorable cost--success trade-off than non-adaptive baselines, substantially reducing VLM calls at matched success rate, and the result transfers to a real SO-101 arm. The generalist is invoked at a low frequency, and the specialist runs at every control step and produces actions by combining the generalist's most recent output with the latest observation. Adaptive Generalist Calling sec:adaptive_calling Existing dual-system VLAs fix the generalist call interval to a single value chosen offline, which over-invokes in easy phases and under-invokes it in hard ones. We instead formulate generalist calling as a periodic call/skip decision. At each decision point, a time step at which the rule fires, an invocation policy selects an action from based on the running context, choosing whether to invoke at this point or to defer the call to the next one. The objective is to find that maximizes task success while minimizing the number of generalist invocations: where denotes task success rate, the number of generalist calls per rollout, and trades efficiency against accuracy. Casting calling as an explicit decision problem subsumes the static-frequency setting (where deterministically calls every steps) and exposes the headroom available to scene-conditioned invocation policies. Realizing requires meeting two preconditions surfaced in Section~ sec:dual_system_formulation . The architecture must remain interval-flexible so that adaptive calling does not inherit the collapse, and the invocation signal must be computable online from quantities already produced at inference time so that the trigger itself does not erode the throughput advantage of the dual-system design. title: GeoBridge-VLA: Geometry-Aware Residual Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models encode semantic information from vision-language pretraining, but manipulation also requires precise spatial reasoning. We present GeoBridge-VLA, a two-stage method for learning geometric features from a pretrained VLA's frozen visual encoder and using them for action prediction. Stage I trains a feature bridge and geometry decoder with depth supervision. Stage II freezes these modules and trains a gated residual interface together with the action-side projections and action expert. The residual augments the existing visual tokens without adding a second image encoder or increasing the token count. Deployment requires RGB, robot state, and language, but no depth observations. Under matched evaluation conditions, GeoBridge-VLA achieves 70.9% success on LIBERO, compared with 60.0% for SmolVLA. Disabling the residual in the same trained checkpoint reduces success from 70.90% to 69.85%, with mixed effects across suites. On a physical ROBOTIS OMY robot, GeoBridge-VLA succeeds in 148 of 200 trials (74.0%) across four tasks, compared with 108 of 200 (54.0%) for SmolVLA.

INTRODUCTION sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models extend pretrained vision-language representations to language-conditioned robotic manipulation rt2,openvla,pi0,smolvla . Their pretrained representations provide strong semantic priors for recognizing objects, interpreting instructions, and generalizing across diverse scenes. Robotic manipulation, however, also depends on geometric properties such as depth, relative position, object extent, and local spatial relationships. Representations optimized primarily for semantic alignment do not necessarily preserve this information with the precision required for physical interaction. Recent work has addressed this limitation through explicit depth or 3D observations, external spatial representations, calibrated camera geometry, and auxiliary geometric supervision. SpatialVLA introduces 3D-aware spatial representations~ spatialvla , DepthVLA incorporates a pretrained depth module~ depthvla , FALCON injects features from a spatial foundation model~ falcon , G VLA introduces calibrated camera geometry into the visual-token stream~ g3vla , and GIFT shapes intermediate policy representations through control-oriented structural supervision ~ gift . We investigate whether the frozen visual hierarchy of a VLA can provide depth-supervised features for action prediction without a separate image encoder, additional geometry tokens, or depth observations at deployment. We refer to this adaptation as geometry retrofit. GeoBridge-VLA first learns a geometric readout from frozen intermediate visual features, then transfers the resulting features to the action policy. Here, geometry refers to the representation learned through depth supervision. In Stage I, a feature bridge maps selected encoder features to a geometry decoder. We train the bridge and decoder using simulator ground-truth depth for LIBERO and teacher-generated pseudo-depth for OMY. In Stage II, we freeze both modules and train a gated residual interface that adds decoder features to the native visual tokens during action learning. The two paths share the VLA's visual encoder, preserving the token count and existing conditioning pathway. We evaluate GeoBridge-VLA across all four LIBERO manipulation suites and on a physical ROBOTIS OMY platform. The complete adaptation pipeline improves manipulation success over the SmolVLA baseline in simulation and physical robot evaluation, while a same-checkpoint residual intervention tests the trained policy's sensitivity to the learned geometry-to-action pathway. Detailed results are reported in Sec.~ sec:results . The main contributions of this work are: We formulate geometry integration in pretrained VLAs as a geometry retrofit problem and introduce a shared-hierarchy pathway that learns a depth-supervised geometric readout directly from frozen intermediate VLA features without adding a separate image encoder to the deployed policy. We propose a two-stage geometry acquisition and geometry-to-action transfer strategy in which depth supervision first adapts the feature bridge and geometry decoder, after which they are frozen and a gated residual interface transfers their representation into the native visual-token space for action learning. We evaluate the resulting policy across all four LIBERO suites and on a physical ROBOTIS OMY robot under depth-free deployment, and further analyze shared-encoder depth prediction and same-checkpoint residual intervention to examine geometry acquisition and the trained policy's sensitivity to geometry-to-action transfer. Related Work sec:related-work Monocular Depth Estimation Transformer-based monocular depth estimation has progressed from DPT and ZoeDepth to large-scale foundation models such as Depth Anything V2 and Depth Anything 3~ dpt,zoedepth,depthanythingv2,da3 . CLIP-based approaches further demonstrate that depth-related information can be recovered from frozen vision--language representations: DepthCLIP exploits patch--text correlations, while SPACE-CLIP directly decodes semantic and structural features from a frozen CLIP vision encoder ~ depthclip,spaceclip . These works primarily target depth prediction; GeoBridge-VLA instead uses depth supervision to adapt geometric information for closed-loop action generation. Vision-Language-Action Models VLA models extend pretrained vision--language representations to robotic control. RT-2 and OpenVLA demonstrate large-scale vision--language-to-action transfer~ rt2,openvla , while uses flow matching for continuous action generation~ pi0 . Recent systems also emphasize efficient policy design and deployment, including OpenVLA-OFT, TinyVLA, and SmolVLA ~ openvlaoft,tinyvla,smolvla . We use SmolVLA as the policy backbone throughout our action-policy experiments. Geometry-Aware Vision-Language-Action Models Recent VLA systems incorporate geometric or spatial structure through several mechanisms. Explicit 3D approaches use depth, point clouds, or dedicated spatial representations: 3D-VLA couples 3D perception and action generation ~ 3dvla , FP3 and PointVLA operate on point-cloud features ~ fp3,pointvla , and 3D-CAVLA combines depth perception with task-oriented spatial reasoning~ 3dcavla . Other methods improve spatial reasoning without requiring metric depth at deployment. IVRA reuses affinity information from the native visual encoder at inference~ ivra , while RetoVLA repurposes Register Tokens for spatial reasoning~ retovla . FALCON injects features from an embodied spatial model~ falcon , and GIFT imposes geometry-aware structural supervision on intermediate policy representations~ gift . Other approaches incorporate geometric structure into VLA policies through different mechanisms. SpatialVLA predicts depth and back-projects image features into egocentric 3D structure~ spatialvla . G VLA injects calibrated camera geometry through geometric encodings and cross-view fusion ~ g3vla , while GP3 and AugVLA-3D introduce dedicated spatial encoders or VGGT-derived 3D features before action prediction~ gp3,augvla3d . QDepth-VLA and DepthVLA incorporate dedicated depth experts or pretrained depth transformers~ qdepthvla,depthvla , whereas Evo-Depth extracts implicit depth features from RGB and progressively aligns depth-aware modulation with action learning~ evodepth . Concurrent GaussVLA lifts semantic and depth features into compact 3D Gaussian tokens for geometric reasoning~ gaussvla . GeoBridge-VLA instead learns a depth-supervised geometric readout directly from intermediate features of the frozen native VLA visual encoder and transfers the resulting representation through a gated residual interface. This separates geometry acquisition from geometry-to-action transfer while requiring neither a second image encoder nor additional visual tokens at deployment. title: How (and How Not) to Use Data Augmentation in VLA Post-Training
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 workshop RoboPAD. Code and videos at https://bramgrooten.nl/vla-augm/
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models currently demonstrate strong performance in a wide range of real-world robotics tasks. However, they often still lack the generalization ability to handle large visual out-of-distribution shifts. Post-training of VLAs with reinforcement learning (RL) has been shown to benefit robustness, but significant room for improvement remains. In this work, we systematically study the effect of image augmentation on VLA post-training. We find that it is crucial to augment only the critic module during RL updates, while leaving the actor's input clean during both rollouts and updates. For $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.5 this raises out-of-distribution success on LIBERO-Plus by $7.8$ and $10.0$ points respectively, while augmenting the actor collapses training entirely. We investigate a range of augmentation types and strengths, and provide practical recommendations for improving generalization in VLA post-training.

However, they often still lack the generalization ability to handle large visual out-of-distribution shifts. Post-training of VLAs with reinforcement learning (RL) has been shown to benefit robustness, but significant room for improvement remains. In this work, we systematically study the effect of image augmentation on VLA post-training. We find that it is crucial to augment only the critic module during RL updates, while leaving the actor's input clean during both rollouts and updates. For and GR00T N1.5 this raises out-of-distribution success on LIBERO-Plus by and points respectively, while augmenting the actor collapses training entirely. We investigate a range of augmentation types and strengths, and provide practical recommendations for improving generalization in VLA post-training. Code and videos are available at: Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as capable generalist robot policies, yet their performance degrades sharply under visual shifts that are common in the real world: new backgrounds, lighting, distractors, and camera poses fei2025liberoplus . A promising route to closing this gap is post-training pretrained VLAs with reinforcement learning (RL), which has been shown to improve execution and semantic generalization by liu2025rlvla . However, the authors also indicate that RL post-training alone does not consistently improve robustness to visual out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts, leaving a central limitation for real-world deployment unsolved. Image augmentation is a natural, low-cost solution with a long history of improving visual robustness in deep RL, and the question of where to inject augmentation within an actor-critic network is well studied. hansen2021svea stabilized Q-learning by augmenting the value path while keeping the bootstrap target clean, and almuzairee2024recipe later showed that, for standard convolutional policies, augmenting both actor and critic inputs (with a clean target network) is more effective. Yet this line of work studies small CNN encoders with Gaussian or categorical actors, a regime far from modern vision--language--action models. In VLAs the visual encoder is a large pretrained VLM whose features risk being corrupted, and the actor is a flow-matching head through which gradients must propagate. Whether existing augmentation recipes transfer to this setting remains unknown. In this work, we provide the first systematic study of image augmentation for VLA post-training. We ablate where augmentation is applied (actor vs.\ critic), what type of augmentation is used, and how strongly it can be pushed before training collapses. Our central finding inverts prior wisdom: for VLAs post-trained with PPO, critic-only augmentation is most effective, and augmenting the actor is detrimental to training dynamics, which is the opposite of the conclusion drawn for convolutional policies~ almuzairee2024recipe . shows both halves of that result: what the augmented observations look like, and what applying them in the wrong place does to post-training. Based on these results, we distill practical rules of thumb for robust VLA post-training. Prior Work on Data Augmentation for VLAs Vision-language-action models and RL post-training. VLA models combine a pretrained vision-language backbone with an action head and are typically trained by imitation learning on large demonstration datasets~ kim2024openvla, black2025pi0, black2025pi05, bjorck2025groot . A growing line of work further fine-tunes VLAs with online reinforcement learning~ guo2025irevla, lu2026vlarl, li2026simplevlarl, zang2025rlinfvla, deng2025vlarlsurvey , including methods designed specifically for diffusion and flow-matching action experts~ ren2025dppo, zhang2025reinflow, lyu2026fpo . These approaches mainly improve in-distribution task success. In a controlled study, liu2025rlvla find that RL post-training improves execution and semantic generalization, but yields little to no gain on visual out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts such as background and texture changes. How the backbone is adapted matters too: hu2026simplerecipe show that on-policy RL with low-rank adaptation preserves a VLA's performance in continual learning over a sequence of tasks. Data augmentation in visual RL. Image augmentation has a long history of improving sample efficiency and generalization in visual RL~ laskin2020rad, yarats2021drq, ma2025augsurvey , and the question of how to apply augmentation within the update has been studied in detail. hansen2021svea stabilize Q-learning by augmenting the value path while keeping the bootstrap target clean, raileanu2021drac regularize policy and value toward invariance across augmentations, grooten2024madi mask distracting image regions, and almuzairee2024recipe conclude that augmenting both actor and critic inputs, while keeping the target network clean, is most effective. All of these works, however, consider small convolutional encoders with Gaussian or categorical actors, a regime far from modern VLAs with pretrained VLM backbones and flow-matching action experts. Robustness and augmentation for VLAs. Robustness benchmarks show that VLAs are brittle under visual perturbations; on LIBERO-Plus, for instance, success rates can collapse from 95 to below 30 under modest lighting or background changes~ liu2023libero, fei2025liberoplus . Several recent methods target this gap. grover2025preserving improve visual robustness by preserving pretrained VLM representations during fine-tuning. On the RL side, zhang2025robustvla add Jacobian and smoothness regularizers during post-training, xie2026strongvla decouple robustness learning from task alignment in a two-stage curriculum, and peng2026pairvla introduce paired auxiliary losses that enforce invariance to task-preserving visual changes and sensitivity to task-altering ones. Other works move augmentation out of the RL update entirely: gao2026sword apply style augmentation inside a learned world model, shi2026beyond rely on domain-randomized simulation for sim-real co-training, and xue2025resample augment the demonstration data itself via exploratory sampling. Where should augmentation be applied? Despite this activity, no prior work studies where image augmentation should be injected during RL post-training of VLAs---actor, critic, or both---even though this placement question is well understood for conventional visual RL~ hansen2021svea, raileanu2021drac . The closest works answer adjacent questions: peng2026pairvla achieve visual robustness in VLAs through auxiliary paired losses rather than augmentation, and almuzairee2024recipe study augmentation placement only for small convolutional policies. Our work fills this gap with a systematic study of where augmentation should be applied, what type works best, and how strong it can be during VLA post-training. Experimental Framework Augmentation Suite sec:framework Models and post-training. We study two VLAs that both pair a VLM backbone with a flow-matching action head, but couple the two differently. In ~ black2025pi05 the action expert shares one attention stack with the image and language tokens of a PaliGemma-style VLM, attending into them directly, and the robot's proprioceptive state reaches the model as discretized tokens appended to the prompt. In GR00T N1.5~ bjorck2025groot We use the GR00T N1.5 release; it has no separate publication, so we cite the GR00T N1 paper that introduces the architecture. the head is instead a diffusion-transformer (DiT) that cross-attends to the features of an Eagle VLM, and proprioception enters through a separate encoder. For both VLAs, we start from a LIBERO-Spatial supervised fine-tuning (SFT) checkpoint and post-train it with PPO~ schulman2017ppo for up to epochs using RLinf~ zang2025rlinfvla . Every epoch collects episodes ( sequential rollout rounds over parallel environments) with each episode capped at steps. We use a value head that takes the VLM's final features as input, so the critic and the actor share one backbone pass unless augmentation is applied to only one of them ( ). To run PPO on VLA models, we need the log-probability of the action taken, and a flow-matching head does not provide one. An action chunk is produced by integrating a deterministic ODE from a prior draw , which gives no tractable density over actions. We therefore use Flow-SDE~ chen2025pirl , which takes the ODE-to-SDE conversion of Flow-GRPO~ liu2025flowgrpo and adapts it to flow-based VLAs. Replacing the deterministic integration with an equivalent SDE that preserves the model's marginals at every timestep turns each denoising step into a Gaussian transition whose density is available in closed form. The denoising chain itself becomes the stochastic policy that PPO optimizes, and exploration comes from the injected noise. Optimization settings, learning rates and batch sizes are listed in . Augmentation suite. All augmentations act on the observation images and are applied only in the training forward pass. Rollouts and evaluations always see clean observations, so the behavior policy and every reported success rate are measured on unaugmented inputs. During training we adjust both camera views (base and wrist), using either overlay and/or shift augmentations. Random overlay~ hansen2021soda , inspired by mixup~ zhang2018mixup , convexly blends each observation with a natural image drawn from a fixed bank, , with unless stated otherwise. The bank holds ten images from each of the classes of the ImageNet Winter21 release~ deng2009imagenet , and each draw is additionally randomly resized, cropped and flipped, so the effective overlay distribution is far larger than the image count. A fresh overlay is drawn per sample and shared across the two camera views, so one blend roughly corresponds to a single scene change observed from both viewpoints. shows both camera views of one observation before and after augmenting at the default strength. In of we sweep the full range of . Random shift~ yarats2021drq pads the observation by pixels and takes a random crop back to the original resolution ( ), independently per camera as two physically mounted cameras may move separately. The pad is sized relative to the observation rather than copied outright: of pixels is a shift, matched to the -pixel pad DrQ~ yarats2021drq applies to its inputs ( ), so the perturbation ratio stays comparable at our higher resolution. We use replicate padding, repeating the edge pixels. We also consider the composition of both augmentation types, see . Benchmarks and metrics. We train on LIBERO-Spatial~ liu2023libero , a suite of ten tabletop manipulation tasks that share objects but differ in spatial arrangement and target location. We report in-distribution (IND) success rate on the training suite itself: each of the ten tasks is run with seeds, giving evaluation episodes per checkpoint. To examine generalization capability, we further measure out-of-distribution (OOD) performance on LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025liberoplus , which perturbs the LIBERO tasks along seven annotated axes. We report the five visual axes---background textures, light conditions, objects layout, camera viewpoints and sensor noise---comprising of the tasks. Each of the tasks is evaluated once, and we report the unweighted mean over the five axis success rates. See for examples of tasks from each LIBERO-Plus category used in this work. title: Do VLAs Understand and Adapt to the Objects They Handle, or Simply Replay Learned Behaviors?
summary: This paper asks whether VLA generalization is grounded in a global understanding of objects' physical properties that enables policies to adapt their motion to unseen setups, or if policies simply replay the motions they've learnt that happen to succeed in new setups. The former reflects genuine generalization; the latter reflects incidental robustness. We first examine awareness of physical properties in seven VLAs by applying linear probing and representational similarity analysis (RSA) to their activations. We find that physical properties, including mass, fragility, deformability, friction and size are less decodable than non-physical properties such as semantic category, material, sound and price in nearly every modality stream. Compared with their base VLMs, robot pre-training weakens the linear encoding of physical properties in the language stream. Neither pre-training nor downstream fine-tuning strengthens the alignment between physical-property differences and activation distances. We then ask whether the weak physical information present in these activations shapes the actions a VLA generates. In a controlled LIBERO case study, we increase the mass of an in-domain object and signal the change through language or vision. Most VLAs use similar lifting behaviour for the heavier and original-mass objects, leading to task success declines. The few exceptions change their behaviour in response to lexical or visual cues rather than to mass itself. These results suggest that VLAs encode physical properties weakly and do not reliably use them to adapt their motion.

Introduction Vision Language Action models (VLAs) trained on large robot corpora show some robustness to unseen objects and environments~ liberopro,liberoplus,liberox,liberopara,quest,liberogen . A fundamental question, however, remains: is this generalization grounded in a global understanding of object physical properties, e.g. mass and deformability, that lets the policy adapt its motion to new setups, or does it just replay the motions they've learnt in training, and assume they are robust in unseen setups? We examine two dimensions. Awareness: do VLAs represent the physical properties of the objects they manipulate in their latent representations? Following~ vlaprobesym,vlaprobeval,featobs,rsa,rsanlp , we quantify awareness with two metrics. Decodability fits a linear probe to the model's activations and asks whether a property can be read out of them; representation geometry uses representational similarity analysis (RSA) to ask whether pairwise distances between object activations track differences in that property, such that objects with similar property values are represented similarly. Across seven widely used VLAs on the OXE and DROID datasets, we find that all physical properties, including mass, fragility, deformability, friction and size, are less decodable than the other properties, such as category, material, sound and price, in almost every modality stream, and no stream's pairwise activation distances align most strongly with differences in a physical property. Moreover, physical properties are less decodable from the language stream after robot-interaction pre-training and downstream fine-tuning than in the corresponding base VLMs, while neither stage strengthens the alignment between physical-property differences and activation distances (Sec.~ sec:experiments ). Behavioral adaptation: do VLAs adapt their actions to changes in objects' physical properties? We answer this with a controlled case study of mass in LIBERO (Sec.~ case_study ). As shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser , we select manipulable containers from LIBERO, preserve their geometry while adding the mass of realistic contents, and signal the change through language (top row in Fig.~ fig:teaser ) or vision (bottom row in Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Six VLAs execute tasks with mass-amended and original objects under otherwise identical setups. Success falls for mass-amended objects, since for most VLAs the lifting-phase actions deviate no further from the original. Three policies are exceptions, but none tracks mass by exhibiting the human pattern of lifting heavier objects more slowly. Instead, the action divergence arises from either lexical rewording or pixel-level changes. As a conclusion, the results suggest that VLAs encode physical properties weakly and do not reliably use them to adapt their motion. Related Work Probing VLA representations. Linear probes are widely used in LLMs, where affine readouts recover high-level concepts encoded as activation directions~ linrep,catgeom . Applied to VLAs, they reveal symbolic object and action states~ vlaprobesym , value-like success structure~ vlaprobeval , and observable end-effector variables such as yaw and gripper aperture~ featobs . Richer techniques expose complementary structure; for example, sparse autoencoders recover motion primitives, task semantics and episode-specific features~ sae . We use linear probes for their simple, uniform readout across architectures. Prior work shows that robot training can degrade broad multimodal capabilities and pretrained representations, with retention depending on the action representation and training recipe~ vlm2vla,preserverep,vlatrace . We study this degradation through the lens of object representations, asking which physical properties are retained or lost; our analysis is therefore complementary rather than a rediscovery of the broader effect. Representational similarity analysis. Introduced in systems neuroscience~ rsa , RSA relates two systems through their dissimilarity structures and is a standard tool for connecting neural and symbolic representations in language models~ rsanlp . We apply it to VLAs to ask what a probe cannot: whether a property organizes the representation. A property can be linearly decodable yet contribute nothing to the distances between object embeddings. Object physical properties. PhysObjects~ physobjects annotates mass, fragility, deformability, material and other properties in household-object images, and uses them to ground a VLM that improves object selection by a high-level LLM planner. Human-norm resources provide reference labels for some properties, including measured mass in YCB~ ycb and size in THINGSplus~ thingsplus ; we use these to validate our annotation (Sec.~ sec:annotation ). That line of work targets task planning, i.e. which object to pick for a goal, whereas we target motion execution: whether a policy's low-level actions reflect the properties of the object it holds. Dataset and Annotation sec:annotation In this paper we augment three widely-used datasets: OXE~ oxe , DROID~ droid , and LIBERO~ libero , with commonsense object-property annotations elicited from GPT-4.1. We restrict our study to the pick-and-place task family, and from each dataset select the one-hand-manipulable objects: for OXE, for DROID, and for LIBERO (e.g.\ apple, mug, moka pot). For each object we annotate twelve properties spanning physical mechanics, semantic identity and everyday context: mass, fragility, deformability, friction, size, material, sound Whether the object is characteristically associated with producing a sound, e.g.\ a bell or blender vs.\ a towel. , price, category , location , colour The object's most characteristic colour. , and disposability Whether the object is typically single-use and discarded after use (e.g.\ a napkin) rather than reused (e.g.\ a mug). . We refer to the first five as physical properties: by common sense, they directly affect how an object is grasped, lifted and placed. Among these, mass, fragility, deformability, friction, size, sound and price are ordinal, and material, category, location, colour and disposability are categorical. For a categorical property we query GPT-4.1 one object at a time by name, e.g.\ ``In what type of room is a \ object\ most typically found?'' for location, and record its chosen label from a fixed label set. For an ordinal property we instead pose pairwise comparisons by name, ``Which is more X, \ object \ or \ object \ ?'', over every within-dataset pair (each asked in both orders to cancel order bias). We then fit a Bradley-Terry (BT) model~ bt to the resulting win matrix to obtain a per-object score and a ranking within each dataset. Annotation validity. We assess GPT-4.1's annotations against human-labelled reference datasets. For the categorical properties we report classification accuracy and Cohen's against a human gold label: category ( , ; THINGSplus~ thingsplus ) and material ( , ; PhysObjects~ physobjects ). For the ordinal properties we report the balanced accuracy of GPT-4.1's pairwise ``which is more X?'' judgments against the human-norm ordering: size (THINGSplus~ thingsplus ), sound (Amsel et al.~ amsel ), mass (YCB measured mass~ ycb ), and fragility and deformability against the PhysObjects physobjects . Every accuracy above meets or exceeds the inter-human-annotator agreement that PhysObjects requires to accept a human gold label~ physobjects , so we treat the GPT-4.1 labels as trustworthy. The remaining properties, friction, price, location, colour and disposability, have no established human dataset and are annotated by GPT-4.1 without validation. LIBERO's simulated mass does not reflect an object's real-world weight. Every object is assigned a uniform density ( ) with no explicit mass, so MuJoCo computes each object's mass as density collision-mesh volume, i.e. a pure size proxy that ignores material and contents. Because the LIBERO fine-tunes were trained under this physics, for LIBERO we discard the GPT-4.1 real-world mass annotation and label mass with the simulator's density-derived value instead. Models and Methodology sec:methodology We study seven widely used VLA policies spanning the three dominant action-decoding paradigms: autoregressive discrete tokens ( -FAST~ pi0fast , OpenVLA~ openvla ), flow-matching action experts ( ~ pi0 , ~ pi05 , SmolVLA~ smolvla , GR00T-N1.7~ groot,grootn17 ), and JEPA-style latent prediction (VLA-JEPA~ vlajepa ). We ask whether these models internally represent object physical properties, rather than merely mapping pixels or text to actions. Borrowing from mechanistic interpretability in LLMs, we study the geometry of the frozen models' layer-wise activations through linear probing and representational similarity analysis (RSA), asking where and how those latent representations encode each object property (property details in Sec.~ sec:annotation ). Latent representation extraction. Fig.~ fig:arch shows how we extract frozen latent representations from the two mainstream VLA architecture classes, autoregressive (top) and flow-matching (bottom). Consider a frame of a trajectory in which the robot manipulates object . title: Controllable and Photorealistic Pedestrian Risky Motion Generation for End-to-End Driving Safety Evaluation
summary: Evaluating end-to-end autonomous driving under rare, safety-critical vehicle-pedestrian interactions requires photorealistic, sensor-level scenarios. However, trajectory-based scenario generators cannot synthesize raw visual observations, whereas video-based approaches lack controllability. To bridge this gap, we present ControlPed, a novel framework that combines trajectory-level conflict synthesis with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to generate photorealistic, motion-controllable safety-critical scenarios. Built upon HazardPed, a dataset derived from 10,352 traffic videos comprising 422 conflict trajectories, HD maps, and 857 annotated 3D human motions, ControlPed first generates conflict trajectories, lifts them into 3D human motion sequences via text-conditioned motion diffusion, and finally renders multi-view sensor observations using animatable 3DGS avatars. Safety evaluation in 88 rendered photorealistic scenarios reveals that seven leading end-to-end driving models suffer a severe performance drop, with their mean HDScore plunging from 88.8 to 47.4, exposing major failure modes under dangerous pedestrian behaviors. The dataset and testing benchmarks will be released to facilitate safety assessment of vehicle-pedestrian interactions.
full_text: Evaluating end-to-end autonomous driving under rare, safety-critical vehicle-pedestrian interactions requires photorealistic, sensor-level scenarios. However, trajectory-based scenario generators cannot synthesize raw visual observations, whereas video-based approaches lack controllability. To bridge this gap, we present ControlPed, a novel framework that combines trajectory-level conflict synthesis with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to generate photorealistic, motion-controllable safety-critical scenarios. Built upon HazardPed, a dataset derived from 10,352 traffic videos comprising 422 conflict trajectories, HD maps, and 857 annotated 3D human motions, ControlPed first generates conflict trajectories, lifts them into 3D human motion sequences via text-conditioned motion diffusion, and finally renders multi-view sensor observations using animatable 3DGS avatars. Safety evaluation in 88 rendered photorealistic scenarios reveals that seven leading end-to-end driving models suffer a severe performance drop, with their mean HDScore plunging from 88.8 to 47.4, exposing major failure modes under dangerous pedestrian behaviors. The dataset and testing benchmarks will be released to facilitate safety assessment of vehicle-pedestrian interactions. INTRODUCTION Evaluating end-to-end autonomous driving requires sensor-level safety-critical data, since raw observations are directly mapped to future trajectories~ hu2023planning . However, high-risk vehicle-pedestrian interactions are rare in real-world driving logs. This motivates synthesizing vehicle-pedestrian conflict scenarios at the sensor-level to evaluate models under realistic deployment conditions~ zhou2025hugsim . Existing approaches for safety-critical scenario generation follow trajectory-based or video-based paradigms. For trajectory-based methods, adversarial~ liu2026adv methods often generate unnatural trajectories, and learning-based~ lin2025causal methods suffer from data scarcity. Both of them lack multi-view video rendering. In contrast, video-based methods satisfy sensor-level requirements~ liu2026safegen,fu2025controllable , but lack behavioral controllability. Recent technical advances provide new ways to address these challenges. 3DGS converts driving logs into photorealistic scenes~ chen2025omnire , text-conditioned motion generation models enable fine-grained control~ tevet2022human , and animatable avatars facilitate dynamic integration~ lei2024gart . However, because existing motion datasets focus on daily tasks~ punnakkal2021babel , models trained on them fail to capture safety-critical pedestrian dynamics~ huang2024stablemofusion . Bridging this gap requires constructing safety-critical pedestrian datasets to train generative models for controllable, photorealistic scene editing and end-to-end algorithms evaluation. Our key insight is that safety-critical scenario generation requires hierarchical decomposition: macro-level collision paths governed by trajectory control, micro-level actions guided by joint dynamics, and sensor-level inputs realized via photorealistic rendering. To this end, we propose ControlPed, a three-stage framework comprising trajectory generation, motion synthesis, and photorealistic rendering. Trained on 422 real conflict trajectories and 857 hazardous human motion sequences (Fig.~ fig:framework a), ControlPed couples a conflict trajectory generator with a text-driven motion diffusion model (Fig.~ fig:framework b–c). A hard root constraint guarantees strict alignment between generated motions and target trajectories. Animatable avatars are subsequently composited into 3DGS scenes to render photorealistic camera videos (Fig.~ fig:framework d). Finally, these synthesized scenarios serve to evaluate seven end-to-end driving models, closing the loop from conflict synthesis to safety assessment (Fig.~ fig:framework e). This work makes the following key contributions: HazardPed Dataset: We present HazardPed, a safety-critical dataset that combines real conflict trajectories, HD maps, and human motions. It bridges the scarcity of risky interaction data, providing a prior for controllable pedestrian scenario generation. ControlPed Generator: We propose ControlPed, a controllable scenario synthesis method that couples trajectory-level conflict generation with text-conditioned motion diffusion. It achieves sensor-level photorealism without sacrificing fine-grained pedestrian control. Safety Evaluation Benchmark: We establish a photorealistic benchmark to evaluate autonomous driving safety. This benchmark enables third-party testing agencies and regulatory bodies to assess algorithm reliability before real-world deployment. RELATED WORK Safety-Critical Scenario Generation Trajectory-based scenario generators synthesize hazardous interactions via behavior perturbation~ liu2026adv,jing2026counterscene or traffic priors~ lin2025causal . However, their 2D bird's-eye-view representations strip away key pedestrian dynamics essential for vision-based end-to-end models. Conversely, video-based approaches introduce sensor-level realism via asset insertion or pose-guided editing~ liu2026safegen, fu2025controllable , yet lack fine-grained trajectory or human control. Asset insertion struggles to enforce precise terminal collision states, while 2D pose editing lacks metric grounding, preventing control over real-world vehicle–pedestrian distances. Consequently, achieving joint controllability over macro trajectories and micro pedestrian motions in photorealistic rendering remains an open challenge. Human Motion Generation and Datasets Text-conditioned human motion generation models, built on diffusion architectures~ tevet2022human, huang2024stablemofusion , synthesize diverse motions from language but lack spatial grounding to specify coordinate dynamics. Although recent spatial control techniques incorporate trajectory or sparse joint constraints~ cohan2024flexible,xie2024omnicontrol,shafir2024human , their applicability remains bounded by the underlying training data. Standard motion benchmarks built on AMASS, HumanML3D, and BABEL focus almost exclusively on daily activities~ zhu2023human . Consequently, critical conflict dynamics, such as abrupt dodging or freezing under imminent vehicle threat, remain remarkably scarce, hindering the generation of safety-critical scenarios. Scenario Reconstruction and End-to-End Evaluation 3DGS enables photorealistic rendering and has been widely adopted in driving scenario reconstruction~ zhou2024drivinggaussian . To handle dynamic objects, recent approaches decouple foreground actors from background modeling, allowing moving entities to be controlled independently~ chen2025omnire . Advances in pose-driven animatable avatars further free pedestrians from rigid log replaying, enabling the insertion of hazardous human behaviors into reconstructed scenes. For safety evaluation, existing paradigms face clear trade-offs: open-loop tests on passive logs lack reactivity, simulators exhibit a pronounced sim-to-real gap. Recently, reconstruction-based closed-loop simulations combine realism with interactivity by evaluating models on rendered real-world scenes~ zhou2025hugsim , yet they lack critical pedestrian-involved hazards. Therefore, injecting controllable pedestrian behaviors into photorealistic reconstructed scenes is essential for end-to-end safety evaluation. HAZARDPED DATASET To enable controllable injection of hazardous pedestrian motions and resolve the scarcity of safety-critical interaction data, we construct HazardPed by filtering dynamic interactions from web videos and open-source datasets. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:dataset , HazardPed integrates diverse vehicle-pedestrian conflict trajectories, aligned HD maps, and paired text-conditioned human motion data. Safety-critical scenario dataset We collected 10,352 real-world traffic videos from YouTube and public datasets~ kotseruba2016joint . Following the PedGen pipeline, we performed 2D pedestrian tracking, camera pose estimation, and SMPL body fitting, retaining 3,497 valid clips after post-processing~ liu2025learning . Object trajectories were extracted using YOLO11 and BoT-SORT~ khanam2024yolov11,aharon2022bot . To map 2D detections into global world coordinates, homography matrices for static CCTV feeds were calibrated based on average human height, while UniDepthV2 and DROID-SLAM estimated camera intrinsics and ego-vehicle poses for dashcam feeds~ liu2026monocular . Finally, Mask2Former~ cheng2022masked extracted road semantics, yielding 422 scenarios with 566 vehicle-pedestrian conflict pairs. Human Motion Extraction and Annotation Following human verification, 1,473 valid motion clips were retained. We adopted the vocabulary format of BABEL~ punnakkal2021babel for action annotation. Human motions were rendered into video frames, allowing Claude to generate initial textual descriptions and action categories. Precise temporal boundaries for action segments were then established using frame-wise kinematic signals. Upon final human review, we obtained 586 navigation motion clips and 271 hazardous reaction motion clips. Each annotated sample consists of a pedestrian motion sequence paired with textual annotations, denoted as , where across frames. Here, and specify root translation and orientation, while captures the rotations of 21 body joints. The scalar indicates the action category, and represents the natural language description.
