title: Arm-wise Compositional Generalization in Dual-Arm Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Generalization in multi-arm collaboration can be studied as composing familiar atomic skills in new ways across arms. However, existing evaluations offer limited insight into which training and architectural choices support this ability under different coordination requirements. We introduce \textbf{ACG-Bench}, a benchmark for \emph{Arm-wise Compositional Generalization} that provides a common testbed for studying skill recomposition in dual-arm policies. It contains 23 task--condition pairs across 8 task families, with 6 in-domain conditions and 17 unseen compositions covering reordering, synchronization, their combination, and cross-task composition. All methods receive the same per-arm atomic prompts, and success requires achieving the task goal while satisfying physical milestones and specified order or timing constraints. Using $π_{0.5}$ as a common vision-language-action backbone, we compare representative data-augmentation and architectural strategies with shared source data and a common evaluation protocol. Our architectural study examines arm-token grouping, skill-specific LoRA adapters (SkillLoRA), and arm-wise attention (AWA), highlighting the complementarity of skill-conditioned parameters and attention structure. Combining these choices yields \textbf{AE-VLA}, which achieves 21.53\% generalization success in simulation, compared with 2.94\% for Single $π_{0.5}$, 3.06\% for MA-VLA, and 5.53\% for two independently controlled $π_{0.5}$ policies. On physical SO101 robots, AE-VLA reaches 39.00\% mean success across five unseen conditions, compared with 10.00\% for the strongest baseline. These findings provide empirical guidance for designing dual-arm policies that generalize beyond fixed training routines.
full_text: Experiments sec:experiments Experimental Setup sec:experimental_setup Common pretrained backbone. Single , both policies in Dual , our MA-VLA implementation~ zhang2026mavla , and all four Token Group settings initialize their backbones from the same pretrained checkpoint~ intelligence2025pi_ . This design keeps the pretraining source fixed across all comparisons. For MA-VLA, we replace the original backbone with , and all reported MA-VLA results use this adapted implementation. In Dual , each arm is controlled by an independent policy that receives its own wrist view together with the shared global view. We omit TwinVLA~ im2026twinvla from the quantitative comparison because its pretrained weights differ from those of , which would confound architectural differences with differences in pretraining. These choices enable a more controlled comparison with respect to pretrained initialization. Training and methods. Using the pooled source data in Section~ sec:macg , we train the single-policy variants for 30,000 steps with batch size 32 on two NVIDIA A800 GPUs. Single predicts both arms with the base model. Dual trains a separate policy for each arm. All receive the same per-arm skill prompts at evaluation; SkillLoRA also uses skill labels to train its routers. Test set and averages. Each method runs 100 episodes per condition with seeds 1000--1099, for 2,300 episodes across the 23 conditions. We average results equally over conditions. The generalization mean includes all 17 non-in-domain conditions, so the four groups have weights . Metrics. Constraint-compliant success rate (CCSR) counts episodes that reach the goal and meet the required milestones, order, and timing: Here, denotes the number of valid successful episodes, while denotes the total number of evaluated episodes. Normalized progress is defined as the fraction of required milestones completed under these scoring rules and is used to measure partial task execution. For Sync, the allowable event-time gap is 20\,s for Can in Basket, 15\,s for Object in Cabinet, and 45\,s for all other tasks. For Can in Basket, task completion is determined by environment success, while Sync additionally requires satisfaction of the 20\,s event-time constraint. If an arm-wise collision occurs, the corresponding episode is considered a failure. We therefore set its success score to zero while retaining the measured progress. Appendix~ appendix:scoring provides the complete scoring rules. Main Results sec:main_results Figure~ fig:regime_results shows a large gap between in-domain and compositional success. Single falls from 37.00 in-domain CCSR to 2.94 on the generalization set. MA-VLA reaches 3.06 and Dual reaches 5.53 on this set. The combined AE-VLA setting reaches 21.53 , a gain of 18.59 points over Single and 16.00 over Dual. It reaches 26.50 on Reorder, 22.00 on Sync+Reorder, and 40.00 on Cross-task Combination. Pure Sync remains difficult: AE-VLA reaches 8.67 . Its in-domain success is 27.17 , below all three baselines. Progress gives a different view. AE-VLA and Dual complete similar fractions of required milestones on the generalization set (44.25 and 40.64 ), yet their full success rates differ widely. Thus, local progress does not imply successful completion of the required combination. For example, on synchronization tasks, Dual can grasp the objects but lacks the waiting and coordination needed between arms, causing collisions between arms and task failure. Single and MA-VLA also show low progress (10.94 and 9.83 ). Gains also vary across tasks. AE-VLA reaches 79 on Stack Bowls/Reorder versus 4 for Dual, and 54 on Cube in Bowl/Cross-task versus 0 . Dual is stronger on several other conditions, including Object in Cabinet/In-domain and Burger Fries/Sync. Single is best on Push Cubes/In-domain; MA-VLA is best on Stack Cubes/In-domain. Table~ tab:macg_task_results reports all 23 conditions, including cases where the baselines do better. Design Choices and Their Interaction sec:ablation Table~ tab:macg_ablation shows the complete comparison. Token Group raises generalization CCSR from 2.94 to 3.82 , with almost no change in progress. Adding SkillLoRA alone reaches 6.00 ; adding AWA alone reaches 5.82 . Their combination reaches 21.53 . AWA alone has higher progress than SkillLoRA alone (28.84 versus 19.02 ), but not higher full success. The gain from AWA is 2.00 points without SkillLoRA and 15.53 with it. The difference, 13.53 points, measures their interaction. The two choices work better together for these trained models. Appendix~ appendix:architecture_results gives the results for each condition. This improvement has an in-domain cost. AWA lowers Token Group from 45.00 to 25.00 in-domain CCSR, and Token Group + SkillLoRA from 41.33 to 27.17 . The comparison also has limits: SkillLoRA adds both weights and router supervision; AWA changes both cross-arm and within-chunk attention. The four settings separate the effects of these two design choices, but do not isolate each change within them. Real-world SO101 Results sec:real_world We use two 6-DoF SO101 arms with one global and two wrist cameras. Training demonstrations cover Stack Bowls, Stack Cubes, and Push Cubes, collected with LeRobot teleoperation~ cadene2024lerobot . Cube in Bowl is held out: its cube pick-and-place skill is learned from Stack Cubes and tested with a bowl target. We evaluate three in-domain and five unseen conditions with distractor objects. Each method has 20 trials per condition, giving 640 trials in total. Appendix~ appendix:so101 describes the setup and scoring. AE-VLA reaches 39.00 mean success on the five unseen conditions, compared with 2.00 for Single, 6.00 for MA-VLA, and 10.00 for Dual (Table~ tab:real_robot_results ). It leads on four of the five conditions, including Stack Bowls/Sync (12/20 versus 0/20 for every baseline). Push Cubes/Sync is the exception: Dual reaches 6/20 and AE-VLA reaches 2/20. In-domain, AE-VLA reaches 60.00 , below Dual's 70.00 . The real-robot results thus also show improved generalization with some loss of in-domain success. Figure~ fig:real_robot shows example phases.

title: Towards Quadruped-Provided Localization and Active Tracking for Micro-UAVs
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures. Submitted version (before peer review) of a paper accepted at CLAWAR 2026, Cranfield, UK, 14 to 16 September 2026. The published version, titled "Towards Quadruped-Provided Localization and Active Tracking for Nano-UAVs", will appear in the CLAWAR 2026 proceedings (Springer, Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems)
summary: Micro unmanned aerial vehicles (micro-UAVs) are small enough to reach confined spaces that larger robots cannot access, but too small to carry the sensing and computing power required for autonomous flight. We move the localization stack entirely off the aerial platform onto a quadruped robot with a 7-degree-of-freedom (DOF) arm, which supplies the micro-UAV (27 g bare, 42 g with fiducial markers) its full 6-DOF pose. A camera at the arm's end-effector detects AprilTag fiducial markers on the drone and composes that observation with the quadruped's own self-localization to place the drone in a shared map frame, so the ground robot localizes its partner, rather than only tracking it relative to the camera. The arm acts as an actively-controlled observer, repositioning to keep the drone in view as both robots move; the drone carries only an inertial measurement unit and fuses the external pose to fly commanded setpoints. In lab flights the external pose is accurate to 12-16 mm, enough to fly the drone autonomously within 2-5 cm of motion-capture-fed control. Having the quadruped actively follow the drone reduces the tracking error from 11.0 cm to 6.9 cm by holding the camera in the close range, where the markers are most accurate.
full_text: Towards Quadruped-Provided Localization and Active Tracking for Micro-UAVs Alejandro Lorite Mora Andrés Faíña IT University of Copenhagen, Rued Langgaards Vej 7, Copenhagen 2300, Denmark,\\ \ lori, anfv\ @itu.dk \\ Helix Lab, Campus Kalundborg 3, 4400 Kalundborg, Denmark\\ Novo Nordisk A/S, Hallas Alle 1, 4400 Kalundborg, Denmark Micro unmanned aerial vehicles (micro-UAVs) are small enough to reach confined spaces that larger robots cannot access, but too small to carry the sensing and computing power required for autonomous flight. We move the localization stack entirely off the aerial platform onto a quadruped robot with a 7-degree-of-freedom (DOF) arm, which supplies the micro-UAV (27\,g bare, 42\,g with fiducial markers) its full 6-DOF pose. A camera at the arm's end-effector detects AprilTag fiducial markers on the drone and composes that observation with the quadruped's own self-localization to place the drone in a shared map frame---so the ground robot localizes its partner, rather than only tracking it relative to the camera. The arm acts as an actively-controlled observer, repositioning to keep the drone in view as both robots move; the drone carries only an inertial measurement unit and fuses the external pose to fly commanded setpoints. In lab flights the external pose is accurate to 12--16\,mm, enough to fly the drone autonomously within 2--5\,cm of motion-capture-fed control. Having the quadruped actively follow the drone reduces the tracking error from 11.0\,cm to 6.9\,cm by holding the camera in the close range, where the markers are most accurate. INTRODUCTION Traversing narrow passages and highly constrained environments generally necessitates the use of small robotic platforms. However, reducing the robot's size also limits the payload capacity available for sensors, onboard computation, and communication systems. This trade-off is evident in current aerial inspection applications, which are predominantly performed using relatively large unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). These platforms can carry advanced sensing suites and powerful onboard processors, enabling autonomous navigation and operation in complex environments. Their large size, however, prevents them from accessing the confined or hazardous spaces that applications such as search-and-rescue missions and infrastructure inspection often require. In contrast, micro-scale UAVs possess the agility and compact form factor required to access narrow and cluttered spaces that are inaccessible to larger platforms. Nevertheless, their limited payload capacity significantly restricts their sensing and computational capabilities, preventing fully autonomous navigation in such environments. As a result, micro-UAVs often rely on external infrastructure, offboard computation, or human assistance to safely traverse and operate within confined spaces. A micro-UAV that cannot localize itself must obtain its pose either by adding onboard sensing or by receiving it from an external source. Scaling the payload up is the usual answer when a global navigation satellite system (GNSS) is unavailable, as in indoor drone flight~ jarraya_gnss_denied_2025 : visual-inertial odometry (VIO) and light detection and ranging (LiDAR) simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) are the standard methods at the kilogram scale~ qin_vinsmono_2018,geneva_openvins_2020,xu_fastlio2_2022 , but they degrade in featureless or poorly-lit environments and cannot run on sub-30\,g platforms, because the stereo or LiDAR sensors and the VIO/SLAM computation exceed the payload, computing power, and power a micro-UAV can carry. Micro-UAVs instead rely on lighter methods such as optical flow or learned visual navigation~ palossi_nanodrone_2019 , which also degrade where visual texture is weak, as it often is in the confined spaces micro-UAVs are meant to reach. The other option is to receive the pose from an external source. Micro-UAVs commonly rely on external infrastructure for this. Motion capture (MOCAP) with Crazyswarm2~ honig_crazyswarm2 provides centimeter accuracy but requires a pre-installed array of cameras. Ultra-wideband (UWB) localization, which estimates range from fixed radio anchors, shares the same pre-setup constraint. Fiducial markers are the standard low-cost option. AprilTag~ olson_apriltag_2011 is the most widely used, and its accuracy and failure modes are well characterized~ kalaitzakis_fiducial_2021 . Recent open micro-UAV frameworks build on fiducial-marker localization for the same reason~ chiun_star_2024 ; but in all such work the observing sensor is fixed or rigidly mounted to the platform being localized. Repositioning the observer instead---moving it to keep the target in view---is an instance of active perception~ bajcsy_active_2018 and, at the control level, visual servoing~ chaumette_vs_2006 , but both classically serve the observer's own task rather than sustaining the external localization of a separate, non-sensing robot. A common alternative is to let a ground vehicle help localize the UAV, providing mapping and localization support. Such cooperative UAV and unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) teams have been studied for GNSS-denied navigation with complementary sensing across platforms. UWB cooperative localization~ queralta_uwb_2020 requires radios on both platforms. The most closely related work is by Akhihiero et al.~ depetrillo_ugv_uav_2024 , where a UGV provides mapping, self-localization, and UAV state estimation in subterranean environments using UGV LiDAR and UWB, but the formulation requires either UAV or UGV to be stationary during state updates. Gross et al.~ gross_aerial_2019 make similar architectural choices with UGV LiDAR plus stereo and IMU on the UAV. In all of these the UAV still carries its own localization sensors---stereo, inertial measurement unit (IMU), altimeter---and the ground robot only refines that estimate rather than replacing it. Despite the growing interest in cooperative robotic systems, the problem of enabling localization for sensing-constrained micro-UAVs through information provided by a ground robot remains insufficiently studied. In our system the micro-UAV carries only an IMU, with no exteroceptive sensing and no way to localize itself, so the ground partner supplies its entire absolute 6-DOF pose while both robots move. The drone's onboard extended Kalman filter (EKF) fuses that external pose with its IMU to follow position setpoints. A quadruped with a 7-DOF arm estimates the drone's pose externally from observing AprilTags on the drone, with the arm acting as an actively-controlled perception platform that repositions to keep the drone in view. The estimate is produced in the quadruped's map frame rather than only relative to the camera, so the ground robot localizes the drone rather than merely tracking it. That pose is ready for a mapping-and-planning module to consume; integrating that module is the natural next step and is not evaluated here. Our contributions are (i)~the integrated localization-and-tracking system---AprilTag-anchored external pose estimation with an actively-controlled arm---for a micro-UAV with no localization sensing, deployed end-to-end in the Robot Operating System (ROS\,2); and (ii)~preliminary validation of the approach in lab settings. The external estimate localizes the drone to 12--16\,mm once a constant calibration bias is removed. This is accurate enough to fly the drone autonomously along commanded trajectories, within a few centimeters of motion-capture-fed control. Moreover, active arm tracking improves rather than degrades the pose, because it holds the drone in the close range where fiducial accuracy is higher, so the quadruped's own motion helps rather than harms the estimate it provides. METHOD System Overview sec:overview We use a quadruped robot with an arm that provides the perception capabilities for drone localization. All sensing, estimation, and control run on the quadruped, while the drone is only a thin actuator that executes setpoints. The ground platform is a Boston Dynamics Spot~ boston_dynamics_spot with the Spot Arm and a Jetson AGX Orin 64\,GB Developer Kit (Fig.~ fig:system ). It localizes itself from its five stereo RGBD cameras, a gray-scale camera pointing to the ground, and an IMU. The aerial platform is a Crazyflie~2.1+ (27\,g bare, 92\, \,92\, \,29\,mm) with no positioning sensors; it carries a custom chassis with four 36h11 AprilTags (58.5\, \,58.5\,mm) on its lateral faces for visibility from any azimuth, bringing the flight mass to 42\,g. A Crazyradio PA (2.4\,GHz, USB) plugged into the Jetson removes the need for a separate ground station. To report position accuracy we use an OptiTrack MOCAP system of eight PrimeX 13W cameras covering a 4\, \,4\, \,2.5\,m volume; both robots carry reflective markers tracked by it. All software runs in ROS\,2 Humble~ macenski_ros2_2022 in an Ubuntu 22.04 Docker container deployed on the Jetson PC, with packages for the quadruped's ROS\,2 driver~ bdai_spot_ros2 , the micro-UAV control stack~ honig_crazyswarm2 , the AprilTag detector (apriltag ros), and our integration code. Two paths run concurrently (Fig.~ fig:arch ): a perception path that fuses the quadruped's sensors and the arm-mounted camera into the drone's pose, and a command path that carries trajectory setpoints to the drone. The control system consumes a single composed transform, (section sec:localization ). Because this pose is already expressed in the map frame, it is also what an on-board planner would need, so a mapping-and-planning module can be added later without changing the perception path. Drone Localization in the Map Frame sec:localization The goal of this stage is to know where the drone is---its full 6-DOF pose, position and orientation---expressed in the same global map frame that Spot uses to navigate, so that the aerial and ground platforms share one coordinate system. Since the drone carries no positioning sensors, this pose is recovered entirely from the arm camera's view of the on-board AprilTags together with Spot's own self-localization. The estimate is assembled as a chain of coordinate transforms, each linking one frame to the next: Fiducial detection. Detecting the drone's AprilTags yields the camera-to-drone transform , the final two links of the chain in Eq.~ eq:tf_chain . With markers on four lateral faces the camera sees one or two tags at a time. When more than one is visible we use the single strongest detection by decision-margin followed by Perspective-n-Point (PnP)-covariance trace, then compose with a static transform to obtain . This process runs on the CPU. Pose stream and watchdog. The pipeline emits one map-frame pose per detection and does not extrapolate between detections, so during a detection gap it simply publishes nothing. Tolerance to short gaps instead comes from the drone's onboard EKF, which coasts on its IMU until the next external pose arrives. A safety watchdog complements this: if the drone is airborne and no pose update arrives within a short timeout, it commands an immediate landing, so the drone is never left flying without a position estimate when it leaves the camera's view. Active Tracking sec:tracking The quadruped's arm acts as an actively-controlled perception platform, repositioning to keep the drone in the hand camera's field of view. When the drone moves away from the center of the view, a new optimal camera position is calculated. Then, inverse kinematics (IK) is solved with the Spot Arm IK service to compute the required joint angles. The onboard locomotion controller handles foothold planning and dynamic balance. Finally, the quadruped walks and moves the arm simultaneously to re-center the drone in the image. title: When and What to Prune? Stage-Aware Visual Token Pruning for Efficient VLA
summary: Visual token pruning is an effective way to accelerate vision-language models and is especially useful for vision-language-action (VLA) inference, where many visual tokens must be processed before predicting robot actions. Existing pruning methods usually estimate which tokens can be pruned based on attention scores or feature diversity, retaining tokens that are either highly attended or visually different from others. However, most of them use fixed pruning schedules, such as pruning once at a preset layer or pruning at uniformly spaced layers. Such schedules can be risky for VLA models, because the model may not know which visual regions matter for the action in early layers. Tokens that look unimportant at first may become useful after the model combines visual observations with the language instruction. In this work, we propose SAPrune, a training-free visual token pruning framework for efficient VLA inference. Instead of pruning at fixed layers, SAPrune uses a small calibration set to observe how action-to-visual attention changes across layers, and chooses pruning layers only after the attention pattern becomes more reliable. At each selected layer, SAPrune applies a dual-path pruning rule: one path protects strongly attended visual tokens from pruning, while the other prevents useful surrounding context from being discarded. Experiments on LIBERO, SIMPLER, and real-world robotic tasks show that SAPrune prunes 87.5% of visual tokens and achieves up to 1.718x inference speedup while maintaining competitive task success rates.
full_text: Visual token pruning is an effective way to accelerate vision-language models and is especially useful for vision-language-action (VLA) inference, where many visual tokens must be processed before predicting robot actions. Existing pruning methods usually estimate which tokens can be pruned based on attention scores or feature diversity, retaining tokens that are either highly attended or visually different from others. However, most of them use fixed pruning schedules, such as pruning once at a preset layer or pruning at uniformly spaced layers. Such schedules can be risky for VLA models, because the model may not know which visual regions matter for the action in early layers. Tokens that look unimportant at first may become useful after the model combines visual observations with the language instruction. In this work, we propose SAPrune, a training-free visual token pruning framework for efficient VLA inference. Instead of pruning at fixed layers, SAPrune uses a small calibration set to observe how action-to-visual attention changes across layers, and chooses pruning layers only after the attention pattern becomes more reliable. At each selected layer, SAPrune applies a dual-path pruning rule: one path protects strongly attended visual tokens from pruning, while the other prevents useful surrounding context from being discarded. Experiments on LIBERO, SIMPLER, and real-world robotic tasks show that SAPrune prunes 87.5 of visual tokens and achieves up to 1.718 inference speedup while maintaining competitive task success rates. Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently shown strong potential for embodied decision making by mapping visual observations and language instructions directly to robot actions~ brohan2023rt1,zitkovich2023rt2,oneill2024openx,octo2024,kim2025openvla,black2024pi0 . Despite their effectiveness, VLA inference remains computationally expensive because a large number of visual tokens must be propagated through deep Transformer layers~ kim2025openvla,xu2025vlacache,yang2025efficientvla,liu2025vlapruner . Visual token pruning is therefore a natural direction for reducing latency and computation, as shown in prior studies on efficient Vision Transformers and large vision-language models~ rao2021dynamicvit,liang2022evit,bolya2023tome,chen2024fastv,huang2024ivtp,zhang2025sparsevlm,sun2025lvpruning,alvar2025divprune . Although recent studies have shown substantial redundancy in VLA inference, most pruning-oriented acceleration methods still decide token removal from local importance cues, visual saliency, feature-space diversity, or their fixed combinations~ chen2024fastv,zhang2025sparsevlm,huang2024ivtp,sun2025lvpruning,zhang2025vispruner,alvar2025divprune,yang2025efficientvla,liu2025vlapruner . This treats pruning mainly as a static token-selection problem. Such a formulation is insufficient for action generation, where visual evidence does not remain fixed across depth: it gradually emerges, redistributes, and stabilizes as the model forms an action decision. Moreover, visual distinctiveness alone does not imply decision usefulness, since tokens that are geometrically diverse may still be irrelevant to the current action. These limitations motivate us to reconsider VLA pruning from two questions: when pruning becomes reliable, and what action-relevant evidence should be preserved. To understand when visual tokens can be safely pruned during VLA inference, we analyze the attention from action-related states to visual tokens across Transformer layers. Figure~ fig:attention_dynamics shows that early layers attend to a broad set of visual tokens, while middle and deep layers gradually concentrate on tokens related to the target action. Figure~ fig:obs2 further quantifies this trend using the top- attention mass: the mass increases quickly from shallow to middle layers and then changes more slowly. This suggests that early layers have not yet clearly determined which visual tokens are useful for the action. Therefore, pruning too early may remove tokens that become important later, motivating us to delay pruning until the attention pattern becomes more stable. We further compare different pruning criteria in Fig.~ fig:obs3 . Attention-only selection tends to concentrate on dominant regions and may miss supportive context, whereas feature-space diversity-based selection may retain tokens that are visually distinctive but weakly related to the current action. These observations suggest that attention-only selection, feature-space diversity-based selection, and their fixed combination are all insufficient for aggressive VLA pruning. Based on these principles, we propose SAPrune, a training-free visual token pruning framework for efficient VLA inference. SAPrune first selects pruning layers from rollout-level action-attention dynamics, and then applies a dual-path retention mechanism at each selected layer. The attention-core path preserves directly action-relevant tokens, while the functional-diversity path selects complementary tokens using query-conditioned functional signatures. Experiments on LIBERO~ liu2023libero , SIMPLER~ li2024simpler , and real-world robotic tasks show that SAPrune retains only 32 visual tokens, prunes 87.5 of the original visual tokens, and achieves up to 1.718 speedup while maintaining competitive task success rates. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models extend large vision-language models by introducing an action modality, enabling robots to predict executable actions from visual observations and language instructions. Representative generalist robot policies include RT-1~ brohan2023rt1 , RT-2~ zitkovich2023rt2 , Open X-Embodiment / RT-X~ oneill2024openx , Octo~ octo2024 , OpenVLA~ kim2025openvla , ~ black2024pi0 . Early efficient Vision Transformer methods, such as DynamicViT~ rao2021dynamicvit , EViT~ liang2022evit , and ToMe~ bolya2023tome , reduce computation through token sparsification or merging. title: Encoded but Not in Control: Revealing the Grounding Gap in Vision-Language Robot Policies
summary: Instruction following is central to language-conditioned robot policies: language should determine what to do when the same scene permits multiple valid actions. Yet successful execution alone cannot establish whether a policy follows the instruction or infers the task from the scene. We study this ambiguity through scene-preserving instruction interventions, using valid target substitutions, arbitrary nouns, and unrelated sentences while holding the scene fixed. We evaluate vision-language-action (VLA) policies and world-action models (WAMs) in simulation and in real-world experiments. Our analysis addresses three questions: (a) Does task success imply instruction following? When instructions request a different visible object, all evaluated policies predominantly approach and pick up the incorrect original target associated with the scene. (b) Is this failure caused by language insensitivity? Instruction perturbations affect task performance. A layerwise action lens shows intermediate action predictions respond to these perturbations. Linear probes accurately recover instructed targets, indicating modified instructions are encoded despite rarely determining target selection. (c) Why does encoded language fail to control action? Attention analysis indicates weak instruction-token contributions to action generation. Target-token attention can remain focused on the original object, revealing a mismatch between target encoding and visual grounding. UMAP and shared non-negative matrix factorization show target information remains accessible within representations increasingly organized by scene identity. Our findings expose a grounding gap concealed by nominal success and provide a diagnostic framework. They further establish a concrete criterion for progress: policies should reliably follow valid changes in user intent, even when they conflict with scene-favored behavior.

Introduction Language-conditioned robot policies promise a natural interface for specifying what a robot should do in an environment. Recent VLAs~ intelligence2025pi_,bjorck2025gr00t and WAMs~ yuan2026fast,li2026causal demonstrate strong performance across manipulation tasks, embodiments, and visual environments, commonly evaluated by task success under a given instruction and environment. However, task success alone does not establish that the instruction determined the behavior. In many robot datasets, a scene is repeatedly paired with one target object or task, so the scene alone may suffice to infer the demonstrated behavior without resolving the requested behavior. A policy can consequently achieve high success by exploiting scene--task correlations while its ability to follow language remains unclear. Instruction following requires evidence that changing a valid instruction in a fixed scene redirects behavior toward the newly specified target. Evaluations using linguistic perturbations and modality ablations reveal brittleness and task-dependent language sensitivity in VLA policies~ fei2025libero, zhou2025libero, guo2026robustness, dong2026does, shi2026vla . More directly, LIBERO-CF and LangGap expose instruction-following failures under alternative feasible instructions in fixed scenes~ fang2026vision, hou2026langgap , while InstructMove constructs scenes where language must distinguish among multiple feasible actions~ zhao2026instructmove . Mechanistic analyses further find that prompt information can remain decodable despite limited behavioral use, with action generation relying strongly on visual inputs~ grant2026not . Building on these findings, we use scene-preserving instruction interventions to investigate how target-selection failures relate to the encoding, visual grounding, and contribution of instruction information to action generation, linking behavioral failures to action-level responses and internal representations across VLA and world-action models. Part I: Does nominal task success imply instruction following? We revisit this question across VLA and WAM policies, with additional real-world experiments. When a valid instruction requests another object in the same scene, the policies predominantly approach and manipulate the original target. We refer to this directional preference as a scene-conditioned behavioral prior. It reveals a failure that standard success rates cannot expose: a policy may successfully reproduce the expected behavior for a familiar scene without allowing language to determine which behavior it executes. Part II: Is target-conflict failure caused by language insensitivity? This failure cannot be attributed simply to absent linguistic influence. Controlled instruction perturbations produce systematic, task-dependent changes in policy performance. A layerwise action lens shows that intermediate action predictions respond differently to target substitutions and random sentences, evidencing language sensitivity in action generation. Linear probes also recover target and scene identities from fine-tuned representations with high accuracy, so target information remains available despite incorrect object selection. Policies thus respond to language at behavioral and representational levels, yet the failure persists even when the modified instruction affects action predictions and its target remains encoded---motivating a closer look at how this information contributes to action selection. Part III: If target information is encoded, why does it fail to control action? Attention contribution analysis shows instruction tokens contribute little to action generation relative to visual inputs, and target-token attention can stay fixed on the original object even after the instruction names a different target. UMAP reveals a shift from object-based to scene-based clustering after fine-tuning; shared non-negative matrix factorization likewise identifies transitions from object-dominated to scene-dominated components in both and GR00T N1.7. High target decodability thus coexists with limited instruction contribution, misaligned visual attention, and increased scene dependence, characterizing why encoded language does not reliably guide target selection. We describe this dissociation as a representation-to-control grounding gap: linguistic information can be represented within a policy without reliably governing action selection. Our analyses distinguish sensitivity to language, accessibility of target information, and behavioral adherence to the instruction. These target-selection failures also extend to the evaluated world-action models, showing that visual prediction objectives alone do not ensure instruction following. Our findings motivate a stricter grounding criterion: a valid change in instruction should reliably select a different behavior within the same scene. We hope this work encourages evaluations that test such control directly and provides a diagnostic basis for investigating where encoded instructions fail to guide action. Ultimately, progress should be measured by how reliably robots act on the user's current intent, even when it conflicts with familiar scene-task associations. Related Work -conditioned robot policies. Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions. Recent models such as couple a pretrained vision-language backbone with a dedicated action expert that generates continuous action chunks through flow matching ~ intelligence2025pi_ . GR00T N1 adopts a dual-system architecture in which a vision-language module interprets visual observations and language instructions, followed by a diffusion transformer that generates continuous motor actions ~ bjorck2025gr00t . World action models (WAMs) instead incorporate explicit visual-dynamics modeling into policy learning. LingBot-VA adopts an autoregressive diffusion framework that jointly learns future-frame prediction and policy execution, using a shared latent space and a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture to integrate visual and action tokens~ li2026causal . Fast-WAM retains video co-training during training but removes explicit future prediction at test time, directly producing actions from the learned world representations ~ yuan2026fast . These complementary architectures motivate our evaluation of , GR00T N1.7, LingBot-VA, and FastWAM, allowing us to examine whether instruction-grounding failures persist across both VLA and world-action modeling paradigms. and improving instruction following. Recent studies investigate if task success reliably reflects language grounding. LIBERO-PRO reports persistent behaviors under corrupted instructions~ zhou2025libero , while LIBERO-Plus evaluates robustness to linguistic, visual, and physical perturbations~ fei2025libero . Multilingual evaluation further reveals step-dependent language sensitivity~ dong2026does . To test semantic control more directly, LIBERO-CF and LangGap vary instructions within existing scene layouts~ fang2026vision,hou2026langgap , while InstructMove introduces semantic distractors that require language-dependent action selection~ zhao2026instructmove . Complementary methods strengthen language conditioning through counterfactual language--action augmentation in navigation~ glossop2026cast , Bayesian training objectives~ lian2026langforce , counterfactual action guidance~ fang2026vision , and instruction augmentation coupled with guidance against a vision-only prior~ zhan2026stable . Building on these studies, we connect behavior under scene-preserving instruction interventions to internal policy representations. Target substitutions test semantic redirection, whereas arbitrary nouns and random sentences diagnose language dependence without necessarily specifying executable alternatives. representations and behavioral influence. Probing studies distinguish decodable information from its use by a model, emphasizing the need for controls when interpreting probe accuracy~ belinkov2022probing,hewitt2019designing . In robotics, lu2025probing decode symbolic object and action states from OpenVLA for monitoring within the cognitive architecture. Using counterfactual prompts, activation injection, sparse autoencoders, and probes, grant2026not identify distinct VLM and action-expert roles and report decodable prompt categories despite weak behavioral sensitivity in . We build on these findings by pairing instruction interventions with layer-wise analyses of target and scene information across VLA and WAM policies, examining how instructed-target representations relate to action selection when language and scene-associated behavior conflict. Our experiments cover LIBERO (Spatial, Object, Goal, Long)~ liu2023libero , the clean and randomized settings of RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin , and six real-world manipulation scenes. These environments support a broad evaluation of instruction sensitivity. title: Mobile-4DGS: Unified Static-Dynamic Real-time Mobile Gaussian Splatting
summary: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have achieved remarkable performance in novel view synthesis, yet deploying both static and dynamic Gaussian representations on resource-constrained mobile devices remains challenging due to heavy storage, redundant primitives, and costly per-frame computation. We present Mobile-4DGS, a unified lightweight framework for high-fidelity real-time static and dynamic Gaussian rendering on mobile platforms. For compact appearance modeling, we introduce a Monte Carlo Specular Energy Aggregator that compresses high-order radiance residuals into the first-order Spherical Harmonics (SH), together with an Attribute-Conditioned SH Enhancement module whose predicted offsets are pre-baked before inference. We further propose a Multi-View Alpha-Based Densification and Pruning strategy to suppress redundant primitives while maintaining multi-view consistency. For dynamic scenes, we develop a compact explicit 4D representation by constructing second-order Gaussian motion, learnable temporal support, and a binary static-dynamic partition, enabling continuous-time modeling without runtime deformation networks. Based on this partition, a Depth-Order Certificate selectively reuses previously committed depth orders to reduce re-projection, sorting, merging, and index-buffer updates during playback. Extensive experiments on static and dynamic scenes demonstrate that Mobile-4DGS substantially reduces storage and rendering overhead while maintaining competitive visual quality, enabling real-time 3D and 4D Gaussian Splatting on mobile devices. \textcolor{magenta}{\href{https://xiaobiaodu.github.io/mobile-4dgs-project/}{Code has been released: https://xiaobiaodu.github.io/mobile-4dgs-project/}}.

Introduction Recent advancements in 3D scene reconstruction~ pami1,pami2,pami4,pami6,yifan2019differentiable, npc and novel view synthesis~ nerfstudio,mildenhall2021nerf,chen2023mobilenerf,pami5,pami3,pami7 have been driven by 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl2023gaussiansplatting . By representing scenes as millions of explicit and differentiable 3D Gaussians, 3DGS delivers high-fidelity, real-time rendering on desktop hardware. This capability has enabled diverse applications across autonomous driving~ yan2024streetgs, du2024dreamcar, du20243drealcar , navigation~ du2020learning, du2023object, du2021vtnet , and virtual reality~ vrgs, long2023wonder3d, liu2023one, shen2023anything . Despite these successes, efficiently deploying static and dynamic Gaussian Splatting on resource-constrained mobile devices remains a critical bottleneck. Mobile-GS~ mobilegs is the first to deploy 3DGS on mobile devices and achieves real-time rendering. It identifies the sorting process in the original volume rendering as causing slow rendering for mobiles. Therefore, it proposes an order-independent rendering pipeline to replace the traditional volume rendering so as to achieve fast rendering on mobiles. However, removing the sorting process causes Gaussian rendering in an arbitrary order, causing transparency artifacts in regions with overlapping geometry. Although Flux-GS~ du2026monte maintains the original sorting process and achieves faster rendering, it cannot support dynamic rendering~ 4dgs in our daily 4D space. The two lines of work therefore leave the same tension unresolved: giving up the sort buys throughput at the price of correct compositing, whereas keeping it means paying for a depth order that a 4D scene has to rebuild at every playback frame, together with the upload of the resulting index buffer. In our experiments, we identified four primary bottlenecks that hinder the efficient deployment of Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) on mobile devices: (1) Third-Order Spherical Harmonics Overhead: Prior methods~ hanson2024speedy, lee2024compact, zhang2025gaussianspa, liu2025maskgaussian, hou2024sort commonly rely on third-order Spherical Harmonics (SH) to model complex, view-dependent radiance. However, third-order SH requires 48 floating-point parameters per Gaussian primitive. Scaled across millions of Gaussians, this creates prohibitive storage overhead and heavy memory bandwidth consumption during rasterization. (2) Redundant Primitive Densification: Lightweight 3DGS variants, such as Mobile-GS~ mobilegs and MEGS2~ chen2025MEGS2 , typically adopt standard single-view gradient-based densification~ kerbl2023gaussiansplatting . This approach aggressively spawns excess primitives, leading to overfitting and inflated point counts. The resulting primitive redundancy severely impacts training efficiency, storage footprint, and inference latency on the resource-constrained edge devices. (3) MLP-based Dynamic Representation: Previous works~ 4dgs,sc-gs,yang2024deformable leverage neural networks to model temporal variation, introducing non-trivial per-frame deformation inference and limiting rendering efficiency on resource-constrained devices. (4) Per-Frame Depth Ordering under Motion: Primitive motion continuously changes the relative depth of Gaussians, invalidating previously cached depth orders. As a result, the renderer must repeatedly re-project primitives, recompute their ordering, and update the draw list during playback, introducing additional runtime and data-transfer overhead. In this work, we present Mobile-4DGS, a mobile real-time Gaussian Splatting method designed to deliver high-fidelity rendering with significantly fewer parameters. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser , our proposed Mobile-4DGS achieves rendering quality comparable to existing baselines while utilizing fewer Gaussian primitives, thereby outperforming Mobile-GS~ mobilegs in inference speed. Our framework is built upon four technical innovations: (1) Unified Mobile Static-Dynamic Representation: We extend the static Mobile-GS/Flux-GS foundations to a compact continuous-time representation in which each dynamic Gaussian requires only eight additional temporal scalars. Static scenes are represented as the zero-motion special case, allowing both modes to share the same appearance, compression, density-control, and rendering pipeline. (2) Monte Carlo Specular Energy Aggregator: As shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser_sh , our approach is motivated by the observation that substantial radiance information can be compressed into a lower-order subspace without compromising view-dependent specular features. We propose a Monte Carlo Specular Energy Aggregator that aggregates high-order specular energy into a compact representation, effectively preserving the complex lighting characteristics. Furthermore, we decouple the SH representation into a view-independent base component and directional view-dependent components, allowing for a substantial reduction in SH memory overhead compared to traditional third-order baselines without the need for expensive offline distillation or pre-training. To recover the fine detail lost during this compression, we introduce an Attribute-Conditioned SH Enhancement module. This module utilizes a lightweight Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to model contextual offsets based on intrinsic Gaussian properties. More importantly, these offsets are statically baked into the explicit Gaussian parameters prior to inference, ensuring that this enhanced view-dependent modeling does not introduce additional computational overhead during inference. (3) Multi-view Alpha-based Densification and Pruning strategy: We further address the inefficiency inherent in the standard single-view gradient-based densification strategy, which often lacks multi-view structure consistency. We propose a Multi-view Alpha-based Densification and Pruning strategy that employs stratified camera sampling and alpha-weighted error accumulation across multiple viewpoints. With multi-view guidance, this strategy ensures a more compact representation by accurately pruning redundant primitives while focusing densification on regions with high multi-view reconstruction error. (4) Depth-Order Certificate for 4D Playback: The learned partition is exactly binary, so the depth order of the static subset depends on the camera alone and is cached for the whole clip, while a closed-form bound on the travel of the animated subset yields a per-frame depth-order certificate (DOC) that decides whether the committed draw list is still the sorted one. A frame that passes the certificate skips re-projection, sorting, merging and the index upload. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Mobile-4DGS offers a robust and scalable solution for mobile real-time rendering. By achieving powerful first-order SH representation while maintaining competitive visual quality, our framework paves the way for the deployment of high-fidelity 3DGS on mobile devices. The same framework also keeps 4D playback affordable on the device: the exact certificate leaves the rendered image untouched on every frame it reuses, and the budget branch confines the reordering it admits to primitives whose footprints already overlap. to Prior Conference Versions. This paper substantially extends our previous Mobile-GS~ mobilegs and Flux-GS~ du2026monte papers. Mobile-GS established a mobile-oriented Gaussian rendering pipeline together with a distillation-based appearance representation, whereas Flux-GS investigated Monte Carlo aggregation for compact static Gaussian Splatting. The present journal version unifies these foundations under a single deployment-oriented framework and extends them to dynamic scenes through explicit second-order motion, learnable temporal support, temporally stratified optimization, and quantized temporal attributes. It further incorporates a shared cross-platform rendering pipeline for both static and dynamic scenes. Importantly, static rendering is treated as a zero-motion special case of the same explicit representation. title: VLA-ZO: Fast Zeroth-Order Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Adapting vision-language-action (VLA) models to deployment-time distribution shifts is important for reliable robotic operation, but conventional first-order adaptation can exceed the memory budget of inference-oriented deployment platforms. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization offers a forward-only alternative with inference-level memory, but accurate gradient estimation requires many perturbation queries, making naive ZO prohibitively slow for large VLA models. We present VLA-ZO, a framework for fast ZO adaptation that exploits the structure of VLA computation. By confining adaptation to the action side, VLA-ZO keeps the expensive vision-language prefix frozen and reuses its conditioning states across perturbation queries and optimizer steps, while schedule-aware prefetching hides state-transfer overhead. On LIBERO camera-viewpoint shifts, VLA-ZO reduces end-to-end adaptation time by 25.59$\times$ at $q=16$ and 32.54$\times$ at $q=64$ relative to baseline ZO, while improving average task success from 48.27% without adaptation to 58.17% and 63.58%, respectively. These results show that making ZO faster can make larger query budgets practical, providing a promising path toward resource-efficient VLA adaptation on deployment platforms.

Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are emerging as a general interface for robotic control~ kim2024openvla, BlackK-RSS-25, black2025pi , but deploying a fixed policy is often insufficient in real-world environments. Changes in camera viewpoint, appearance, and operating conditions shift the observation distribution away from that seen during training, causing VLA policies to degrade sharply under such shifts. Specifically, the success rates of state-of-the-art VLAs collapse from to below under modest perturbations to camera pose and robot initial state~ fei2025liberoplusindepthrobustnessanalysis . Recent work has explored one-shot adaptation~ Li_2026_CVPR, 10.1007/978-3-032-37574-2_24 , in which a VLA policy is adapted using a single demonstration from a target environment. This setting enables data-efficient post-deployment adaptation to address these distribution shifts. This adaptation, however, must run on the deployment platform itself, under a compute and memory budget provisioned for inference rather than training. Conventional first-order adaptation fits this setting poorly (Figure~ fig:motivation-concept , left): backpropagation requires retaining intermediate activations that can otherwise be discarded during inference, substantially increasing memory requirements~ 3495724.3496671, Yang_2023_CVPR . Even with gradient checkpointing enabled, this overhead grows with batch size: for , first-order adaptation uses 20.27 GiB of peak memory at batch size 16 and 54.69 GiB at batch size 64, compared with the corresponding inference-level footprints of 12.74 GiB and 27.71 GiB for forward-only ZO. The relative gap therefore increases from to . Moreover, gradient checkpointing trades memory for additional recomputation and does not remove the need for a backward-capable execution path. These requirements make first-order adaptation difficult to accommodate in inference-oriented deployment stacks as VLA models scale. This motivates zeroth-order (ZO) optimization as a natural alternative (Figure~ fig:motivation-concept , right), as it enables adaptation using only forward evaluations without backpropagation. Rather than explicitly computing gradients through backpropagation, ZO methods estimate gradients by perturbing model parameters and comparing the resulting objective values using only forward evaluations~ duchi2015optimal,nesterov2017random,malladi2023finetuning . By estimating parameter updates solely from forward evaluations, ZO avoids backpropagation and substantially reduces the memory requirements for adaptation, making it attractive for memory-constrained devices as well as deployment environments where backward execution is unavailable or undesirable. Despite these advantages, the potential of ZO optimization for adapting VLA policies remains largely unexplored. In this work, we first show that ZO optimization can effectively adapt VLA policies under deployment-time distribution shifts, but at a substantial runtime cost from repeated forward evaluations (Figure~ fig:motivation ). This trade-off is governed by the query budget , the number of random perturbation directions evaluated per optimization step, each as a pair of forward passes. A larger improves the gradient estimate, allowing adaptation quality to approach first-order performance while peak memory remains at the inference level. The same knob, however, also determines the computational cost: every additional direction requires two more forward passes through the full model, causing adaptation time to grow with and quickly exceed that of first-order adaptation. Because modern VLAs contain expensive vision and language components, naively applying ZO can therefore require hours of adaptation. Thus, the main obstacle to practical ZO-based VLA adaptation is not whether it works, but whether it can run fast enough. Related Work VLA adaptation. Recent work has increasingly studied data-efficient adaptation of pretrained VLA policies from limited target-domain supervision~ li2025controlvla,zhang2026alignthensteer,ijcai2026p569,nguyen2026foca . At the extreme of this low-data regime, one-shot methods adapt a VLA policy using only a single target-domain demonstration. FTM and FLA enable such adaptation to novel camera viewpoints~ Li_2026_CVPR , while DART addresses visual and embodiment shifts and considers domain-level adaptation across tasks~ 10.1007/978-3-032-37574-2_24 . Our focus is complementary: rather than developing a new adaptation method, we study how to reduce the computational cost of zeroth-order VLA adaptation under deployment-time compute and memory constraints. Zeroth-order optimization. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization estimates gradients from perturbed forward evaluations without backpropagation. MeZO~ malladi2023finetuning enables LLM fine-tuning with approximately the memory footprint of inference and reports performance comparable to backpropagation on several language tasks. Subsequent benchmarking examines how task alignment and optimizer design affect ZO fine-tuning~ zhang2024revisiting , while SubZero explores low-rank perturbations in random subspaces~ Yu_2025_ICCV . For execution efficiency, MobiZO parallelizes perturbation evaluations through Multi-Perturbed LoRA within existing inference engines~ gao-etal-2025-mobizo . In general deep-network training, DeepZero combines sparse coordinate-wise gradient estimation with reuse of features preceding the perturbed layer and forward parallelization~ chen2024deepzero . title: Future Anchored Verification and Online Recovery for World Action Models
summary: World action models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic manipulation. They act by first predicting how a task should be performed and then decoding the actions from that future. However, the remaining actions are invalid once execution drifts from the prediction. Simply replanning from the already out of distribution state rarely restores what the task still requires; existing execution monitors decide when to stop, but not what to restore. We observe that the answer is already in hand: the future the WAM predicted before acting depicts exactly the states it intended to pass through. We introduce FAVOR (Future Anchored Verification and Online Recovery), a lightweight framework that keeps these predicted frames as anchors and uses them for verification and recovery. An Anchor Verifier compares each observation with its anchor, together with the executed actions, to flag deviations that break the task. Anchor-Guided Recovery uses a vision-language model to turn the flagged anchor into a short corrective instruction. Under strengthened instruction guidance, the WAM executes this instruction to return to the intended future. It then resumes the task. FAVOR raises the task success of the base WAM from 97.85% to 98.10% on LIBERO and from 72.60% to 72.98% on LIBERO-Plus without modifying the policy.

Introduction sec:intro World action models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic manipulation. They work in a forward and backward way: they first predict the visual future a task should pass through and then decode the actions that realize the future du2023unipi,tian2025seer,wu2024gr1,zhu2025uwm,ye2026dreamzero,yuan2026fastwam,li2026lingbotva,kim2026cosmos,ye2026gigaworld,zhou2026tau0wm,wam2026tutorial . Unlike policies that map current observations and task instruction directly to actions chi2023diffusionpolicy,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0 , every action is thus grounded in an explicit future of where the scene should go. That future is only a plan. Imprecise actions or external disturbances can push the scene off the predicted path, invalidating the remaining actions li2026badwam,wang2026trustimagination . Simply replanning from the deviated state, however, offers little help: WAMs are trained on successful demonstrations ross2011dagger,laskey2017dart,reichlin2022back , so neither the future predicted from such an unfamiliar state nor the actions decoded from it can be trusted. Execution monitors for WAMs help by flagging when the remaining actions should no longer be trusted wang2026trustimagination,liu2026checkvla,zhang2026foresight,agia2025sentinel,xu2025faildetect , but say nothing about what to restore. Recovery methods address this gap, but obtain their target from outside the policy dai2024racer,pan2026vlacorrector . This raises a natural question: can a WAM tell when execution has left its plan, and find its way back on its own? Our observation is that the target of recovery is already in the policy's hands. The future the WAM predicted depicts the states it intended to pass through, and the actions were generated under its guidance, so the actions remain valid exactly as long as the scene follows it. When a deviation occurs, this prediction still shows the condition that was lost, such as a mug held in the gripper, and that state lies in the region where the policy was trained. A deviation therefore invalidates the remaining actions, but not the states they were meant to establish. This suggests a simple principle: use the policy’s own predicted future as an anchor. Following this principle, we propose (Future Anchored Verification and Online Recovery), which keeps the predicted frames as anchors and uses them both to verify execution and to guide recovery. Two challenges stand in the way. (1) Not every mismatch is a deviation: the anchor is an image produced by a generative model and may contain visual artifacts, so pixel-level differences do not necessarily imply a semantic mismatch. (2) The challenge is to convey the anchor to the policy and elicit the intended correction: the anchor is an image, whereas a WAM accepts only an observation and an instruction. Moreover, it leans on visual context and largely ignores the instruction: with the observation fixed, the original and the empty instruction yield nearly identical attention maps (Figure~ fig:attn-prompt ). The anchor must therefore be conveyed through a corrective instruction, and the influence of that instruction must be strengthened to elicit the intended correction. For challenge (1), we introduce the Anchor Verifier, which compares each observation with its anchor together with the executed actions and tracks the mismatch along the chunk. It thus responds to deviations that break the task rather than to any visual difference. For challenge (2), we introduce Anchor-Guided Recovery to return the scene to a state the policy knows how to continue from. It hands the alarmed anchor, the current observation, and the task to a vision-language model, which issues one short instruction naming the condition to restore rather than the pixels to reproduce. The frozen WAM then executes it under strengthened instruction guidance to reach the intended future before deviation. We evaluate on LIBERO liu2023libero and LIBERO-Plus fei2025liberoplus . raises the task success of the base WAM from 97.85 to 98.10 on LIBERO and from 72.60 to 72.98 on LIBERO-Plus. The Anchor Verifier separates failed from successful episodes with an AUROC of 0.992, above distance-based and learned detectors gu2025safe,xu2025faildetect . In summary, our main contributions are as follows: A future-anchored view of WAM execution: the future predicted before acting serves not only as a reference for verifying execution but also as the target that recovery should restore. The Anchor Verifier, which grounds execution verification in the WAM's own predicted future and executed actions, identifying when the scene no longer supports continuation. The Anchor-Guided Recovery, which translates the alarmed anchor into a corrective instruction and strengthens instruction guidance, enabling a WAM to use its own predicted future as a recovery goal and return to a state from which the original task can continue. Related Work sec:related World Action Models and Future Prediction Joint video--action models couple anticipated visual changes with robot actions in a single generative process~ zhu2025uwm,ye2026dreamzero,shen2025videovla,li2025uva,cen2025worldvla,zhou2026tau0wm,li2026lingbotva,ye2026gigaworld,kim2026cosmos , whereas cascaded interfaces pass visual future states as explicit conditions to inverse dynamics models (IDMs)~ du2023unipi,ko2023avdc,black2023susie,hu2024vpp,tian2025seer,wu2024gr1,liang2025video . The role of prediction depends on the inference interface: Fast-WAM separates the benefit of video co-training from that of explicit future generation at test time~ yuan2026fastwam . Related efforts use video models as simulators or reward sources~ yang2023unisim,escontrela2023viper,guo2025ctrlworld and diagnose whether generated futures follow the commanded actions~ chen2026worldecho,liu2026wav,li2026badwam . We focus on WAMs whose predicted future states condition action generation and thus accompany the resulting actions. In these interfaces, and in work on aligning visual features and instructions with action decoding~ qiu2026agra,he2026sgwam,liu2026oawam , the predicted future is an input to action generation and plays no further role once the actions are produced. FFDC is the exception: it retains the prediction and compares it with incoming observations to judge whether the remaining actions can still be trusted, shortening execution or replanning when they cannot~ wang2026trustimagination . HarnessWAM also intervenes during WAM execution, but monitors subgoal completion rather than the prediction~ gu2026harnesswam . Here, as in adaptive-horizon methods~ wang2026trustimagination,wang2026limits,nie2026pace , the signal only decides whether to continue, and replanning starts from the deviated state. Execution Verification and Recovery Execution monitoring for learned policies draws on internal features, action consistency, and semantic progress~ gu2025safe,agia2025sentinel,xu2025faildetect,du2023successvqa,duan2025aha,zhao2026verispace,liu2026checkvla,zhang2026foresight,ma2024gvl,li2026vlasafety . A detector, however, says only that something went wrong, not what state to return to. Existing recovery methods obtain their target from outside the acting policy. Planner-level loops revise behavior from environmental feedback and constraint violations~ huang2023inner,guo2023doremi,zhou2024code , and test-time language correction takes the instruction from a human~ liu2022sirius,liu2023olaf,shi2024yay . Policy-level recovery for VLAs is learned from failure-and-recovery data~ liu2023reflect,dai2024racer,li2024selfcorrectvla,ye2025robofac or inferred by an auxiliary predictive component, either a dynamics model~ pan2026vlacorrector or imagined states toward which recovery is directed~ shin2026b2ff,zhang2026core . Each obtains its objective at the cost of training or a second model, and none derives it from the plan the policy was executing. takes the objective from that plan: the future the WAM predicted before acting is what recovery restores. Since a WAM accepts only an observation and an instruction, the VLM only translates this future into an instruction rather than estimating a target of its own. In the WAM considered here, an IDM decodes actions from the predicted future, so the influence of a corrective instruction on execution depends largely on how it shapes future generation. Yet the WAM used here exhibits limited sensitivity to instruction changes, producing largely unchanged outputs across different instructions (Figure~ fig:attn-prompt ). On the policy side, prior work makes corrections effective by training on them~ liu2022sirius,liu2023olaf,shi2024yay or by aligning visual features and instructions with action decoding~ qiu2026agra,he2026sgwam,liu2026oawam . title: A Safe Action Is Not Enough: Feasible-Future Decoding for Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary:
A safe action is not necessarily a viable one. A frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policy can favor a locally admissible move that leaves no policy-supported route to safe task completion. We call this the feasibility-likelihood gap: likelihood ranks the next move, while feasibility depends on the futures it leaves open.
  To bring those futures into the decision, we derive the exact next-block marginal of the history-conditioned policy-environment trajectory law restricted to safe task completion. The derivation reveals a candidate-dependent feasible-future mass: its support records whether safe completion remains possible under the frozen continuation process, while its magnitude measures how much weighted safe-completion mass remains. Since exact evaluation is impractical online, we develop a selective finite-candidate approximation and establish conditions for recovering the best retained viable candidate.
  Our alarm-triggered, training-free reranker VICS-G lowers mean cumulative safety cost by 1.9%-57.5% across six Safety-CHORES settings while remaining within 2.5 percentage points of policy sampling in success and 0.82 steps in mean episode length. Our approach offers a promising and practical path toward safer task completion, grounded in an exact policy-relative target yet requiring neither policy retraining nor online rollouts.

Introduction sec:introduction An action can look safe in the moment and still steer the agent into a dead end. Under a frozen vision-language-action ( ) policy, even a likely, locally admissible move may leave no policy-supported route to safe task completion. We call this the feasibility--likelihood gap. The navigation example in shows why completion belongs in the safety story: reducing cost by ending an episode early can leave the task unfinished. VLA policies bring broad semantic and motor priors to robot control, learned from large-scale vision--language pretraining and robot demonstrations. Systems such as RT-2~ brohan2023rt2 , PaLM-E~ driess2023palme , OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla , Octo~ octo2024 , and ~ black2024pi0 illustrate this breadth. Given an observation , instruction , and interaction history , the policy defines a_ t:t+H-1 ( , , ). These priors express what the policy has learned to favor, but do not by themselves establish whether it can finish safely. Deployment-time constrained decoding gives us a way to revisit action selection as execution unfolds, while keeping the underlying policy fixed~ zhang2025safevla,kapoor2025safedec,hsu2021safety . Looking ahead in robotics means reasoning about a future that the action alone does not determine. In autoregressive language generation, appending a candidate token fixes the next symbolic prefix~ ji2025inferenceguard . A robot's next state also depends on the world in which it acts: s_ t+H P( s_t,a_ t:t+H-1 ). Under partial observability and execution uncertainty, the same observable history and action block can lead to different successor states, with different reachability, visibility, and collision geometry. A safe-completion target must therefore account for both future policy choices and environment dynamics. We begin with a law over complete trajectories and work back to the next decision. Weighting the joint policy--environment trajectory law by reward and cost, restricting it to safe task completion, and marginalizing over future continuations yields an exact next-block marginal. This marginal brings together the action prior, local reward--cost terms, and the weighted mass of safe, successful continuations---the feasible-future mass. This mass is relative to the policy whose futures we are considering. When it is zero, the frozen policy--environment process assigns no probability to safe completion after that action, even if another controller could still succeed. And even when a safe route remains, the policy may place little mass on the continuations that follow it. We therefore distinguish support, which records whether safe completion remains possible, from magnitude, which measures how much weighted continuation mass is preserved. Exact evaluation is generally impractical online, but a decoder may still recover the preferred action from a much smaller comparison. Our selective finite-candidate approximation combines policy likelihood, local robustness, and a bounded continuation term. A gate first decides whether the sampled action is worth revisiting; only then does the decoder rerank a small candidate set. The gate buys efficiency at a price: a dead end it accepts never reaches the reranker. We account for this risk alongside errors in candidate availability, support handling, and approximate scoring, deriving conditions under which the best retained viable candidate can still be recovered. These ideas lead to (Viability-Corrected Sampling), a training-free reranker that draws on the current observation and interaction history. Across six Safety-CHORES settings~ zhang2025safevla , , its generic rollout-free configuration, consistently lowers observed safety cost while keeping task completion and episode length close to policy sampling. Measuring all three together~ fan2026safevlabench keeps the practical aim in focus: reducing harm while the robot continues toward its goal. We also ask how this picture changes when execution becomes less predictable, or when the decoder can afford a glimpse ahead.
