title: Odyssey: A Closed-Loop Benchmark for Long-Horizon Real-World Driving with Explicit Navigation Routes
summary: Closed-loop evaluation of end-to-end driving requires continuous rollouts that reveal how earlier decisions affect subsequent driving. However, existing benchmarks evaluate only short segments and fail to capture later consequences. Ambiguous directional commands also obscure the intended navigation objective. We introduce Odyssey, a closed-loop benchmark for long-horizon driving comprising 100 scenarios, each reconstructed from a 100-second nuPlan driving log to preserve the context of navigation maneuvers and traffic interactions. To provide a consistent navigation objective, Odyssey replaces directional commands with explicit standard-definition (SD) map routes that specify which roads to follow, while sensor-based planning determines local driving actions. Throughout these rollouts, diffusion-based refinement of 3DGS-rendered images reduces rendering artifacts along the ego trajectory. To assess how effectively planners follow these routes and prepare for upcoming maneuvers, we introduce SD Route Compliance and Pre-Lane Change Score. These assessments are complemented by RouteDS, which extends the Driving Score with penalties for SD-route deviations and failed lane preparation. We adapt state-of-the-art planners, including vision-language-action (VLA) models, and evaluate their navigation performance using these metrics. Odyssey highlights open questions in route representation and integration for E2E driving. Benchmark code and adapted baselines will be released publicly.
full_text: Closed-loop evaluation of end-to-end driving requires continuous rollouts that reveal how earlier decisions affect subsequent driving. However, existing benchmarks evaluate only short segments and fail to capture later consequences. Ambiguous directional commands also obscure the intended navigation objective. We introduce Odyssey, a closed-loop benchmark for long-horizon driving comprising 100 scenarios, each reconstructed from a 100-second nuPlan driving log to preserve the context of navigation maneuvers and traffic interactions. To provide a consistent navigation objective, Odyssey replaces directional commands with explicit standard-definition (SD) map routes that specify which roads to follow, while sensor-based planning determines local driving actions. Throughout these rollouts, diffusion-based refinement of 3DGS-rendered images reduces rendering artifacts along the ego trajectory. To assess how effectively planners follow these routes and prepare for upcoming maneuvers, we introduce SD Route Compliance and Pre-Lane Change Score. These assessments are complemented by RouteDS, which extends the Driving Score with penalties for SD-route deviations and failed lane preparation. We adapt state-of-the-art planners, including vision-language-action (VLA) models, and evaluate their navigation performance using these metrics. Odyssey highlights open questions in route representation and integration for E2E driving. Benchmark code and adapted baselines will be released publicly. Introduction r 0.47 fig:intro_2 A central challenge in autonomous driving is reliable navigation through complex traffic environments that ensure safety and comfort, as well as efficient progress toward an intended destination. With the growing availability of large-scale driving data, planning-oriented end-to-end (E2E) paradigms have gained prominence~ uniad, diffusiondrive, safedrive, drivor , in which driving systems directly map onboard sensor observations to driving decisions. Such planners should be evaluated by their ability to sustain safe driving as the vehicle interacts with its environment over time. Since open-loop evaluation independently compares decisions at individual time steps against recorded driving logs, it cannot capture their downstream effects. Accounting for downstream effects via closed-loop evaluation is essential to assess driving performance under evolving traffic conditions. For E2E planners, closed-loop evaluation requires sensor observations that reflect the consequences of the ego vehicle's actions. Neural rendering provides this feedback by reconstructing 3D real-world scenes from driving logs and rendering new observations from the simulated ego pose. Early approaches relied on neural radiance fields (NeRFs)~ unisim, neurad, emernerf , whose volumetric rendering incurs substantial computational cost. To reduce this cost, recent methods adopt 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ drivinggaussian, splatad, hugs, omnire for faster rendering while maintaining high visual fidelity. These developments have supported growing research on neural-rendering-based closed-loop benchmarks~ neuroncap, hugsim, alpasim for E2E planners. However, existing benchmarks are limited in assessing a planner's ability to handle long-term driving tasks (see Figure~ fig:intro_1 (a)). One limitation of existing closed-loop benchmarks~ neuroncap, hugsim is their short evaluation horizon, typically limited to approximately 20 seconds. Such short rollouts are insufficient to fully assess the navigation capabilities of E2E planners, particularly when navigation requires a sequence of coordinated maneuvers. For example, as shown in Figure~ fig:intro_2 (a), completing an upcoming right turn may require changing lanes in advance. However, the evaluation may terminate before the turn occurs, making it hard to assess the planner's ability to complete the maneuver sequence. Furthermore, high-level meta-action commands used in many E2E benchmarks~ nuscenes, navsim, navsimv2, hugsim, wod_e2e provide ambiguous guidance for navigation in real-world driving scenarios. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:intro_1 (a), a directional command such as ``turn right'' may correspond to multiple possible maneuvers. For example, if two right exits occur in succession, the command alone does not indicate which exit the planner should take. Annotating these commands in real-world driving datasets may not accurately reflect the driver's intended maneuver~ openscene , as shown in Figure~ fig:intro_2 (b). Reliable long-horizon evaluation therefore requires more explicit navigation guidance than high-level meta-action commands alone can provide. Another challenge is maintaining high rendering quality throughout long-horizon closed-loop simulations. When the ego vehicle deviates from the trajectory recorded during data collection, rendering quality may deteriorate because novel viewpoints lack sufficient observational support. The resulting artifacts can distort the visual input to E2E planners, influence their subsequent decisions, and undermine the reliability of both planning and evaluation. In addition, existing evaluation setups do not accurately model changes in traffic signals or pedestrian motion, further limiting their ability to represent realistic driving scenarios. In this paper, we introduce Odyssey, a real-world closed-loop benchmark for evaluating E2E driving models over long-horizon rollouts. Odyssey uses neural rendering to reconstruct 3D scenes and support realistic closed-loop simulations. Each scenario includes an explicit navigation route represented on a standard-definition (SD) map. By combining long-horizon evaluation with explicit route guidance, Odyssey enables a comprehensive assessment of models’ ability to navigate complex road structures safely—a capability that existing benchmarks have not adequately evaluated. For these extended rollouts, Odyssey builds on the explicit geometric representation of 3D Gaussian Splatting~ 3dgaussian , followed by diffusion-based refinement for improving visual fidelity. Using OmniRe~ omnire , we reconstruct continuous 100-second driving environments with rigid vehicles and deformable pedestrians whose motion is controlled independently of the static background. We further apply its time-conditioned deformation field to traffic lights to model changes in their color states throughout the sequence. To reduce blur and recover missing detail at novel ego poses, we apply single-step diffusion refinement~ difix3d, fixer to the rendered camera images without modifying the underlying scene representation or simulated state. Odyssey provides navigation routes as explicit guidance for E2E planners. By specifying the intended sequence of road segments, they resolve the ambiguity inherent in directional commands and eliminate the need to determine when to issue individual high-level meta-action commands. For each scenario, we construct an SD-map route from trip data of the data-collection fleet. However, this road-level representation encodes only coarse road-level topology and does not specify lane-level structure or the precise goal location that a driving model should reach. E2E planners must therefore interpret the high-level route jointly with the scene perceived by onboard sensors and translate it into a concrete, scene-consistent navigation goal. This requires the planner to reason about how an abstract road-level route is translated to appropriate lane-level maneuvers within the current road geometry. Odyssey establishes a foundation for evaluating such reasoning capability of E2E planners. We design the closed-loop benchmark to enable systematic comparison of different E2E planners. We curate 100 scenarios from the raw nuPlan data~ nuplan2 , covering sequences of complex navigation maneuvers and diverse road topologies. We further introduce two evaluation metrics, termed Pre-Lane Change Score and RouteDS, which assess whether the vehicle is appropriately positioned for upcoming navigation maneuvers, as well as driving safety and progress along the intended route. We evaluate a set of baseline planners adapted from recent state-of-the-art E2E and vision-language-action (VLA) models, incorporating navigation routes as additional input. Our main contributions are as follows: We introduce Odyssey, a high-fidelity real-world closed-loop benchmark for evaluating whether E2E planners can sustain safe and goal-directed driving under explicit route guidance over long-horizon rollouts. We evaluate planners over continuous rollouts based on recorded 100-second sequences, with explicit SD-map routes that resolve ambiguities in high-level driving commands and enable consistent assessment of navigation performance across complex road topologies. We develop a closed-loop simulation framework that combines the structural consistency of 3DGS with diffusion-based refinement to improve rendering fidelity when ego-vehicle motion reveals poorly reconstructed or previously unobserved regions. We will release the benchmark, evaluation code, and baseline results to enable reproducible comparison and facilitate further research on long-horizon closed-loop evaluation for autonomous driving. Related Work Open-loop displacement metrics overlook how planning actions affect subsequent driving~ nuscenes, stp3, uniad . NAVSIM introduces simulation-based driving metrics~ navsim , and NAVSIM v2 adds pre-rendered feedback~ navsimv2 . Continuous replanning further requires observations from the ego poses reached after executing successive actions. Neural simulators provide this feedback in reconstructed environments~ unisim, neurad, neuroncap, hugsim, alpasim . However, short evaluation sequences can end before earlier lane choices affect later navigation~ neuroncap, hugsim . Assessing these consequences also requires a consistent navigation objective. Directional commands can leave consecutive branches ambiguous~ uniad, vad, navsim, hugsim , obscuring whether route deviations reflect planning errors or insufficient guidance. Nearby target points provide spatial guidance but limited context for upcoming route choices~ carla, bench2drive . Odyssey addresses these temporal and navigational limitations through extended closed-loop rollouts with explicit SD-map routes, assessing whether successive decisions support safe progress along the intended road sequence. Odyssey sec:odyssey Odyssey provides a closed-loop simulation platform for evaluating long-horizon navigation along explicit routes on an SD map. Within each scene reconstructed from a 100-second driving log, the planner predicts a local driving trajectory based on camera observations and route guidance. The simulator advances the ego vehicle along the predicted trajectory and uses a neural rendering engine to generate new camera observations from its updated pose. We evaluate planner performance in terms of driving safety, route progress, adherence to the road-level route, and lane selection before intersections. Scenario Curation sec:long_horizon Odyssey comprises 100 driving scenarios curated from nuPlan~ nuplan2 . To capture diverse driving situations over extended sequences, we combine RefAV~ refav -based tagging with human review of navigation maneuvers and traffic interactions. The distribution of individual tags is reported in Figure~ fig:curation (a). The selected scenarios contain multiple maneuver and interaction tags, with the number of tags per scenario shown in Figure~ fig:curation (b). The selected set includes 13 scenarios involving traffic lights and 47 involving pedestrians, covering both signal compliance and safety around vulnerable road users. Within this set, we prioritize scenarios with complex road layouts and sequences of navigation maneuvers. Figure~ fig:curation (c) shows representative routes involving successive turns, branching roads, and lane changes. In particular, scenarios with a lane change followed by a turn allow us r 0.44

title: MarvisNav: Making Memory Visible on Route Choices for Zero-Shot Object Navigation
summary: When searching for an object, people choose their next move by considering both likely target locations and places already explored. The current view can cue place-associated memories, bringing target relevance and prior exploration into the same spatial context. In many zero-shot object navigation (ZSON) methods, however, vision-language models (VLMs) infer promising search areas from egocentric images, while exploration history is represented separately, e.g., as text or maps. This separation either requires an additional fusion step or leaves the correspondence between memory and route choices implicit for the VLM to recover. We instead make exploration memory directly visible on visual route choices. We propose MarvisNav, a ZSON framework that maintains a topological graph and projects candidate nodes together with their exploration states onto egocentric views as memory-bearing visual route choices. These states capture local exploration progress beyond binary visitation. By binding exploration state directly to each visual candidate, MarvisNav enables the VLM to jointly evaluate target relevance and exploration state without a separate post-hoc fusion or reranking stage. Without policy training, MarvisNav achieves state-of-the-art performance on HM3D (81.2% SR and 42.5% SPL), while remaining competitive on MP3D. It also outperforms representative VLM-based methods with far fewer VLM calls (e.g., 7.5% of WMNav). Real-robot experiments across diverse scenes further validate its practical deployability. Beyond MarvisNav, our study shows that memory representation shapes VLM decisions and ZSON performance, highlighting that effective memory use depends not only on its availability, but also on how it is represented. Code and project page will be available at \url{https://wangjincheng1998.github.io/MarvisNav/}.
full_text: When searching for an object, people choose their next move by considering both likely target locations and places already explored. The current view can cue place-associated memories, bringing target relevance and prior exploration into the same spatial context. In many zero-shot object navigation (ZSON) methods, however, vision-language models (VLMs) infer promising search areas from egocentric images, but exploration history enters the decision through separate representations, e.g., as text or maps. This separation either requires an additional fusion step to align semantic evidence with exploration state, or leaves the correspondence between memory and route choices implicit for the VLM to recover. We instead make exploration memory visible directly on visual route choice. We propose MarvisNav, a ZSON framework that maintains a topological graph and projects candidate nodes together with their exploration states onto the egocentric perception as memory-bearing visual route choices. These topological states capture local exploration progress beyond binary visitation. By binding exploration state directly to each visual candidate, MarvisNav enables the VLM to jointly evaluate target relevance and exploration state and make the final high-level selection without a separate post-hoc fusion or reranking stage. Without policy training, MarvisNav achieves state-of-the-art performance on HM3D ( SR and SPL), while competitive on MP3D. Moreover, it outperforms representative VLM-based methods with far fewer VLM calls (e.g., of WMNav). Real-robot experiments across diverse scenes further validate its practical deployability. Beyond MarvisNav, our study shows that memory representation shapes VLM decisions and ZSON performance, highlighting that effective memory use in ZSON depends not only on its availability, but also on how it is represented. Code will be released at https://wangjincheng1998.github.io/MarvisNav/ Introduction Imagine a robot asked to find an office chair in a home it has never seen. To succeed, it needs to infer where the target is likely to be and explore efficiently. This challenge is formalized as Object Navigation. Standard supervised methods are typically trained on a closed set of target categories~ chaplot2020object,chaplot2021seal,poni,HIEM , limiting their ability to generalize to new objects. Zero-shot Object Navigation (ZSON) instead leverages pretrained semantic knowledge to search for novel targets without category-specific training~ zson,chen2023not,CoWs,openfmnav , making it a key step toward open-world tasks. ZSON is a long-horizon search problem under partial observability~ 2025cvpr . When the target is not visible, the agent needs to use semantic cues to infer promising search areas. Existing methods obtain such guidance through visual-semantic alignment, which scores target relevance from visual observations ~ CoWs,vlfm,apexnav , or contextual semantic reasoning, which exploits scene context and spatial relations~ esc,sgnav,cognav . Recently, generative Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have been widely adopted for object search, leveraging strong multimodal understanding and broad knowledge for richer semantic and spatial reasoning over observations. Long-horizon search, however, requires a sequence of high-level decisions. A VLM does not by itself maintain the agent's exploration state across successive decisions. VLM-based methods therefore maintain explicit memory~ wmnav,openfrontier to avoid re-selecting semantically promising but already searched areas. Semantic guidance and exploration memory, however, are often met in separate representations. VLMs form semantic judgments from the current egocentric view, whereas exploration memory may be carried as separate textual histories or dense maps. Bringing the two together therefore requires an additional fusion or alignment step before decision-making. When memory remains outside the VLM, the system must explicitly define how it changes the model's semantic judgment~ wmnav,openfrontier , for example through hand-crafted candidate filtering or score adjustment. This places part of the choice outside the VLM and may constrain or override its judgment. When memory is instead supplied to the VLM, external fusion may be avoided, but the alignment problem remains. A textual history records past events in language, whereas a top-down map lays them out in an allocentric frame~ wu2026rememnav,History-Augmented,habibpour2025think . Neither is expressed in the egocentric view the agent is reasoning over. The VLM must therefore infer how remembered places relate to the current view before using that memory to decide where to search next (Fig.~ fig1 , left). Consider how a person searches for the chair in an unfamiliar house. They make both judgments from the same view, seeing which doorways look promising and which lead to areas already searched. A searched room is dismissed at a glance, while a doorway seen earlier remains a candidate if it still opens onto unexplored space. By making exploration cues visible on the corresponding spatial choices in views, we may then be able to give VLMs a similar decision interface, so that semantic evidence and exploration state are read together rather than aligned across representations. To this end, we introduce MarvisNav, a ZSON framework that makes exploration memory visible to VLMs by grounding it directly on visual route choices. We first reduce continuous exploration into sparse high-level decisions, where the VLM selects among navigable search directions. We derive these choices from a Reduced Voronoi Graph (RVG)~ voronav , where selected junctions serve as decision sites and local paths define candidate directions associated with reachable nodes. We extend this representation into a State-Aware RVG that associates each candidate with a local exploration state indicating whether nearby connected space may remain unexplored. At each decision, MarvisNav projects visible RVG paths into the egocentric RGB views and annotates candidates with local identifiers and exploration states, forming memory-bearing visual route choices (Fig.~ fig1 , right). A VLM then jointly evaluates target relevance and exploration state on these choices and selects an identifier in a single query. The selected identifier directly specifies the next navigation goal, enabling memory-conditioned route selection without additional semantic-memory fusion. We evaluate MarvisNav on standard indoor ZSON benchmarks, where it achieves strong performance without policy training. It also outperforms representative VLM-based methods with far fewer VLM queries, demonstrating practical efficiency for long-horizon navigation. We further validate its practical deployability on a Go2 robot across diverse scenes. Beyond MarvisNav, our study further demonstrates that exploration-memory representation can substantially affect both VLM preferences and navigation performance. These findings highlight the need to consider not only what an agent remembers, but also how that memory is made visible and associated with its choices. Related Work Semantic Guidance and Spatial Choices in ZSON. ZSON asks an agent to find an object in an unseen environment without category-specific training. A central problem in ZSON is determining where the target is likely to be found. Early approaches transfer pretrained vision-language knowledge to navigation through multimodal goal embeddings and open-vocabulary localization~ zson, CoWs . Later methods score the similarity between observations and the target with a pretrained image-text model~ clip and accumulate it in maps to guide exploration toward promising areas~ vlfm,apexnav,openfmnav . Large-language models (LLMs) extend this guidance beyond visual similarity by reasoning about object-room relations, scene context, and spatial structure esc,sgnav,cognav . VoroNav follows this line and uses a Voronoi Graph to organize navigable paths and sparse observation locations for language-model reasoning voronav . More recently, generative VLMs have moved this reasoning onto the egocentric image, judging which directions look promising without an intermediate textual description~ wmnav,DRIVE-Nav . This shift requires spatial alternatives to be presented in a form that the VLM can visually inspect and select~ som, PIVOT , while remaining tied to navigation goals that the agent can execute. Recent works provide such an interface by rendering frontiers directly into the observation as selectable navigation goals openfrontier . However, these visual choices indicate where the agent can go, but not whether unexplored space remains beyond each option, preventing direct joint reasoning over semantic promise and exploration state for VLM. Exploration Memory in VLM-Based Object Navigation. A VLM query does not retain exploration state across successive decisions, so VLM-based ZSON methods maintain explicit memory to avoid repeatedly considering already searched areas. Some methods keep memory outside the VLM's semantic reasoning: exploration history may restrict the candidates before querying VLMs~ DRIVE-Nav,openfrontier , or adjust its preference afterward through fixed filtering or score modification~ wmnav,instructnav . In both cases, semantic evidence and exploration state are evaluated separately and combined by an external rule, placing part of the decision outside the VLM and constraining its judgment. A more direct alternative is to expose the memory to the VLM itself. Text-based methods serialize past observations or actions into the prompt~ History-Augmented,wu2026rememnav,dynavlm for VLM reasoning. However, the VLM must implicitly associate this linguistic history with the current visual choices, which can make route-memory correspondence ambiguous. Rendering exploration history into a top-view map reduces that alignment problem by placing candidates and explored regions in a shared coordinate frame~ topvnav . However, reasoning directly over such a map moves the VLM away from the egocentric visual domain in which its perception and semantic reasoning are most naturally trained~ wmnav . A further step is to bring memory into the VLM's egocentric view itself. Mem2Ego~ mem2ego projects candidate choices and visited locations into the view as separate markers. This preserves egocentric reasoning, but the correspondence between a candidate and its visitation memory must still be inferred from their image-space proximity. Moreover, a visited marker indicates where the agent has been, but not whether unexplored space remains beyond that location. Our work instead grounds topological exploration memory explicitly onto visual choices, indicating whether unexplored connected space remains beyond each choice. This allows the VLM to jointly reason over semantic evidence and exploration state, without recovering correspondences across representations or relying on external rules. Motivation: How Memory Representation Shapes Decisions? sec:motivation Before introducing our method, we conduct a motivating study of how the representation of exploration memory shapes VLM decisions in ZSON. Generative VLM-based methods choose where to explore by evaluating visual navigation choices, making memory representation part of the decision context. While prior methods represent exploration history in diverse ways, comparatively less attention has been paid to how the representation itself affects VLM decision-making. To study this effect in a controlled setting, we keep the scene and target fixed and vary only how exploration memory is represented, as illustrated in Fig.~ motivation . The five representations span progressively tighter integration between exploration memory and the VLM's visual choices. title: SimForcing: Distilling Simulation Motion Priors into Real-Domain Robot World Models
summary: Action-conditioned robot world models must respond precisely to robot trajectories while preserving realistic visual dynamics, yet learning both from heterogeneous robot videos remains challenging. Simulation offers structured motion supervision, but appearance differences hinder direct transfer, and inaccurate simulation predictions can misguide real-video generation. We present SimForcing, a simulation-guided framework that uses simulation both as a source of transferable motion knowledge and as a controllable reference for prediction. First, we transfer motion knowledge from a simulation teacher through latent-motion distillation, aligning temporal changes in latent space to internalize motion priors while mitigating the influence of appearance differences. Second, we introduce multi-block simulation conditioning with condition dropout to exploit predicted simulation trajectories without relying excessively on their accuracy. Our simulation-conditioning classifier-free guidance scheme unifies these two ideas by balancing predictions based on internalized motion knowledge with those additionally guided by simulation latents. The jointly trained student generates both simulation conditions and real-domain videos, requiring no additional world model at inference. On Bridge, SimForcing achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and FVD among the compared methods without external embodied pretraining. Evaluation on InternData-A1 further supports its applicability across robot datasets. Moreover, using our trained world model to initialize a vision-language-action model improves LIBERO success, suggesting its utility for downstream policy learning. \url{https://github.com/Wang-Xiaodong1899/SimForcing}
full_text: Introduction sec:introduction Recent advances in large-scale video generation and world foundation models~ wan2025wan,chi2025wow,ali2025cosmos2.5,ma2026lingbotvideo , have expanded the potential of learned visual dynamics for embodied intelligence. Beyond video synthesis, these models can generate training experiences for robot policies~ jang2025dreamgen and support the improvement of vision-language-action (VLA) models through synthetic rollouts~ guo2026vlaw . Benchmarks such as WorldArena~ shang2026worldarena further assess their utility as data engines, policy evaluators, and action planners. Despite this progress, visually convincing predictions do not necessarily ensure reliable physical interactions or strong downstream performance~ shang2026worldarena . For robotic manipulation, a key challenge remains: learning precise responses to continuous action trajectories while preserving realistic appearance and temporally coherent scene dynamics. Existing approaches address this problem through different training paradigms, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser . One approach learns video prediction directly from real robot videos and their associated actions such as IRASim~ zhu2024irasim and Ctrl-World~ guo2025ctrlworld . This provides direct supervision for action-conditioned generation, but learning precise action responses and complex visual dynamics jointly from real videos remains challenging. Another approach introduces an explicit visual structure. For example, RoboDream~ ye2026robodream anchors generation to rendered robot motion and conditions on scene and object priors. Such compositional inputs provide additional control, while requiring the corresponding priors to be constructed and supplied. Qwen-RobotWorld~ zhang2026qwenrobotworld also needs scene video as prior. However, the potential of simulation data to improve real-video prediction without additional priors remains underexplored. Simulation provides structured supervision for action-dependent motion, complementing the appearance and interaction diversity of real videos. Transferring this knowledge nevertheless presents two challenges. First, appearance differences complicate direct matching between simulated and real observations. Second, predicted simulation trajectories are imperfect; a real-domain model that relies too heavily on them may inherit their errors. These challenges motivate transferring motion knowledge through temporal differences in latent space to mitigate the influence of appearance differences, while controlling the model's reliance on potentially inaccurate simulation predictions. We present SimForcing, a novel world modeling framework that addresses these challenges through motion knowledge transfer and controllable simulation guidance. To transfer motion knowledge across domains with different appearances, we first train a mixture-of-transformers world model on synthetic rollouts with trajectory augmentation, learning action-dependent motion from diverse robot trajectories. The resulting model initializes the student and serves as a frozen teacher. Our key transfer mechanism is latent-motion distillation, which aligns temporal differences between adjacent teacher and student video latents rather than directly matching their appearances. This motion-focused supervision internalizes the teacher's simulation-derived priors within the student, directly enhancing its ability to predict real-world video dynamics. Joint flow-matching and motion-distillation objectives on paired simulated and real videos further develop prediction capabilities in both domains within the same student, without requiring additional scene or object decomposition. To benefit from explicit simulation predictions without becoming overly dependent on their accuracy, we introduce multi-block simulation conditioning with condition dropout. Injecting simulation latents into multiple video transformer blocks provides a motion reference throughout generation, while latent corruption and condition dropout train the student to handle imperfect or absent simulation guidance. At inference, we introduce a simulation-conditioning classifier-free guidance (CFG) that combines predictions from branches with and without simulation latent input, balancing explicit simulation guidance with the student's internalized motion priors. This design enables the model to exploit reliable simulation predictions while limiting the influence of inaccurate ones. The jointly trained student generates both the simulation conditions and real-domain videos, requiring no additional world model at inference. Experiments on Bridge show that SimForcing outperforms Ctrl-World, EnerVerse-AC, and a GeniWorld reimplementation across PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and FVD, improving both reconstruction fidelity and perceptual similarity. It also achieves lower LPIPS than Cosmos-Predict2.5 with substantially faster inference. Evaluation on InternData-A1 supports its applicability across robot datasets, while ablations demonstrate the complementary benefits of motion distillation and simulation conditioning. Beyond video prediction, initializing a downstream VLA with the pretrained world-model experts improves average LIBERO success from to under action-only training relative to Wan DiT initialization, with gains also observed in the other training settings. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce SimForcing, a robot world model framework for transferring motion knowledge from simulation to real-world video prediction in latent space, internalizing simulation-derived motion priors within the world model. We propose a controllable mechanism for exploiting simulation predictions while limiting overreliance on inaccurate guidance. Our simulation-conditioning CFG scheme combines this explicit guidance with the motion knowledge internalized through distillation. We outperform state-of-the-art methods on Bridge across PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and FVD, and demonstrate the framework's applicability to InternData-A1 dataset. LIBERO experiments preliminarily validate the pretrained video expert's utility for policy learning. Related Work sec:related_work Generative World Models for Embodied Interaction Large-scale video generators provide increasingly capable visual priors for world modeling~ wan2025wan,agarwal2025cosmospredict1,ali2025cosmos2.5,chi2025wow , with recent efforts extending pretraining and adaptation toward embodied interaction. Qwen-RobotWorld~ zhang2026qwenrobotworld uses natural-language actions to predict future visual trajectories across manipulation, navigation, and driving, while LingBot-Video~ ma2026lingbotvideo scales mixture-of-experts video pretraining with robot-oriented data. DreamGen~ jang2025dreamgen adapts video generators to target robot embodiments and recovers action labels through inverse dynamics or latent action models, producing synthetic trajectories for policy learning. RoboScape~ shang2025roboscape incorporates physical priors through joint RGB--depth prediction and keypoint-based temporal consistency. PhysisForcing~ zhang2026physisforcing improves physical consistency using supervision constructed through a multi-model pipeline involving point tracking, depth-aware region selection, and semantic relation extraction. In contrast, our latent-motion distillation derives supervision directly from temporal differences in a simulation-pretrained teacher's predicted video latents, without constructing explicit depth, point-trajectory, or semantic-relation targets. Action-conditioned world models connect robot controls to predicted visual outcomes. IRASim~ zhu2024irasim learns from historical observations and continuous actions, while AVID~ rigter2024avid adds an action-conditioned adapter to a frozen video diffusion model. Dynamic World Simulation~ he2025worldsim combines action conditioning with a motion-reinforced objective. EnerVerse-AC~ jiang2025enerverse uses multi-level action conditioning for multiview generation, and Ctrl-World~ guo2025ctrlworld supports policy-in-the-loop simulation with frame-level control and temporal memory. Other methods encode control as spatial visual signals: RoboMaster~ fu2025robomaster uses collaborative robot--object trajectories, ABot-PhysWorld~ chen2026abot combines spatial action injection with physics-aligned training, and OSCAR~ wu2026oscar uses rendered kinematic skeletons across embodiments. EA-WM~ yang2026eawm projects actions and kinematic states into camera-aligned visual action fields, with event-aware bidirectional fusion supervised by VAE-encoded frame differences. Masked Visual Actions~ alzayer2026masked reveals robot or object motion in masked videos, unifying forward and inverse world modeling through a shared pixel-space control interface. FlowWAM~ chen2026flowwam adopts optical flow for video prediction and policy learning, while RynnWorld-Teleop~ zhao2026rynnworld uses hand-pose conditioning for real-time teleoperation. Recent efforts further incorporate 3D and 4D structure into embodied prediction and control. TesserAct~ zhen2025tesseract jointly generates RGB, depth, and normal sequences for 4D scene reconstruction. Robo4DGen~ liu2025robo4dgen introduces cross-view pointmap supervision for geometrically consistent multiview prediction, while MVISTA-4D~ wang2026mvista generates arbitrary-view RGB-D futures through cross-view and cross-modality feature fusion. RoboStereo~ zhang2026robostereo couples action-conditioned RGB and pointmap generation through a dual-tower diffusion architecture, and RynnWorld-4D~ zhao2026rynnworld4d jointly predicts RGB, depth, and optical flow to model appearance, geometry, and motion. Kinema4D~ xu2026kinema4d uses URDF-based kinematics to construct robot pointmap trajectories as control signals for synchronized RGB and pointmap generation. CausalWM~ xu2026causalwm sequentially predicts optical flow, 3D pointmaps, and RGB videos, using intermediate predictions as context for subsequent generation. PointWorld~ huang2026pointworld instead models scene dynamics directly as 3D point flows, representing robot actions in the same space and learning across embodiments from real and simulated manipulation data. X-WAM~ guo2026xwam further couples multiview RGB-D prediction with robot action generation, using a lightweight depth branch and asynchronous denoising to decode actions with fewer steps than video. WAM4D~ li2026wam4d uses spatial register tokens and future-depth supervision to transfer geometric priors into video--action representations, removing the geometric readout branch for efficient action inference. Our work addresses the complementary problem of transferring simulation-derived motion knowledge into real-domain video prediction, combining latent-motion distillation with simulation guidance generated by the same model. World Action Models World action models couple visual prediction with robot control. VPP~ hu2024vpp , Video Policy~ liang2025videopolicy , DiT4DiT~ ma2026dit4dit , and mimic-video~ pai2025mimicvideo learn action policies from predictive video representations. Unified World Models~ zhu2025uwm , Motus~ bi2025motus , LingBot-VA~ li2026lingbotva , and DreamZero~ ye2026dreamzero jointly model future observations and actions, connecting world modeling with policy learning. UniT~ chen2026unit develops shared visual-action tokens for human-to-humanoid transfer, while Cosmos Policy~ kim2026cosmospolicy and World-Value-Action Model~ li2026worldvalueaction incorporate value prediction for planning. Future RGB modeling is a common visual learning objective in video-based WAMs~ zhu2025uwm,ye2026dreamzero , although auxiliary representations vary; Motus~ bi2025motus , for example, also learns latent actions from optical flow. Beyond direct action generation, learned world models support policy evaluation~ li2025worldeval,li2026dworldeval , reinforcement-learning-based policy improvement~ jiang2026wovr , and paired video-action data synthesis~ lang2026vag

title: Recursive Video In-Context Learning for Agentic Robot
summary: LLM agents that orchestrate frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policies improve across episodes through text memory, which records what the agent did but not how the task is done. A demonstration video shows it, but fits poorly into an agent's context. The full video slows every turn, fixed keyframes lose the contact detail that decides whether a grasp holds, and what the agent needs shifts from the task's structure while planning to the frames around each contact. We introduce Recursive Video In-Context Learning (RV-ICL), a training-free method that turns a demonstration into a hierarchy the agent navigates rather than a prompt it receives. The hierarchy is built from the sub-events of the demonstration, such as grasps and releases. Its levels grow finer, from keyframes of the whole task to phases, moments and short clips, and are exposed through read-only tools. The agent reads the coarse levels before planning. During execution it re-enters the hierarchy whenever a step needs more detail and loads only the clip of its current sub-goal. One demonstration per task is enough. Built on RPent, RV-ICL raises success from 92.6% to 96.5% on LIBERO-PRO and from 86.7% to 95.8% on LIBERO-Plus.
full_text: LLM agents that orchestrate frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policies improve across episodes through text memory, which records what the agent did but not how the task is done. A demonstration video shows it, but fits poorly into an agent's context. The full video slows every turn, fixed keyframes lose the contact detail that decides whether a grasp holds, and what the agent needs shifts from the task's structure while planning to the frames around each contact. We introduce Recursive Video In-Context Learning ( ) , a training-free method that turns a demonstration into a hierarchy the agent navigates rather than a prompt it receives. The hierarchy is built from the sub-events of the demonstration, such as grasps and releases. Its levels grow finer, from keyframes of the whole task to phases, moments and short clips, and are exposed through read-only tools. The agent reads the coarse levels before planning. During execution it re-enters the hierarchy whenever a step needs more detail and loads only the clip of its current sub-goal. One demonstration per task is enough. Built on RPent, raises success from 92.6 to 96.5 on LIBERO-PRO and from 86.7 to 95.8 on LIBERO-Plus. Introduction Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as the deliberative layer of robot systems. They decompose instructions, localise objects, and call learned visuomotor policies for the contact-rich steps they cannot perform analytically~ ahn2022saycan,liang2023cap,huang2022innermonologue . Recent agentic harnesses push this design further. HarnessVLA~ zhang2026harnessvla , released as the RPent framework, exposes a frozen VLA as one retryable primitive among a few analytic ones. A coding agent orchestrates them and improves across episodes through text memory: recipes, lessons and failure rules. Under distribution shift, this design outperforms end-to-end VLAs by a wide margin. How far the agent can improve, however, is bounded by what text can record. The agent writes its memory from its own execution traces, so the memory describes its calls and their outcomes rather than the task itself. It can record that a grasp failed, but not what a successful execution looks like: which object is taken first, from which side the hand approaches, how high the object is lifted, when the gripper opens. Such knowledge is spatial and temporal, and it is hard to put into words. What is hard to put into words is easy to show: a video of the task captures all of it, frame by frame. Such a video is also cheap to obtain. A human demonstration only requires recording a person actually performing the task, with no action labels or other annotation. Large models can learn from demonstrations placed in their context, in text~ brown2020gpt3 and with interleaved images~ alayrac2022flamingo . This suggests letting the agent watch a demonstration of its task, much as a person watches a how-to video before trying something new. But in what form should the video enter the agent's memory? The obvious answers fail for three reasons. (i) Length. A demonstration spans hundreds of frames, and the agent re-reads its whole context at each of its tens to hundreds of turns. Long contexts also degrade how well models use their content~ liu2024lost . (ii) Resolution. A few keyframes are affordable, but they drop the frames around each contact, which decide whether a grasp holds or a placement registers. (iii) Timing. What the agent needs changes over the episode: the task's structure before it acts, and the frames around a particular contact once it reaches that step. No fixed presentation of the video can satisfy all three constraints at once. Since each moment of the episode calls for a different part of the demonstration, why not let the agent watch just that part, and only at that moment? Methods for long documents and long videos already take this route: instead of reading everything, the language model navigates a hierarchical index~ sarthi2024raptor,wang2024videoagent,packer2023memgpt . We bring this idea to embodied agents, which decide from their own progress when to look closer: before a delicate contact, at the start of a new sub-goal, or after a step goes wrong. We build such an index over a demonstration and call the method Recursive Video In-Context Learning ( ) . The index is a tree whose levels grow finer: event-driven keyframes of the whole task, the phases between sub-events, the moments around each sub-event, and short clips from any camera ( a). The agent reads the coarse levels before planning and does not collect clips up front. Whenever it needs more detail during execution, the agent re-enters the tree at the node of its current sub-goal and pulls only the relevant clip ( b). The demonstration is thus consulted recursively, at the level of detail and the moment the agent's progress calls for. requires no training, no change to the VLA, and one demonstration per base task. The hierarchy is built from the sub-events of the demonstration, the instants at which one sub-task ends and the next begins. The same construction therefore applies to any task that decomposes into sub-tasks. We make the following contributions: 0em We introduce video in-context learning to tool-using robot agents: their text memory cannot record what a successful execution looks like, but a demonstration video shows it frame by frame ( ). We propose Recursive Video In-Context Learning ( ), which lets the agent look only at the part of the demonstration its current step needs, by giving it recursive access to a hierarchy built from the demonstration's sub-events ( ). On LIBERO-PRO, raises the success rate of HarnessVLA from 92.6 to 96.5 , above every baseline, and on LIBERO-Plus from 86.7 to 95.8 across seven kinds of perturbation. On the long LIBERO-10 tasks it gains up to 12 points, where keyframes or the whole video of the same demonstration gain at most 2 ( ). Related Work sec:related LLM agents for robot manipulation Language models entered robotics as planners over pre-trained skills. SayCan~ ahn2022saycan scores LLM proposals by learned affordances, ProgPrompt~ singh2023progprompt and Code as Policies~ liang2023cap write programs over perception and control APIs, and VoxPoser~ huang2023voxposer composes 3D value maps for a motion planner. Inner Monologue~ huang2022innermonologue feeds execution feedback back to the planner, and Voyager~ wang2023voyager accumulates a library of verified skills. A recent line of agentic harnesses puts a coding agent in charge of a frozen VLA. HarnessVLA~ zhang2026harnessvla exposes the VLA as a retryable primitive and learns its operating range from text memory; Robo-Harness K1~ li2026robokharness augments such agents with perception; CaP-X~ fu2026capx benchmarks coding agents for manipulation; RATS~ zhang2026rats learns through play; and RAPID~ liu2026rapid synthesises agent programs from demonstrations. The knowledge these systems carry across episodes is textual or programmatic. keeps the harness unchanged and adds a visual record of how the task is performed, together with a protocol for consulting it. Learning from demonstrations in context In language models, a few demonstrations in the prompt suffice to specify a task~ brown2020gpt3 , although models draw mostly on their format and label space rather than the exact input--label mapping~ min2022rethinking . Flamingo~ alayrac2022flamingo extends in-context learning to interleaved images. In robotics, one-shot imitation has been learned by meta-learning from human videos~ yu2018daml and by video-conditioned policies~ jain2024vid2robot . In-context imitation has been achieved by tokenising demonstrations as keypoints for an off-the-shelf LLM~ dipalo2024kat , by training a policy to continue interleaved demonstration trajectories~ fu2024icrt , and by conditioning a VLA on structured demonstrations~ xu2026stellavla . When an LLM acts directly as the policy, one-shot demonstrations yield no aggregate gain~ zhang2026astrarobodojo . All of these present the demonstration once, as a prefix for the next actions. Our agent makes tens to hundreds of decisions per episode, so the question is not only whether to show a demonstration but which part, and when. Recursion in language-model reasoning and retrieval sec:related-recursion Recursion lets a bounded model handle inputs and problems that exceed its context. Recursive summarisation condenses a book into a tree of summaries read top-down~ wu2021recursively , and RAPTOR~ sarthi2024raptor retrieves from such a tree at the level of abstraction a question requires. For long videos, VideoAgent~ wang2024videoagent and VideoTree~ wang2025videotree likewise inspect only the frames or branches a question needs. Recursive decomposition splits a problem as needed. ADaPT~ prasad2024adapt decomposes a sub-task further only when the executor fails on it, THREAD~ schroeder2025thread spawns child threads that return only what the parent needs, and Recursive Language Models~ zhang2025rlm call themselves over slices of a context too long to read at once. Tree of Thoughts~ yao2023tot searches over such trees of intermediate steps. A related family decides when to fetch information. FLARE~ jiang2023flare retrieves when upcoming tokens are uncertain, and Self-RAG~ asai2024selfrag learns to request retrieval on demand. Reflexion~ shinn2023reflexion and Self-Refine~ madaan2023selfrefine feed the outcome of an attempt into the next one, and MemGPT~ packer2023memgpt pages information between a bounded context and external storage. brings recursion to an embodied agent. The demonstration is a tree read at the level each decision requires, and the agent descends whenever its progress in the physical task calls for more detail: before a delicate contact, at a new sub-goal, or after a step goes wrong. At turn the agent conditions on its context and emits a call . The context holds , the text memory of HarnessVLA, the current camera images and the history of calls and results. The episode ends when the agent calls or reaches its step or time limits. It succeeds if the simulator's goal predicate holds. adds a demonstration of the same base task, recorded in a different scene, and a second, read-only tool set whose calls return views of . The design question is which views offers and when the agent should request them, given that every view stays in once loaded. We segment at its sub-events , the instants at which one sub-task ends and the next begins. Every task that decomposes into sub-tasks has such instants, so the construction below applies to it unchanged. Manipulation tasks expose their sub-events in the recorded state. An object is grasped when the gripper closes and released when it opens, and a drawer or door is opened or closed when its joint moves. title: SteadySplats: Resampling of Low-Variance Gaussians for High-Fidelity Stochastic Rendering
summary: Stochastic order-independent transparency enables efficient and elegant rendering of primitive-based radiance fields like 3D Gaussian Splatting models, but remains impractical due to the inherent visible noise in the output. We propose a principled approach to minimize high-frequency noise, addressing its sources at the representation and image synthesis level. During stochastic rendering, our history-based spatial resampling scheme drastically accelerates image convergence, while temporal importance resampling ensures coherence under camera movement. During training, a color regularizer implicitly reduces the variance along view rays in the 3DGS models. With these properties, our optimized, Vulkan-based renderer effectively mitigates output noise at low and high sample counts, achieving a substantial 13~dB PSNR increase in quality over previous stochastic methods at 1 sample per pixel and quickly converging to sorted 3DGS with an average L1 error of less than $10^{-4}$.

Introduction sec:intro HTML 218f8d HTML 5EC962 The rapid evolution of novel view synthesis has been largely driven by the advent of radiance fields and, more recently, primitive-based representations in particular. Methods such as 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233dgs have demonstrated exceptional visual fidelity and real-time rendering capabilities by modeling complex scenes as unstructured collections of volumetric primitives. Traditionally, fast rendering of these representations relies on alpha-blending sorted primitives using a tile-based rasterizer. Stochastic order-independent transparency (OIT) presents an elegant, efficient alternative for rendering primitive-based radiance fields. By probabilistically sampling visible primitives rather than sorting them, stochastic OIT dramatically simplifies and accelerates the rendering pipeline. However, despite its structural advantages, this approach has remained largely impractical for novel view synthesis. The stochastic nature of the visibility evaluation inherently introduces high-frequency noise in the resulting images ( ~ ). Across novel view trajectories, this uncorrelated noise manifests itself as severe temporal flickering and ``boiling'' artifacts~ schied2017spatiotemporal , to which human visual perception is sensitive. Mitigating this issue and suppressing these artifacts below visible thresholds requires accumulating hundreds of samples per pixel, which directly negates the performance advantages of sorting-free rendering~ kheradmand2025stochasticsplats . In this work, we propose solutions that make stochastic order-independent transparency practical for high-fidelity rendering by aggressively tackling noise at both ends of the pipeline: training and inference. All of our contributions are implemented in a high-performance Vulkan-based renderer: Color Variance Regularization: A training objective that penalizes high-variance primitive configurations, implicitly conditioning the 3D model to produce less noise during stochastic sampling. History-Based Spatial Resampling: An efficient, inference-time resampling technique to massively accelerate convergence of image synthesis with minimal bias. Temporal Consistency: We demonstrate that under mild assumptions, spatio-temporal resampling can be implemented as a recursive exponential moving average filter to efficiently mitigate temporal artifacts. Stratifying samples using per-primitive Spatio-Temporal Blue Noise further improves convergence. We demonstrate that our combined approach successfully renders clean, high-fidelity images at low sample counts, achieving higher frame rates than vanilla 3DGS with near-indistinguishable quality. Related Work sec:related_work 3D Gaussian Splatting and the Sorting Bottleneck. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a highly efficient representation for real-time novel view synthesis~ kerbl20233dgs . Traditionally, it relies on a tile-based rasterizer that strictly sorts semi-transparent primitives based on a per-primitive depth to perform deterministic alpha-compositing. However, this global sorting operation is computationally expensive, scales poorly with increasing scene complexity, especially on low-end hardware, and introduces temporal discontinuities known as ``popping'' artifacts when slight camera movements alter the primitive order. Several methods have attempted to address these limitations. StopThePop~ radl2024stopthepop eliminates popping through computationally intensive per-pixel sorting based on the maximal Gaussian response. Alternatively, exact volumetric intermixing can be achieved by ray tracing of constant density ellipsoids~ mai2024ever or by reconstructing the transmittance function from analytic moments~ muller2025moment . Other approaches approximate alpha-blending via proxy-guided weighted blending~ liu2025duplex or order-independent accumulation with a K-buffer~ hahlbohm2025hybrid to bypass full radix sorting. Weighted sum rendering~ hou2025sort, du2026mobile completely eliminates sorting during training and inference at the cost of reduced image quality. Order-Independent and Stochastic Transparency. To fundamentally circumvent the sorting bottleneck, recent literature has adapted stochastic order-independent transparency (OIT). Originally introduced to 3D graphics by Enderton et al.~ enderton2010stochastic , stochastic transparency replaces sorted alpha-blending with a randomized Monte Carlo estimator. StochasticSplats~ kheradmand2025stochasticsplats successfully integrates this estimator into 3DGS by keeping each fragment as an opaque sample with probability equal to its alpha value, completely bypassing depth-sorting while accurately blending overlapping Gaussians. Similarly, Gaussian Point Splatting~ rijsdijk2026gaussian treats Gaussians as discrete point clouds, sampling pixel-sized opaque points independently and splatting them via 64-bit atomics to achieve massive parallelism. While these approaches eliminate the need for sorting, they inherently introduce severe high-frequency noise into the rendered images and must rely on expensive sample accumulation or temporal anti-aliasing (TAA)~ karis2014high,yang2020survey . Stochastic approaches can also be applied to ray tracing 3D Gaussians for relightable reconstruction~ xu2026stochastic and semi-transparency~ sun2025stochastic . Stochastic Gaussian Splatting~ aira2025modeling moves the stochasticity into the Gaussian parameters themselves in order to estimate reconstruction uncertainty. Denoising and Resampling. Early real-time denoising relied heavily on analytical spatial and temporal filters, most notably Spatiotemporal Variance-Guided Filtering (SVGF)~ schied2017spatiotemporal to accumulate temporal history while preserving edges. As deep learning matured, denoising networks such as kernel prediction networks~ mildenhall2018burst, vogels2018denoising, fan2021real , neural bilateral grids~ meng2020real , and Deep Learning Super Sampling~ nvidia_dlss_developer, nvidia_dlss_rayreconstruction gained popularity. Spatiotemporal Reservoir Resampling (ReSTIR)~ wyman2023gentle and descendant methods~ zhang2024area, kettunen2023conditional, ouyang2021restir, hedstrom2025restir, zeng2025restir directly improve the quality of the Monte Carlo integration in a principled manner before the denoising step. By leveraging temporal history and spatial neighbors, the impact of each individual sample is amplified. Preliminaries sec:preliminaries In this section, we detail how the stochastic paradigm diverges from traditional 3DGS rendering. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) 3D Gaussian Splatting represents complex scenes as an unstructured collection of anisotropic 3D Gaussians~ kerbl20233dgs . Each Gaussian primitive is defined by a set of optimizable parameters , which encode its mean position ( ), 3D covariance matrix ( ), opacity ( ), and view-dependent color ( ), typically modeled using spherical harmonics. To synthesize a novel view, these 3D Gaussians are ``splatted'' to a screen-space 2D Gaussian distribution and depth using an affine approximation for projection~ zwicker2001EWA . We denote by the set of Gaussians intersecting the pixel , by the alpha-blending factor of Gaussian , and by the final pixel radiance, which is classically computed by evaluating the volume rendering equation through deterministic alpha-compositing~ kerbl20233dgs : where denotes all intersecting primitives located in front of primitive along the ray. In standard 3DGS, primitives are sorted by prior to blending, which simplifies the transmittance to . While this sorted alpha-blending ensures a stable and noise-free image, the global sorting operation imposes significant computational overhead and memory bandwidth bottlenecks, limiting scalability, especially on low-power devices, and producing temporal popping artifacts~ radl2024stopthepop . Stochastic and Order-Independent 3DGS sec:stochastic StochasticSplats~ kheradmand2025stochasticsplats fundamentally alters the rendering pipeline by adapting stochastic order-independent transparency (OIT)~ enderton2010stochastic . Rather than sorting primitives globally, stochastic transparency replaces deterministic alpha-blending with an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator. The two approaches are contrasted in . The core idea is to probabilistically assign fully opaque samples to a pixel according to the fragments' alpha-blending factors, evaluating the color without any sorting. The radiance is estimated by randomly and independently sampling Gaussian indices from a probability mass function : , each Gaussian is sampled with exactly its blending weight from . A single draw thus yields an unbiased one-sample estimate of the pixel color, . In practical hardware implementations, is sampled by leveraging standard, unsorted rasterization with a Z-buffer. For each fragment, a uniform random number is sampled; the fragment is kept as fully opaque if , and discarded otherwise. The Z-buffer then retains the nearest kept fragment, whose index therefore follows . Gaussian Point Splatting produces samples from the same underlying distribution using a massively parallelized point-sampling technique. As such, its output is near-identical to StochasticSplats except for small biases introduced by approximations. Further details can be found in . Temporal Reuse. Because 1-sample stochastic splats produce noisy raw frames, temporal accumulation is essential for stability. Existing methods address this in two distinct ways. StochasticSplats maintains an unweighted Cumulative Moving Average (CMA), where is the sample drawn in frame , is the reprojection of into the previous frame, and counts the accumulated samples, resetting the sample counter whenever relative depth error exceeds a threshold . Gaussian Point Splatting instead uses a fixed-weight exponential moving average (EMA) with a bounded temporal window, borrowing AABB color clamping from standard temporal anti-aliasing (TAA)~ karis2014high,salvi2016temporal to suppress ghosting by restricting reprojected history to within standard deviations of the local color mean. Method sec:method The noise produced by stochastic 3DGS methods kheradmand2025stochasticsplats, rijsdijk2026gaussian is a direct result of the variance in the Monte Carlo estimator , which determines its root-mean-square error: To reduce this error, either the color variance at each pixel must be decreased or the sample count increased. title: StageVLN: Spatial and Trajectory Auxiliary Guidance for Efficient Vision-Language Navigation
summary: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) policies increasingly benefit from strong semantic priors provided by large vision-language models (VLMs). However, standard action supervision does not explicitly encourage intermediate representations to preserve scene geometry, relative orientation, or global episode progress. Incorporating depth estimators, explicit maps, point clouds, or geometry foundation models at inference can provide such structure but introduces additional computation, memory overhead, and architectural dependence during deployment. We introduce StageVLN, a training framework that shapes navigation representations through privileged spatial and trajectory guidance while preserving the original inference pathway. A frozen geometry foundation model provides multi-level spatial guidance to hierarchical navigator states, while relative-heading and expert-route progress objectives provide complementary trajectory-state supervision. All auxiliary components are used only during training and removed at deployment. On R2R-CE validation-unseen, StageVLN achieves 56.3\% SR and 51.4\% SPL with a 4B-parameter backbone, without an additional geometry encoder at inference. On RxR-CE, it achieves 54.3\% SR without additional navigation training data or a geometry encoder at inference.

On RxR-CE, it achieves 54.3 SR without additional navigation training data or a geometry encoder at inference. INTRODUCTION Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) tasks require an agent to process natural language instructions and egocentric visual observations to generate actions that reach a goal through diverse environments. The Room-to-Room (R2R) benchmark anderson2018vision established an instruction-grounded evaluation framework within real scanned scenes. Subsequently, Room-Across-Room (RxR) ku2020room extended this paradigm to support greater language and trajectory diversity, while Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) krantz2020beyond further transitioned the task from discrete navigation graphs to continuous 3D spaces. In continuous settings, merely recognizing referenced objects is insufficient; navigation policies must also relate the visible structure of the environment to traversable motion, maintain spatial orientation across sequential observations, and continuously localize their position along the requested route. Recent RGB-only systems zhang2024navid, zhang2024uni, cheng2024navila, wei2025streamvln, zhang2026embodied increasingly integrate VLMs into navigation policies, leveraging images, video context, memory, or world-action modeling objectives to learn more robust behaviors. However, their strong semantic priors do not guarantee that the hidden representations used for action prediction preserve the geometric and trajectory structure required for navigation in complex environments. A direct solution is to incorporate pretrained geometry models wang2025vggt, wang2026vggt into the inference pipeline, or to fuse depth, point clouds, maps, or latent 3D features directly into the navigation policy. While this paradigm has proven effective for spatial understanding in VLMs fan2026vlm, zhang2026spatialstack, wang2026learning and has recently been adapted for VLN zeng2026janusvln , it introduces extra runtime dependencies and increases deployment costs, particularly on real-world robots with constrained hardware. To address this limitation, our central question is: can geometric guidance and trajectory-state supervision improve the navigator while preserving its original deployment pathway? This perspective aligns with the broader principles of learning via auxiliary objectives and intermediate representation distillation hinton2015distilling, lopez2015unifying , while adapting them to the temporal structure of embodied navigation. We propose StageVLN, a general framework for spatial and trajectory auxiliary guidance. The central idea is to introduce complementary supervision at three levels of navigation structure, progressing from local scene geometry to relational orientation and finally to global trajectory state. During training, a frozen geometry encoder provides multi-level spatial information by supervising intermediate visual states via representation distillation. Additionally, relative heading prediction encourages the learning of a relational orientation structure across observations, while progress prediction provides the agent with a global estimate of its position along the expert trajectory. Crucially, these objectives are applied strictly at training time, allowing the navigator to retain the benefits of geometric and trajectory supervision without requiring auxiliary components at inference. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:stagevln_overview , our contributions are threefold: We introduce a training-only hierarchical geometry-teacher mechanism that transfers spatial representations into multiple navigator layers without requiring geometric feature fusion at inference time. We propose a unified spatial-and-trajectory training formulation that combines multi-level spatial feature distillation with relative-heading and expert-route progress supervision. We conduct extensive navigation evaluations and comprehensive component analyses, demonstrating improvements in success-related metrics while characterizing localization trade-offs and distinguishing auxiliary-free deployment from measured system efficiency. RELATED WORK sec:related_work Vision-Language Models for Navigation Recent VLN methods adapt pretrained vision-language models to predict actions from egocentric observations and instructions. NaVid~ zhang2024navid uses monocular video for end-to-end navigation, while Uni-NaVid~ zhang2024uni extends video-based action modeling to multiple embodied navigation tasks. NaVILA~ cheng2024navila connects language-conditioned navigation with legged locomotion through intermediate movement commands. StreamVLN~ wei2025streamvln addresses long observation streams through slow--fast context modeling, memory compression, and KV-cache reuse. StageVLN addresses the complementary problem of supervising the spatial and trajectory information encoded within an RGB--language policy. It introduces additional training objectives while preserving the base policy's observation interface and action-generation architecture at deployment. Geometry-Aware Representations and Spatial Distillation Geometry foundation models provide representations learned from geometric prediction tasks. VGGT~ wang2025vggt , for example, jointly predicts camera parameters, depth, point maps, and point tracks from images. JanusVLN~ zeng2026janusvln combines visual-semantic and spatial-geometric features with separate implicit memories for navigation. In spatial question answering, SpatialStack~ zhang2026spatialstack integrates geometric features at multiple language-model layers, demonstrating the value of hierarchical geometry--language fusion. Both designs compute geometric features as part of the inference pathway. An alternative is to transfer teacher representations during training. FitNets~ romero2015fitnets established intermediate-feature supervision as a mechanism for knowledge transfer. More directly related, Spatial Forcing~ li2026spatial aligns intermediate visual embeddings of manipulation VLAs with pretrained geometric representations while leaving their inference architecture unchanged. Auxiliary Supervision for Navigation Auxiliary objectives have long been used to improve navigation representations beyond action imitation. The self-monitoring agent~ ma2019selfmonitoring introduces progress estimation to support instruction grounding. AuxRN~ zhu2020auxiliary jointly learns trajectory retelling, progress estimation, next-orientation prediction, and cross-modal matching; its progress objective already uses soft step-fraction targets with cross-entropy supervision. However, these auxiliary objectives do not explicitly transfer spatial representations from a pretrained geometry model into the navigation policy. StageVLN combines hierarchical geometric feature transfer with two trajectory-state targets. Its heading objective supervises the accumulated relative rotation between historical and current views, rather than the orientation of the next expert action. Its progress target measures the fraction of expert forward actions already completed, excluding turns, and is predicted from a pre-action hidden state without access to the supervised action token. Together with current-view geometric alignment, they provide supervision for scene structure, inter-observation orientation, and route-level state. All auxiliary components, including the geometry teacher, are removed at inference, retaining the original RGB–language navigation pathway. title: KineWorld: Action-Induced Transport Fields for Embodied World Modeling
summary: Embodied world models predict the visual consequences of candidate actions before execution. However, existing action-conditioned world models often adopt uniformly weighted visual generation objectives that can be misaligned with embodied prediction needs. Even with explicit motion conditioning, these objectives can underemphasize spatially sparse changes that are critical to interaction. We propose KineWorld, a transport-aware world-modeling framework that extends robot kinematics from motion conditioning to the spatial allocation of generative supervision. Kinematic Transport Lifting (KTL) constructs renderer-derived, camera-aligned transport fields from commanded robot motion. Transport-Aware World Diffusion (TAWD) calibrates their motion support on the video-latent grid and reweights future-RGB flow matching through a normalized mixture of uniform and transport-focused distributions. We train KineWorld using ALOHA-AgileX bimanual manipulation data from RoboTwin 2.0. KineWorld achieves an EWMScore-P of 68.95 in single-view evaluation and a TWB-Score of 54.82 in multi-view evaluation. These results support a shift from appearance fitting toward action-consequence modeling for embodied decision-making.
