However, existing action-conditioned world models often adopt uniformly weighted visual generation objectives that can be misaligned with embodied prediction needs. Even with explicit motion conditioning, these objectives can underemphasize spatially sparse changes that are critical to interaction. We propose , a transport-aware world-modeling framework that extends robot kinematics from motion conditioning to the spatial allocation of generative supervision. Kinematic Transport Lifting (KTL) constructs renderer-derived, camera-aligned transport fields from commanded robot motion. Transport-Aware World Diffusion (TAWD) calibrates their motion support on the video-latent grid and reweights future-RGB flow matching through a normalized mixture of uniform and transport-focused distributions. We train KineWorld using ALOHA--AgileX bimanual manipulation data from RoboTwin~2.0. KineWorld achieves an EWMScore-P of 68.95 in single-view evaluation and a TWB-Score of 54.82 in multi-view evaluation. These results support a shift from appearance fitting toward action-consequence modeling for embodied decision-making. Introduction sec:introduction World Action Models (WAMs) enable robots to anticipate how the visual world will evolve under candidate actions before executing them in the physical environment. By generating action-conditioned future observations, these models can serve as predictive simulators for policy learning, action evaluation, planning, and synthetic experience generation. Recent advances in large-scale video generation further provide strong appearance and dynamics priors, making it possible to construct visually realistic robot rollouts from limited embodied data zhu2024irasim,guo2025ctrlworld,liao2025genieenvisioner . Existing world action models (WAMs) improve action responsiveness through numerical action tokens, learned latent codes, and spatially aligned conditions such as embodiment masks, action images, optical flow, and projected kinematic fields zhu2024irasim,guo2025ctrlworld,wang2026latentwam,liao2025genieenvisioner,chen2026flowwam . Yet motion conditioning does not itself alter the spatial weighting of the primary RGB-generation objective. When action-responsive regions occupy only a small part of the frame, uniform token averaging can bias optimization toward static appearance. Motion-sensitive auxiliary objectives and flow-branch reweighting address related concerns zhu2024irasim,chen2026flowwam . We further use robot kinematics to guide future-RGB supervision, aligning the model's learning priorities with action consequences. This raises a key question: how can robot kinematics guide the learning of action consequences? Our key insight is that action conditioning and supervision allocation serve different purposes: the former specifies what motion to generate, whereas the latter determines which prediction errors receive greater weight during training. Robot kinematics provides a geometry-derived prior for this allocation by identifying where commanded robot motion is expected to appear in the camera view, without relying on generated future frames. This suggests using kinematic transport not only as a generation condition, but also as a spatial prior for the primary video-generation objective. Building on this insight, we introduce , a transport-aware training framework for action-conditioned world modeling. Kinematic Transport Lifting (KTL) constructs camera-aligned transport, while Transport-Aware World Diffusion (TAWD) calibrates its motion support on the video latent grid and converts the resulting support into a normalized mixture distribution for the RGB flow-matching objective. The resulting objective redistributes supervision while preserving the aggregate token weight, without adding inference parameters or sampling steps. This extends kinematic priors from generation conditions to learning guidance for interaction- and decision-oriented world prediction. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: Action-Consequence-Oriented Learning. We distinguish visual extent from interaction importance, motivating kinematics-guided learning of interaction-critical local changes. Framework. We propose , a transport-aware framework with KTL and TAWD. KTL constructs camera-aligned transport from the commanded rollout, while TAWD reweights RGB flow matching via a normalized mixture on the latent grid, preserving token weight and sampling. Benchmark Evaluation. Trained on RoboTwin~2.0 ALOHA--AgileX bimanual manipulation data chen2025robotwin2 , KineWorld achieves an EWMScore-P of 68.95 and a TWB-Score of 54.82 in single-view and multi-view evaluation, respectively. Our framework and evaluations provide the community with a reference for action-consequence-oriented world modeling. Related Work sec:related_work World Action Models. World Action Models (WAMs) increasingly leverage pretrained video generators to connect visual prediction with robot control guo2025ctrlworld,liao2025genieenvisioner . Existing approaches include action-conditioned video prediction zhu2024irasim,guo2025ctrlworld , joint video-action generation unified_video_action , and action decoding from visual latent representations liao2025genieenvisioner . Recent systems further broaden this paradigm. RealWonder connects physical actions to video generation through simulated RGB and flow liu2026realwonder , while CLAP integrates heterogeneous action representations for cross-embodiment learning liu2026clap . However, advances in generative architectures and action interfaces do not inherently prioritize interaction-critical changes in the primary RGB objective. When these changes occupy few visual tokens, uniform weighting can underemphasize their contribution. KineWorld addresses this complementary problem through kinematics-guided allocation of future-RGB supervision. Action Representations for WAMs. Existing WAMs encode robot actions as numerical tokens, learned latent codes, or spatially grounded visual cues zhu2024irasim,latent_action_model,unified_video_action . Recent methods align actions with the visual domain through embodiment masks bridgev2w , multi-view action videos action_images , optical flow chen2026flowwam , and camera-aligned kinematic fields eawm . Beyond conditioning, FlowWAM reweights its flow-branch loss using reference-relative latent deviations chen2026flowwam , while EA-WM uses frame-difference supervision to guide cross-stream fusion eawm . In contrast, KineWorld uses kinematic transport to directly reweight future-RGB flow matching without introducing auxiliary objectives. title: RealtimeWAM: One-Step Asynchronous World Action Models
comment: The code and checkpoints are available at $\href{https://github.com/ModelTC/LightX2V/tree/main/examples/realtimewam}{\text{this https URL}}$
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) incorporate visual representations from video generation backbones to guide action prediction. Recent efficient WAMs adopt Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architectures and compute video representations once for reuse by the action expert. However, intra-expert iteration (\ie, multi-step action denoising) and inter-expert waiting (\ie, sequential execution of the video and action experts) still limit inference efficiency. To this end, we present RealtimeWAM, an extremely efficient WAM variant with one-step action generation and asynchronous inference, addressing these two bottlenecks. To reduce intra-expert iteration, we propose Teacher-Anchored Consistency Distillation (TACD) to address a local-global error gap: low local consistency error alone does not guarantee accurate final actions. TACD supplements local consistency with explicit supervision from the frozen teacher's multi-step rollout endpoint, enabling accurate one-step action generation. Additionally, we propose Cross-Expert Wavefront Pipelining (CEWP) to eliminate unnecessary expert-level waiting. It overlaps the two experts through block-wise sharing of the video KV cache, synchronizing only immediately before the corresponding action attention consumes it. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks (\eg, LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin) and model variants (\eg, Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM) demonstrate the superiority of RealtimeWAM. Notably, RealtimeWAM maintains near-lossless performance (\ie, $<1\%$ drop) across these benchmarks while delivering significant end-to-end speedup (\eg, $\sim25\times$ on H100). Our code and checkpoints are available via this \href{https://github.com/ModelTC/LightX2V/tree/main/examples/realtimewam}{link}.
full_text: Experiments sec:experiments Implementation Details lab:setup We implement RealtimeWAM based on Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fast and Faster-WAM~ zhao2026faster , yielding RealtimeWAM and RealtimeWAM , respectively. We freeze the Video Expert and optimize only rank-128 low-rank adaptation (LoRA)~ hu2021lora parameters in the Action Expert. In Teacher-Anchored Consistency Distillation (TACD), we obtain the teacher endpoint through a 10-step rollout of the frozen teacher and set the teacher-anchored loss weight to . Training proceeds for 30 , 000 iterations with AdamW, a learning rate of , and a weight decay of . We set the exponential moving average (EMA) decay to . For a fair comparison, all evaluated step-distillation methods, including distribution matching distillation (DMD)~ yin2024improved , consistency distillation~ song2023consistency , and MeanFlow distillation~ geng2025meanflow,gu2026anyflow , adopt the same training settings. Moreover, we compare against other efficient WAMs, including Flash-WAM~ akbari2026flash and Light-WAM~ li2026light . For latency evaluation, we include VAE encoding time but exclude text encoding time, as instructions are encoded only once per episode. Evaluation Benchmarks We evaluate RealtimeWAM on LIBERO~ liu2023libero , RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin , and LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025liberoplus , using task success rate as the evaluation metric. On LIBERO, we evaluate four task suites: Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long. For RoboTwin 2.0, we follow the multi-task training setting in previous work~ yuan2026fast , training on 50 tasks using a total of 2 , 500 clean demonstrations and 25 , 000 randomized demonstrations. We evaluate performance under both clean and randomized conditions. To assess out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness, we further evaluate success rates on all seven perturbation subsets of LIBERO-Plus. We additionally evaluate RealtimeWAM on real-world dual-arm manipulation tasks (see Appendix~ app:garment_folding ). Main Results RoboTwin 2.0. We report detailed results on RoboTwin 2.0 (Tab.~ tab:main_results ). Notably, RealtimeWAM achieves a success rate of 90.84 with one-step action generation using only LoRA fine-tuning, incurring a reduction of just 0.67 compared with 10-step Fast-WAM. Surprisingly, RealtimeWAM achieves nearly lossless performance with one-step action generation, attaining a success rate of 92.64 with a reduction of only 0.29 compared with 10-step Faster-WAM. It also considerably outperforms other efficient WAMs ( , 81.41 for one-step Flash-WAM) and step-distillation baselines ( , 88.22 for DMD ). LIBERO. A similar trend is observed on LIBERO (Tab.~ tab:main_results ). RealtimeWAM achieves an overall success rate of 97.0 with one-step action generation, matching the performance of 10-step Fast-WAM. Compared with directly reducing Fast-WAM to a single denoising step (95.0 ), RealtimeWAM improves the success rate by 2.0 , demonstrating the effectiveness of step distillation in preserving policy performance. It also outperforms one-step Flash-WAM (95.1 ) and DMD (96.1 ), while remaining competitive with Light-WAM (97.2 ). Detailed results for individual LIBERO task suites are provided in Appendix~ app:libero_results (Tab.~ tab:libero ). LIBERO-Plus. We further evaluate robustness to distribution shifts on LIBERO-Plus (Tab.~ tab:libero_plus ). With one-step action generation, RealtimeWAM achieves an overall success rate of 73.0 , only 0.6 below Faster-WAM (73.6 ). It slightly improves performance under camera, sensor-noise, and layout perturbations, indicating that step distillation largely preserves out-of-distribution robustness. Ablation Study lab:ablaion Effect of different components. We first validate the effectiveness of the key components of our distillation framework (Tab.~ tab:ablation_study ). Fine-tuning the Video Expert during action step distillation reduces the overall success rate while introducing additional training overhead ( , longer training time and higher peak memory usage, as reported in Appendix~ app:limitation ). With the Video Expert frozen, augmenting with , yielding Teacher-Anchored Consistency Distillation (TACD), further improves the reported overall success rate from 89.85 to 90.84 . This improvement is consistent with our analysis: the teacher anchor provides an endpoint reference from the complete teacher trajectory, supplementing local consistency supervision with an explicit endpoint constraint to mitigate global deviations that the local objective may leave unresolved. Choice of teacher rollout steps . We further present results for different numbers of teacher rollout steps (Tab.~ tab:teacher_steps ). With , the rollout may produce a less accurate approximation to the exact clean endpoint , resulting in a larger numerical integration error and weaker endpoint supervision. This setting achieves a success rate of 90.39 , which improves to 90.84 when increases to 10. Further increasing to 20 yields no additional improvement (90.77 ) while requiring more teacher computation. We therefore adopt to balance policy performance and teacher rollout cost. title: TAPDreamer: Transferable Adversarial Patches for World Action Models
summary: World models learn to predict how their environment will evolve, making them an important foundation for general-purpose robotic control. Yet world action models depend on camera inputs whose manipulation can corrupt the visual representations used across tasks and action policies. Existing attacks on these models optimize against the victim's actions or predicted futures and therefore require access to target-model outputs. In this paper, we propose an attack, TAPDreamer, against world action models that instead uses a public encoder alone to construct a fixed local perturbation that transfers across tasks and action architectures. TAPDreamer requires no target-policy queries. Our key insight is that interactions between patch-induced changes in attention weights and value vectors broadcast a nearly identical representation shift far beyond the patch footprint, and this shift remains stable across task observations. Guided by this insight, TAPDreamer uses six frames from one source task to maximize the global L1 distance between clean and patched encoder representations. In closed-loop evaluation, one frozen patch per benchmark, covering about 6.5% of the input, reduces FastWAM's success rate from 97.7% to 0.0% across 40 LIBERO tasks and from 90.8% to 0.0% across 50 RoboTwin tasks; matched random patches retain 81.5% and 79.2% success. The same patches reduce success to 2.1% and 0.8% on two DreamWAM configurations and to 10.0% on Motus. These results show that protecting downstream action generation alone is insufficient: defenses for world action models must also secure shared visual encoders against persistent local perturbations.
full_text: World models learn to predict how their environment will evolve, making them an important foundation for general-purpose robotic control. Yet World Action Models (WAMs) rely on camera inputs, and manipulating those inputs can corrupt the visual representations that underpin their tasks and action policies. Existing attacks on these models optimize against actions or predicted futures and require access to victim outputs or generation modules. We propose , a transferable fixed local patch whose pixel optimization uses only a public visual encoder and requires no target-policy queries. Its design addresses two requirements: a local modification should affect representations beyond its footprint, and the resulting disturbance should persist across observations. We optimize a fixed local patch on six frames from one source task by maximizing the mean L1 distance between clean and patched encoder outputs over all latent positions and channels. Mechanism analysis reveals that interactions between patch-induced changes in attention weights and value vectors broadcast a nearly identical representation shift beyond the patch footprint, while a shared perturbation response persists across task observations despite differences in clean latents. In closed-loop evaluation, one frozen patch per benchmark, covering about 6.5 of the input, reduces FastWAM's success rate from 97.65 to 0.00 across 40 LIBERO tasks and from 90.86 to 0.00 across 50 RoboTwin tasks; matched random patches retain 81.45 and 79.20 success. The same patches reduce success to 1.45 and 1.00 on two DreamWAM configurations and to 10.60 on Motus. Behavioral analysis connects these representation shifts to grasping failures and separates rapid command recovery after patch removal from persistent physical consequences. These results show that protecting downstream action generation alone is insufficient: WAM defenses must also secure shared visual encoders against persistent local perturbations. Introduction sec:intro World Action Models (WAMs) are emerging as a powerful foundation for general-purpose robotic control. Rather than predicting actions from the current observation alone, a WAM learns how the visual world evolves together with the robot's actions. This world-modeling objective captures objects, spatial relationships, and motion, and can support action generation either through explicit future imagination~ ref_unipi,ref_robodreamer or through representations learned during video prediction~ r1 . By unifying visual prediction and control, WAMs promise policies that can reason about the consequences of their actions and replan as the environment changes~ ref_uwm,ref_dreamzero . This coupling, however, also creates a security risk. Current WAM pipelines implicitly trust the visual representation on which world prediction and action generation are built. This assumption is fragile. Cameras expose a direct, externally accessible input channel. Moreover, visual encoders are often reused across tasks and models, making the exposed channel transferable among tasks. A perturbation that corrupts this shared interface can therefore bypass model-specific action heads. If the channel remains exposed, a perturbation can be injected consistently. In this paper, we investigate whether an attacker can exploit this vulnerability and launch attacks against WAMs that transfer to unseen tasks and models. We propose (illustrated in Figure fig:teaser ), a transferable attack that applies a patch on visual inputs to WAMs. maximizes the displacement of the final latent produced by visual encoder. The search uses a few demonstration frames from a single source task. Once the patch is found, the patch pixels, area, and position are frozen and the same artifact is deployed unchanged throughout each episode and across target tasks and models. Throughout the attack, does not require action labels, task rewards, simulator, victim-model weights, or policy outputs, making simple and inexpensive to initiate. We evaluate on 40 LIBERO tasks and all 50 RoboTwin tasks. consistently outperforms attack baselines. On FastWAM, a single frozen patch covering approximately of the input reduces task success from to on LIBERO and from to on RoboTwin. Random patches retain and success, respectively. The same frozen patches also transfer across WAM architectures without retraining or target-model queries: success falls from and with matched random patches to and on DreamWAM-uncond and DreamWAM-joint, and from to on Motus. We further trace how a fixed patch causes failure during closed-loop control. title: Wiring Matters: Injection Topology and Initialization of Affordance Heads in Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Dense affordance supervision is an appealing auxiliary signal for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, yet naively co-training an affordance head can severely damage instruction following. We present a controlled study of how to wire such a head into a modern VLA on the LIBERO benchmark. Our recipe reads the backbone through a stop-gradient and re-injects an intermediate head feature into the action expert via a learned bridge. The stop-gradient is a precondition: letting affordance gradients reach the backbone drops the policy below the headless base (85.5% vs. 93.1%). With the backbone protected, a same-budget 2*2 ablation over injection topology (concatenation vs. residual) and bridge initialization (zero vs. random) shows initialization is the dominant lever. The best wiring, an actively initialized residual bridge, reaches 96.2%, matching the far more elaborate three-expert AffordanceVLA (95.8%) with under 1% extra parameters. Two probes explain the mechanism: ground-truth affordances fed as an input hurt, and inference-time zeroing shows a lazy bridge acts only as a training-time regularizer while an active bridge becomes load-bearing.
full_text: Dense affordance supervision is an appealing auxiliary signal for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, yet naively co-training an affordance head can severely damage instruction following. We present a controlled study of how such a head should be wired into a modern VLA on the LIBERO benchmark. Our recipe reads the backbone through a stop-gradient and re-injects an intermediate head feature into the action expert via a learned bridge. The stop-gradient is a precondition: letting affordance gradients reach the backbone drops the policy below the headless base ( vs.\ ). With the backbone protected, a same-budget ablation over injection topology (concatenation vs.\ residual) and bridge initialization (zero vs.\ random) shows initialization is the dominant lever. The best wiring, an actively initialized residual bridge, reaches , matching the far more elaborate three-expert AffordanceVLA ( ) with under extra parameters. Two probes explain the mechanism: ground-truth affordances fed as an input hurt, and inference-time zeroing shows a lazy bridge acts only as a training-time regularizer while an active bridge becomes load-bearing. INTRODUCTION Vision-language-action (VLA) models have rapidly become the dominant recipe for language-conditioned robot manipulation. A large vision-language backbone, pretrained on internet-scale image-text data, is fine-tuned by imitation to map camera observations and a natural-language instruction to low-level actions rt2,openvla,octo,pi0,groot . The recipe inherits the backbone's open-vocabulary perception and its language grounding, and recent flow-matching action experts pi0 have pushed success rates on standard benchmarks such as LIBERO libero above the 90 mark. Yet the supervision these models receive is curiously indirect. The action loss constrains only the trajectory; nothing in the objective ever tells the model where in the scene the interaction should happen. Which object the instruction refers to, which part of it to grasp, and where to place it must all be discovered implicitly, by correlating pixels with future gripper positions across the demonstration corpus. The failure modes of imitation-trained VLAs mirror this gap. In our experiments, a strong 2B-parameter policy is nearly saturated on suites that test object diversity or spatial layout ( ), but loses most of its remaining errors in two places. The first is instruction disambiguation: scenes containing several plausible targets where only the language picks out the right one. The second is long-horizon tasks, where a small placement error early in the episode compounds. Both are precisely the situations in which an explicit, spatially grounded notion of ``the place to act next'' should help. Affordances offer exactly that notion. The term, originating in ecological psychology gibson , denotes the action possibilities a scene offers an agent; in robot learning it has been operationalized as dense maps of contact or interaction regions where2act,vrb,moka . Affordance labels are attractive as auxiliary supervision for three reasons. First, in simulation they are free: the physics engine knows every contact between gripper and object, so pixel-accurate interaction maps can be extracted from existing demonstrations without human labeling. Second, they are dense: a per-pixel heatmap carries orders of magnitude more spatial signal per frame than a single action vector. Third, they are task-aligned: predicting where to interact next requires resolving the instruction, binding it to an object, and localizing a part, which are the exact sub-skills whose failures dominate VLA error budgets. It is therefore no surprise that several recent systems build affordances into VLAs deva,affordancevla . What is surprising is how inconsistent the reported outcomes are, and how much architectural machinery is deployed to make the signal help. AffordanceVLA affordancevla , the strongest published system, introduces a purpose-built three-expert mixture-of-transformers with a dedicated affordance-generation expert and a two-stage curriculum, and its own ablation shows that removing the second stage costs almost ten points. Our starting point was the opposite experience: attaching a straightforward affordance head to a VLA and co-training hurt, collapsing instruction-following performance. The same auxiliary task, on the same benchmark, can evidently help or harm depending on integration details that papers rarely state, let alone ablate. This paper treats those details as the object of study. Our method rests on three wiring decisions. The first is a stop-gradient: the affordance head reads intermediate backbone layers, but its loss never updates the backbone. This is not a stylistic choice. Ablating it flips the sign of the whole intervention, dropping goal-conditioned success from the s to and making the head-equipped policy worse than the headless base. With the backbone protected, the head's only channel of influence on the policy is a single learned bridge that re-injects an intermediate head feature into the visual tokens conditioning the action expert. This bridge is defined by two remaining bits of wiring, and we ablate both under a strictly identical data, budget, and seed protocol: Injection topology: the head feature is either concatenated with the visual tokens and linearly re-projected, which re-mixes (and can distort) the pretrained features, or added as a residual, which preserves them exactly. Bridge initialization: the injection weight starts at zero (``lazy'': the policy begins identical to the base and must earn a dependence on the head) or at a standard random initialization (``active'': the head's feature participates at full magnitude from the first step). These bits swing the result by more than the presence of the head itself. Initialization is the dominant lever, worth to points on either topology; topology contributes a further half point, and only under active initialization. The best cell, residual injection with active initialization, lifts the average success on LIBERO from to , with the gains concentrated exactly on the two failure modes above (Goal , Long ). . (1)~A simple affordance-head recipe (stop-gradient + feature re-injection) that lifts a strong VLA from to average success on LIBERO, on par with the dedicated mixture-of-transformers AffordanceVLA ( ) affordancevla at a fraction of its architectural complexity. (2)~A stop-gradient ablation showing gradient isolation is a precondition: with affordance gradients flowing into the backbone, the head makes the policy worse than the headless base ( vs.\ , with goal-conditioned success collapsing to ). The sign of the entire intervention flips on this single bit. (3)~A same-budget factorial ablation showing that, once the backbone is protected, initialization of the injection bridge, not its topology, is the dominant lever. Active initialization adds / points over lazy on the concatenation/residual topologies respectively, a two-way internal replication. Topology contributes at most , and only under active initialization. (4)~Two mechanism probes. Ground-truth affordance maps supplied as an input hurt ( points), showing the signal must be internalized by prediction rather than injected as data. Inference-time zeroing of the injected feature is a free diagnostic that separates two regimes. Under a lazy bridge the head is a pure training-time regularizer whose benefit survives ablation. Under an active bridge the affordance pathway becomes load-bearing, and it additionally lifts long-horizon success from to . RELATED WORK Vision-language-action models Casting manipulation as next-action prediction on top of a pretrained vision-language model was popularized by RT-2 rt2 , which showed that web-scale semantics transfer into control when actions are emitted as tokens. Subsequent open efforts scaled the recipe across embodiments and datasets: Octo octo and OpenVLA openvla established open-weight generalist policies, pi0 replaced autoregressive action decoding with a flow-matching action expert conditioned on backbone features, and GR00T~N1 groot extended the approach toward humanoid platforms. A parallel line augments the visual side of VLAs with explicit spatial structure, e.g.\ 3D position encodings in SpatialVLA spatialvla or intermediate visual sub-goals in CoT-VLA cotvla . Our study is orthogonal to the backbone choice and concerns only how auxiliary dense supervision should be attached. The StarVLA platform and the QwenPI model sec:qwenpi We conduct all experiments in StarVLA starvla , an open-source, ``Lego-like'' codebase for VLA development in which every functional component (model, data pipeline, trainer, configuration, and benchmark evaluation) is factored into plug-and-play modules with high cohesion and low coupling. The platform lets a VLM backbone be paired with interchangeable action experts and evaluated under standardized pipelines across benchmarks including LIBERO, RoboCasa, and CALVIN. This modularity is not incidental to our study but instrumental. A controlled wiring ablation is only meaningful if inserting the head, swapping the bridge topology, or changing an initialization touches nothing else in the stack. StarVLA's factoring makes each of our variants a small, isolated diff against an otherwise frozen training and evaluation pipeline. Our base policy is StarVLA's QwenPI instantiation, which realizes the design pi0 on a modern open backbone. A Qwen3-VL-2B VLM qwenvl , a natively multimodal model pairing a ViT vision tower with a language decoder, encodes the camera views and the instruction. Action generation is delegated to a layerwise flow-matching action expert: a DiT that carries a noisy action chunk and denoises it under a conditional flow-matching objective, attending at each of its layers to the hidden states of the corresponding VLM layer. Compared with autoregressive action tokenization rt2,openvla , this keeps actions continuous and chunked while letting the expert read the backbone at every depth, which is precisely the interface our affordance bridge later writes into. Affordances for manipulation The original notion of affordance, the action possibilities an environment offers gibson , entered robot learning as the problem of predicting where and how an agent can interact. Where2Act where2act learns per-pixel actionability scores for articulated objects from simulated interaction; VRB vrb distills contact regions and post-contact trajectories from human videos; MOKA moka elicits affordance points from a VLM zero-shot via visual prompting and executes them open-loop. These works treat the affordance predictor as the product. Closer to us are systems that use affordances in service of an end-to-end policy: DeVA deva co-trains dense affordance and depth heads on a video-generation backbone for embodied control, and AffordanceVLA affordancevla interleaves an affordance-generation expert with action generation inside a three-expert mixture-of-transformers, trained with a two-stage curriculum. Both report that affordance awareness improves manipulation, but both couple the signal to substantial bespoke architecture, which leaves open what the minimal effective coupling is. Our result, a stock VLA plus one head and one linear bridge matching AffordanceVLA on LIBERO, suggests the architecture is not the essential ingredient; the wiring is. Auxiliary objectives, gradient interference, and bridges Auxiliary losses have long been used to shape representations, from the self-supervised auxiliary tasks of UNREAL in RL unreal to depth and segmentation heads in perception stacks. The risk is equally well documented: auxiliary gradients can interfere destructively with the primary task pcgrad . Our preliminary experiments reproduce exactly this failure, with the affordance loss collapsing instruction following when backpropagated into the backbone. Our stop-gradient design sidesteps interference s

title: MaRO-GS: Mask-Robust Object-Centric Gaussian Splatting from Inconsistent Multi-view Masks
comment: Accepted to ACCV 2026. Project page: https://eunjikim02.github.io/marogs/
summary: We address the challenge of accurate 3D object reconstruction from multi-view images in Gaussian Splatting. Existing object-level 3DGS methods reconstruct the entire scene rather than directly optimizing the target object, even when only the target object is needed, which incurs substantial computational overhead. They also rely on 2D segmentation masks to associate Gaussians with objects, but these masks are often inconsistent across views. Such inconsistencies corrupt Gaussian optimization and produce incorrectly supervised Gaussians that degrade object reconstruction fidelity. To overcome these limitations, we propose MaRO-GS, a 3DGS framework that directly optimizes target-object Gaussians from object-masked multi-view images and remains robust to inconsistent supervision. For reliable supervision, mask-reliability view filtering excludes unreliable views. Object-supported Gaussian density control suppresses Gaussians irrelevant to the target object and prevents background densification, while Silhouette-aligned Object Loss maintains object-focused optimization. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate that MaRO-GS improves PSNR, segmentation accuracy, and computational efficiency, with the largest PSNR gain of 2.05 dB on the small-object LERF-Mask dataset.
full_text: MaRO-GS: Mask-Robust Object-Centric Gaussian Splatting from Inconsistent Multi-view Masks Eunji Kim Gahyeon Kim Gianella Cravioto Dong-hun Lee Chaewon~Moon Chae-yeong Song Sang-hyo Park School of Computer Science and Engineering\\ Kyungpook National University, Daegu, Republic of Korea\\ \ now0104, hwang190190, gianellacrv9, hy05205,\\ moonchaewon2, yeongsong, s.park\ @knu.ac.kr \\ Equal contribution\\ Corresponding author We address the challenge of accurate 3D object reconstruction from multi-view images in Gaussian Splatting. Existing object-level 3DGS methods reconstruct the entire scene rather than directly optimizing the target object, even when only the target object is needed, which incurs substantial computational overhead. They also rely on 2D segmentation masks to associate Gaussians with objects, but these masks are often inconsistent across views. Such inconsistencies corrupt Gaussian optimization and produce incorrectly supervised Gaussians that degrade object reconstruction fidelity. To overcome these limitations, we propose MaRO-GS, a 3DGS framework that directly optimizes target-object Gaussians from object-masked multi-view images and remains robust to inconsistent supervision. For reliable supervision, mask-reliability view filtering excludes unreliable views. Object-supported Gaussian density control suppresses Gaussians irrelevant to the target object and prevents background densification, while Silhouette-aligned Object Loss maintains object-focused optimization. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate that MaRO-GS improves PSNR, segmentation accuracy, and computational efficiency, with the largest PSNR gain of 2.05 dB on the small-object LERF-Mask dataset. Introduction sec:intro 3D object reconstruction is essential for applications such as object editing~ xie2026objectmorpher,yenphraphai2024image,ni2025decompositional , AR/VR~ shen2025gaussianshopvr , and 3D content creation~ ni2025decompositional . Despite the importance of 3D object reconstruction, recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ 3dgs research has primarily focused on improving scene-level reconstruction quality~ zeng2025frequency,chao2025textured,zhang2024fregs and computational efficiency~ pup, hanson2025speedysplat,dai2025efficient,radsplat . To support object-centric reconstruction, several methods have extended 3DGS to enable object-level reconstruction~ Ye2024GaussianGrouping, Zhu2025ObjectGS, zhang2025cob, mazzucchelli2026bea, hu2026sagd, jain2024gaussiancut . However, as illustrated in ~ , these approaches reconstruct the entire scene before extracting the target object, which incurs unnecessary computational overhead. Furthermore, they rely on SAM kirillov2023segment -generated masks that are inconsistent across views, thereby destabilizing Gaussian optimization and degrading object reconstruction quality. To improve object extraction quality, recent methods propose boundary refinement strategies~ zhang2025cob, mazzucchelli2026bea, hu2026sagd or enforce cross-view mask consistency via tracking and voting~ Ye2024GaussianGrouping, Zhu2025ObjectGS . The former refines object boundaries to mitigate extraction artifacts, yet reconstructing the entire scene still incurs substantial computational overhead. The latter ensures cross-view object identity consistency but does not assess individual mask reliability, so inaccurate masks are still used as supervision during optimization. Meanwhile, Trace3D~ shen2025trace3d identifies inconsistent masks via instance weight tracing but corrects rather than filters inaccurate masks, which allows erroneous supervision into the optimization process. To address these challenges, we propose MaRO-GS (Mask-Robust Object-centric Gaussian Splatting), a framework for direct optimization of target-object Gaussians from object-masked multi-view images under inconsistent mask supervision. Mask-reliability view filtering establishes reliable mask supervision by identifying and excluding unreliable views during training. Inconsistent mask supervision can also lead to unnecessary Gaussian densification around object boundaries and background regions. Object-supported Gaussian density control suppresses densification outside the target object and removes Gaussians irrelevant to the object to maintain a compact object-centric representation while improving reconstruction quality. In addition, the silhouette-aligned object loss further constrains optimization with object-focused photometric and silhouette supervision, encouraging the reconstructed object to align with the target object silhouette. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MaRO-GS improves PSNR over existing methods, with the largest gain of 2.05 dB on the small-object LERF-Mask dataset~ Ye2024GaussianGrouping while directly reconstructing the target object without scene-level reconstruction. As a complementary analysis, we evaluate target object reconstruction quality from object-centric viewpoints. We propose MaRO-GS, a mask-robust framework for object-centric 3DGS that directly optimizes target-object Gaussians from object-masked multi-view observations under inconsistent mask supervision. We propose mask-reliability view filtering, which stabilizes object-centric optimization by identifying and excluding unreliable views during training. We introduce object-supported Gaussian density control, which removes Gaussians irrelevant to the target object and constrains densification for a compact, high-fidelity object representation. We provide object-centric and mask-error robustness evaluations that complement conventional scene-level evaluation for assessing target-object reconstruction quality, particularly under small object regions and inconsistent masks. Related Work sec:relatedwork Scene-level Reconstruction in 3DGS Recent 3DGS~ 3dgs research has substantially improved scene-level reconstruction fidelity through enriched Gaussian representations and adaptive density control~ lu2024scaffold,kheradmand20243d,ye2024absgs,chao2025textured,zeng2025frequency . Other studies have instead focused on improving computational efficiency through pruning and compression techniques~ LightGaussian,minisplatting,pup,eagles,C3DGS,hanson2025speedysplat,niedermayr2024compressed,radsplat . However, these scene-level 3DGS methods are designed for entire scene reconstruction and do not account for individual objects within the scene. Object-level Reconstruction in 3DGS Several methods~ Ye2024GaussianGrouping, Zhu2025ObjectGS, zhang2025cob, shen2025trace3d, mazzucchelli2026bea have extended 3DGS to support object-level reconstruction. For example, ObjectGS Zhu2025ObjectGS introduces object-aware anchors, COB-GS zhang2025cob and Trace3D shen2025trace3d address boundary ambiguity through Gaussian refinement, and BEA-GS mazzucchelli2026bea improves object extraction via boundary and occupancy losses. However, these methods perform scene-level Gaussian optimization prior to object extraction, which results in unnecessary computational overhead. Since scene-level reconstruction optimizes Gaussian primitives for the entire scene, Gaussians near object boundaries receive supervision from both object and background regions. As a result, ambiguous Gaussians emerge, which limits object extraction quality despite various boundary refinement strategies~ zhang2025cob, shen2025trace3d, mazzucchelli2026bea . Unlike these approaches, MaRO-GS directly reconstructs the target object from object-masked multi-view images and applies object-supported Gaussian density control to better constrain Gaussian optimization around the target object. 2D Mask Supervision in 3DGS Recent object-aware methods have leveraged 2D masks predicted by SAM kirillov2023segment and lifted them into 3D representations~ Ye2024GaussianGrouping,jang2025identity, shen2024flashsplat, yang2024gaussianobject,hu2026sagd, jain2024gaussiancut . This enables applications such as object extraction, segmentation, and scene editing in 3DGS. Although SAM provides powerful segmentation capabilities, it produces inconsistent masks across views for the same object. These inconsistencies manifest in both object boundaries zhang2025cob, shen2025trace3d, mazzucchelli2026bea and mask granularity choi2024click . They introduce conflicting supervision signals into the reconstruction process. As a result, object-centric Gaussian optimization becomes unreliable and reconstruction quality degrades. To address this, Gaussian Grouping~ Ye2024GaussianGrouping and ObjectGS~ Zhu2025ObjectGS adopt different strategies to establish cross-view mask consistency. Specifically, Gaussian Grouping employs the DEVA cheng2023tracking tracker for cross-view object ID tracking, while ObjectGS uses majority voting to assign object IDs. In both cases, the focus remains on cross-view object ID consistency rather than assessing the reliability of individual 2D mask predictions. Consequently, inaccurate masks can still be used as supervision during optimization. Trace3D shen2025trace3d also addresses multi-view mask inconsistency via GIT-based instance weight tracing. However, as it is designed for multi-object segmentation within a fully reconstructed scene, its consistency enforcement operates across all objects simultaneously rather than explicitly identifying and filtering low-quality masks for a target object. Despite their differences, these methods do not explicitly filter inconsistent masks to ensure clean supervision for object-centric reconstruction. In contrast, MaRO-GS removes unreliable views through mask-reliability view filtering and provides cleaner supervision. Methods We propose MaRO-GS (Mask-Robust Object-centric Gaussian Splatting), illustrated in . Our method first formalizes the object-centric reconstruction task ( ). To ensure reliable optimization under imperfect mask supervision, we introduce mask-reliability view filtering, which enforces geometric consistency across training views ( ). We further propose object-supported Gaussian density control to suppress background Gaussians and concentrate density around target objects ( ). Finally, we design a Silhouette-aligned object loss function that prioritizes object regions during optimization ( ). This unified design transforms conventional scene-level 3DGS into an object-centric reconstruction pipeline for robust and high-fidelity results under inconsistent mask supervision. Object-centric 3D Gaussian Splatting sec:task We formalize object-centric 3DGS for accurate and efficient reconstruction of a target object by directly performing Gaussian optimization on object-masked observations, without reconstructing the entire scene. Specifically, given an RGB image and binary object mask , we construct an object-masked observation: where denotes element-wise multiplication. This masking operation removes irrelevant scene regions and focuses the optimization on the target object. However, simply applying object masks is insufficient, as optimization becomes directly dependent on their quality and consistency. When masks are inaccurate or inconsistent across views, the same 3D region may be supervised as foreground in one view and background in another, which corrupts Gaussian optimization and adaptive density control. Therefore, object-centric 3DGS requires robust optimization under imperfect mask supervision, which motivates the designs in the following sections. Mask-Reliability View Filtering sec:filtering Since MaRO-GS directly optimizes an object-centric Gaussian representation from masked observations, the reliability of each object mask directly determines the quality of supervision. However, segmentation models such as SAM~ kirillov2023segment often produce view-dependent mask errors, including missing object regions, boundary inaccuracies, and background inclusions. As shown in , even a small number of erroneous masks can disturb Gaussian optimization and lead to rendering artifacts in multiple views. This indicates t

title: GS-Pool: Object-Level Change Detection in 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Factories, museums and surveyors photograph the same space months apart and need to know which objects changed. When each visit is reconstructed with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), a direct comparison of the two reconstructions does not answer this. Training is stochastic, so two reconstructions of an unchanged space never coincide, and the second visit is often a quick re-scan with far fewer photographs. We propose GS-Pool, which takes two independently reconstructed Gaussian fields of the same space and returns the changed objects in each, together with their masks. SAM2 masks of each visit's photographs are lifted onto the Gaussians that render them and merged into an object pool, so every decision is taken once per object in 3D. We introduce a photographic carrier, the 3DGS training loss of each input reconstruction against the other visit's photographs, backpropagated to the Gaussians that rendered each pixel. We combine it with GS-Diff's geometry and colour terms and our distilled DINOv3 features. This evidence is compared with that of the objects present in both visits, which sets a change threshold for each scene. On PASLCD, GS-Pool reaches mIoU/F1 scores of 0.751/0.846 against 0.644/0.758 for GS-Diff, the strongest prior method, a gain of 17%/12%. Its mIoU is also 36%, 40% and 57% above that of O-SCD, PlenoCI and MV-3DCD, and it reaches 0.855 mIoU on CL-Splats, 33% above MV-3DCD. Each changed object is returned as a set of Gaussians with the evidence behind its decision, which an inspector can review in 3D.

Introduction Consider a room photographed on two visits, several months apart. Between the visits, objects in this room have changed, the light is different and the camera path is different. We assume that the two reconstructions of the room are built independently with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). They share no primitives, and their primitives differ in number and placement. The goal is to report only which objects changed, a question many factories, museums and surveyors ask. Change detection in 3D Gaussian Splatting is usually posed as a dense problem. For example, and fuse per-view cues into a change field over the Gaussians. ~ gsdiff , the strongest prior method, compares the two primitive sets directly, renders a change score per primitive and thresholds the rendered score at a fixed in every pixel. These methods make pixel-level decisions, with a threshold fixed in advance, about objects that may span thousands of primitives. Two reconstructions of the same unchanged space never coincide, because 3DGS training is stochastic and each visit is photographed along a different camera path. We refer to this difference as drift, as ~ gsdiff does. A difference computed between the two reconstructions therefore mixes change with drift. Unlike the primitives, the photographs that were used for training carry no reconstruction drift. therefore lets the reconstructions propose a set of candidate object changes directly from the primitive space, and the photographs of the other visit confirm or reject them. Geometry and colour alone can miss a different object in the same place, so we also distill a semantic field, generated from a foundation model, into the primitives. keeps 's drift model, geometry and colour kernels and observability weight unchanged. Related work Change detection in image space. The longest line of prior work compares two photographs of the same place. Early methods compute or learn a pixel- or superpixel-wise difference between paired viewpoints~ sakurada_change_2015, alcantarilla2018street, daudt2018fully, varghese2018changenet . Later methods also accommodate viewpoint change with supervision~ cyws2d, cyws3d, lin2025robust . The most recent methods drop change labels and build on frozen foundation models~ kim2025towards, cho2025zero, goldilocs . For all these methods, the unit of decision is either a pixel or a bounding box in one image pair. In terms of change detection performance, the strongest 2D method, CYWS-2D, evaluated in~ mv3cd , reaches 0.273 mIoU on PASLCD. Change detection with 3D reconstructions. Rendering one visit's reconstruction using the other visit's camera pose removes the need for matching viewpoints~ kruse2024splatpose, liu2024splatposeplus, zhou2023pad, lu20253dgs, jiang2025gaussian . Recent methods evaluated on PASLCD decide per primitive. thresholds per-view 2D change maps and fuses them into a change channel optimised on the Gaussians~ mv3cd . ~ oscd localises each incoming image against the reference splat and fuses per-view cues by a self-supervised objective. Its per-view cue is the 3DGS training loss against each incoming frame, fitted into a separate per-Gaussian change parameter. Our photographic carrier instead carries that loss through the rasteriser onto each visit's own primitives, in both directions between two independent reconstructions, and pools it per object. ~ gsdiff compares the two primitive sets directly, modelling reconstruction drift and weighting each primitive by its Fisher information. is the closest method to ours, and its kernels are adopted unchanged (Section~ sec:evidence ). Parallel work, PlenoCI~ plenoci , compares renders of two instance-aware reconstructions along image edges, with thresholds selected per scene, and classifies each change as geometric or appearance-based through analytic plenoptic derivatives. PlenoCI works well on unchanged scenes, flagging few pixels between two of their reconstructions, but on PASLCD's changed scenes its mIoU is below that of state-of-the-art methods. instead runs on standard reconstructions and calibrates its change threshold on each scene. Galappaththige et al.~ u3dgs attribute reconstruction residuals to primitives as an uncertainty measure that suppresses false detections, while our photographic carrier instead attributes the training loss against the other visit's photographs, as evidence of change. Object-level change detection. These methods typically make per-pixel or per-primitive decisions. SceneDiff~ scenediff decides per object, similar to us. It introduces a benchmark of paired video clips with consistent object identities across visits, and it compares foundation model features between overlapping frames, with depth and poses predicted by a feed-forward network. It builds no reconstruction, and its output is a mask per frame. takes two independently trained reconstructions and returns each changed object as a set of primitives in its reconstruction. Thus, while both methods decide per object, their inputs and outputs differ. Model-to-model comparison. Comparing two models of a place predates radiance fields, in bitemporal point clouds~ c2c, LAGUE201310, yew2021city, de2023siamese , robotic maps~ schmid2022panoptic, fu2022planesdf, zhu2024living and between photographs and a city model~ taneja2011image . For splats the question has mostly been posed as update~ cheng2025lt, zeng2025gaussianupdate, yugay2025gaussian, ackermann2025clsplats or as registration assuming no change~ gaussreg, siren . Most point-cloud methods (SLAM-based) compare geometry alone, and map-based methods maintain one map that is updated as a robot revisits a place. The splat update methods localise change in order to retrain the changed region of an existing reconstruction from new photographs, rather than comparing two independent reconstructions. Semantic fields. Image foundation model features are often distilled into neural radiance fields and Gaussian splats~ dff, n3f, lerf, feat3dgs, langsplat, gaussiangrouping , where the added feature channels support editing, querying or segmentation of a scene. We distill DINOv3~ dinov3 features into each reconstruction with its Gaussians held fixed, and use the distilled features as one source of change evidence. By contrast, SAM2~ sam2 only segments the photographs into object masks (Section~ sec:pool ). Benchmarks. PASLCD~ paslcd, mv3cd has five indoor and five outdoor scenes, each in two instances, one under consistent and one under varied lighting. Each instance pairs a reference capture of 50 to 109 photographs with an inference capture of 25 annotated test views, and a joint COLMAP solve. CL-Splats~ ackermann2025clsplats photographed five real scenes twice, with objects changed between the two captures. No change masks are available, so we annotated the masks ourselves (Appendix~ sec:clsplats ). Method takes two independently reconstructed Gaussian fields and of the same space, sharing a camera frame, and returns the changed objects in each together with their masks. These two reconstructions serve as inputs that pass sequentially through five stages, allowing each change decision to be traced back through the evidence behind it. Each stage is presented in this order below (Figure~ fig:pipeline ). We refer to as the reference visit and the inference visit, the visit for which the change map is evaluated. The photographs supply the segments, their tracking and the photographic evidence aggregated on the primitives, and they confirm or reject the changes proposed in 3D. The final mask renders the changed objects' selected primitives. Inputs. Each visit is reconstructed independently by an unmodified 3DGS trainer at its published defaults. We use vanilla 3DGS~ 3dgs and FastPGSR, the FastGS~ fastgs acceleration of PGSR~ pgsr . The two reconstructions share a camera frame, which takes as given. Stage 1: the distilled semantic field We attach a semantic descriptor to every primitive. DINOv3 (ViT-L/16) features are extracted from the undistorted views, reduced by one PCA to dimensions, and distilled onto the primitives as in Feature 3DGS~ feat3dgs : a per-primitive feature vector is rendered by gsplat~ gsplat with the same alpha compositing as colour and optimised to match every view's upsampled patch features. The reconstruction itself is held fixed: splat positions, scales, rotations, opacities and colour are not optimised, only is. The PCA is fitted to both visits together, so the two visits' features lie in one feature space and can be compared directly. Stage 2: the object pool sec:pool The pool turns primitives into objects: SAM2 segments each visit's photographs and the segments are lifted onto the splat. Segments of the same object are merged. Segments. SAM2 runs on the keyframes, a subset of each visit's photographs. On keyframe it returns a label map, an image that gives each pixel the id of at most one segment, and segment is the mask of the pixels with id . The two visits are segmented independently with approximately the same number of photographs per viewpoint: the visit with more photographs (usually ) is sub-sampled evenly along its capture to at most the number of the other visit's photographs, all of which are keyframes.
